meta.source: Southern Waters Aquatic Restoration Success Stories.xlsx
meta.note: Compiled by AI-assisted research of public sources (Oct 2026); not confirmed by the partners involved. Locations approximate (~2 decimals).

stories.title: Conasauga Habitat Connectivity for Trispot Darters
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program); National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; Murray and Whitfield county road departments
stories.desc: A $1,457,500 National Fish Passage Program project replacing undersized barrier culverts on county-owned roads in the Conasauga system with structures that pass aquatic organisms. The work is intended to restore movement and genetic connectivity and reopen spawning habitat for the federally threatened trispot darter and the blue shiner, while improving road resilience and reducing flooding at the crossings.
stories.notes: FY2024 National Fish Passage Program award; project page gives no completion status, so treat as in progress. Counties from the FY24 award listing.

stories.title: Mill Creek / Rocky Flats Fish Passage – Chattahoochee National Forest
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Georgia; USDA Forest Service (Chattahoochee-Oconee NF); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Southeast Fish Passage Team; Georgia DNR; Lyndhurst Foundation; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; Pond & Company; Contech
stories.desc: Two failing, perched metal pipe culverts at the Rocky Flats crossing of Mill Creek, a Conasauga River tributary, were replaced in September 2019 with a 34-ft-span bottomless aluminum box culvert, and a sinkhole that had been dumping sediment into the creek was stabilized. The ~$269K project reopened about six miles of trout-stream habitat to the federally listed blue shiner, trispot darter and several listed mussels, and restored access to 1,000+ acres of national forest.

stories.title: Holly Creek Watershed Restoration – Culverts, Fencing, Banks and Buffers
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife; USDA Forest Service; Limestone Valley RC&D Council; Coosa River Basin Initiative; The Nature Conservancy; USDA NRCS; Federal Highway Administration; Conasauga River Alliance; private landowners (e.g., Ward Farm)
stories.desc: Along Holly Creek, a Conasauga tributary with one of the richest fish and mussel faunas in North America, partners have replaced fish-blocking culverts on national-forest headwaters, fenced cattle out of the stream, stabilized banks with live stakes and coir mesh, planted 50-ft riparian buffers, regraded a mile of eroding dirt road, planted 3,000+ live stakes along 1.8 miles of creek, and reintroduced endangered mussels. The $60,500 Ward Farm project alone stabilized nearly two acres of bank and recruited neighboring farmers.

stories.title: Rock Creek Culvert Replacement at Peeples Road Spur – Holly Creek Watershed
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Georgia; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; Georgia Power (funding); Georgia Aquatic Connectivity Team; private landowners
stories.desc: An undersized culvert on Rock Creek, a major tributary of Holly Creek in the Conasauga watershed, was flagged by a 2019 survey and then blew out in a March 2021 flood, stranding landowners. In April 2021 it was replaced with a pre-fabricated bottomless arch culvert, restoring a stable road crossing and open passage for the Holly Creek aquatic community, which includes federally listed darters, shiners and mussels.

stories.title: Holly Creek Livestaking and Road Regrading (Partners for Fish and Wildlife)
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife (Georgia Ecological Services); Limestone Valley RC&D Council; Coosa River Basin Initiative; Georgia Environmental Protection Division; Georgia DNR; Dalton Public Schools; four private landowners
stories.desc: In February 2023 seven volunteers installed more than 3,000 live stakes along 1.8 miles of Holly Creek bank over four days to stabilize banks and reduce sedimentation. A companion road project regraded a one-mile eroding dirt road, added more than ten waterbars, repaired dips and culverts and placed over 110 tons of gravel to cut runoff into the creek. The work is expected to support recovery of seven listed and two at-risk aquatic species and improve more than 0.4 mile of designated critical habitat.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, NGO, schools, private landowners)
stories.notes: Reported in the Georgia ES field office highlights page; county not stated in source, inferred from Holly Creek location. Closely related to, but distinct from, the broader Holly Creek watershed entry.

stories.title: Holly Creek Streambank Restoration and Riparian Buffer (CRBI)
stories.orgs: Coosa River Basin Initiative; Limestone Valley RC&D Council; U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service; Georgia EPD (Section 319); volunteer private landowner
stories.desc: On a volunteer landowner's property near Chatsworth, partners regraded eroding banks of Holly Creek and planted native vegetation. Georgia EPD's FFY2022 nonpoint source report records more than 300 feet of bank restored with a riparian buffer installed, and CRBI has since published a 'Conservation Corridor of Holly Creek' story map building on the work.

stories.title: Mulkey Creek Culvert Replacement at Duncan Ridge Road
stories.orgs: Trout Unlimited; USDA Forest Service (Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest); Hartline Construction; local quarry and trucking businesses
stories.desc: In 2026 Trout Unlimited, with Forest Service support, replaced an aging, structurally unsound and debris-prone pipe culvert under Duncan Ridge Road on Mulkey Creek with a new crossing designed for aquatic organism passage and heavier loads. The roughly $650,000 project, TU's first major AOP build in Georgia, reconnects wild brown and rainbow trout habitat in the Blue Ridge headwaters and routed spending through a local contractor, suppliers and lodging.

stories.title: Holly Creek Watershed Restoration, Conasauga River
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife (Georgia Ecological Services); Limestone Valley RC&D Council; Coosa River Basin Initiative / Upper Coosa Riverkeeper; The Nature Conservancy; USDA Forest Service; USDA NRCS; Conasauga River Alliance; Georgia DNR; Federal Highway Administration; private landowners
stories.desc: A long-running watershed partnership on Holly Creek and Dill Creek, tributaries of the Conasauga River, combining streambank stabilization, livestock exclusion fencing, riparian buffer planting, septic and poultry-waste improvements, mussel augmentation and replacement of culverts with fish-passable crossings. At the Ward Farm a 50-foot buffer now lines nearly two acres of creek frontage; roughly seven miles of Holly Creek have been conserved and cattle are out of the water with vegetation returning. The Conasauga supports about 90 native fish species and work targets amber darter, frecklebelly madtom and listed mussels.
stories.water: Holly Creek / Dill Creek, Conasauga River
stories.notes: County inferred from Chatsworth dateline; the story does not name it. Ongoing multi-decade effort with completed on-the-ground components.

stories.title: Park Creek Elementary Stream & Riparian Restoration for Trispot Darter
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife; Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division; Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute; Whitfield County Schools / Park Creek Elementary; Limestone Valley RC&D; The Nature Conservancy
stories.desc: The federally threatened trispot darter spawns in a stream on Park Creek Elementary's 67-acre campus in Dalton, so partners worked with the school to restore the stream channel and riparian habitat and build an outdoor education program, culminating in a 2023 Earth Day restoration event. The campus is now a protected spawning site and was named a 2025 Georgia Water Coalition Clean 13 honoree.

stories.title: Open-Bottom Culverts for the Trispot Darter – Upper Coosa Basin
stories.orgs: Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division; Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership; The Nature Conservancy; Limestone Valley RC&D Council; Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute; Dalton State College; University of North Georgia; USFWS; local governments; private landowners; NFWF America the Beautiful Challenge
stories.desc: Under an America the Beautiful Challenge grant, Georgia DNR and partners assessed more than 1,600 road-stream crossings in the trispot darter's Upper Coosa range (2024–2025) and prioritized perched culverts that block the threatened darter's winter spawning runs into small tributaries. Four barrier culverts have been replaced with open-bottom structures and a cost-shared culvert is being installed on a working farm. (Pin is placed at Dalton as the regional center; individual sites are not named in the source.)

stories.title: Upper Soque River – Agricultural BMPs and Streambank Restoration (delisted 2012)
stories.orgs: Georgia EPD; City of Clarkesville; Soque River Watershed Partnership; NC State University; North Georgia Technical College; participating landowners; U.S. EPA (Section 319)
stories.desc: A Section 319 grant ($447K + $298K match) implemented 65 agricultural practices on 812 acres, including 46,442 linear feet of cattle exclusion fencing, stream crossings, off-stream wells and heavy-use-area protection, plus 500 linear feet of eroding bank restored with natural channel design and rain gardens in town. Fecal coliform was removed as an impairment for the 29-mile segment in 2012.

stories.title: Soque River Headwaters Stream Restoration (Savage-Roberts Farm)
stories.orgs: Chattahoochee Riverkeeper; U.S. EPA; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Savage-Roberts Farms (private landowner); Soque River Watershed Association; Southeast Waters AmeriCorps
stories.desc: In 1998 a severely eroding 1,300-ft reach of the Soque River on a Habersham County farm was rebuilt using natural-channel bank restoration techniques then new to Georgia, with a replanted riparian buffer. Bank-pin monitoring showed erosion became negligible even after heavy rains, sediment yield dropped, fish habitat diversity increased, and stream temperatures fell as the riparian canopy matured.

stories.title: Lower Soque River – Cattle Exclusion and Natural Channel Design (delisted 2014)
stories.orgs: Georgia EPD; City of Clarkesville; Soque River Watershed Association; ~20 participating farmers; NC State University; U.S. EPA (Section 319)
stories.desc: Section 319 grants (~$790K federal + $550K match, 2008–2014) funded 81,053 linear feet of cattle exclusion and cross-fencing, six stream crossings, off-stream watering and heavy-use-area protection (excluding ~1,715 cattle from surface waters), plus 585 linear feet of eroding streambank restored with natural channel design and urban stormwater BMPs. Fecal coliform was removed as an impairment for the 6-mile segment on Georgia's 2014 303(d) list.

stories.title: Riverview Farms – Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Buffer on the Coosawattee
stories.orgs: Riverview Farms (Swancy family, private organic farm); Georgia Water Coalition (Clean 13, 2018)
stories.desc: This 500-acre certified-organic family farm in Gordon County keeps cattle and hogs out of a one-mile stretch of the Coosawattee River and maintains a natural forested buffer along the bank, farming without synthetic inputs since 2000. The river supplies drinking water to Calhoun and Gordon County downstream; the farm was named a 2018 Clean Water Hero as a model of voluntary private-land stewardship.

stories.title: Fourmile Creek Livestock Exclusion Project
stories.orgs: Forsyth County; Georgia EPD (Section 319); participating cattle producers
stories.desc: Completed in 2020, the project installed 13,266 linear feet of woven-wire livestock exclusion fence, four hardened stream crossings and three watering ramps to keep cattle out of Fourmile Creek, an Etowah-basin stream impaired for bacteria. Post-project monitoring showed bacteria counts decreasing since 2017, with modeled load reductions of 35% for sediment, 26% for phosphorus and 17.5% for nitrogen.

stories.title: Etowah River at Canton – Livestock Exclusion, Bank Restoration and Septic Repairs (delisted 2010)
stories.orgs: Limestone Valley RC&D Council; Upper Etowah River Alliance; Cherokee County; City of Canton; The Nature Conservancy; Georgia EPD; USDA NRCS & FSA; Reinhardt College; participating landowners
stories.desc: Between 2006 and 2011 partners installed rural and urban BMPs on the 20-mile Etowah segment above Lake Allatoona: a livestock exclusion project, a manure stackhouse, a streambank restoration, nine septic repairs, five rain gardens and eight stormwater controls, backed by ~$125K of EQIP funds to Cherokee County farmers. 2009 sampling met fecal coliform criteria in all four seasons and Georgia EPD removed the segment from the 2010 303(d) list.

stories.title: Crayfish Creek Restoration below Buford Dam
stories.orgs: Trout Unlimited (Upper Chattahoochee & Oconee River chapters, Georgia Council); National Park Service (Chattahoochee River NRA); Georgia DNR; U.S. Forest Service; USDA NRCS; Gwinnett County Soil & Water Conservation District; Columbia Engineering; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; Georgia Power; UGA 5 Rivers Club
stories.desc: Starting in fall 2021, TU volunteers and 17 partner organizations restored 500 linear feet of an eroding Chattahoochee tributary a few miles below Buford Dam (later officially named Crayfish Creek): three obsolete culverts were removed, banks were regraded and stabilized with coir matting, and invasive plants were replaced with natives. A $7,500 Embrace-A-Stream grant grew into a ~$250,000 project with 300+ volunteers over 11 workdays, protecting a robust Chattahoochee crayfish population and young-of-year wild brown trout.

stories.title: Raccoon Creek Stream Restoration – Paulding Forest WMA
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division; Paulding County; Kennesaw State University; Georgia Power; USDA NRCS; Georgia Forestry Commission; Coosa River Basin Initiative; USFWS
stories.desc: In 2013 The Nature Conservancy restored a 1.2-mile stretch of Raccoon Creek, an Etowah tributary that is the only Etowah darter habitat below Lake Allatoona, to improve fish habitat and stabilize eroding banks. More than 43% of the watershed is now permanently protected, isolated Cherokee darter populations were reconnected, and southern rainbow mussels were found in 2013 for the first time in decades. Georgia DNR was a 2017 Clean 13 honoree for the work.

stories.title: Raccoon Creek Road Culvert-to-Bridge Replacement
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; Coosa River Basin Initiative; Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division; Paulding County; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Georgia Power (funding); Kennesaw State University (monitoring)
stories.desc: A four-cell box culvert on Raccoon Creek Road inside Paulding Forest WMA, a long-standing fish-passage barrier, was removed in 2019 and replaced with a free-span bridge completed in February 2020. The crossing reconnected spawning habitat for the federally endangered Etowah darter and threatened Cherokee darter plus 40+ other native fishes; a KSU graduate student is tracking fish movement above and below the new bridge.

stories.title: Raccoon Creek Culvert Replacement, Paulding Forest WMA
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Georgia; Georgia Department of Natural Resources; Paulding County; Coosa River Basin Initiative; Kennesaw State University; US Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: A multi-box culvert blocking Raccoon Creek inside the Paulding Forest Wildlife Management Area was removed in 2019 and replaced with a free-span bridge, a fish-passage priority since the early 2000s. Raccoon Creek supports the federally endangered Etowah darter and federally threatened Cherokee darter along with 43 other native fish species. A Kennesaw State graduate student is monitoring fish movement above and below the new bridge to measure the passage benefit.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate within Paulding Forest WMA.

stories.title: White Dam Removal – Middle Oconee River
stories.orgs: UGA Warnell School of Forestry & Natural Resources; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program); Georgia Aquatic Connectivity Team; Georgia Water Coalition (Clean 13 recognition)
stories.desc: In July 2018 UGA's Warnell School worked with a USFWS crew to remove an 88.5-ft section of the obsolete 1911 White Dam in Whitehall Forest, leaving the historic powerhouse in place. The first dam removal in Georgia to need both state and federal approvals, it reconnected roughly 18 miles of river, restored fish passage, and opened a longer, safer paddling run from Tallassee to Barnett Shoals. Lessons learned seeded the Georgia Dam Removal Handbook.

stories.title: Candler Park Brook Daylighting and Natural Channel Restoration
stories.orgs: City of Atlanta Parks & Recreation; Candler Park Neighborhood Organization; Park Pride; Georgia EPD (Section 319); Freedom Park Conservancy; Peavine Watershed Alliance; Mary Lin & Paideia schools; Candler Park Conservancy
stories.desc: An $875K project removed ~850 ft of collapsing concrete culvert, daylighted ~1,850 ft of buried headwater stream in a natural channel design, replanted the riparian buffer with native vegetation and black willow live stakes, and routed stormwater through bioretention and detention basins. Four years later the macroinvertebrate index improved, native mosquitofish colonized a formerly fishless stream, and beavers created ~1.3 acres of wetland used by wading birds and amphibians.

stories.title: Wise Creek Bank Stabilization on the Ocmulgee River
stories.orgs: Georgia River Network; U.S. Forest Service (Oconee National Forest); Georgia DNR; Georgia Power; Robust Redhorse Conservation Committee; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation
stories.desc: At the Wise Creek access on the Ocmulgee River, 190 linear feet of severely undercut bank were stabilized and revegetated and the access road was rebuilt to stop sediment from washing into the river. The work protects shoal spawning habitat used by robust redhorse being reintroduced to the Ocmulgee; before-and-after photos show the bank fully stabilized.

stories.title: Williamson Swamp Creek – Livestock Exclusion and Streambank Protection (delisted 2010)
stories.orgs: Pine Country RC&D Council; Washington & Jefferson County Soil Conservation District; USDA NRCS (EQIP); Georgia EPD; participating landowners
stories.desc: From 2004–2006 partners installed heavy-use-area protections, pasture plantings, alternative livestock watering with stream-exclusion fencing, and critical streambank protection using ~$159K of Section 319 funds, producer match and >$837K of EQIP. 2007 monitoring showed all 20 samples met dissolved-oxygen criteria and the 9-mile segment was delisted in 2010.

stories.title: Oconee River Spawning Gravel Augmentation for Robust Redhorse
stories.orgs: Georgia DNR Wildlife Resources Division; Robust Redhorse Conservation Committee (Georgia Power, USFWS, USGS, universities); Georgia Power
stories.desc: To rebuild spawning habitat for the robust redhorse, a large sucker rediscovered in the Oconee in 1991 after 122 years, 1,019 tons of washed gravel in three size classes were barged and pumped onto four shoal sites between Milledgeville and Dublin in 2009–2010. Low-flow monitoring found the gravel persisted at every site, creating new spawning beds in a river where fine sediment had buried natural gravel.

stories.title: Eagle & Phenix and City Mills Dam Removals – Chattahoochee River
stories.orgs: Uptown Columbus, Inc.; City of Columbus; Phenix City, AL; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; Georgia Power; McLaughlin Whitewater Design Group; Batson-Cook Construction; Chattahoochee River Conservancy
stories.desc: Between 2012 and 2013 the 1882 Eagle & Phenix Dam and the City Mills Dam were breached in downtown Columbus, draining a 45-acre impoundment and restoring about 2.3 miles of free-flowing river and long-inundated Fall Line shoals. The $24M+ public/private project created the nation's longest urban whitewater course and re-exposed shoal habitat that supports the native shoal bass.

stories.title: Upatoi Creek Tributary Dam Removals – Chattahoochee Fall Line
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Georgia; Columbus State University (monitoring); The Coca-Cola Foundation (funding); Georgia Aquatic Connectivity Team
stories.desc: On TNC land in the Upatoi Creek watershed near Fort Benning, three failing earthen dams were partially removed (completed around 2020). New channels were built to Natural Channel Design principles, including a bypass channel at Little Pine Knot dam; banks were stabilized and replanted with natives, and an undersized culvert was replaced with a low-water crossing. Columbus State monitoring since 2019 has documented fish and crayfish moving into the reopened upper reaches of two streams.

stories.title: Mill Creek (Ogeechee) – Livestock Exclusion and Pasture BMPs (delisted 2014)
stories.orgs: Central Savannah River RC&D Council; Georgia EPD; USDA NRCS; Ogeechee River Soil & Water Conservation District; local landowners
stories.desc: A $313K Section 319 grant (total $523K with landowner cost-share, 2010–2013) funded 42 agricultural BMPs on six producer properties, including fencing livestock out of the stream with alternative watering sources and planting pasture to cut erosion. The 16-mile segment, impaired for low dissolved oxygen since 2004, was removed from Georgia's impaired waters list in 2014.

stories.title: Upatoi Creek Earthen Dam Removals and Stream Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Georgia; Columbus State University (School of Environmental Sciences); The Coca-Cola Foundation
stories.desc: TNC removed three high-priority failing earthen dams on its own land in the Upatoi Creek watershed, a Chattahoochee River tributary near Fort Benning and Columbus, and replaced an undersized culvert with a low-water crossing. Work included partial dam removal, a new bypass channel at the Little Pine Knot dam, natural-channel-design stabilization structures, streambank stabilization and riparian revegetation with native grasses and shrubs. Columbus State University monitoring from 2019 through summer 2021 documented fish and crayfish moving through the restored channels.
stories.notes: County not stated on the source page; Upatoi Creek forms the Muscogee/Chattahoochee county line near Fort Benning. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Burton 4-H Center Living Shoreline – Tybee Island
stories.orgs: UGA Marine Extension & Georgia Sea Grant; Georgia 4-H / Burton 4-H Center; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; City of Tybee Island; Chatham County MPC; One Hundred Miles; The Nature Conservancy
stories.desc: In 2016 an eroding bank on Horse Pen Creek at the Burton 4-H Center was stabilized with a living shoreline of bagged recycled oyster shell and native marsh plants, built with volunteers and students. The project stopped bank erosion while creating oyster and salt marsh habitat and is now an outdoor classroom for thousands of 4-H students.

stories.title: Skidaway Island State Park Living Shoreline
stories.orgs: UGA Marine Extension & Georgia Sea Grant; Georgia State Parks (Georgia DNR); Georgia Coastal Management Program / NOAA
stories.desc: A 110-linear-foot living shoreline of bagged recycled oyster shell and native plants was installed along the Sandpiper Trail at Skidaway Island State Park to stabilize an eroding marsh bank and reduce stormwater runoff. The site demonstrates the technique to park visitors and adds oyster and marsh-edge habitat on a public park shoreline.

stories.title: Harris Neck National Wildlife Refuge Living Shoreline, Barbour River
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Savannah Coastal Refuges); descendants of the Harris Neck community; South Atlantic Salt Marsh Initiative partners; Pew Charitable Trusts; Georgia Conservancy
stories.desc: An 800-foot living shoreline of oyster shell, native marsh plants and logs is being built on the Barbour River at Harris Neck National Wildlife Refuge to halt erosion threatening the refuge dock, boat ramp and a local crabbers' dock, with $511,530 in funding. The project also protects Gould Cemetery and a culturally significant baptismal tree, and is carried out under a 2020 memorandum of understanding with descendants of the Harris Neck community. It is one piece of a regional effort to restore or enable migration of one million acres of South Atlantic salt marsh.
stories.notes: Funded and designed as of the March 2024 story; construction completion not confirmed on the page. County stated in the story only in historical context.

stories.title: Ashantilly Living Shoreline – Sapelo Island (Georgia's first)
stories.orgs: Georgia DNR Coastal Resources Division; Sapelo Island National Estuarine Research Reserve (NOAA); The Nature Conservancy; UGA Marine Extension & Georgia Sea Grant
stories.desc: In 2010 an eroding creek bank at the Ashantilly dock on Sapelo Island was stabilized with bagged oyster shell and native marsh plants instead of a bulkhead, the first living shoreline built on the Georgia coast. The structure held through two major hurricanes while recruiting live oysters and marsh vegetation; it was refurbished in 2022 after the dock was replaced.
stories.water: Tidal creek, Doboy Sound / Sapelo Island

stories.title: Tolomato Island Private-Property Living Shoreline
stories.orgs: Private landowner; UGA Marine Extension & Georgia Sea Grant; Georgia DNR Coastal Resources Division
stories.desc: In 2021 a private landowner on Tolomato Island stabilized 95 linear feet of eroding tidal-creek bank with vegetated concrete block mat, a granite riprap toe and native plantings rather than a hard bulkhead. Oysters have since colonized the base of the structure and vegetation has filled in the upper bank, showing the approach works on residential shorelines.

stories.title: Hog Creek – Cattle BMPs, Riparian Planting and Grade Stabilization (delisted 2006)
stories.orgs: Seven Rivers RC&D Council; Ware County Soil Conservation District; USDA NRCS (EQIP); Ware County; Georgia EPD; local producers
stories.desc: Between 2000 and 2005 producers installed heavy-use-area foundations, a grade-stabilization structure to stop streambank failure, pasture seeding and riparian-zone planting, and wells and ponds to keep livestock out of the creek, while Ware County adopted erosion, septic and drainage ordinances. With only $17K of 319 funds plus producer match and EQIP, 2003 monitoring met standards and the 10-mile segment was delisted for fecal coliform in 2006.

stories.title: Mosquito Creek Living Shoreline – Little St. Simons Island
stories.orgs: UGA Marine Extension & Georgia Sea Grant; Georgia DNR Coastal Resources Division; The Nature Conservancy; Sapelo Island NERR; Little St. Simons Island (private landowner); NOAA Community-based Restoration Program
stories.desc: A failing wooden bulkhead on Mosquito Creek at the private Little St. Simons Island lodge was removed and replaced with a living shoreline of bagged oyster shell and native plants. Follow-up lift-net monitoring by UGA found greater abundance and diversity of fish, crabs and shrimp at the living shoreline than at comparison sites, including sheepshead that had not been recorded there before.
stories.water: Mosquito Creek, Little St. Simons Island

stories.title: Spring Creek Road Erosion and Culvert Repairs, Miller County
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife; Golden Triangle Resource Conservation & Development Council; Miller County Road Department; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife (West Georgia / Florida Panhandle)
stories.desc: Eroding county dirt roads alongside Spring Creek were rebuilt to stop sediment delivery to the creek: roadbeds were raised and graded over a granite and fabric base, larger culverts were installed, and ditches were rebuilt, riprapped and seeded. FWS paid for materials and the county supplied labor. The sediment had been degrading habitat for listed and at-risk freshwater mussels including shiny-rayed pocketbook and oval pigtoe; the rebuilt roads are also more stable and less prone to flooding for local residents.
stories.notes: Town not named in the story; Colquitt is the Miller County seat and nearest town on Spring Creek.

stories.title: Jekyll Creek Thin-Layer Sediment Placement for Salt Marsh Resilience
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Savannah District); Georgia DNR Coastal Resources Division; Jekyll Island Authority
stories.desc: About 5,000 cubic yards of sediment dredged from Jekyll Creek were sprayed in thin layers over a five-acre, low-elevation salt marsh to raise its surface by up to a foot so Spartina can keep pace with sea-level rise, a first-of-its-kind beneficial-use pilot in Georgia. Treatment and control plots are being monitored for marsh-grass recovery as a model for using maintenance dredging to restore drowning marsh.

stories.title: Noyes Cut Ecosystem Restoration – Satilla River Estuary
stories.orgs: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Section 1135); Georgia DNR Coastal Resources Division; Satilla Riverkeeper; local property owners
stories.desc: Man-made navigation cuts dug decades ago let salt water short-circuit into the headwaters of Umbrella and Dover creeks, destroying the salinity gradient and silting in the creeks. After more than a decade of advocacy, the Corps filled Dynamite Cut and closed Noyes Cut, restoring natural tidal flow to over 4,700 acres of salt marsh and 33 miles of tidal creeks that serve as nursery habitat for shrimp, blue crab, striped bass, shad, seatrout and red drum.

stories.title: Piscola Creek – National Water Quality Initiative Farm BMPs
stories.orgs: USDA NRCS (EQIP / NWQI); Georgia EPD; U.S. EPA; Southern Georgia Regional Commission; participating farmers, ranchers and forest landowners
stories.desc: After Piscola Creek was named an NWQI priority watershed, NRCS invested $1.65M of EQIP (2012–2014) in conservation crop rotation, cover crops, nutrient management, livestock fencing and watering systems, and microirrigation on 9,811 acres in Brooks County. 2014 monitoring showed the 13-mile downstream section meeting dissolved-oxygen criteria and Georgia EPD recommended it for delisting in the 2016 Integrated Report.

stories.title: Naked Creek Natural Channel Design Restoration – New River State Park
stories.orgs: New River Conservancy (lead); New River State Park / NC Division of Parks & Recreation; NC Land and Water Fund; Foggy Mountain Nursery and Stream Restoration; Appalachian State University; Town of Jefferson; U.S. EPA Section 319
stories.desc: After the state park acquired a 110-acre parcel in 2015, partners restored ~4,873 ft of Naked Creek using natural channel design: banks were resloped to reconnect the floodplain, four culverted sections were daylighted, cross vanes, rock vanes, log structures and boulder clusters were installed, and more than 9,080 native trees and shrubs were planted in the riparian zone. The benthic rating improved from fair to good-fair and the 1.1-mile impaired segment was delisted in 2020.

stories.title: Meadow Fork Trout Habitat Improvement and Bank Stabilization
stories.orgs: NC Wildlife Resources Commission (Habitat Conservation Program); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; National Park Service / Blue Ridge Parkway; private landowner
stories.desc: On a livestock-degraded reach of Meadow Fork near Laurel Springs, NCWRC biologists built a new 120-ft meander with pool-riffle sequence (leaving the old bend as an oxbow amphibian pool), installed rock weirs, rock vanes and root wads for trout cover, regraded an eroding bank, established a riparian buffer and fenced 1,262 ft of stream from cattle. The low-cost project (under $5,000) produced a stable channel, reduced sediment and thermal loading, and allowed suppressed streamside alders to recover.

stories.title: Upper Dan River Agricultural BMPs
stories.orgs: NC DEQ Division of Water Resources; NC Agricultural Cost Share Program; Stokes and Rockingham SWCDs; local farmers; U.S. EPA Section 319
stories.desc: Starting with a 2008 Section 319 seed project and follow-on projects in 2011, 2014 and 2016, partners installed ~20,767 ft of livestock exclusion fencing, ~12,400 ft of heavy-use protection, watering tanks, wells and pipelines, 3.5 acres of critical-area plantings, and converted 35+ acres of cropland to sod-based rotation. Two Dan River assessment units totaling 14.2 miles were delisted for fecal coliform in 2012 and benthic scores improved from fair to good-fair.

stories.title: Ward Mill Dam Removal, Watauga River
stories.orgs: Ward family (owner); American Rivers; MountainTrue; Blue Ridge RC&D Council; Watauga County SWCD; USFWS National Fish Passage Program; Wildlands Engineering; Appalachian State University; NC Division of Water Resources; Patagonia; Bonneville Environmental Foundation; MountainTrue (Watauga Riverkeeper); Blue Ridge Resource Conservation and Development Council; Buncombe County Soil and Water; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Ward family (landowners)
lpOrgs: Blue Ridge Resource Conservation and Development
stories.desc: A 20-foot-tall obsolete hydropower dam that had blocked the Watauga River for roughly 80 years was removed in 2021 after the owners surrendered the hydropower license. The project reconnected about 140 miles of river and tributary habitat (25 mainstem miles) and was ranked tier-one, priority-one in North Carolina's aquatic barrier assessment tool. Monitoring by Appalachian State University tracks recovery of native brook trout, tangerine darters, green floater mussels and Eastern hellbenders.
stories.notes: Height, mileage and partner list confirmed in American Rivers' 2021 report PDF (DamList2021_Report_02172022_FINAL3.pdf); narrative confirmed on the blog page linked here. Also documented at: https://mountaintrue.org/ward-mill-dam-removal-connects-aquatic-habitat-makes-river-healthier/

stories.title: Shull's Mill Dam Removal, Watauga River
stories.orgs: American Rivers; MountainTrue; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; State of North Carolina (funding)
stories.desc: A concrete dam that had stood on the upper Watauga River for more than 150 years was removed in 2024, upstream of the earlier Ward Mill removal. Together the two removals created a 78-mile corridor of free-flowing water. Eight Eastern hellbenders - a salamander whose populations have declined about 70 percent - were found and safely relocated during the work, and when Hurricane Helene struck in October 2024 the dam-free reach passed the flood without the structural failure engineers believed the old dam would have suffered.
stories.notes: Removal year 2024 confirmed by the 2024 annual dam removal summary table (town listed as Vilas, Watauga County).

stories.title: Powdermill Creek Culvert Removal – Roan Highlands
stories.orgs: Trout Unlimited; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; NC Division of Parks and Recreation; Wildlands Engineering; Wildlife Conservation Society
stories.desc: TU and NCWRC removed a perched, clogged and undersized culvert on Powdermill Creek on NC State Parks property in the Roan Highlands, one drainage over from Roaring Creek, stabilized the channel to reference conditions and regraded the banks. The $35,420 project opened miles of upstream coldwater habitat for native brook trout and other stream life.

stories.title: Roaring Creek Culvert Replaced with Clear-Span Bridge – Roan Highlands
stories.orgs: Trout Unlimited (Southern Appalachian program); Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy; Wildlands Engineering; Duke Energy Water Resources Fund; Rocky River Chapter of TU; private landowner
stories.desc: In 2017 TU replaced an undersized, perched 36-inch culvert on Roaring Creek (North Toe River watershed) that repeatedly failed in floods and blocked aquatic organism passage with a 40-ft clear-span steel-and-timber bridge, and restored the channel to reference conditions. The ~$25,000 private-lands project reopened coldwater habitat for native brook trout and other stream organisms.

stories.title: Smith Creek Watershed Restoration – Wake Forest
stories.orgs: Town of Wake Forest; NC Division of Water Resources; NC Clean Water Management Trust Fund; Wake County SWCD; Franklin County SWCD; Wake County Open Space; NC State University Stream Restoration Program; Sound Rivers; Duke Energy
stories.desc: Following a 2012 Section 319-funded watershed plan, Wake Forest implemented ten priority stream restoration and stabilization projects (including the Ailey Young Park dam removal and head-cut repair with pocket wetlands), added benthic habitat structures, improved riparian buffers and created a 28-acre Smith Creek greenway, and adopted a stricter local erosion control program. A 4-mile segment to the Neuse River regained good-fair benthic and fish ratings and was delisted in 2018.

stories.title: Roanoke River Floodplain Reconnection – Big Swash, Pollocks Ferry, Company Swamp
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in North Carolina; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; NOAA; East Carolina University; NC Land and Water Fund; Roanoke/Tar River Gun Club; Smith Family Foundation; Bass Pro Shops; private landowners
stories.desc: After mapping ~1,400 barriers on the lower Roanoke floodplain, TNC and partners are replacing undersized road culverts with fish-friendly bridges and low-water crossings. At Big Swash 14 barriers were removed to reconnect 8+ miles of tributary and 500+ acres of floodplain forest; Pollocks Ferry reconnected 3 miles, Whites Millpond 52 miles of floodplain, and Town Swamp and Company Swamp ~1.1 miles each. eDNA, trap and electrofishing monitoring confirm blueback herring, shad and other species using the restored waterways.

stories.title: Bald Creek Watershed Restoration – Cane River
stories.orgs: NC Division of Mitigation Services; Yancey County SWCD; NC Agriculture Cost Share Program; NC Division of Water Resources; NC Clean Water Management Trust Fund; NC Cooperative Extension; U.S. EPA (Section 319)
stories.desc: A 2007 DMS project on Bald Creek tributaries restored 1,335 ft and enhanced 3,144 ft of stream with natural channel design, riparian buffer planting, invasive removal, floodplain and wetland restoration, livestock exclusion fencing and removal of a small dam; the Ag Cost Share program added over 22,000 ft of exclusion fencing and at least 15 failing septic systems were repaired. Fecal coliform fell from 1,276 to 174 col/100 mL, and in 2018 Bald Creek plus four tributaries were removed from the 303(d) impaired list.

stories.title: Lower Roanoke River Culvert-to-Bridge Fish Passage Replacements
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in North Carolina; US Army Corps of Engineers; US Fish and Wildlife Service (Roanoke River National Wildlife Refuge)
stories.desc: TNC has been replacing undersized road-crossing culverts in the lower Roanoke River floodplain with fish-friendly bridges; the culverts trapped migrating fish and impounded floodwaters on the floodplain. When complete the project will reconnect eight miles of river to its floodplain within a 140-mile floodplain corridor running from the Atlantic to the first dam. Monitoring with eDNA, fish traps and electrofishing indicates anadromous blueback herring and shad are now using the barrier-free waterways.
stories.notes: Partially complete: several crossings replaced and fish passage documented, with more barriers remaining. BOUNDARY CAUTION: the lower Roanoke corridor spans Martin, Bertie and Washington counties; Washington County is outside the extent. Placed at Williamston (Martin County), inside the extent. Specific crossing names, counties and years are not given on the source page.

stories.title: Little Ivy Creek Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Restoration
stories.orgs: Madison County SWCD (lead); NC Division of Soil & Water Conservation; NC Division of Water Quality; Madison County; UNC Asheville; Clean Water Management Trust Fund; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; TVA
stories.desc: In this Ivy River headwater watershed, the SWCD worked with farmers to install 48,500 ft of livestock exclusion fencing, 170 alternative watering facilities, 31 acres of riparian buffer, 1,500 ft of stream restoration, rotational grazing on 830 acres, and farm road stabilization. The biological score rose from fair (2002) to good (2007) and a 2.6-mile segment was delisted in 2008.
stories.water: Little Ivy Creek (Ivy River / French Broad)

stories.title: Milburnie Dam Removal – Neuse River
stories.orgs: Restoration Systems LLC (owner/funder, mitigation bank); American Rivers; NC Division of Mitigation Services
stories.desc: In November 2017 Restoration Systems began removing the obsolete Milburnie Dam, the last barrier to migratory fish on the Neuse between Falls Lake and the Atlantic and the site of 15 drownings in its hydraulic. The 6-mile impoundment returned to free-flowing river, reopening historic spawning habitat for American shad and striped bass and making the lower Neuse one of the longest free-flowing river reaches in the Southeast. The project was privately funded as a mitigation bank with a perpetual conservation easement.

stories.title: Black Duck Island Living Shoreline – near Oregon Inlet
stories.orgs: North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; Cross Trail Outfitters; Albemarle & Associates; Coastal Wildlife Consultants; Native Shorelines; NC Land and Water Fund
stories.desc: On a rapidly eroding 68-acre dredge-spoil island in Pamlico Sound near Oregon Inlet, partners completed ~2,600 ft of granite living shoreline in August 2024, with 100-ft gaps for fish passage and water circulation and oyster castles for reef habitat, followed by marsh planting in spring 2025. The structure is designed to slow erosion of the island's marsh and bird habitat and re-establish stabilizing marsh grass.

stories.title: Fourth Creek Livestock Exclusion Project
stories.orgs: Carolina Land and Lakes RC&D; Iredell and Rowan SWCDs; NC Agriculture Cost Share Program; U.S. EPA Section 319
stories.desc: Between 2003 and 2006 the project installed 18,328 ft of livestock exclusion fencing, 18 alternative watering facilities, a stream crossing, 2.18 acres of critical-area plantings and manure management equipment on Piedmont farms along Fourth Creek, with five public field days at demonstration sites. The 5.8-mile segment was fully delisted for fecal coliform and turbidity in 2010.

stories.title: Ramseur Dam Removal, Deep River
stories.orgs: American Rivers (lead); Town of Ramseur; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; state and federal permitting agencies; American Rivers
stories.desc: A river-rock dam built in the early 1900s to power a sawmill and later the Columbia Manufacturing Company - with broken gates, exposed rebar and water seeping through - is being taken out of the Deep River at Ramseur. American Rivers reports that as the dam comes down the Deep River will flow freely for the first time in more than a century, restoring passage for native fish, aquatic salamanders and freshwater mussels in the Cape Fear basin. The town is pairing the removal with a state trail greenway, a Deep River blueway paddle trail, and new trailheads and river access points.
stories.notes: Article dated March 2026 describes removal underway; no completion date given. County not stated on the page (Ramseur is in Randolph County). Also documented at: https://www.americanrivers.org/ramseur-dam-removal/

stories.title: Pea Island Recycled-Shell Oyster Patch Reefs (Restaurant to Reef)
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in North Carolina; North Carolina Coastal Federation (Restaurant to Reef); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Pea Island NWR); Outer Banks restaurants and volunteers
stories.desc: Oyster shell recycled from ~30 Outer Banks restaurants (over 3,280 bushels collected 2018–2022) is returned to the sound to build reefs; in spring 2023 volunteers placed ~300 bushels to create new patch oyster reefs in the sound behind Pea Island NWR. TNC reports its NC oyster program has built over 3,000 linear feet of reef and ~50 acres of deep-water sanctuary; the Pea Island reefs slow wave energy to reduce marsh erosion while providing habitat for up to 300 species.

stories.title: Pocosin Lakes NWR Peatland Hydrology Restoration
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; The Nature Conservancy; The Conservation Fund; Ducks Unlimited; NC State University; East Carolina University; Duke University; NC DEQ; APNEP; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; USDA NRCS
stories.desc: Roughly 44,000 acres of the refuge's pocosin peatland had been ditched and drained; since the 1990s USFWS and partners have installed dikes, canal plugs and water control structures to retain rainwater, re-wetting more than 37,000 acres in one of the largest wetland restoration projects in the country. Outcomes include restored seasonal water levels and waterfowl habitat, reduced catastrophic peat-fire risk, improved water quality and resistance to saltwater intrusion, with a final Water Management Plan adopted in 2023 and $27 million in IRA funding for further work.
stories.water: Pocosin peatlands (Alligator & Scuppernong rivers, Pungo Lake)

stories.title: Unnamed Dam Removal, Deep River tributary (Chatham County)
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: An unnamed dam on an unnamed tributary of the Deep River in Chatham County was removed in 2024 as part of ongoing barrier removal in the Cape Fear basin. Removal restores free flow and aquatic organism passage on a small tributary stream. The annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2024 dam removal summary table (PDF verified). Exact site not given; lat/lon is an approximate county centroid on the Deep River corridor.

stories.title: Lockville Dam Removal, Deep River
stories.orgs: American Rivers (project partner lead); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program)
stories.desc: Removal of Lockville Dam, a derelict former hydropower dam that is the most downstream barrier on the Deep River in the Cape Fear River basin and was breached in 2023. The $500,000 National Fish Passage Program project is intended to restore habitat and passage for the federally endangered Cape Fear shiner and the Atlantic pigtoe mussel while improving water quality, climate resilience and paddling recreation.
stories.notes: FY2024 National Fish Passage Program award; county from the FY24 award listing, not the project page.

stories.title: Swannanoa River and Haw Creek Streambank Restoration (RiverLink)
stories.orgs: RiverLink (lead); City of Asheville; Town of Black Mountain; Buncombe County; NC DWQ; Warren Wilson College; Biltmore Estate; Trout Unlimited Land of Sky Chapter; U.S. EPA Section 319
stories.desc: RiverLink led restoration of 8,814 ft of streambank with riparian plantings on Haw Creek and the Swannanoa River, removed invasive exotic plants along 1,950 ft of Haw Creek, secured conservation easements for a 300-ft buffer along 1.3 stream miles at Azalea Park plus a 7-acre wetland, and built rain gardens in Black Mountain. Annual sediment load dropped by more than 500 tons and two Swannanoa segments (2.6 and 11.5 miles) were delisted in 2008 and 2010.

stories.title: Beaverdam Creek Dam Removal, Pigeon River headwaters
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: Beaverdam Creek Dam in Haywood County was removed in 2024, restoring free-flowing conditions and aquatic organism passage in the upper Pigeon River system of the southern Blue Ridge. American Rivers' 2024 annual list records the removal but does not report height, reconnected mileage or partners.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2024 dam removal summary table (PDF verified); the table lists the waterbody as Pigeon River, Haywood County. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Lake Mattamuskeet Invasive Carp Removal and SAV Restoration
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Mattamuskeet NWR); NC Wildlife Resources Commission; Hyde County; North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC DEQ; NC State University; UNC Institute of Marine Sciences; commercial fishermen
stories.desc: After submerged aquatic vegetation in the 40,000-acre lake collapsed to zero, partners adopted a DEQ-approved Watershed Restoration Plan (2019) and attacked the main cause: ~1 million invasive common carp. Carp-exclusion barriers were installed at the four outfall tide gates, 102,000 bluegill were stocked (2023) to eat carp eggs, and contracted netting removed carp through February 2026; the 2026 technical report found the carp population far below 2018 levels and under its impairment threshold, setting the stage for SAV recovery.

stories.title: Richland Creek Agricultural BMPs and Streambank Restoration – Waynesville
stories.orgs: Southwestern NC RC&D Council; Haywood SWCD; Haywood Waterways Association; Town of Waynesville; NC Clean Water Management Trust Fund; Pigeon River Fund; TVA; USDA NRCS; NC State University; NC Wildlife Resources Commission
stories.desc: To address sediment and fecal coliform from livestock and failing septics in Waynesville's water-supply watershed, partners installed 5,055 ft of livestock exclusion fencing, 1,120 ft of channel stabilization, 5,375 ft of critical-area plantings, check dams, heavy-use areas, a stream crossing and septic repairs between 2005 and 2011. Fish IBI scores rose from poor to good-fair, fish counts nearly doubled, darters appeared for the first time, and a 1.6-mile segment was delisted in 2010.

stories.title: Ela Dam Removal, Oconaluftee River
stories.orgs: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians; American Rivers; Mainspring Conservation Trust; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program); Northbrook Carolina Hydro II (owner); Southern Environmental Law Center; American Whitewater; Swain County; Great Smoky Mountains National Park; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; N.C. Wildlife Resources Commission; Northbrook Energy; Swain County Soil and Water Conservation District; U.S. Forest Service; USACE; N.C. Wildlife Federation
stories.desc: Removal of the ca. 1925 Ela Dam, the only physical barrier on the Oconaluftee River, which has smothered the streambed downstream (worsened by a 2021 accidental sediment release) and cut the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians off from ancestral waters. The roughly $16-20 million project will excavate 150,000-200,000 cubic yards of impounded sediment, restore downstream streambanks and reconnect about 549 stream miles to the Tuckasegee River for sicklefin redhorse, Appalachian elktoe mussel and eastern hellbender. About $16 million of the cost has been secured, including $6 million federal and a $4 million National Fish Passage Program award.
stories.notes: Not yet removed as of the page's Sept 2026 update: detailed removal plan being finalized, contingent on full funding and surrender of the hydropower license. Included as a major in-progress project. FWS project page: https://www.fws.gov/project/ela-dam-removal-project

stories.title: McDowell Creek Stream Restoration – Birkdale to Gilead Road
stories.orgs: Mecklenburg County Storm Water Services; Town of Huntersville; Town of Cornelius; City of Charlotte Stream and Wetland Mitigation Bank; NC Land and Water Fund; U.S. EPA Section 319
stories.desc: In this rapidly urbanizing watershed draining to Mountain Island Lake, Huntersville adopted a low-impact development ordinance (2003) and partners restored 10.3 miles of stream, including a 2.1-mile reach from Birkdale Village to Gilead Road completed in 2016 with bank stabilization and in-stream habitat structures, plus 550+ stormwater control measures (~$12M total). EPT abundance rose significantly, suspended solids dropped 48% (2005–2021), and a 2.7-mile segment moved off the impaired category in 2020.

stories.title: Mills River Source Water Protection and Streambank Restoration
stories.orgs: Mills River Partnership; NC Division of Water Quality; Clean Water Management Trust Fund; U.S. EPA; USDA Forest Service; NRCS; NC State University; City of Hendersonville; City of Asheville; Henderson County SWCD; Trout Unlimited
stories.desc: Upstream of the Hendersonville drinking-water intake, partners restored nearly 4,700 ft of streambank, planted 7.8 acres of riparian buffer, secured three conservation easements totaling 192 acres, relocated two agrichemical mixing stations away from the river, stabilized 10 miles of logging roads, and installed 2,580 ft of cattle fencing with stock trails and water tanks. The 1.9-mile segment improved from Poor (1998) to Good-Fair (2002), meeting aquatic life standards.

stories.title: Clear Creek Restoration and 'Stream Doctor' Program
stories.orgs: Mud Creek Restoration Council; Henderson County Cooperative Extension; NC Division of Water Quality; NC Ecosystem Enhancement Program; Tennessee Valley Authority; NC State University; Henderson County
stories.desc: Partners restored 5,425 ft of stream on Clear Creek tributaries, installed a pasture watering system, reduced orchard pesticide spraying on 392 acres, and had landscapers trained through the 'Stream Doctor' program complete eight backyard streambank stabilization projects totaling 1,300 ft. NC DWQ delisted 2.5 miles in 2006 and another 2.7 miles in 2012 after biological ratings improved to Good.

stories.title: AR-293 Mouse Harbor Estuarine Reef – Pamlico Sound
stories.orgs: NC Division of Marine Fisheries Artificial Reef Program; USFWS Sport Fish Restoration Program; Coastal Recreational Fishing License grants; Native Shorelines; NATRX
stories.desc: In 2023 DMF established a new 15-acre inshore reef (AR-293) in Mouse Harbor near Pamlico Point with 200 reef balls and 100 3D-printed concrete units, and in 2026 added 200 more reef balls, experimental 'QuickReef' cubes and 1,200 tons of limestone marl. The hard structure provides oyster settlement substrate and refuge for juvenile finfish, crabs and shrimp on otherwise featureless sound bottom.

stories.title: Lower Mud Creek / Ochlawaha Bog Restoration
stories.orgs: NC Ecosystem Enhancement Program (now DMS); Henderson County SWCD; NC Cooperative Extension; Carolina Mountain Land Conservancy (now Conserving Carolina); Land of Sky Regional Council; NC Division of Water Resources; Clean Water Management Trust Fund; TVA; NC State University
stories.desc: Above Hendersonville, partners took 30 acres of farm field out of production at Ochlawaha Bog, restoring ~1,045 ft of stream, planting 16.65 acres of riparian buffer and restoring ~5 acres of wetland (2011), then stabilized 1,275 ft of eroding streambank with native vegetation and 930 ft of eroding farm road in the Lewis Creek subwatershed (2013). Benthic scores improved from Poor to Good-Fair and the 2.23-mile Lower Mud Creek segment was removed from the 303(d) list in 2014.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, county, land trust, private landowners)

stories.title: Reedy Creek Stream Restoration – Charlotte
stories.orgs: Charlotte-Mecklenburg Storm Water Services; Mecklenburg County Park & Recreation; private landowners (conservation easements)
stories.desc: At and around Reedy Creek Nature Preserve in east Charlotte, Storm Water Services reconnected deeply incised, eroding channels to their floodplains with stable, properly sized channels, restoring 26,000+ ft of stream, protecting 15,000+ ft of headwater streams and 4+ acres of wetlands, and establishing forested riparian areas under conservation easement. Constructed 2017–2019 with monitoring through 2024, the project won NAFSMA's first-place Green Infrastructure Award.

stories.title: Cedar Rock Creek Ford Replaced with Bottomless Culvert – Pisgah National Forest
stories.orgs: Trout Unlimited; USDA Forest Service (Pisgah Ranger District); NC Wildlife Resources Commission; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Duke Energy Water Resources Fund
stories.desc: On a state road crossing in the Catheys Creek watershed of Pisgah National Forest, partners removed a concrete low-water ford with two embedded 24-inch culverts and replaced it with an 18-ft bottomless culvert designed for vehicle traffic. The ~$297,000 project restored aquatic organism passage in a TU priority brook trout catchment in the upper French Broad basin.
stories.water: Cedar Rock Creek (Catheys Creek / French Broad)

stories.title: Catheys Creek Culvert Replacements – Pisgah National Forest
stories.orgs: Trout Unlimited (Southern Appalachian Program, Pisgah Chapter); USDA Forest Service, National Forests in North Carolina; NC Land and Water Fund; Wildlands Engineering; Bass Pro Shops & Cabela's Outdoor Fund
stories.desc: Under its Southern Appalachian Watershed Resiliency Initiative, TU replaced two adjacent undersized culverts at the confluence of Catheys Creek and a tributary with large open-bottom culverts sized for flood flows, removing a complete fish barrier in a stream holding native brook trout and wild brown trout. Construction began in late summer 2024, survived Hurricane Helene undamaged, and was completed in late spring 2025 at about $800,000.

stories.title: Walnut Creek Culvert Removal and Bridge – Franklin
stories.orgs: Mainspring Conservation Trust; NC Wildlife Resources Commission (Aquatic Organism Passage program); private landowner
stories.desc: In 2018 Mainspring removed a fish-blocking culvert on Walnut Creek near Pine Grove Baptist Church on Highlands Road in Franklin and replaced it with a bridge, funded through NCWRC's Aquatic Organism Passage program. Up to 14 additional fish species from the Cullasaja / Little Tennessee system can now reach the creek's cooler water in summer, and fish washed downstream in storms can return upstream.

stories.title: Senator Jean Preston Oyster Sanctuary Network – Brant Island / Maw Point
stories.orgs: North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC Division of Marine Fisheries; NOAA; NC Central University; NCSU CMAST; NC Aquarium on Roanoke Island; RTI International
stories.desc: Since 2009 the Coastal Federation and DMF have built a network of 15 harvest-protected oyster sanctuaries in Pamlico Sound (789 acres of protected habitat), with the newest reefs at Brant Island and Maw Point built in 2025–2026 under a $14.9 million NOAA grant. The reefs supply significant oyster spat to wild populations across the sound, and an RTI study found every $1 invested returns $1.71 in benefits, 143 jobs and $34 million added to the coastal economy (2013–2023).
stories.water: Pamlico Sound (Brant Island Shoal / Maw Point)

stories.title: Lakey Creek Culvert Removal and Fish Passage
stories.orgs: Mainspring Conservation Trust; NC Wildlife Resources Commission; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; private landowner
stories.desc: Following 2013 riparian buffer restoration (1,750 ft of buffer, 1,300 live stakes), Mainspring in early 2016 removed a failing culvert that blocked upstream fish movement on Lakey Creek, replaced it with a steel-and-wood bridge, and placed logs and other natural structures to create resting pools. Funded by NCWRC with USFWS support, the project reopened the tributary to Little Tennessee River fishes.

stories.title: Swan Island Oyster Sanctuary (50 Million Oyster Initiative)
stories.orgs: North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC Division of Marine Fisheries; NOAA Community-based Restoration Program; NC General Assembly; Grady-White Boats
stories.desc: Between 2017 and 2019 the Coastal Federation and NC DMF built a 40-acre subtidal oyster sanctuary from ~80,600 tons of limestone marl and granite in Pamlico Sound near the mouth of the Neuse River, the centerpiece of the 50 Million Oyster Initiative. DMF monitoring found densities up to 2,000 oysters per square meter (~136 million oysters on the reef), nearly three times the initiative's goal; the project also planted 154 acres of harvestable cultch reefs.

stories.title: Little Tennessee River Tributary Stream Restoration (Partners for Fish and Wildlife)
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife (Asheville and Georgia field offices); North Carolina State Historic Preservation Office; private landowner; Macon County
stories.desc: A Partners for Fish and Wildlife stream restoration on an unnamed tributary to the Little Tennessee River in Macon County. Before construction, FWS staff and an archeologist completed a phase I survey, digging and sifting 20 test holes; no artifacts were found, the site report was filed with the state historic preservation office and the stream restoration moved forward in 2026.
stories.notes: Stream not named in the story; coordinates approximate near Franklin / Coweeta. Story documents the pre-construction survey and confirms restoration proceeded.

stories.title: Brasstown Creek Watershed Restoration – Hiwassee River
stories.orgs: Hiwassee River Watershed Coalition (lead); Clay County and Cherokee County SWCDs; Blue Ridge Mountain SWCD (GA); TVA; NC Division of Soil & Water Conservation; USDA NRCS; Clean Water Management Trust Fund; 47 private landowners
stories.desc: From 1995 to 2004 partners revegetated 160 acres of critically eroding streamside land, installed ~6.2 miles of livestock exclusion fencing, reconstructed unstable channelized reaches using a stable reference-reach pattern, and created or protected 48 acres of forested riparian buffer. Macroinvertebrate scores climbed from Fair (1994) to Excellent (2004); the creek was delisted in 2000 and TVA modeling showed ~25% less suspended sediment.

stories.title: Cedar Island Oyster Sanctuary
stories.orgs: North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC Division of Marine Fisheries; NC General Assembly; NOAA
stories.desc: The Coastal Federation and DMF constructed more than 15 acres of harvest-protected oyster reef in Pamlico Sound near Cedar Island National Wildlife Refuge using quarried limestone marl and crushed concrete recycled from NC bridge demolitions. The reef is expected to support at least 15 million oysters and filter up to 750 million gallons of water per day; sanctuaries make up ~6% of Pamlico Sound reef area but contribute nearly 40% of the sound's oyster population.

stories.title: Steeles Mill Dam Removal, Hitchcock Creek
stories.orgs: City of Rockingham; American Rivers; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; NOAA
stories.desc: A late-1800s cotton-mill dam, decommissioned by 1999, was removed from Hitchcock Creek at Rockingham in 2009, reopening about 15 miles of upstream spawning habitat in this Pee Dee River tributary. The project restored access for American shad, hickory shad, American eel, striped bass, Atlantic sturgeon and the federally endangered shortnose sturgeon. It also created a 14-mile blue trail with primitive campgrounds, two river access areas and a boat launch, and protected roughly 100 acres of bottomland forest.
stories.notes: County not stated on the page; Rockingham is the seat of Richmond County, NC.

stories.title: Angola Bay Game Land Pocosin Rewetting
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in North Carolina; NC Wildlife Resources Commission
stories.desc: TNC and NCWRC restored hydrology on 7,500 acres of ditched pocosin peatland at Angola Bay Game Land, installing 37 water control structures across 140 miles of ditches (2023–2024). In 2025 the second phase planted nearly 250,000 native seedlings, including 147,000+ globally rare Atlantic white cedar, on former loblolly plantation, re-wetting peat more than six feet deep to cut carbon emissions, reduce wildfire risk and improve wetland habitat.
stories.water: Angola Bay pocosin (Northeast Cape Fear headwaters)

stories.title: Fort Macon State Park Living Shoreline
stories.orgs: North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC Division of Parks and Recreation; NC Land and Water Fund; Quible & Associates; Carolina Marine Structures; Native Shorelines
stories.desc: To halt severe erosion on the park's northern soundside next to the Coast Guard station, a ~2,400-ft granite sill was installed in early 2024 and marsh grasses were planted behind it by contractors and volunteers in spring 2024 and 2025. The project rebuilds salt marsh nursery habitat for crabs, shrimp and shellfish, protects diamondback terrapin habitat, and is expected to reduce sand shoaling into the Beaufort Inlet channel.

stories.title: Morris Landing Clean Water Preserve Living Shoreline – Stump Sound
stories.orgs: North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC Division of Marine Fisheries; NC Land and Water Fund; NOAA Restoration Center; Restore America's Estuaries; Onslow County Soil & Water; Atlantic Coastal Fish Habitat Partnership; Duke Energy Foundation
stories.desc: On a 52-acre preserve purchased in 2004, the Coastal Federation built six phases of living shoreline (2005–2021) using stone sills, oyster-shell bag reefs, concrete oyster domes and loose-shell sills, with volunteers planting thousands of smooth cordgrass seedlings. The sills restored a vibrant salt marsh behind them, and the site's shell stockpile and loading pier raised the state's annual recycled-shell deployment from ~9,000 to 20,000–30,000 bushels; ~1,860 ft of living shoreline is now maintained here.

stories.title: Cape Fear River Lock & Dam #1 Rock Arch Rapids
stories.orgs: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Wilmington District); Cape Fear River Watch; Cape Fear River Partnership; NOAA; NC Wildlife Resources Commission
stories.desc: In 2012 the Corps and partners built a rock arch rapids (nature-like fishway) over Lock & Dam #1 on the Cape Fear River, allowing striped bass, American shad, river herring and Atlantic and shortnose sturgeon to pass the dam for the first time in more than 100 years. Monitoring showed passage could be improved, so the rapids were modified in late 2021; fish passage at Lock & Dams #2 and #3 is now being planned.

stories.title: Carolina Beach State Park Tidal Wetland Restoration
stories.orgs: North Carolina Coastal Federation; NC Division of Parks and Recreation; NOAA, USFWS and NC DEQ (natural resource trustees); U.S. EPA; Greenfield Multistate Environmental Response Trust; UNC Wilmington; NC Sea Grant
stories.desc: Funded with natural-resource-damage settlement money from the Kerr-McGee (Navassa) Superfund site, the Federation and State Parks restored about 10 acres of tidal wetland between the Sugarloaf and Swamp Trails over three phases: invasive Phragmites was removed by burning, herbicide and cutting, fill was excavated to create a shallow tidal slough, and native wetland vegetation was planted with help from more than 260 volunteers.
stories.water: Cape Fear River estuary / Snow's Cut

stories.title: Matthews Creek Dam Removal, Mountain Bridge Wilderness
stories.orgs: Naturaland Trust; Trout Unlimited; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A dam on Matthews Creek in the Mountain Bridge area of the Blue Ridge Escarpment was removed in 2019 to restore habitat for South Carolina's native southern Appalachian brook trout. American Rivers' South Carolina Dam Removal Handbook features it as a case study and describes the project as producing excellent results for brook trout habitat restoration. The removal reconnected headwater trout habitat in a protected mountain watershed.
stories.water: Matthews Creek (Middle Saluda / Saluda River headwaters)
stories.notes: Case study 3 in the SC Dam Removal Handbook (PDF verified); the appendix text itself was truncated in the fetch, so location is inferred from Matthews Creek in the Jones Gap / Caesars Head area of Greenville County. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Burrell's Place Dam Removal, Chattooga headwaters
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; South Carolina Department of Natural Resources; Naturaland Trust; U.S. Forest Service; Mountain Bridge Chapter of Trout Unlimited; American Rivers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A 15-foot-tall, 165-foot-long headwater dam built in 1935 was removed on 2 March 2022 from an unnamed branch of Pigpen Creek, a tributary of the federally designated Wild and Scenic Chattooga River. The project is expected to restore about three miles of stream for native southern Appalachian brook trout. It was one of three South Carolina removals recorded nationally that year.
stories.water: Unnamed tributary to Pigpen Branch (Chattooga River)
stories.notes: Detail (height, length, 3 miles, partners, 2 March 2022 date, 1935 build year) from the project write-up in American Rivers' 2022 dam removal summary PDF. Lat/lon approximate within Oconee County's Chattooga headwaters.

stories.title: Cane Creek and Little Cane Creek livestock exclusion
stories.orgs: Friends of Lake Keowee Society (lead); SCDHEC; Oconee County Soil and Water District; USDA NRCS; Clemson University; Oconee County Cattlemen's Association; City of Walhalla; ENTRIX, Inc.; local residents
stories.desc: A three-year project beginning in 2006 installed 6,933 feet of livestock exclusion fencing, 17 alternate watering sources with 2,680 feet of supply pipeline and 15 protected heavy-use areas, addressed 18 onsite wastewater systems, and replaced 500 feet of damaged sewer line in Walhalla. In the year after the project both monitored sites met the state fecal coliform standard, with exceedance rates of 8.33 percent on Cane Creek and 9.80 percent on Little Cane Creek.
stories.water: Cane Creek and Little Cane Creek
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story; sites met standards but the document does not state a formal delisting.

stories.title: Gills Creek culvert replacements for the Carolina heelsplitter
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Aquatic Habitat Restoration Team, South Carolina Ecological Services, Orangeburg National Fish Hatchery); SC Department of Natural Resources; Lancaster County
stories.desc: Three undersized, perched round culverts on Gills Creek were replaced with bottomless arch culverts, restoring passage for the endangered Carolina heelsplitter mussel and its host fish, the bluehead chub, and reconnecting more than five miles of designated critical habitat. The work accompanied propagation at the Orangeburg Mussel Conservation Center, which produced more than 5,000 mussels and released close to 2,000 between 2016 and 2021, with over 1,000 stocked into South Carolina streams in 2021 alone.
stories.notes: Gills Creek in Lancaster County holds roughly a third of remaining Carolina heelsplitter habitat. Coordinates approximate to the creek within the county.

stories.title: Tyger River streambank protection and livestock exclusion
stories.orgs: SCDHEC; Clemson University Cooperative Extension; USDA NRCS; Spartanburg, Greenville and Union soil and water conservation districts and Cattlemen's Associations; Duke Energy Foundation; U.S. EPA; landowners
stories.desc: In the 820-square-mile Tyger River watershed, partners installed 27,385 feet of livestock exclusion fencing and an equal length of streambank and shoreline protection, 19 alternative water source units, 15,193 feet of pipeline, livestock stream crossings and 14,994 square feet of heavy-use area protection, and repaired 114 rural septic systems. Four monitoring sites were reported fully supporting recreational use in the 2012 Integrated Report, and peak fecal coliform levels across 20 stations dropped from about 8,800 to under 2,300 cfu/100 mL.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans Greenville, Spartanburg, Union and Newberry counties; coordinates approximate to the watershed center.

stories.title: Culvert Replacements for Fish Passage in South Carolina (Lynches and Saluda rivers)
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program); USDA Forest Service (project partner lead)
stories.desc: Road crossings on a tributary of the Lynches River and on the Saluda River that were not designed for aquatic organism passage, and that push excess road fill into the stream, are being replaced with bottomless arch culverts. The $860,000 project is intended to restore stream function, let fish and mussels move upstream and reduce sediment delivery to downstream mussel beds; the stream is designated critical habitat for the endangered Carolina heelsplitter. The FWS project page lists 10.1 stream miles reopened.
stories.notes: FY2022 National Fish Passage Program award; project status listed as In Development despite a stream-mile figure. Two separated sites; coordinates given for the Lancaster County site.

stories.title: Thompson Creek riparian planting and cattle exclusion
stories.orgs: U.S. EPA; SCDHEC; USDA NRCS; Pee Dee Resource Conservation and Development Council; Chesterfield County Soil and Water Conservation District; SC Department of Natural Resources; local landowners
stories.desc: Partners installed about 53,000 feet of fencing to exclude cattle from Thompson Creek, 106 acres of tree and shrub planting, 26 acres of pasture and hayland planting, 24,648 feet of pipeline, 37 watering facilities, five wells and 974 acres of conservation tillage, and repaired 34 failing septic systems. Average fecal coliform levels fell about 81 percent at station PD-246 (3,064 to 570 cfu/100 mL) and 58 percent at PD-247 between 2003 and 2008.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story; water quality improved substantially but the creek was not delisted.

stories.title: Wrenn Farms Pond Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Wrenn Farms Pond Dam on a tributary of the Catawba River in Lancaster County was removed in 2022, draining an impoundment and restoring free-flowing stream conditions and aquatic organism passage. The national annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2022 dam removal summary table (PDF verified). Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Coneross and Beaverdam Creek buffers, fencing and septic repair
stories.orgs: SCDHEC; Clemson University; USDA NRCS; Oconee County Soil and Water Conservation District; Oconee County Cattlemen's Association; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Across the 47,016-acre Coneross and 9,099-acre Beaverdam Creek watersheds, landowners installed 80 agricultural BMPs including planted riparian buffers and field borders, cattle exclusion fencing, alternative water sources, waste-storage sheds and compost facilities, and 38 failing septic systems were repaired or replaced. Beaverdam Creek was removed from the 303(d) list in 2000 and the Coneross Creek site in 2002, and by December 2005 all three monitoring stations met South Carolina's fecal coliform standards.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate to the Coneross Creek watershed between Westminster and Seneca.

stories.title: Rocky Creek livestock exclusion, buffers and filter strips
stories.orgs: SCDHEC; Research Planning, Inc.; City of Columbia; Clemson University Cooperative Extension Service; U.S. EPA; participating farmers
stories.desc: Seven farms in the 127,872-acre Rocky Creek watershed installed nearly 50,000 feet of livestock exclusion fencing plus more than 65 other practices including vegetated buffers and filter strips, stream crossings, alternative watering systems, no-till planting and manure storage, and failing septic systems were repaired. Three of four monitoring sites improved from 'not supporting' to 'partial support' of recreational use and geometric mean fecal coliform levels fell at all four stations.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans Chester and Fairfield counties; progress toward, not attainment of, standards.

stories.title: Enoree River livestock exclusion fencing and stream crossings
stories.orgs: SCDHEC; Clemson University Cooperative Extension; USDA NRCS; Spartanburg, Laurens and Union soil and water conservation districts and Cattlemen's Associations; Enoree River Educational Board; landowners
stories.desc: A three-year CWA Section 319 project across 195,417 acres of the Enoree River watershed installed 29,577 feet of fencing to keep livestock out of streams, 40,554 square feet of heavy-use area protection, 8,850 feet of waterline, 11 concrete water tanks, two stream ramps and two stream crossings, and repaired nine failing septic systems. By the 2014 assessment the Enoree River at US 221 had dropped from 17 to 3 percent bacteria exceedances and Beards Fork Creek from 21 to 0 percent, both now fully supporting recreational use.
stories.water: Enoree River and Beards Fork Creek
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Implementation spanned Laurens, Spartanburg and Union counties; coordinates approximate to the lower watershed.

stories.title: Rabon Creek livestock exclusion and vegetative plantings
stories.orgs: Upper Savannah Council of Governments; Clemson University Extension; Laurens County Water and Sewer Commission; USDA NRCS; Laurens Cattlemen's Association; SCDHEC; local landowners
stories.desc: Between 2007 and 2010 partners installed 22,215 linear feet of fencing, 14 watering facilities, two watering gaps, 10,918 square feet of heavy use area protection and 1.5 acres of vegetative plantings, restricting 320 head of livestock from waterways, and repaired 44 failing septic tanks. South Rabon Creek (station S-322) met water quality standards in 2010-2011 monitoring and was reported fully supporting its recreational use in the 2016 CWA 303(d) assessment, with estimated reductions of 645 tons of sediment and 4,611 lb of nitrogen.
stories.sector: Partnership (regional COG, university, federal, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed also extends into Greenville County.

stories.title: Fishing Creek riparian buffers and livestock exclusion
stories.orgs: SCDHEC; Research Planning, Inc.; USDA NRCS; Chester and York County Cattlemen's Associations and conservation districts; Clemson University Extension; York County Engineering; U.S. EPA; local landowners
stories.desc: Eleven agricultural landowners on 13 farms in the 288-square-mile Fishing Creek watershed established 182 acres of vegetative riparian buffers and 104,000 feet of fencing that excluded 675 cattle and 42 horses from streams, plus 12 alternative water sources, five water control structures, a constructed wetland and 10 septic repairs. Two of 11 monitoring sites met South Carolina fecal coliform standards after implementation and seven others showed declining bacteria levels.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans York and Chester counties; partial attainment only, not a full delisting.

stories.title: Lake Hartwell fish habitat structure installation
stories.orgs: SC Department of Natural Resources (Freshwater Fisheries Research); Clemson University
stories.desc: SCDNR has been placing artificial habitat structures in coves of Lake Hartwell to rebuild fish habitat in a reservoir whose fishery was damaged by PCB contamination, and is assessing the resulting changes in the fish community with Clemson University. A 2015 pilot assessment estimated about 250 largemouth bass over 12 inches in a single 100-acre treated cove, and the study design compares coves with and without installed habitat.
