stories.notes: Agency project page is dated 2015; current status not confirmed. Lake Hartwell spans Anderson, Oconee and Pickens counties in SC.

stories.title: Upper Little Pee Dee River streambank protection and livestock exclusion
stories.orgs: Pee Dee Resource Conservation and Development Council; Dillon and Marlboro Soil and Water Conservation Districts; USDA NRCS; SC Department of Natural Resources; SCDHEC; U.S. EPA; private landowners
stories.desc: On a 12.6-mile reach of the Upper Little Pee Dee River, 14 farms installed 24,484 feet of streambank and shoreline protection, 16,709 feet of livestock exclusion fencing, five alternate water sources, 8.9 acres of pasture planting and 4,624 acres of nutrient management, with 25 septic systems repaired. By 2008 only 5 percent of samples exceeded the fecal coliform standard and SCDHEC removed the river from the impaired waters list that year.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story (delisted 2008). Monitoring station PD-029E lies northwest of Dillon; Marlboro County also participated.

stories.title: Upper Northlake Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Upper Northlake Dam on an unnamed tributary of Rocky Creek at Greenwood was removed in 2022, restoring free flow on a Saluda basin tributary. The national inventory records the removal but does not report height, reconnected mileage or partners.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2022 dam removal summary table (PDF verified). Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Flint Hill Church Fish Passage and Flood Control Project, Horsepen Creek
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program); Upper Savannah River Land Trust
stories.desc: Replacement of an undersized culvert system on Horsepen Creek less than a mile upstream of designated critical habitat for the endangered Carolina heelsplitter mussel. The $400,000 project is intended to protect downstream mussel beds, let mussels and their host fish move upstream, and end the road closures and emergency-access problems the existing culverts cause during high water. The FWS project page lists 12 stream miles reopened.
stories.notes: FY2023 National Fish Passage Program award; status listed as In Development. Coordinates approximate within Greenwood County.

stories.title: Scape Ore Swamp streambank protection and grazing BMPs
stories.orgs: Santee-Wateree Resource Conservation and Development Council; Lee and Kershaw Soil and Water Conservation Districts; USDA NRCS; SC Department of Health and Environmental Control; SC Department of Natural Resources; U.S. EPA; private landowners
stories.desc: Landowners along the 11.8-mile main stem of Scape Ore Swamp installed 1,100 feet of streambank and shoreline protection, 4.5 acres of vegetated filter strip, 188 acres of prescribed grazing, 943 acres of nutrient management, nine waste storage structures and NRCS-funded riparian buffers and fencing. Fecal coliform exceedances fell from 33 percent of samples in 2002 to 4 percent by 2012. SCDHEC found the waterbody no longer impaired and the 2012 Integrated Report listed it as fully supporting contact recreation.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Kershaw County partners also participated.

stories.title: Smith Swamp streambank stabilization and livestock BMPs
stories.orgs: Pee Dee Resource Conservation & Development Council; Santee-Wateree RC&D; Marion, Dillon and Horry Soil and Water Conservation Districts; USDA NRCS; SC Department of Natural Resources; Clemson University Cooperative Extension; SCDHEC; local landowners
stories.desc: Across the 23,350-acre Smith Swamp watershed, 18 cattle farms installed 77,265 feet of streambank stabilization, sensitive-area protection and cross-fencing, 484 acres of prescribed grazing and runoff management, 25 acres of critical-area stabilization, 12 wells and 39 troughs, and 108 failing septic systems were repaired. Station PD-187 improved from not supporting to fully supporting recreational use and Smith Swamp was removed from the CWA 303(d) impaired waters list for fecal coliform in 2014.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story (delisted 2014).

stories.title: Congaree Creek Dam Removal
stories.orgs: American Rivers; Congaree Riverkeeper; South Carolina Department of Natural Resources; City of Cayce; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Aquatic Habitat Restoration Team)
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: An obsolete 15-foot-tall, 40-foot-wide dam that created a dangerous current at the head of a canoe trail was removed from Congaree Creek at Cayce in May 2019. The removal reconnected ten miles of mainstem Congaree Creek for herring, shiners and darters that need access to different parts of the stream. Follow-up photos four and a half months later show the creek flowing freely and the paddling hazard eliminated.
stories.notes: County not stated on the page; Cayce is in Lexington County, SC. Also referenced as a case study in American Rivers' South Carolina Dam Removal Handbook.

stories.title: Brunson Swamp rotational grazing and livestock exclusion
stories.orgs: Horry Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Horry County; Grand Strand Water and Sewer Authority; Town of Aynor; SCDHEC; local landowners
stories.desc: The Horry, Aynor and Dogbluff Water Quality Project installed 1,600 feet of fencing excluding 359 livestock from waterways, began rotational grazing on 593 pasture acres, added nine wells, 28 storage tanks and 9,450 feet of pipeline for alternative livestock water, and repaired 120 failing septic systems in this blackwater tributary of the Little Pee Dee River. Estimated reductions were 8,704 lb of nitrogen, 2,170 lb of phosphorus and 114 tons of sediment, and E. coli exceedances at station PD-370 fell from 35 to 18 percent between 2011 and 2018.
stories.sector: Partnership (conservation district, federal, local government, landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 story; water quality improved but the swamp remains listed as impaired.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Oaks Creek at Oyster Landing, Murrells Inlet
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; community volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built in Oaks Creek near Oyster Landing at Murrells Inlet in 2001, in the program's first season, and expanded in 2003. Volunteers placed bagged shell in the intertidal zone to add oyster settlement substrate in the inlet's tidal creek network.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reefs at Murrells Inlet (Oyster Landing and Huntington Beach)
stories.orgs: SC Department of Natural Resources (SCORE program); North Inlet-Winyah Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve; Huntington Beach State Park; volunteers
stories.desc: SCORE built recycled-shell oyster reefs on Oaks Creek near Oyster Landing at Murrells Inlet in 2001 and 2003, at Huntington Beach State Park near the education center pier in 2003, and at Horseshoe Creek within a larger shell planting in 2004. These reefs mark the northern end of SCORE's 200-mile restoration range and support volunteer monitoring in the Murrells Inlet estuary.
stories.water: Oaks Creek / Horseshoe Creek, Murrells Inlet
stories.notes: Reef count and area not published per site.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Huntington Beach State Park, Murrells Inlet
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; South Carolina State Park Service (Huntington Beach State Park)
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built near the education center pier at Huntington Beach State Park on Murrells Inlet in 2003. The reef adds intertidal oyster settlement substrate in the inlet's salt marsh and sits beside a public education facility used for estuary interpretation.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: St. Stephen Fish Lift, Santee River Rediversion Canal
stories.orgs: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Charleston District; South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A fish lift was built into the St. Stephen Powerhouse on the Santee-Cooper Rediversion Canal in 1985 to restore migratory fish passage blocked by the dam, the only fish lift in South Carolina. It lifts fish from the tailrace into Lake Moultrie, reopening access to Lake Marion and the Congaree and Wateree rivers upstream. SCDNR operates and monitors the lift, which can move thousands of fish per day; passed species include American shad, blueback herring, striped bass, blue catfish and the federally endangered shortnose sturgeon, and passage statistics have been tallied since 1987.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate, taken from the St. Stephen powerhouse location. Page verified by WebFetch; it links to separate passage-statistics pages for 1987-2014 that were not fetched.

stories.title: Boyd Living Shoreline, Morgan Park, Georgetown
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; Darnall W. and Susan F. Boyd Foundation; Boeing South Carolina; Coastal Carolina University; Shoreline Restoration Group; Baruch Institute; SC Department of Environmental Services; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; The Nature Conservancy in South Carolina; US Army Corps of Engineers
stories.desc: TNC built a one-acre living shoreline at Morgan Park in Georgetown to slow erosion from boat wakes and high tides, combining near-shore wattle fence sills made from 63 bundles of branches with an offshore wooden pole breakwater that reduces wave energy. Construction began in 2024 and was completed in 2025, funded by a $997,000 gift from the Boyd Foundation plus Boeing South Carolina support, with volunteer labor and community ambassadors. Coastal Carolina University conducted baseline and post-installation monitoring of sediment accumulation and habitat use.
stories.notes: Waterbody not named on the source page (it refers to the East Bay/Morgan peninsula); county inferred from Georgetown, SC. No measured outcomes reported yet. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Bulls Bay / Shellfish Area 7 oyster reef planting and livestock exclusion
stories.orgs: Charleston Soil and Water Conservation District; SCDHEC; SC Department of Natural Resources; The Nature Conservancy; USDA NRCS; U.S. Forest Service; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Charleston County; Town of McClellanville; U.S. EPA; local landowners
stories.desc: More than 11,000 bushels of oyster shell were planted in 2010 and 2012 to rebuild reefs in Shellfish Harvesting Area 7, including on Tibwin Creek, alongside 10,300 feet of livestock fencing with 20-foot vegetated buffers around drainage ditches, 62 septic system replacements and pet-waste stations. Seven monitoring sites in the Awendaw Creek and Bulls Bay watersheds now meet state fecal coliform standards, were removed from the 303(d) list in the 2014 assessment, and the shellfish beds reopened to harvest.
stories.water: Bulls Bay, Awendaw Creek, Tibwin Creek, Graham Creek
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story (delisted 2014).

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Jeremy Creek, McClellanville
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Town of McClellanville; community volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built in Jeremy Creek beside the McClellanville town boat landing in 2001 and expanded in 2002. The reef adds intertidal oyster settlement substrate in the working-waterfront creek that serves the village's shrimp and oyster fleet.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: Jeremy Island oyster castle reef, Cape Romain
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge); SC Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: TNC and partners deployed Oyster Castle units at Jeremy Island in the Cape Romain area to rebuild intertidal oyster reef and protect eroding marsh edge, part of a broader program testing Oyster Castles as reef building blocks within Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge. The work is tied to TNC's South Carolina coastal resilience program and the South Atlantic Salt Marsh Initiative.
stories.notes: TNC's page describes the site only in a photo caption; scale and exact dates are not published there.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Cape Romain AICW near Graham Creek
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service); Virginia Military Institute and Old Dominion University student volunteers; SC Department of Natural Resources (SCORE program); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge); volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: Volunteers built recycled-shell oyster reefs along the Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway near Graham Creek inside Cape Romain, over four consecutive build seasons from 2014 through 2017. VMI and Old Dominion University student groups and other volunteers placed shell bags along eroding AICW shorelines, adding oyster settlement substrate and buffering boat-wake erosion in a refuge setting.
stories.water: Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway near Graham Creek, Cape Romain
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate to the AICW reach inside Cape Romain. Refuge affiliation inferred from the Cape Romain location; the page names only the student volunteer groups.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Daniel Island, Wando River
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (stimulus) funding
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built on the Wando River at Daniel Island in 2010, beside the fishing pier on the island's nature trail, using federal stimulus funding. The reef provides intertidal settlement substrate and shoreline buffering along a publicly accessible stretch of the Wando.
stories.notes: Daniel Island straddles Berkeley and Charleston counties; listed as Berkeley. Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: Goldbug Island Living Shoreline
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in South Carolina; The Nature Conservancy; SC Department of Natural Resources; local partners
stories.desc: TNC converted an eroding Goldbug Island shoreline, damaged by heavy waves and boat traffic, into a stabilized living shoreline. The restored site now supports healthy marsh grass and oysters across multiple size classes, confirmed by volunteer oyster measurements. Before-and-after photos on the project page document the change, and the site is cited as the precedent for TNC's later Georgetown living shoreline.
stories.notes: Completion year, scale and waterbody are not stated on the source page; town/county inferred from Goldbug Island near Mount Pleasant, SC. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Alhambra Hall, Mount Pleasant
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Town of Mount Pleasant; Moultrie Middle School; Wando High School; South Carolina State Ports Authority; SCDNR Marine Resources Research Institute (SCORE); Students Today Leaders Forever; Charleston County Park and Recreation Commission; Patriots Point Naval and Maritime Museum; SC Department of Natural Resources (SCORE program); Marine Resources Research Institute; volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: Volunteers built and expanded an intertidal oyster reef with recycled shell at Alhambra Hall on Charleston Harbor in Mount Pleasant over three build seasons in 2011, 2012 and 2013. Students from Moultrie Middle and Wando High schools worked alongside the Town of Mount Pleasant and the SC State Ports Authority to bag shell and place it along the shoreline, adding hard substrate for oyster settlement and shoreline protection at a heavily used public waterfront park.
stories.notes: Site details verified on the SCORE site-descriptions page; per-site acreage and bushel counts are not published. Coordinates approximate to Alhambra Hall.

stories.title: SCDNR large-scale oyster shell planting, 15 coastal sites
stories.orgs: SC Department of Natural Resources (Marine Resources Research Institute); NOAA National Marine Fisheries Service; SC Saltwater Recreational Fisheries License program; South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, Marine Resources Research Institute; SC Saltwater Recreational Fishing License program
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: Between 2002 and 2004 SCDNR planted just under 280,000 square feet (6.4 acres) of oyster and whelk shell, about 88,000 bushels, at 15 sites along the South Carolina coast to provide hard substrate for juvenile oyster settlement, funded by saltwater fishing license proceeds. NMFS funding in 2005 extended planting to additional acreage outside the Public Oyster Grounds. SCDNR monitored shell loss, siltation, erosion, oyster recruitment and growth, and reports that some plantings were undercut by rapid siltation and shell loss from boat wakes, which drove trials of mesh covers, shell bags and geotextile underlayment.
stories.notes: Statewide program, not a single point; the 15 individual sites are not named on the page. Coordinates are the MRRI/Charleston program base, used as a placeholder. Mixed outcome is stated candidly on the source page.

stories.title: SCORE community oyster reef restoration program (statewide)
stories.orgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SCORE program); volunteer groups, schools, municipalities and private landowners statewide; SC Department of Natural Resources (Marine Resources Research Institute); NOAA Coastal Services Center; coastal municipalities, parks and schools; more than 25,000 volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: The South Carolina Oyster Restoration and Enhancement (SCORE) program has recycled over 100,000 bushels (more than 1,800 tons) of oyster shell and used volunteer labor to build 225 constructed reefs at dozens of intertidal sites along 200 miles of coast from Murrells Inlet to Hilton Head since 2001. The program reports more than four acres of restored oyster habitat; monitored reefs recruit new oysters and attract estuarine fish and invertebrates, and in several places marsh grass has advanced behind the reefs.
stories.water: Intertidal creeks and estuaries, SC coast
stories.notes: Program-level entry covering 44 named restoration sites across Charleston, Beaufort, Colleton, Georgetown and Jasper counties; individual sites listed separately below.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Ashley River at Brittlebank Park
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Summerville Saltwater Anglers; College of Charleston students; Mason Preparatory School students and families; City of Charleston (Plymouth Avenue Park); community volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A volunteer-built recycled-shell oyster reef was constructed on the Ashley River across from Brittlebank Park in downtown Charleston over three seasons in 2012, 2013 and 2014. Summerville Saltwater Anglers, College of Charleston students and Mason Prep families placed bagged shell in the intertidal zone to create settlement substrate and stabilize the urban riverbank.
stories.notes: Per-site acreage not published. Coordinates approximate to Brittlebank Park.

stories.title: SCDNR experimental oyster reefs and marsh regrowth monitoring
stories.orgs: SC Department of Natural Resources (Marine Resources Research Institute); S.C. Sea Grant Consortium
stories.desc: SCDNR built experimental intertidal oyster reefs with Sea Grant support and monitored shoreline erosion for 6 to 70 months at 15 intertidal sites, where erosion was running about one-half to two inches per month. At several reef-protected sites, marsh vegetation regrew within two to three years, and at one site the marsh edge advanced an average of 12 feet over four years, demonstrating oyster reefs as a shoreline stabilization tool.
stories.water: Intertidal creeks and marsh edge, SC coast
stories.notes: Sites are not individually named on the agency page; date range approximate.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Bowens Island, Folly Creek
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Bowens Island Restaurant; community volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: One of the earliest SCORE sites, a recycled-shell oyster reef was built in Folly Creek in front of Bowens Island Restaurant on James Island in 2001 and expanded in 2003 and 2004. The build was featured on the television program Dirty Jobs. The reef added intertidal settlement substrate in a creek that supplies the restaurant's long-standing oyster roast tradition.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate to Bowens Island. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reefs at Bears Bluff, Wadmalaw Island
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Bears Bluff National Fish Hatchery (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service); Boy Scouts of America Camp Ho Non Wah; SC Department of Natural Resources (SCORE program); Bears Bluff National Fish Hatchery; volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: Volunteers built recycled-shell oyster reefs at the Bears Bluff hatchery site on Wadmalaw Island in 2008 and 2009 and expanded them in 2013, restoring intertidal oyster habitat on the Wadmalaw River. SCORE monitors reef recruitment and growth at the site; Wadmalaw Island also hosts SCORE reefs at Boy Scout Camp Ho Non Wah (2001, 2002 and three added reefs in 2006) and Rockville (2001).
stories.notes: Reef count and area not published per site.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Bass Creek, Kiawah Island
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Town of Kiawah Island community volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built in Bass Creek on Kiawah Island, off Ocean Course Road, in 2004 and expanded in 2006. The reef adds intertidal oyster settlement substrate in a barrier-island tidal creek.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Big Bay Creek, Edisto Beach State Park
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; South Carolina State Park Service (Edisto Beach State Park); ACE Basin Interpretive Center; SC Department of Natural Resources (SCORE program); SC State Park Service; volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built in Big Bay Creek at Edisto Beach State Park, between the Live Oak boat landing and the ACE Basin Interpretive Center, with builds in 2002, 2003, 2006 and then annually from 2008 through 2014. The repeated expansions created a long run of intertidal oyster habitat along a state park shoreline that doubles as a public interpretive site.
stories.notes: Listed on the SCORE page as the Edisto site. Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Coosaw Cut at Hutchinson Island, ACE Basin
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Beaufort Marine Institute; Sun City Hilton Head volunteers; area schools; Dataw Island community volunteers; SC Department of Natural Resources (SCORE program); ACE Basin National Estuarine Research Reserve; volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: This is one of SCORE's longest-running sites: recycled-shell oyster reefs were built and repeatedly expanded on the Intracoastal Waterway adjacent to Hutchinson Island in the ACE Basin in 2007, 2009 and then every year from 2011 through 2017. Beaufort Marine Institute students, Sun City volunteers and area schools placed shell bags along the Coosaw Cut shoreline to add oyster habitat and reduce wake-driven marsh erosion.
stories.water: Coosaw Cut / Intracoastal Waterway, ACE Basin
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate to Hutchinson Island in the ACE Basin. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: Laurel Bay Living Shoreline, MCAS Beaufort
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in South Carolina; US Department of Defense; Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort; NOAA; The Nature Conservancy; U.S. Department of Defense; volunteers
stories.desc: Volunteers and TNC built an Oyster Castle living shoreline along Laurel Bay at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort in 2025, captioned on the project page as completed oyster restoration. The work is funded by a $6.8 million NOAA Transformational Habitat Restoration and Coastal Resilience grant awarded in July 2023 for a four-year program; the grant plan calls for a 2,000-foot Oyster Castle reef on the Broad River shoreline. The reef is intended to stabilize eroding military-installation shoreline while rebuilding oyster and marsh habitat.
stories.notes: Final installed length is not confirmed on the page (2,000 ft is the grant plan); no measured outcomes reported. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Battery Creek stormwater retrofit and shellfish bed reopening
stories.orgs: City of Beaufort; Beaufort County; SCDHEC (now SC Department of Environmental Services); U.S. EPA; private property owner
stories.desc: The Burton Hill M2 Regional Water Quality Retrofit repaired and enlarged a private pond so it could capture and treat runoff from a 470-acre sub-basin of the 9,874-acre Battery Creek watershed, using settling and UV exposure to cut bacteria, and added outfall ditch enhancement. The project reduced fecal coliform loading by 9.0E12 CFU; six shellfish monitoring stations were reclassified from restricted to approved, reopening 948 acres of estuarine water to harvest on October 1, 2020, with two more stations reclassified effective October 1, 2022.
stories.water: Battery Creek (Beaufort River / Port Royal Sound)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Stormwater/pond retrofit rather than in-channel habitat work, but the outcome was reopening of 948 acres of estuarine shellfish habitat. Original 2020 story: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-10/documents/sc_battery_creek_1905_508.pdf

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Battery Creek near Port Royal
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; community volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built on Battery Creek near Port Royal in 2010 and expanded in 2011. Volunteers placed shell bags in the intertidal zone to create oyster settlement substrate in a Beaufort County tidal creek.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Fripp Inlet at Hunting Island State Park
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; South Carolina State Park Service (Hunting Island State Park)
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built near the Nature Center at Hunting Island State Park on Fripp Inlet, with builds each year from 2006 through 2010. The repeated expansions added intertidal oyster settlement substrate along a barrier-island park shoreline known for chronic erosion.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Callawassie Creek
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Callawassie Island community volunteers
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built in Callawassie Creek near the Sugar Mill Park dock on Callawassie Island in 2001 and expanded in 2002. The reef adds intertidal oyster settlement substrate along a residential island shoreline in the Colleton River system.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Trask Boat Landing, Colleton River
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; community volunteers; SCDNR Waddell Mariculture Center (SCORE)
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built at the H.E. Trask Sr. boat landing on the Colleton River near Bluffton and expanded in most years between 2002 and 2010, making it one of SCORE's most repeatedly expanded Beaufort County sites. Volunteers placed bagged shell in the intertidal zone next to a heavily used public landing to add oyster settlement substrate and stabilize the bank.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate to the Trask landing. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: SCORE oyster reef, Pinckney Island National Wildlife Refuge
stories.orgs: SCDNR SCORE; Pinckney Island National Wildlife Refuge (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)
lpOrgs: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
stories.desc: A recycled-shell oyster reef was built at Pinckney Island National Wildlife Refuge in 2001, one of the first SCORE sites constructed in the program's launch year. Volunteers placed bagged shell in the intertidal zone to add oyster settlement substrate on refuge shoreline near Hilton Head.
stories.water: Mackay Creek / Port Royal Sound tidal creeks
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate to Pinckney Island NWR. Per-site acreage not published.

stories.title: May River headwaters stormwater retrofits and shellfish reopening
stories.orgs: Town of Bluffton; Beaufort County; SCDHEC; NOAA; SC Department of Natural Resources; University of South Carolina; Clemson University; SC Sea Grant Extension; Palmetto Bluff Conservancy; Friends of the Rivers; Trust for Public Land
stories.desc: A multiphase program in the May River headwaters retrofitted a stormwater lagoon with a reuse irrigation system that cut annual stormwater volume roughly 60 percent, enhanced an outfall ditch with filter socks, and added about 8,000 square feet of pervious parking and a bioretention cell, while sewer mains replaced septic systems at more than 80 homes, 31 of them within a 500-foot waterfront buffer. Estimated fecal coliform reductions reached 1.97E12, station 19-19C met the shellfish standard, and harvesting reopened for the season beginning October 1, 2021.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Primarily stormwater and sewer work; included for the estuarine shellfish habitat outcome. Phase 3 sewer conversion ongoing.

stories.title: Riverton Dam Removal, North Fork Shenandoah River
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; City of Front Royal; Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources
stories.desc: The Riverton Dam on the North Fork Shenandoah River at Front Royal was removed in 2005 by USFWS and the City of Front Royal under DWR's fish passage program. The removal restored free flow at the confluence area of the North and South Forks and reconnected upstream habitat on the North Fork.
stories.notes: DWR's table of contents lists 2011 but the page body states 2005. Miles reopened not reported.

stories.title: Mountain Run Agricultural BMPs, Smith Creek Watershed
stories.orgs: Shenandoah Valley Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; U.S. Forest Service
stories.desc: Partners installed agricultural best management practices on two Mountain Run segments totaling about 6.6 miles in the Smith Creek watershed, including livestock exclusion fencing, riparian forest and riparian buffers, streambank protection, animal waste control facilities, improved pasture and hayland and cover crops, funded through state cost-share, the Water Quality Improvement Fund, CREP and a Section 319 grant. Benthic macroinvertebrate communities improved and biological monitoring scores generally met the aquatic life support threshold. Both segments were removed from Virginia's impaired waters list in 2014.
stories.water: Mountain Run (Smith Creek tributary, Shenandoah basin)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. This is the Rockingham County Mountain Run in the Smith Creek watershed, not the Culpeper Mountain Run. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Whiteoak Canyon Low-Water Crossing Replacement, Cedar Run
stories.orgs: Piedmont Environmental Council; Trout Unlimited; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Virginia Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office (National Fish Passage Program); Shenandoah National Park
stories.desc: A flood-prone low-water crossing at the Whiteoak Canyon trailhead was replaced in late 2019 with a 35-foot high-water bridge. The new structure restored fish and American eel access to 3.5 miles of stream habitat on Cedar Run, a tributary of the Robinson River, and provides safe public and emergency-vehicle access to the popular Shenandoah National Park trailhead.
stories.water: Cedar Run (Robinson River / Rapidan River basin)
stories.notes: Source photo caption says Rappahannock County; the Whiteoak Canyon trailhead sits on the Madison/Rappahannock line, so county is approximate. Boundary uncertainty: Rappahannock River basin, Atlantic slope.

stories.title: Muddy Creek Nitrate Delisting, Rockingham County
stories.orgs: Shenandoah Valley Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Shenandoah Resource Conservation and Development Council; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Rockingham County Farm Bureau; Virginia Department of Health; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Old Order Mennonite community
stories.desc: Following the 2001 TMDL implementation plan, partners installed 5,514 feet of livestock exclusion fencing and 14 acres of riparian buffers on Muddy Creek plus 108 acres of permanent vegetative cover, 26 acres of no-till forage, 4,030 acres of cover crops, 14 animal waste control facilities, eight loafing lot systems, nutrient management plans on more than 3,200 acres and pre-sidedress soil nitrate testing, together with 41 septic pump-outs and 18 system repairs or replacements. Monitoring in 2007-2008 found no nitrate violations in 15 samples. The 2.17-mile lower segment was removed from the nitrate impairment list in 2010.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Creek remains listed for bacteria and aquatic life. Overlaps the Muddy Creek/Lower Dry River story listed separately. Coordinates approximate. Coordinate corrected during QA to ~15 mi WNW of Harrisonburg, as stated in the source.

stories.title: Muddy Creek and Lower Dry River Livestock Exclusion, Rockingham County
stories.orgs: Shenandoah Valley Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Rockingham County Farm Bureau; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Old Order Mennonite community landowners
stories.desc: Over four years beginning with 2002 Section 319 funding, partners installed 10 miles of livestock exclusion fencing and 1,200 acres of cover crops in the Muddy Creek and Lower Dry River watersheds, added nutrient management plans, manure storage and loose housing barns, and pumped 30 septic tanks while repairing or replacing 13 systems and installing five alternative waste treatment systems. The watershed's Old Order Mennonite community funded much of its own work. Lower Dry River's fecal coliform violation rate fell from a high of 50 percent to 11 percent by 2005, Muddy Creek's from 91 percent in 1998 to 44 percent in 2005, and state staff observed substantial improvement in the Muddy Creek benthic community.
stories.water: Muddy Creek; Lower Dry River (North River / South Fork Shenandoah basin)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story; documented improvement rather than a full delisting at time of publication. Streams lie about 15 miles west-northwest of Harrisonburg; coordinates approximate. Coordinate corrected during QA to ~15 mi WNW of Harrisonburg, as stated in the source.

stories.title: McGaheysville Dam Removal, South Fork Shenandoah River
stories.orgs: City of Harrisonburg; American Rivers–NOAA Community-based Restoration Partnership; Pure Water 2000; Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources
stories.desc: The McGaheysville Dam on the South Fork Shenandoah River was removed in 2004 as part of Virginia's fish passage program. The City of Harrisonburg, American Rivers–NOAA and Pure Water 2000 partnered on the removal, restoring free flow and upstream passage on the South Fork Shenandoah.
stories.notes: Miles reopened not reported. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Upper Robinson River Stream Exclusion and Cover Crops, Madison County
stories.orgs: Culpeper Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; USDA Farm Service Agency (CREP); Chesapeake Bay Livestock Exclusion Initiative
stories.desc: Between 2003 and 2012 landowners along three upper Robinson River segments totaling 7.15 miles installed about 23,530 linear feet (4.5 miles) of livestock stream exclusion fencing, 2,418 acres of small grain and mixed cover crop, 352 acres of harvestable cover crop, 22 septic pump-outs and two alternate waste treatment systems. Bacteria violation rates fell to 6 percent at one monitoring station and 10 percent at another. Two segments were removed from the impaired waters list in 2012 and the third in 2014.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Madison County is inside the extent. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Rockland Dam Partial Removal, North River
stories.orgs: Adjacent landowner; American Rivers–NOAA Community-based Restoration Partnership; Chesapeake Bay Foundation; Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources
stories.desc: Rockland Dam on the North River, a South Fork Shenandoah tributary, was partially removed in 2005 with the adjacent landowner, the American Rivers–NOAA partnership and the Chesapeake Bay Foundation. The partial removal restored flow through the structure and improved upstream fish passage.
stories.notes: Partial removal; miles reopened not reported. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Knightly Dam Removal, Middle River
stories.orgs: Adjacent landowners; Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources
stories.desc: Knightly Dam on the Middle River, a tributary of the South Fork Shenandoah, was removed in 2004 in partnership with the adjacent landowners under DWR's fish passage program. The removal restored free flow and reconnected upstream habitat in the Middle River.
stories.notes: Miles reopened not reported. Coordinates approximate to Middle River in Augusta County.

stories.title: Middle River Livestock Exclusion and Buffers, Augusta County
stories.orgs: Headwaters Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Cooperative Extension; local landowners
stories.desc: Mostly between 2006 and 2014, partners installed about 11.35 miles of livestock exclusion fencing, stream exclusion with managed grazing on 22 acres, cover crops on about 2,832 acres, 114 acres of long-term vegetative cover, 86 acres of planted woodland and buffer filter area, and three animal waste control facilities treating roughly 1,069 tons of livestock waste per year along two Middle River segments. None of 12 E. coli samples from 2009 to 2014 exceeded the standard and VSCI scores of 64 and 67 exceeded the threshold of 60. Both segments, 26.07 miles in all, were delisted in the 2016 Integrated Report.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Funding included CREP and the Virginia Agricultural Cost-share Program. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: South Fork Back Creek Stream Exclusion and CREP Buffers, Augusta County
stories.orgs: Headwaters Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Rockingham County Farm Bureau; local landowners
stories.desc: Between 2000 and 2016, 19 projects on the 6.84-mile South Fork Back Creek installed 24,290 linear feet of stream exclusion fencing with grazing management, 46 acres of CREP riparian forest buffer, 35 acres of woodland buffer filter area, 47 acres of cover crop and 43 acres of fescue conversion with wildlife options, plus repair of about 2,570 feet of existing stream fencing. None of 12 E. coli samples from 2011 to 2016 exceeded standards and benthic samples scored above the VSCI threshold of 60. Bacteria and benthic impairments were removed for 6.48 miles in the 2018 Integrated Report.
stories.water: South Fork Back Creek (South River / Shenandoah basin)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: North Fork Buffalo Creek Cover Crops and Stream Exclusion, Rockbridge County
stories.orgs: Natural Bridge Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Cooperative Extension; local landowners
stories.desc: Between 2010 and 2016 the Natural Bridge Soil and Water Conservation District installed 639 acres of small grain and mixed cover crop, 438 acres of harvestable cover crop, 13 acres of afforestation on crop, hay and pasture land, and 800 linear feet of stream exclusion fencing with grazing management keeping 18 beef cattle out of two segments of North Fork Buffalo Creek totaling 7.58 miles. The $121,002 project drew on the Water Quality Improvement Fund and the Virginia Agricultural Cost-Share Program. Only 1 of 12 samples from 2011 to 2016 exceeded the E. coli standard and both segments were delisted in the 2018 Integrated Report.
stories.water: North Fork Buffalo Creek (James River basin)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Quinn Dam Removal, Tye River
stories.orgs: Dam owners; adjacent landowners; Virginia Organizing Project; American Rivers–NOAA Community-based Restoration Partnership; volunteers; Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources
stories.desc: Quinn Dam on the Tye River near Route 29 was removed in 2007 by the dam owners working with adjacent landowners, the Virginia Organizing Project, the American Rivers–NOAA partnership and volunteers. The removal restored free flow on this James River tributary and reopened upstream habitat for migratory and resident fish.
stories.notes: Nelson County is inside the extent. Mileage reopened not reported by DWR. Coordinates approximate to the Tye River near US 29.

stories.title: Bosher's Dam Vertical Slot Fishway, James River
stories.orgs: Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources; James River Association; City of Richmond; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; NOAA/National Marine Fisheries Service; EPA Chesapeake Bay Program; Virginia Marine Resources Commission; County of Henrico; J.K. Timmons and Associates; English Construction
stories.desc: A $1.5 million vertical slot fishway with 13 pairs of offset baffle walls and resting pools was built on the 10-foot Bosher's Dam and opened March 1, 1999, allowing fish past the dam for the first time since 1823. The fishway reopened roughly 137 miles of the James River mainstem and 168 miles of tributaries and includes a 4-by-7-foot counting window with a live webcam and a trap for biological sampling. Tens of thousands of fish passed in spring 1999, and annual monitoring since shows effective passage of American shad, striped bass, sea lamprey, American eel elvers and more than 25 resident species.
stories.notes: Dam straddles the Richmond city/Henrico/Chesterfield line; coordinates approximate to the dam site.

stories.title: Williams Island (Z-Dam) Notch, James River
stories.orgs: Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources; City of Richmond; James River Association; EPA Chesapeake Bay Program; NOAA/National Marine Fisheries Service; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: In November 1993 a notch 30 feet wide and 2.5 feet deep was cut into the Z-Dam, the most upstream dam on the south channel at Williams Island, to let migratory fish continue upstream. The notch reopened 2.6 miles of the James River between the Richmond dams and Bosher's Dam. The dam pool supplies the City of Richmond's drinking water, so a notch rather than removal was used.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Willis River Bacteria Delisting (2005-2009)
stories.orgs: Peter Francisco Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Farm Bureau; Cattlemen's Association; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
stories.desc: An implementation project running from July 2005 through June 2009 delivered 54 agricultural practices on the Willis River, including about 32 miles of livestock exclusion fencing, more than 129 acres of riparian buffers, dairy loafing lot management, alternative water systems, composting and animal waste storage, improving about 1,780 acres of pastureland, plus 14 septic pump-outs, four repairs and four replacements. Landowners contributed about $317,000. Three segments totaling 34.71 miles were removed from Virginia's 303(d) impaired waters list in 2006 and 2008 once bacteria levels met the primary contact recreation standard.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story; about 60 miles west of Richmond. Distinct from the later Willis River benthic delisting listed separately. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Willis River Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Buffers (2005-2012)
stories.orgs: Peter Francisco Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Health; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Buckingham County Farm Bureau; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
stories.desc: From 2005 through 2012, partners installed about 16.2 miles of livestock exclusion fencing keeping roughly 823 head of cattle out of streams, converted 66 acres of erodible land to forest, planted 36 acres of riparian forest buffer and 50 acres of cover crops, extended a CREP watering system over 35 acres and built three animal waste control facilities, plus 15 septic pump-outs, three repairs and two replacements. The benthic macroinvertebrate community improved to a Virginia Stream Condition Index score of 67 in spring 2011, above the 60 threshold. Both impaired segments (4.83 and 15.2 miles) were delisted in the 2014 Integrated Report.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story (benthic delisting). A separate earlier Willis River bacteria delisting is listed as its own entry. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Manchester and Brown's Island Dam Breaches, James River
stories.orgs: Commonwealth of Virginia; Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources; City of Richmond; Council on the Environment
stories.desc: In January 1989 both the Manchester and Brown's Island dams in downtown Richmond were breached with explosives, creating 100-foot openings near the north shore. Combined with the naturally breached Belle Isle Dam, the work reopened about 6 miles of the James River up to the Williams Island Z-Dam. The breaches are visible from the public catwalk on Brown's Island.
stories.notes: Includes the earlier natural storm breach of Belle Isle Dam, counted within the same 6 miles. Described on the DWR Fish Passage Program page.

stories.title: Baber's Mill Dam Removal, Rock Island Creek
stories.orgs: Weyerhaeuser (landowner/dam owner); Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (State Wildlife Grant funding and Section 106 review); anonymous private foundation; contracted construction firm
stories.desc: The remnant of Baber's Mill Dam, a roughly 6-foot barrier built in 1827 to power a mill on Rock Island Creek in Buckingham County, was removed in April 2024. DWR produced the removal plan, drawings and permits; Weyerhaeuser owned the site and USFWS provided State Wildlife Grant funding. The removal reconnected about 45 upstream functional network miles of Rock Island Creek and its accessible tributaries; sea lamprey now reach the creek and the federally endangered James spinymussel is expected to benefit.
stories.notes: Also listed in American Rivers' 2024 dam removal summary. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Turpin Creek Livestock Exclusion and Buffers, Slate River Watershed
stories.orgs: Piedmont Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Prince Edward County Health Department; local landowners; EPA Section 319 program
stories.desc: From 2013 to 2020 partners installed about 21,471 linear feet of livestock stream exclusion fencing and 472 acres of stream exclusion practices with a 345-foot buffer along the 7.31-mile Turpin Creek in the Slate River watershed, excluding roughly 1,400 cattle, plus animal waste control facilities and 60 residential septic projects. Septic pump-out and maintenance outreach accompanied the on-the-ground work. Turpin Creek now meets its designated recreational use and was removed from Virginia's impaired waters list.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. The PDF cites both the 2018 and 2020 assessment cycles, so the exact delisting year is ambiguous. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Rock Island Creek Stream Exclusion and Cover Crops, Buckingham County
stories.orgs: Peter Francisco Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Health; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Buckingham County Farm Bureau
stories.desc: Between July 2011 and December 2014 landowners along an 8.88-mile segment of Rock Island Creek installed about 6,000 linear feet of stream exclusion fencing that removed 38 head of livestock from the stream, 117 acres of cover crops, 57 acres of long-term no-till and two residential septic projects. During 2009-2014 only 1 of 12 samples (8 percent) exceeded the E. coli standard, down from 29 percent a decade earlier. The segment was removed from the impaired waters list in the 2016 Integrated Report.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Same creek later had Baber's Mill Dam removed in 2024 (listed separately). Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: College Lake Dam Removal, Blackwater Creek
stories.orgs: City of Lynchburg; University of Lynchburg; AECOM
stories.desc: A 35-foot high-hazard dam that overtopped during a 2018 storm was removed from Blackwater Creek at Lynchburg in 2024, reconnecting 43 miles of stream. The sediment-filled former lakebed was converted into an urban wetland that doubles as an outdoor learning site, with river access, an overlook and habitat enhancements. The project removed a significant dam-failure risk to the city while restoring floodplain function.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Lynchburg is in the James River basin of central Virginia and may fall outside the extent. Full write-up verified in the 2024 dam removal summary PDF; photo URL verified on the 'Big Year for Dam Removals in 2024' blog post.

stories.title: Flat Creek Agricultural BMPs, Amelia and Nottoway Counties
stories.orgs: Piedmont Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Amelia and Nottoway county governments; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
stories.desc: Partners carried out 166 agricultural BMP projects in the Flat Creek subwatershed, mainly between 2007 and 2011, including about 4.75 miles of livestock exclusion fencing with alternative cattle watering, two animal waste control facilities, more than 2,200 acres of cover crops, 254 acres of conservation crop rotation, about 85 acres of tree and shrub planting and reforestation, 54 acres of pasture and hayland overseeding and about 18 acres of CREP riparian forest buffer. The BMPs cut loads by an estimated 32,901 pounds of phosphorus, 114,576 pounds of nitrogen and 22,567 tons of sediment, and E. coli violation frequency has trended downward at two monitoring stations since 2007.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story describing improvement, not full attainment. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: New London Dam No. 1 Removal, Orrix Creek
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: New London Dam No. 1 was removed from Orrix Creek in Bedford County in 2022, together with a companion structure immediately upstream. Removal restores free flow and stream connectivity on a small Roanoke-basin tributary. The annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Bedford County, Virginia. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Deep Creek Stream Exclusion and CREP Buffers (delisted 2016)
stories.orgs: Piedmont Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Amelia and Nottoway county governments; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
stories.desc: From 2002 to 2014 landowners along an 11.55-mile segment of Deep Creek installed about 25 miles of stream exclusion fencing, cover crops on several thousand acres, 176 acres of continuous no-till forage, 138 acres of afforestation on former farmland, about 167 acres of CREP woodland buffer and two animal waste control facilities. The share of samples exceeding E. coli standards fell from 34 percent in 1995-2000 to below 10 percent in 2009-2014. The segment was removed from Virginia's impaired waters list in 2016.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. A second Deep Creek story covering different segments is listed separately. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Deep Creek Stream Exclusion, Second Delisting (2008-2018)
stories.orgs: Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Piedmont Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Health; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Amelia and Nottoway county governments; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
stories.desc: Continued agricultural and residential BMP work on Deep Creek in the Appomattox basin included about 14 miles of stream exclusion fencing between 2008 and 2018 that kept roughly 802 livestock out of the creek, together with cover crops, no-till forage, nutrient management, alternative water sources, afforestation, stream protection, woodland buffers and residential septic projects. E. coli exceedance rates fell from 17 percent to 7 percent on a 5.67-mile segment and from 25 percent to 7 percent on an 11.54-mile segment. Both segments were removed from the impaired waters list, in 2016 and 2020.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Overlaps the earlier Deep Creek story listed separately; both are distinct EPA publications covering different segments. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Spring Creek Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Buffers, Prince Edward County
stories.orgs: Piedmont Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; USDA Conservation Reserve Enhancement Program; local landowners
stories.desc: From 2008 to 2020 partners installed more than 31,000 linear feet of livestock stream exclusion fencing and 164 acres of riparian buffer along a 5.47-mile segment of Spring Creek in the Appomattox basin, plus six residential septic projects and septic maintenance outreach. Bacteria exceedances dropped to 3 of 29 samples between 2013 and 2018, below the 10 percent threshold. The creek fully supports its recreation use and was removed from the 303(d) list in the 2020 Integrated Report.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Abutment Dam Denil Fishway, Appomattox River
stories.orgs: Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources; City of Petersburg (dam owner); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; EPA Chesapeake Bay Program; Brasfield Dam owner/hydropower operator (formerly STS Power); Harvell Dam hydropower licensee (FERC); dam owner; federal fish passage funding partners; NOAA; American Rivers; Harvell Dam Corporation; City of Petersburg
stories.desc: DWR designed and built a 4-foot-wide Denil fishway in 2003 on the 5-to-7-foot Abutment Dam, about one mile downstream of Brasfield Dam on the Appomattox River, reopening 1.3 miles of river. In 2009 a section of the dam more than 100 feet wide collapsed mid-river, and that natural breach is now the main migration route up the Appomattox. DWR notes that removing more of the structure would further improve passage.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.fws.gov/project/harvell-dam-removal-appomattox-river-virginia

stories.title: Little Cub Creek Stream Exclusion and Buffers, Appomattox and Charlotte Counties
stories.orgs: Southside Soil and Water Conservation District; Robert E. Lee Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Health; Virginia Cooperative Extension
stories.desc: From 2005 to 2014, about 10 miles of stream exclusion fencing with grazing management and riparian buffers were installed along a 9.21-mile segment of Little Cub Creek, keeping 240 beef cattle out of the water, plus 47 acres of afforestation, 25 acres of long-term no-till, 35 acres of permanent vegetative cover, 32 acres of high-residue tillage and a loafing lot system. About $400,000 in state cost-share and $119,000 from farmers funded the work. E. coli exceedances fell from 33 percent of samples to 8 percent and the segment was delisted in the 2016 Integrated Report.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local districts, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/documents/va_cub-508.pdf

stories.title: Little Sandy Creek Livestock Exclusion and Buffers, Prince Edward County
stories.orgs: Piedmont Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; USDA Farm Service Agency
stories.desc: Between 2007 and 2014 partners installed about 29,529 linear feet (5.6 miles) of livestock stream exclusion fencing plus 2,200 feet of fence maintenance, 18 acres of riparian forest buffer, 770 acres of cover crop and a composter facility along the 7.35-mile Little Sandy Creek in the Appomattox basin, supported by farm visits and farmer-to-farmer outreach. The single-sample bacteria violation rate fell from 22 percent in 2002-2003 to 8 percent in 2009-2010 and 0 percent in 2013-early 2014. A 2.91-mile segment was removed from the impaired waters list in 2012.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Middle Creek Mined Land Reclamation, Tazewell County
stories.orgs: Virginia Department of Mines, Minerals and Energy, Division of Mined Land Reclamation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Claredon National Insurance Company
stories.desc: After a 2000 bond forfeiture by Covenant Coal Corporation, the Division of Mined Land Reclamation reclaimed former mine sites in the watershed of the 11-mile Middle Creek, a Clinch River tributary, between 2000 and 2005, with revegetation, regrading to approximate original contour, removal of abandoned mining equipment and structures, and conversion to unmanaged forestland. Benthic macroinvertebrate scores in 2003 reached 95 percent of the reference stream at both monitoring sites, placing Middle Creek in the non-impaired category, and average conductivity fell to 263 mmhos/cm. DEQ removed Middle Creek from the impaired waters list in 2006 before a TMDL was completed.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Work was watershed-scale mined land reclamation rather than in-channel restoration; included for its documented aquatic biological recovery. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Little River Mill Dam Removal, Clinch River Watershed
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program; Appalachian and Virginia Fish and Wildlife Conservation Offices; Partners for Fish and Wildlife); Canaan Valley Institute; Bowen family (landowners)
stories.desc: A derelict 130-foot-wide, 14-foot-tall mill dam dating to 1818-1834 was notched and then fully removed from the Little River, a major Clinch River tributary, followed by streambank restoration completed in summer 2024. Removal reconnected over 30 stream miles (FWS lists 50 in its quick facts) and restored about 2 miles of in-stream habitat for endangered slabside pearlymussel and fluted kidneyshell and at-risk Cumberland moccasinshell and Tennessee clubshell. Pre-removal surveys found zero mussels above the dam or within 200 m of its base; promising mussel bed development has since been seen downstream.
stories.notes: Status Completed on the FWS project page: https://www.fws.gov/project/clinch-river-watershed-fish-passage-restoration-little-river-mill-dam-removal . $200,000 National Fish Passage Program award.

stories.title: Little River (Bowen Mill) Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source; Dam owner; project partners reported to American Rivers
stories.desc: The Little River Dam, also known as Bowen Mill Dam, was removed at Maiden Spring in Tazewell County in 2024. Removal restores free flow and aquatic organism passage on the Little River, a Clinch River headwater stream in the upper Tennessee basin - one of the most mussel-rich river systems in North America. The annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.notes: Southwest Virginia, upper Tennessee River basin - very likely inside the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Indian Creek Livestock Exclusion and CREP Buffers, Tazewell County
stories.orgs: Tazewell Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Tazewell County Farm Bureau; Town of Richlands; private landowners
stories.desc: Between 2006 and 2016 landowners installed about 16,460 linear feet of stream exclusion fencing with grazing management plus 9 acres of woodland buffer and filter area and 9 acres of CREP riparian forest buffer along 13.67 miles of Indian Creek in the upper Clinch watershed, keeping 30 beef cows and 20 goats out of the stream. Only 1 of 11 samples from 2011 to 2016 exceeded the E. coli standard. Both segments were removed from Virginia's impaired waters list in the 2018 Integrated Report.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/documents/va_clinch-508.pdf

stories.title: Lower Blackwater River Agricultural BMPs, Franklin County
stories.orgs: Blue Ridge Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
stories.desc: Between 2002 and 2012 landowners installed 5.6 miles of livestock exclusion fencing and 333 acres of cover crops in the impaired lower Blackwater subwatershed, with another 8.2 miles of fencing, about 2,650 acres of cover crops and four animal waste storage facilities upstream. Funding totaled about $329,000 in Section 319(h), $205,000 in state cost-share, $9,800 in CREP and $231,000 from landowners. Virginia Stream Condition Index scores rose from 60.7 (spring) and 50.1 (fall) in 2004 to between 69.4 and 76.0 in most post-BMP samples, and the two segments were removed from the impaired waters list in 2014.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. This is the Roanoke-basin Blackwater River in Franklin County, not the Chowan-basin river. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Altice Mill Dam Removal, Blackwater River
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Altice Mill Dam was removed from the Blackwater River at Rocky Mount in Franklin County in 2022, one of six Virginia removals that year. Removal restores free-flowing conditions and fish passage on a Roanoke River tributary. The annual summary records the removal without height, reconnected mileage or partners.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - southern Virginia, Roanoke basin. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Black Creek Mine Land Reclamation and Wetland Enhancement, Wise County
stories.orgs: Red River Coal Company; Virginia Department of Mines, Minerals and Energy, Division of Mined Land Reclamation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; EPA Section 319 program; U.S. Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement Clean Streams Initiative
lpOrgs: Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
stories.desc: Under a 1996 re-mining permit, about 300 acres in the Black Creek watershed, a Powell River tributary near Norton, have been restored through revegetation, regrading to original contour, constructed wetlands, sediment ponds, riparian area restoration, diversion ditches and infiltration channels, with the plan about 75 percent complete. State grants separately funded a wetland enhancement in 2001 and five in-stream habitat structures in 2006. Chemical monitoring shows marked water quality improvement and biological metrics including taxa richness, EPT richness and habitat scores improved from 2001 to 2009, though the Virginia Stream Condition Index reached only 49 by 2009.
stories.sector: Partnership (private coal company, state, federal, NGO)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 story reporting improvement, not a delisting; stream remains impaired pending full plan implementation. Includes constructed wetland and five in-stream habitat structures. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Dumps Creek Channel and Floodplain Restoration, Russell County
stories.orgs: Virginia Department of Mines, Minerals and Energy; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Contura Energy subsidiary; Alpha Natural Resources; Dominion Virginia City Hybrid Energy Center; federal Abandoned Mine Land Reclamation Program
stories.desc: On a 3.54-mile segment of Dumps Creek above its mouth on the Clinch River at Cleveland, partners stopped mine dewatering at two outfalls, cleaned about 21 miles of coalfield streams, converted an old mining pond into a sediment-filtering wetland, planted trees on about 70 acres of mined land, and in 2015 restored about 2,600 linear feet of Dumps Creek by regrading the floodplain and installing in-stream structures. About 1.5 million tons of gob pile was removed from upstream Hurricane Fork. Biological scores stayed above the VSCI threshold of 60, reaching 72.83 in October 2014, total dissolved solids loading fell by about 6.9 million kg per year, and the segment was delisted in 2016.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Includes genuine in-stream and floodplain restoration, not only mine reclamation.

stories.title: Big Chestnut Creek Livestock Exclusion, Pigg River Watershed
stories.orgs: Blue Ridge Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Department of Health; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Franklin County
stories.desc: From 2007 through 2012 landowners along a 12.43-mile segment of Big Chestnut Creek in the Pigg River watershed installed about 9.3 miles of livestock exclusion stream fencing, 53 acres of afforestation on erodible cropland and pasture, 18 acres of cover crops, 7 acres of permanent vegetative cover on critical areas and three replacement septic systems, backed by farm site visits and outreach. The E. coli violation rate dropped from 50 percent in 2001-2004 to 8 percent in 2007-2012. The creek was removed from the impaired waters list in the 2014 Integrated Report.
stories.water: Big Chestnut Creek (Pigg River / Roanoke River basin)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Clinch Valley Agricultural Streamside Best Management Practices
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Virginia (Clinch Valley Program); private landowners; Virginia Tech Freshwater Mollusk Conservation Center; Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources
stories.desc: Since 1995 TNC's Clinch Valley Program has assisted more than 250 landowners in adopting streamside best management practices in the Clinch and Powell river watersheds, including fencing cattle out of waterways and establishing riparian buffers. Volunteers have also re-established native river cane brakes, removed invasive species and cleared trash along the Clinch River. The work targets sediment and nutrient loading in a river system that holds one of North America's richest freshwater mussel faunas.
stories.notes: WEAK ENTRY: cumulative program rather than a dated single project. The source page gives no per-project date, acreage or water-quality results. Placed at a representative Clinch River location in Russell County, VA, inside the extent; coordinates approximate. Include or drop at the compiler's discretion.

stories.title: Byers and Hutton Creeks Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Buffers, Washington County
stories.orgs: Holston River Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Tennessee Valley Authority; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: From 2001 to 2008 landowners in the Hall/Byers and Hutton Creek watersheds installed about 18.3 miles of livestock exclusion fencing, 13 grazing protection systems, 10 animal waste storage facilities, 702 acres of small grain cover crop, 311 acres of harvestable cover crop, 224 acres of riparian forest buffer and 38 acres of permanent vegetative cover. Sediment, nitrogen and phosphorus loads fell by about 19,739 tons, 107,628 pounds and 22,108 pounds respectively. Virginia Stream Condition Index scores rose above 60 at both creeks and 0.48 miles of Byers Creek and 5.15 miles of Hutton Creek were delisted in 2014.
stories.water: Byers Creek; Hutton Creek (Middle Fork Holston River basin)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watersheds lie about 10 miles northeast of Abingdon; coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Middle Fork Holston River Tributaries Stream Fencing and Buffers
stories.orgs: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Tennessee Valley Authority; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Holston River Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; EPA Region 3; volunteers
stories.desc: Beginning in 2001, partners working in four Middle Fork Holston tributaries (Cedar, Hall, Byers and Hutton Creeks) installed 14.2 miles of stream fencing to exclude livestock, grazing management with alternative watering sources and travel lanes, 3,588 acres of improved pasture and 13 acres of riparian forest buffer along Hutton Creek, and upgraded 16 on-site sewage systems while pumping 120 septic tanks. About 70 percent of agricultural producers in the watershed were contacted. Hutton Creek's bacteria levels fell by an annual average of 50 percent from 2000 to 2004, and high fecal coliform values declined in the Byers, Cedar and Hutton Creek watersheds.
stories.water: Cedar, Hall, Byers and Hutton Creeks (Middle Fork Holston River)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story (2005 fact sheet); improvement reported but not a full delisting. Overlaps with the later Byers/Hutton delisting story listed separately. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Powell River Agricultural BMPs and Stream Exclusion, Lee and Wise Counties
stories.orgs: Daniel Boone Soil and Water Conservation District; Lonesome Pine Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Virginia Cooperative Extension; Lee and Wise County Farm Bureaus
stories.desc: From 2002 to 2018 partners installed 136,608 linear feet (about 26 miles) of stream exclusion fencing with grazing management, 172 acres of grazing land management, 40 acres of permanent vegetative cover, 5 acres of riparian forest buffer and 1,250 linear feet of stream diversion and protection across the Powell River watershed, treating 145 tons per year of animal waste. Biological scores rose to 72 (spring) and 79 (fall) on the Virginia Stream Condition Index and bacteria exceedances fell below 10 percent. Two benthic-impaired segments totaling 12.30 miles and two bacteria-impaired segments totaling 4.69 miles were delisted in the 2014, 2018 and 2020 Integrated Reports.
stories.water: Powell River, South Fork Powell River, Town Creek
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Coordinates approximate to the Powell River in Lee County.

stories.title: Stone Creek Acid Mine Drainage Treatment and Bank Protection, Lee County
stories.orgs: Virginia Department of Mines, Minerals and Energy; Daniel Boone Soil and Water Conservation District; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation; Tennessee Valley Authority; Lee County; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: From 2002 through 2012 partners treated acid mine drainage on a 3.33-mile segment of Stone Creek in the Straight Creek watershed, building 1,087 linear feet of open limestone channels, five alkalinity-producing cells, four aerobic wetlands, nine water control structures, 200 linear feet of slurry wall and 100 linear feet of streambank protection, and reclaiming more than 215 acres of mined land mostly back to forest. Virginia Stream Condition Index scores from 2009 to 2013 ranged from 61 to 77, all above the threshold of 60. Stone Creek was removed from the impaired waters list in 2014.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Includes constructed wetlands and streambank protection.

stories.title: Batie Creek Cave Stream Recovery, Lee County
stories.orgs: Virginia DCR Karst Program (Division of Natural Heritage); Virginia Water Resources Center; Virginia Department of Environmental Quality; Cave Conservancy of the Virginias; Virginia Tech; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Tennessee Valley Authority; private lumber company
stories.desc: Improper sawdust disposal at a lumber mill had sent oxygen-depleting leachate into Thompson Cedar Cave and Batie Creek, harming the endangered Lee County cave isopod. Under a consent decree the company removed sawdust from the cave entrance and then removed and reused most of the decomposing pile, after Virginia Tech researchers funded by the Cave Conservancy showed it could amend soil for mined land reclamation, with USFWS and TVA funding transport to reclamation sites. Dissolved oxygen rebounded to 5.8 mg/L by summer 2002 and has stayed healthy at Batie West Spring, aquatic life including the cave isopod returned, and the creek was removed from the impaired waters list in 2006.
stories.water: Batie Creek and Batie East/West Springs (Thompson Cedar Cave stream)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, NGO, university, private company)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Pollution source removal and karst aquatic habitat recovery rather than channel work. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Georges Mill Dam Removal, South Mayo River
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' 2025 national dam removal round-up; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: Georges Mill Dam, the site of seven drownings over the years, was removed from the South Mayo River in 2025 and is highlighted in American Rivers' 2025 national summary. Removal eliminated a lethal low-head hazard and restored free-flowing conditions on a Dan River tributary in the Roanoke basin. The summary article does not give the dam's height or reconnected mileage.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - southern Virginia, Roanoke basin. County and lat/lon inferred from the South Mayo River's course through Patrick County; not stated in the source.

stories.title: Great Dismal Swamp Hydrologic Restoration
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge); conservation partners; Inflation Reduction Act funding
stories.desc: Since the refuge was established in 1974 with a 150-mile legacy ditch network, FWS has installed 45 additional water control structures, bringing the total to 75, and has thinned red maple, planted Atlantic white cedar and applied prescribed fire, with ditch filling and road removal also underway. Rewetting the peat across the 113,000-acre refuge keeps carbon in the ground and reduces catastrophic peat fire risk; the restored peatlands are estimated to sequester about 200,000 tons of carbon per year.
stories.water: Great Dismal Swamp (Lake Drummond; Pasquotank/Chowan drainage)
stories.county: City of Suffolk (VA); extends into Gates and Camden counties, NC
stories.notes: Boundary uncertainty: the swamp drains to the Albemarle/Pasquotank system, and the NC portion includes Camden County, which the brief excludes. Coordinates and county given for the Virginia side. Photo is the story banner (Okefenokee), not Great Dismal Swamp; no Dismal Swamp image on the page.

stories.title: White Mill (Long Mill) Dam Removal, Dan River
