stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source; City of Danville; American Rivers (project reporting); project partners
stories.desc: The White Mill Dam, also recorded as Long Mill Dam, was removed from the Dan River at Danville in 2024, part of a run of Virginia removals that made the state one of the national leaders that year. Removal restores free-flowing conditions on an urban reach of the Dan River in the Roanoke basin upstream of North Carolina. The annual summary records the removal but does not report height, reconnected mileage or partners.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Danville is on the Dan River in the Roanoke/Albemarle basin; include only if southern Virginia is inside the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Marilla Park Streambank Stabilization and Riparian Planting, Deckers Creek
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; Morgantown Board of Parks and Recreation (BOPARC); WV Land Trust; WV Division of Forestry Mountaineer Treeway Program; WV Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: Friends of Deckers Creek targeted a chronically eroding, tree-poor reach of Deckers Creek in Morgantown's Marilla Park, planting over 100 tree saplings along the bank with volunteers and working with engineers on bank stabilization under a 2018 WVDEP grant. The planting reestablishes shade and root structure on an urban stream reach that floods repeatedly, with educational components added at the adjacent rail trail.
stories.notes: Tree planting is complete; the engineered bank stabilization component was described as planned at the time of writing.

stories.title: Deckers Creek Watershed AMD Restoration
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; WV Department of Environmental Protection; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement; US EPA Brownfields program
lpOrgs: Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
stories.desc: Partners reclaimed abandoned coal mine sites and built nine acid mine drainage treatment installations in the Deckers Creek watershed, using sulfate-reducing bioreactors, lime dosers, limestone leach beds, constructed wetlands and settling ponds, with five of them on the Kanes Creek tributary. Since 2002 average pH rose from 6.5 to 7.19, iron fell from 1.4 to 0.6 mg/L and aluminum from 1.00 to 0.4 mg/L. Stocked brown trout now survive year-round in a creek that previously excluded fish and most aquatic insects.
stories.notes: Watershed spans Monongalia and Preston counties, both in extent.

stories.title: Sovern Run Passive AMD Treatment
stories.orgs: Friends of the Cheat; WVU National Mine Land Reclamation Center; WV Department of Environmental Protection (NPS, AML and Mining & Reclamation programs); Office of Surface Mining; NiSource Environmental Challenge; private landowners
stories.desc: Partners built a series of passive acid mine drainage treatment systems on 4.7-mile Sovern Run, a Big Sandy Creek tributary in the Cheat watershed, using open limestone channels, limestone leach beds and separation dams, steel slag check dams and leach beds, and natural wetlands. The roughly $2.2 million effort cut annual loads by about 442,000 lbs of net acidity, 45,000 lbs of aluminum, 33,800 lbs of iron and 3,200 lbs of manganese. Aluminum, iron and acidity met water quality standards at the mouth by 2010, benthic macroinvertebrates rebounded, and landowners report fish and aquatic plants returning on at least 3.3 of 4.7 listed miles.
stories.notes: County not stated in the EPA story; Sovern Run and Rockville are in Preston County, inside the extent. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Valley Point #12 Passive AMD Treatment System
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; WV Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: Built in 2008 and renovated in 2016, the Valley Point #12 system uses upflow limestone wells and anaerobic vertical flow wetlands to treat abandoned mine drainage in the Valley Point area of Preston County before it reaches Deckers Creek. The 2016 renovation addressed mine seepage to improve effectiveness and extend the system's life. It is part of the treatment network credited with restoring year-round brown trout survival in Deckers Creek.
stories.notes: Site-specific outcome data not published; watershed-scale results in the EPA Deckers Creek success story. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Slabcamp Tributary Passive AMD Treatment System
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; WV Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: A passive treatment system of auto-flushing limestone ponds was built in 2015 on an unnamed tributary to Slabcamp Run near Masontown, intercepting several acid mine drainage discharges before they feed a 5.4-acre wetland and then Deckers Creek. It is one of the installations credited with the watershed-wide rise in pH and fall in iron and aluminum that allowed brown trout to survive year-round in Deckers Creek.
stories.notes: Site-specific monitoring results are not published on the project page; outcomes are documented at the watershed scale in the EPA Deckers Creek success story. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Valley Highwall #3 Lime Doser and Settling Ponds
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; WV Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: An active lime doser built in 2010 treats mine water draining toward Kanes Creek and Deckers Creek. After clogging problems from unreacted lime and metal precipitates, a 2019 upgrade added settling ponds and a trompe to improve reliability. It is part of the Deckers Creek treatment network behind the watershed's rise in pH from 6.5 to 7.19 and the return of year-round brown trout.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Kanes Creek South Site #1 Active Lime Treatment
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; WV Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: An active hydrated-lime treatment system was built in 2011 on a tributary to Kanes Creek and upgraded in 2018 to mix lime and mine water more efficiently for metals removal. Together with the other Kanes Creek installations it drove benthic macroinvertebrate density from 6 to 275 organisms per square meter between 2003 and 2012 and returned creek chub, yellow bullhead and green sunfish to reaches that had been fishless.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Upper Deckers Creek SAPS and Satcher Pre-Treatment Pond
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement; WV Department of Environmental Protection
lpOrgs: Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
stories.desc: A successive alkalinity producing system (SAPS) built by OSMRE in 1997 near Upper Deckers Creek Impoundment #5 was expanded by Friends of Deckers Creek in 2012, and the Satcher Pre-Treatment Pond was added to capture an acid mine drainage source the original SAPS did not treat. The expanded system is one of the oldest passive installations in the watershed and contributed to the long-term reduction in iron and aluminum that allowed stocked brown trout to survive year-round in Deckers Creek.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Kanes Creek AMD Treatment
stories.orgs: Friends of Deckers Creek; WV Department of Environmental Protection; US EPA; Office of Surface Mining; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service
stories.desc: Acid mine drainage from Upper Freeport seam mines was treated along 4.3-mile Kanes Creek with sulfate-reducing bioreactors, water-powered lime dosers, limestone leach beds and an anaerobic vertical flow wetland, alongside abandoned mine land reclamation in 1997 and 2003. The lowest reach has met pH and total iron standards more than 90 percent of the time since April 2010. Creek chub, yellow bullhead and green sunfish appeared in sections that held no fish before 2006, and benthic macroinvertebrate density rose from 6 to 275 organisms per square meter between 2003 and 2012.
stories.notes: County not named in the EPA story; Kanes Creek joins Deckers Creek at Reedsville, Preston County, inside the extent. Photo is the Kanes Creek South Site #1 treatment system from deckerscreek.org/projects/.

stories.title: Cheat River Freshwater Mussel Reintroduction
stories.orgs: Friends of the Cheat; US Fish and Wildlife Service; WV Division of Natural Resources; River of Promise partners
stories.desc: Following decades of acid mine drainage treatment that restored water chemistry on the Cheat River main stem, Friends of the Cheat and partners reintroduced freshwater mussels and monitor eastern hellbender using environmental DNA. A 2022 FOC study found freshwater mussels surviving in the main stem for the first time in more than 100 years. Hellbender eDNA has also been detected, indicating recovery of a sensitive, high-water-quality aquatic community.
stories.notes: Mussel survival result is reported in the EPA 2025 in-depth Cheat River success story. Coordinates are a representative main-stem location in Preston County.

stories.title: Cheat River Watershed Acid Mine Drainage Restoration
stories.orgs: Friends of the Cheat; River of Promise partnership; WV Department of Environmental Protection; US EPA Region 3; Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement; WVU National Mine Land Reclamation Center; Trout Unlimited; Anker Energy; Patriot Mining Company
lpOrgs: Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
stories.desc: Since 1995 Friends of the Cheat and the River of Promise partnership have built 20 acid mine drainage treatment systems (open limestone channels, limestone and steel-slag leach beds, settling ponds, constructed wetlands, and one large active lime plant) across the Cheat River watershed, plus streambank tree planting. Watershed pH and alkalinity have risen steadily while iron and aluminum have fallen since 1994. Fish have returned to formerly dead tributaries, walleye now migrate far upstream, eastern hellbender eDNA has been detected, and freshwater mussels were found alive in the main stem in 2022 for the first time in over a century.
stories.notes: Watershed-scale program spanning Preston and Tucker counties, both in extent. An EPA in-depth version (2025) is at https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2025-12/in-depthss_cheatwv_finaldraft_0623_2025toepa_508_0.pdf. Coordinates are the Albright area on the main stem.

stories.title: Muddy Creek AMD Treatment and Fishery Recovery
stories.orgs: Friends of the Cheat; WV Department of Environmental Protection; US EPA; Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement; River of Promise partnership
lpOrgs: Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
stories.desc: After the 1994 T&T mine blowout killed the lower 3.4 miles of Muddy Creek, Friends of the Cheat installed four Section 319-funded passive treatment systems and WVDEP built a roughly $9 million active lime-slurry treatment facility plus an in-stream doser. Median pH rose from 4.3 to 7.3 and median iron and aluminum fell from about 9-10 mg/L to 1 mg/L; acidity loading to the Cheat River went from 11,800 lbs/day to net alkaline. An electroshock survey found no fish in 2015 but 143 fish of nine species in 2019, and brown trout and walleye now use the lower creek.
stories.notes: Photo is from the Friends of the Cheat article 'Fish Tails Tell the Tale' (https://cheat.org/fish-tails-tell-the-tale/) documenting fish caught at the Muddy Creek mouth in 2020.

stories.title: Lambert Run Passive AMD Treatment
stories.orgs: WV Department of Environmental Protection; Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement; WVU National Mine Land Reclamation Center; Guardians of the West Fork; US EPA
lpOrgs: Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
stories.desc: Four passive acid mine drainage treatment systems, including a steel slag leach bed, were installed between 2006 and 2009 on 4.4-mile Lambert Run, which drains an 8-square-mile watershed into the West Fork River near Spelter. Each treated discharge now has a near-neutral pH of about 7.1 to 7.4 and iron and aluminum loads dropped substantially. Benthic macroinvertebrate numbers and diversity increased in the mainstem and about 2.3 of the 4.4 impaired miles have been restored.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate, near the West Fork River confluence at Spelter.

stories.title: Three Fork Creek In-Stream Lime Doser Restoration
stories.orgs: WVDEP Office of Abandoned Mine Lands and Reclamation; West Virginia University; Save the Tygart Watershed Association; US EPA
stories.desc: Nine in-stream lime dosers were installed on Three Fork Creek and its headwater tributaries (Birds, Raccoon and Squires creeks) to neutralize acid mine drainage from about 9,100 acres of pre-SMCRA underground mine pools, with construction starting July 2010 and all systems treating by April 2011. Average pH rose from 5.1 to 7.1, acidity fell from 21.9 to 5.4 mg/L, and dissolved aluminum dropped about 98 percent, leading to delisting for aluminum in 2014. A 2012 survey collected 1,605 fish of 21 species where only a single fish had been found before treatment, and macroinvertebrate taxa rose from 8 to 15.
stories.water: Three Fork Creek (Tygart Valley River tributary)
stories.notes: Watershed spans Taylor and Preston counties, both in extent. Coordinates are near the Tygart confluence at Grafton.

stories.title: Kempton Refuse and Acid Mine Drainage Reclamation
stories.orgs: West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection, Office of Abandoned Mine Lands and Reclamation; Appalachian Clean Streams Initiative; Cowgirl Up Inc. (contractor)
stories.desc: A former coal refuse pile and acid mine drainage site draining to the headwaters of the North Branch Potomac River near Kempton was reclaimed between August 2007 and October 2009 at a cost of $2,357,159, including $439,292 from the Appalachian Clean Streams Initiative. The work addressed health and safety hazards alongside the acid drainage reaching the stream; WVDEP publishes before-and-after photographs of the site.
stories.sector: Public (state AML program with federal funding)
stories.notes: Site straddles the WV/MD line near Kempton; placed on the Preston County side. Drains to the North Branch Potomac, at the northeastern edge of the extent — verify boundary if that matters.

stories.title: West Fork River Restoration (three dam removals)
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Appalachian Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office; West Virginia partners
stories.desc: Three obsolete dams on the West Fork River in north-central West Virginia were removed in 2016, restoring fish passage along the 103-mile river and improving boating access, swimming safety and local water quality including drinking water. State biologists and anglers report improved fishing upstream, and the free-flowing river has become a destination for anglers and boaters.
stories.notes: Boundary caution: northern West Virginia, Monongahela/upper Ohio basin, which may fall outside the Southern Waters extent. Completed project, verified link.

stories.title: Pendleton Creek Strip Stream Channel Restoration
stories.orgs: West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection, Office of Abandoned Mine Lands and Reclamation; Eastern Arrow Corp. (contractor)
stories.desc: At an abandoned strip mine in the city of Thomas, crews sealed stream capture areas where surface flow was disappearing into abandoned underground mine workings, then built restored and relocated stream channels that return drainage to its pre-mining path on Pendleton Creek. Three dangerous impoundments were backfilled and 200 linear feet of highwall was addressed. The $763,450 project ran from July 2010 to June 2011 and was named a recognized AML project by WVDEP.
stories.notes: County inferred from the city of Thomas, which the source names. Restoring surface flow captured by mine workings is the aquatic element; detail on outcomes is not published.

stories.title: Indian Run Aquatic Organism Passage Bridge Replacement
stories.orgs: Friends of the Cheat; AllStar Ecology; Solid Rock Excavating; Canaan Valley Institute; WV Division of Natural Resources; US Fish and Wildlife Service; Appalachian Stewardship Foundation; The Pew Charitable Trusts; private landowner
stories.desc: Friends of the Cheat completed its first aquatic organism passage project in September 2023, replacing a perched double-culvert private driveway crossing on Indian Run, a Tier 3 naturally reproducing trout stream in the Left Fork of Clover Run watershed, with a bridge. The old culverts caught debris in annual floods, eroded banks and blocked fish passage seasonally. The replacement restores year-round trout passage to upstream habitat and, with crossings already improved upstream by the WV Division of Highways and the US Forest Service, completes connectivity on the stream while reducing flood-related bank erosion.
stories.water: Indian Run (Left Fork of Clover Run, Cheat River)
stories.notes: County not stated in the article; Clover Run and its Left Fork are in Tucker County, inside the extent. Coordinates approximate. Not the same Indian Run as the Morgan County EPA 319 story.

stories.title: North Fork South Branch Potomac Streambank Fencing and Riparian Restoration
stories.orgs: North Fork Watershed Association; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service and Farm Service Agency; Potomac Valley Conservation District; Potomac Headwaters RC&D; Trout Unlimited; US EPA; USGS; West Virginia University Extension; Pilgrim's Pride/Wampler-Longacre
stories.desc: Twenty partners worked with farmers across the North Fork of the South Branch Potomac trout watershed to install streambank fencing and alternative livestock watering, roof feeding areas, build waste storage facilities, stabilize and revegetate eroding streambanks, and establish riparian buffers, alongside nutrient management plans for all poultry farms and most livestock farms. More than 85 percent of watershed farmers adopted best management practices. Fecal coliform declined significantly and the North Fork now meets its designated use and is no longer listed as impaired.
stories.water: North Fork of the South Branch of the Potomac River
stories.notes: County not named in the EPA story; the North Fork runs through Pendleton and Grant counties, both explicitly inside the extent. Coordinates approximate near Cabins/Smoke Hole.

stories.title: Upper Buckhannon River Acid Remediation
stories.orgs: Buckhannon River Watershed Association; WV Department of Environmental Protection; WV Division of Natural Resources; Office of Surface Mining; WV Conservation Agency; Canaan Valley Institute; US EPA; Dominion Energy
stories.desc: The Upper Buckhannon Project Team treated acid-impaired tributaries of the 47-mile Buckhannon River with fine limestone granules, sealed and regraded coal refuse areas, armored erosion-prone banks, seeded and mulched disturbed ground, and stocked trout in treated tributaries. Funding included a $2 million Dominion Energy settlement, $90,000 in Section 319 funds and $348,170 in partner match. In one treated tributary pH readings centered near 7.0 and fell below 6.0 only 2 percent of the time, and WVDNR documented year-long trout survival in several streams; WVDEP expected to remove metals impairments from the 303(d) list.
stories.notes: County not stated in the EPA story; the upper Buckhannon lies in Upshur and Randolph counties, both in extent. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Upper Greenbrier River Watershed Fish Passage
stories.orgs: Trout Unlimited (project partner lead); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program); Monongahela National Forest
stories.desc: Removal and replacement of seven culvert barriers in the Upper Greenbrier watershed, including the West Fork and East Fork Greenbrier, as part of a ten-year effort to build 105 miles of connected high-elevation cold-water habitat for brook trout and climate resilience. The $939,500 project also replaces undersized, flood-prone crossings with structures sized for higher flows, improving public safety and recreation access in the Monongahela National Forest. FWS lists 25 stream miles reopened.
stories.water: Greenbrier River (West Fork and East Fork)
stories.notes: FY2023 National Fish Passage Program award; status listed as In Development. Greenbrier drains to the New/Kanawha and Ohio rivers.

stories.title: Sugar Creek and Dogway Fork Limestone Sand Treatment
stories.orgs: WV Division of Natural Resources; WV Department of Environmental Protection Nonpoint Source Program; US EPA
stories.desc: WVDNR applied fine limestone sand to Sugar Creek, a Williams River tributary, and Dogway Fork, a Cranberry River tributary, to neutralize acid deposition in the upper Gauley basin. Typical pH rose from 3.7 to 6.4 in Sugar Creek and from 3.8 to 7.0 in Dogway Fork, both meeting the state 6.0-9.0 criterion. Trout stocking followed and 2.5 miles of Sugar Creek and 6.8 miles of Dogway Fork were restored to viable trout fisheries and removed from the impaired waters list in 2006.
stories.water: Sugar Creek (Williams River) and Dogway Fork (Cranberry River)
stories.notes: Streams lie in Pocahontas and Webster counties, both in extent; Nicholas County is nearby and also in extent. Coordinates are a midpoint between the two treated streams.

stories.title: Morris Creek Passive Treatment and Streambank Stabilization
stories.orgs: Morris Creek Watershed Association; WV Department of Environmental Protection (AML and Nonpoint Source programs); US Office of Surface Mining; US EPA; Trout Unlimited
stories.desc: Four passive treatment systems using wetlands, limestone channels and polishing ponds were installed at Possum Hollow, Blacksnake Hollow, Lower Mainstem and Upper Mainstem by September 2006, followed in 2007-2008 by sediment-reduction work on abandoned roads, culverts, a large slip and eroding streambanks. Metal reductions far exceeded TMDL targets, at roughly 33,248 lbs/yr aluminum, 285,857 lbs/yr iron and 32,320 lbs/yr manganese. Aquatic life returned to a creek that had been unable to support it, including a surviving population of stocked brown trout, and the state proposed delisting in 2010.
stories.notes: Total cost about $1.66 million including roughly $690,000 in Section 319 funds.

stories.title: Woodrow Wilson High School Wetland and Stream Daylighting, Cranberry Creek
stories.orgs: Piney Creek Watershed Association; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; WV Department of Environmental Protection; WV Conservation Agency; WV Division of Natural Resources; US Fish and Wildlife Service; City of Beckley; Beckley Area Foundation; Raleigh County Board of Education; Girl Scouts of Black Diamond Council
stories.desc: An aging 0.75-acre campus pond on Cranberry Creek was drained in April 2021 and converted into an emergent wetland with the natural drainage daylighted and the stream channel rebuilt to NRCS protocols. Invasive plants were replaced with more than 1,750 native plantings, and a pollinator garden, walking bridges and interpretive signage were added. Fecal coliform fell an average of 32 percent as water passes through the wetland, from pre-project levels above 2,300 cfu/100 mL, and the site now supports amphibians, wetland birds, bees and butterflies.
stories.notes: Total cost $126,000 including a $60,000 Section 319 grant. Coordinates are the Woodrow Wilson High School campus in Beckley.

stories.title: Pinnacle Creek Trail 36 Culvert Replacement, Hatfield-McCoy Trail System
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife (West Virginia Ecological Services and Appalachian Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office); Hatfield-McCoy Trail System; Canaan Valley Institute; Tread Lightly; Applied Trails Research; Can-Am; Appalachian Forest National Heritage Area AmeriCorps
stories.desc: On Trail 36 of the Hatfield-McCoy off-road vehicle trail system, an undersized 18-inch culvert that routinely clogged in heavy rain was replaced with a 96-inch culvert and a native vegetation buffer was established along the trail and riparian area during a week of work completed in early April 2025. The project reconnected 1.2 miles of stream habitat on Pinnacle Creek, restored aquatic organism passage, improved flood resilience and lowered maintenance costs, and reduced sedimentation affecting the critically endangered Guyandotte River crayfish.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state trail authority, NGO, corporate)
stories.notes: Completed. Guyandotte River drains to the Ohio River in southern West Virginia.

stories.title: Kitchen Creek Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Buffers
stories.orgs: WV Conservation Agency; Greenbrier Valley Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; US Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife and White Sulphur Springs National Fish Hatchery; Trout Unlimited; private landowners
stories.desc: On 5.5-mile Kitchen Creek, partners installed 11 alternative watering systems (some wind or solar powered), adopted rotational grazing plans meeting NRCS riparian grazing standards, created more than 100 acres of riparian buffer along over 6 miles of stream, and built or repaired three waste storage facilities. Livestock stream access time dropped from 5 percent to 0.12 percent and fecal coliform generally declined after 2009. Brook trout reestablished after a 2013 reintroduction and the dominant nongame fish shifted from dace to sculpin, an indicator of high-quality water.
stories.notes: About $556,560 in Section 319 funds plus state and landowner match. Creek had not yet fully met bacteria standards at time of publication.

stories.title: Carswell Eroding Refuse Stabilization, Laurel Branch
stories.orgs: West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection, Office of Abandoned Mine Lands and Reclamation; Green Mountain Company (contractor)
stories.desc: A failing cut-stone retaining wall above Laurel Branch, which drains to Elkhorn Creek and then the Tug Fork River, was repaired and faced with high tensile-strength steel mesh, and a 20-acre coal refuse area above it was regraded and revegetated. Completed in May 2007 at a cost of $2,542,182, the work stabilized the wall and removed the threat of a landslide or flood delivering the refuse pile into the stream.
stories.notes: Primarily sediment-source stabilization protecting the stream rather than in-channel habitat work; included because the refuse pile was an active sediment threat to Laurel Branch.

stories.title: Windmill Gap Creek Decentralized Wastewater and Wetland Treatment
stories.orgs: Wastewater Treatment Coalition of McDowell County; Canaan Valley Institute; WV Department of Environmental Protection; US EPA; local churches, foundations and Rotary clubs
stories.desc: Canaan Valley Institute designed a decentralized community wastewater system for 23 homes and two businesses in the former coal community of Ashland, routing sewage to constructed wetland cells for secondary treatment and then a low-pressure drainfield, replacing failing septic systems that discharged directly to a 2.8-mile designated trout stream. Fecal coliform levels dropped by more than 98 percent and low-flow samples met state standards by fall 2010. The stream condition index improved from 54.4 (marginal) to 67.7 (suboptimal) with better macroinvertebrate diversity and abundance, and WVDEP planned delisting in 2012.
stories.water: Windmill Gap Creek (North Fork Elkhorn Creek)
stories.notes: The on-the-ground work was a constructed treatment wetland and wastewater system rather than in-channel habitat work, but it is an EPA 319 success story with documented aquatic-life recovery. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Austin Branch Pasture and Heavy-Use-Area Restoration (Red River tributary)
stories.orgs: Sumner County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USEPA Section 319 program; private landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: On this 3.9-mile tributary of the Red River, landowners renovated 47.6 acres of pasture and hayland, armored two heavy-use areas where livestock concentrated (about 30x100 ft and 28x85 ft), and converted 8.1 acres of cropland to grassland between 2003 and 2005. The work targeted siltation from livestock grazing that had caused a poor 2001 biological survey. A 2004 follow-up survey met regional biological goals and TDEC removed Austin Branch from the impaired waters list in 2008.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee. Stream lies southwest of Portland; lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Goose Creek Streambank Restoration, Mountain City
stories.orgs: Town of Mountain City; Appalachian Resource Conservation and Development Council; Johnson, Carter and Sullivan County Soil Conservation Districts; Brushy Fork Environmental Consulting; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; U.S. EPA; local landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Work on 15.4-mile Goose Creek combined in-channel and riparian restoration at Ralph Stout Park - rock vanes to control bed elevation and shear stress, native streambank plantings and interpretive signage - with about 3,536 feet of riparian forest buffer and 1,700 feet of streambank protection funded by Section 319, plus roughly 7,900 feet of agricultural fencing, 4,837 feet of pipeline, seven watering facilities, five stabilized heavy-use areas, access road and well work funded by the state cost-share program. A 2006 habitat assessment at mile 0.1 scored 143, considered good for the region, and testing showed the creek fully supports its designated uses. TDEC removed Goose Creek from the 303(d) list in 2010.
stories.water: Goose Creek (Town Creek, Watauga River basin)
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (Ralph Stout Park, Mountain City).

stories.title: Brush Creek Rotational Grazing and Streambank Protection (Cumberland River)
stories.orgs: Montgomery County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USEPA Section 319 program; private landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: On this 11.6-mile creek flowing to the Cumberland River at Barkley Reservoir south of Clarksville, partners installed 6,080 feet of rotational grazing fence plus 396 feet of additional fencing, 830 feet of livestock pipeline, seven stabilized heavy-use areas, two alternative watering systems, and converted 10 acres of cropland to grass or forest. A 2006 survey at mile 1.9 scored 40 of 42 on the Tennessee Macroinvertebrate Index with a habitat score of 120. TDEC delisted Brush Creek for siltation in 2008.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee. EPA document sometimes misspells it 'Bush Creek'. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Roaring River Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; The Nature Conservancy; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership; Tennessee Tech University; The Nature Conservancy in Tennessee; US Army Corps of Engineers; US Fish and Wildlife Service
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: A dam built in 1973 at the mouth of the Roaring River to block non-game fish from moving up out of Cordell Hull Reservoir was removed in 2017, restoring the impounded reach to flowing-water habitat. The removal reconnected about 78 perennial upstream river miles. Post-removal monitoring by TWRA and Tennessee Tech documented fish assemblages and upstream migration by redhorse; white bass, sauger and smallmouth bass also benefit.
stories.water: Roaring River at Cordell Hull Reservoir (Cumberland River)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee, not East Tennessee; included because the slice covers Tennessee dam removals statewide. Coordinates approximate (dam site at the Roaring River mouth).

stories.title: West Sandy Creek Grade Stabilization and Sediment Basins (Kentucky Lake watershed)
stories.orgs: Henry County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Agricultural Resources Conservation Fund; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; USEPA Section 319 program; local landowners
stories.desc: Ten best management practices were installed in the Kentucky Lake watershed from 1999 to 2005, including three grade-stabilization structures and a terrace in the West Sandy Creek drainage plus water/sediment control basins and grade stabilization on Spring Creek, Clifty Creek and Chapel Branch, along with pasture and hay planting. A 2004 biological survey found 19 total families and 5 EPT families for a Biorecon score of 13 (good). The 15-mile segment running from the West Sandy embayment of Kentucky Lake to the headwaters was removed from the 2006 303(d) list.
stories.water: West Sandy Creek (Kentucky Lake / Big Sandy watershed)
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: West Tennessee. Lat/lon approximate; nearest town not stated in the source.

stories.title: Whites Creek Emergency Watershed Protection Streambank Stabilization
stories.orgs: Davidson County Soil and Water Conservation District; Metro Nashville Water Services; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (Emergency Watershed Protection); Tennessee Department of Agriculture
stories.desc: Streambanks on Whites Creek that had eroded during extreme rain events, threatening nearby land and sewer infrastructure, were stabilized with best management practices under the Emergency Watershed Protection program. The district also runs a Whites Creek watershed cost-share program offering pasture management, riparian buffers, livestock exclusion fencing, rotational grazing, stream crossings, streambank stabilization and alternative watering systems, with completed work including a hay-feeding heavy use area and a watering trough on the Allen Williams farm. Before-and-after photos document the stabilized reach.
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee, Nashville metro. Completion year inferred from the page's 2021 image upload path; the page gives no date or length. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Upper Cherokee Creek Livestock Exclusion
stories.orgs: Washington County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; U.S. EPA; local landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Agricultural best management practices installed from 2003 to 2008 along a 20.8-mile segment of upper Cherokee Creek included fencing to keep cattle out of the stream, a 600-foot pipeline to a new alternative watering tank, and additional cost-shared erosion-control practices. Macroinvertebrate communities recovered, with Semi-Quantitative Single Habitat Assessment scores of 38 and 36 out of 42 at miles 1.0 and 2.5. TDEC removed the segment from Tennessee's 303(d) impaired waters list in 2008.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate; fact sheet names road landmarks rather than a town.

stories.title: Hinds Creek Watershed Restoration
stories.orgs: Hinds Creek Watershed Partnership; Anderson County and Union County Soil Conservation Districts; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Valley Authority; local landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Beginning in 2000, landowners in the Hinds Creek watershed of the lower Clinch River basin fenced cattle out of the creek, planted pasture, hay and riparian zones with native and livestock-friendly species, added streambank protection, installed tanks, troughs and pipeline-fed ponds for alternative water, stabilized heavy-use areas with gravel and geotextile, and built alternative access roads. About $57,700 of Section 319 and state Agricultural Resources Conservation Fund money supported the work toward the 49.5 percent pathogen reduction called for in the 2005 TMDL. Monitoring found E. coli below the single-sample standard and 8.9 miles of Hinds Creek were left off the 2006 303(d) list, with the creek fully supporting all four designated uses.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (mid-watershed).

stories.title: Rock Springs Branch Heavy-Use-Area Stabilization (Caney Fork / Cumberland River)
stories.orgs: Putnam County Soil Conservation District; Smith County Soil Conservation District; DeKalb County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USEPA Section 319 program
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Fifteen acres of heavy-use-area best management practices were installed on two farms along Rock Springs Branch and its tributary Bates Branch in the Caney Fork River watershed to stabilize ground trampled by cattle and cut soil erosion. Follow-up monitoring returned a Biorecon score of 15 of 15 and a habitat score of 137, above the regional habitat goal. The 8.1-mile segment was removed from the 2004 303(d) list because it fully supported fish and aquatic life.
stories.water: Rock Springs Branch / Bates Branch (Caney Fork River, Cumberland basin)
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local districts, private landowners)
stories.notes: Upper Cumberland / Middle Tennessee; partner work also in Smith and DeKalb counties. Lat/lon approximate; nearest town not stated in the source.

stories.title: Dry Creek Diversion Levee and Sediment Dike (Big Sandy River watershed)
stories.orgs: Chickasaw-Shiloh Resource Conservation & Development Program; Benton County Soil Conservation District; Henry County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; USEPA Section 319 program; landowner Mark Hargis
stories.desc: A diversion levee built in 1998 redirected runoff from 83 acres of eroding agricultural field into a controlled outlet where sediment could settle; the field was later enrolled in CRP and planted to grass, and a second dike built in 2004 blocked sediment from 5 more acres. A 2004 biological survey of the 17.8-mile segment found 23 macroinvertebrate families including 4 EPT families, for a Biorecon score of 11 of 15 in the unimpaired range. Dry Creek was removed from Tennessee's 303(d) list in 2006.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowner)
stories.notes: West Tennessee. Lat/lon approximate; nearest town not stated in the source, Camden used as the Benton County seat.

stories.title: College Creek Urban and Agricultural Restoration, Greeneville
stories.orgs: Niswonger Foundation; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; City of Greeneville; Town of Tusculum; Tusculum University; Middle Nolichucky Watershed Alliance; Greene County Soil and Water Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Between 2003 and 2021 partners installed 106 practices in the Sinking Creek-Nolichucky watershed around 9.3-mile College Creek, combining urban measures - catch basins, a constructed wetland, streambank stabilization, an urban wetland pond and a rain garden - with agricultural fencing, alternative watering facilities and heavy-use areas, backed by more than $320,000 in Section 319 funds and more than $190,000 in state cost-share. A 2015 assessment returned a habitat score of 138 against a goal of 128 and a macroinvertebrate score of 36 against a passing score of 32. The entire creek was delisted from the 2020 303(d) list for siltation, habitat alteration and riparian vegetation alteration.
stories.notes: Creek remains listed for E. coli from livestock grazing. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Slop Creek Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Restoration
stories.orgs: Greene County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Valley Authority; U.S. EPA; local landowners; Hamblen County Soil Conservation District; Central Basin Resource Conservation and Development Council
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Along 1.7-mile Slop Creek, a Hale Branch tributary in the Bent Creek subwatershed of the Nolichucky basin, Section 319 funds paid for 200 feet of cattle-exclusion fencing, 0.5 acre of filter strip, three alternative watering facilities, 1,300 feet of pipeline, 400 feet of water diversion and 0.1 acre of heavy-use area protection, with state cost-share adding four more watering facilities, 0.2 acre of heavy-use protection and 1,040 feet of pipeline. A 2005 monitoring station at mile 0.1 scored 36 of 42 on the Tennessee Macroinvertebrate Index (very good) and 132 of 200 on habitat (good). TDEC removed Slop Creek from the impaired waters list in 2008.
stories.water: Slop Creek (Hale Branch / Bent Creek, Nolichucky River)
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-12/documents/tn_covecreek.pdf

stories.title: Obion River Tributary Floodwater Dikes, Miston
stories.orgs: Chickasaw-Shiloh Resource Conservation and Development Council; Tennessee Agricultural Resources Conservation Fund; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; local landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Three earth embankments (dikes) planted to crops or grass were installed in 2004-2005 on a 25.8-mile unnamed tributary of the Obion River near Miston, holding back floodwater and trapping sediment, nutrients and pesticide residues in the Northern Mississippi Alluvial Plain. The stream had scored poorly in a 2001 Biorecon survey and was listed as impaired in 2002. A 2006 evaluation scored 8 of 10, showing support of fish and aquatic life, and TDEC delisted the stream in 2008.
stories.water: Unnamed tributary to the Obion River
stories.notes: West Tennessee, Mississippi River bottoms. Segment spans Dyer and Obion counties; Dyer listed as primary. Lat/lon approximate at Miston.

stories.title: Turkey Creek Livestock Exclusion and Erosion Control
stories.orgs: Hamblen County Soil Conservation District; Smoky Mountain Resource Conservation and Development Council; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; local landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Along a 5.8-mile segment of Turkey Creek just south of Morristown, landowners installed about 2,800 feet of cattle-exclusion fencing, seven alternative watering facilities with roughly 555 feet of pipeline, 2.5 acres of critical-area planting, 0.2 acre of filter strip, a 60-foot roof runoff structure and heavy-use-area protection on more than 0.3 acre. A 2005 assessment found 28 macroinvertebrate genera including 8 EPT genera, giving a Tennessee Macroinvertebrate Index score of 32 of 42. TDEC delisted the segment in 2008 after EPA approved the siltation TMDL.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Nolichucky River Agricultural BMP Restoration
stories.orgs: Cocke, Greene and Hamblen County Soil Conservation Districts; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; local landowners; U.S. EPA
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Landowners along three impaired segments of the Nolichucky River totaling about 23.7 miles installed numerous agricultural best management practices between 2003 and 2008, including 10 acres of pasture and hay planting, heavy-use area protection, filter strips, livestock exclusion fencing, runoff structures and alternative watering facilities. Follow-up monitoring found E. coli geometric means of 5.3 and 20.8 cfu/100 mL, 7 and 11 EPT genera, and a habitat score of 152 of 200 rated good. TDEC removed all three segments from the 2008 303(d) list for E. coli and biological integrity.
stories.notes: Three separate river segments; coordinates are a mid-river point.

stories.title: Squibb Creek 'Rainbow Barrier' Dam Removal
stories.orgs: American Rivers (reporting); project partners not named in source; Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The 'Rainbow Barrier' dam on Squibb Creek, a Nolichucky basin headwater stream in the Cherokee National Forest, was removed in 2024 and recorded in American Rivers' national dam removal database. Barriers of this type were historically installed to keep non-native rainbow trout or non-game fish out of upper reaches; removing it restores longitudinal connectivity on the creek. The compiled summary lists the removal but gives no partner list or quantified outcome.
stories.notes: Minimal detail available: American Rivers' 2024 compiled summary table lists only dam name, river, state, county and year. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Rainbow Barrier Dam Removal, Squibb Creek
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Rainbow Barrier on Squibb Creek in Greene County was removed in 2024. Barriers of this kind were historically installed to keep non-native rainbow trout out of headwater reaches holding southern Appalachian brook trout; its removal restores continuous flow and passage through the creek. The annual list records the removal without reporting dam height, mileage or named partners.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2024 dam removal summary table (PDF verified). Purpose of the 'rainbow barrier' inferred from standard practice; lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Big Sandy River Livestock Exclusion and Grade Stabilization
stories.orgs: Carroll County Soil Conservation District; Henderson County Soil Conservation District; Chickasaw-Shiloh Resource Conservation & Development; Hatchie River Watershed Association; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; USEPA Section 319 program; private landowners
stories.desc: Along a 7.3-mile reach of the Big Sandy River in the Kentucky Lake watershed, partners installed heavy-use-area foundations, grade stabilization structures to halt streambank failure, pasture/hay and riparian-zone plantings, and livestock watering pipelines, wells and ponds to keep cattle out of the stream (2003-2005). Dissolved oxygen rose above 7 mg/L against a 5 mg/L standard, and a 2006 biological survey scored 40 of 42 on the Tennessee Stream Condition Index, well above the regional goal of 32. The segment was delisted for low dissolved oxygen from the 2006 303(d) list.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: West Tennessee. Segment remains listed for E. coli. Lat/lon approximate along the Big Sandy in Carroll County.

stories.title: Harpeth River May 2010 Flood Recovery and Reforestation
stories.orgs: Harpeth Conservancy (Harpeth River Watershed Association); Nashville Waterways Recovery and Restoration Project partners; Metro Nashville-Davidson County; Tennessee Wildlife Federation; volunteers
stories.desc: After the May 2010 flood uprooted more than 10,000 mature trees and stripped riparian zones, Harpeth Conservancy surveyed over 200 sites along the Harpeth River and its tributaries and ran a multi-year recovery effort: more than 60 cleanups with over 2,000 volunteers removed 153 tons of debris, and in 2012 the organization planted 12,656 native seedlings, mostly along the Harpeth. A parallel Nashville Waterway Recovery Project begun in 2011 engaged 776 volunteers for 3,500+ hours and planted more than 7,000 trees in Davidson County. Nearly all flood debris was cleared within two years and annual riparian plantings have continued.
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee; work spanned Williamson and Davidson counties along the Harpeth. Detail also at https://harpethconservancy.org/our-work/science-restoration/environmental-restoration/may-2010-flood-restoration/ . Lat/lon approximate, centered on the Harpeth between Franklin and Bellevue.

stories.title: Kyker Branch Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Restoration
stories.orgs: Greene County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; local landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Along the 2.5-mile Kyker Branch, which flows to the Nolichucky River, landowners installed 16,478 feet of fencing to exclude cattle and establish a riparian zone, three alternative watering facilities, 1,200 feet of water pipeline and 0.1 acre of heavy-use area protection, plus additional voluntary erosion-control practices. A 2005-2006 assessment at mile 0.1 scored 38 of 42 on the Tennessee Macroinvertebrate Index (very good) and 140 of 200 for habitat. TDEC removed the segment from the impaired waters list in 2008.
stories.notes: EPA fact sheet places the branch in Greene County about 7 miles northeast of Parrottsville; coordinates approximate.

stories.title: DeMoss Creek Sediment Basins and Critical Area Planting (South Fork Obion River)
stories.orgs: Carroll County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USEPA Section 319 program; private landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Two water and sediment control basins and one acre of critical area planting were installed on DeMoss Creek west of Trezevant to intercept sediment from eroding non-irrigated cropland and riparian areas. A 2005 biological reconnaissance survey scored 11 on the 1-15 scale with four EPT families and 18 total families, in the good range. Tennessee removed the 24.2-mile impaired segment from the 303(d) list for siltation in 2008.
stories.water: DeMoss Creek (South Fork Obion River watershed)
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: West Tennessee. Lat/lon approximate, west of Trezevant.

stories.title: Crooked Creek Sediment Control Basins and Pasture Planting (South Fork Obion River)
stories.orgs: Carroll County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USEPA Section 319 program; private landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: On a 4.7-mile reach from the mouth at the South Fork Obion River up to Guins Creek, partners built four water and sediment control basins (2004-2008), installed a 780-foot underground drain outlet, planted 3 acres of critical area and 29.5 acres of pasture and hayland in native forage, and added no-till and cover crops. A 2006 biological reconnaissance survey scored 13 of 15 with a habitat score of 155 of 200, and TDEC described the headwaters as 'fully restored.' The segment was delisted in 2008.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: West Tennessee. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Crab Orchard Creek and Laurel Creek Mine Drainage and Agricultural Restoration
stories.orgs: TDEC Land Reclamation Section; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Crab Orchard Creek Restoration Partnership; Emory River Watershed Association; Tennessee Valley Authority; Morgan County Soil Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; University of Tennessee; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Tennessee Scenic Rivers Association; Chota Canoe Club
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: In the Emory River headwaters, partners built eight acid-mine-drainage treatment systems including limestone ponds, a constructed wetland and settling ponds, reclaimed roughly 57 acres of previously mined land with about 1,500 feet of highwall and 2,000 feet of eroding streambank addressed, and installed 37 agricultural best management practices such as exclusion fencing, alternative watering, heavy-use areas and cropland conversion between 2002 and 2016. Manganese fell from as high as 7,480 ug/L in 1999-2000 to 48-600 ug/L, pH returned to 6.10-7.24 and 2012 macroinvertebrate scores of 36 and 32 passed. Tennessee delisted 2.3 miles of Crab Orchard Creek in 2010 and a further 7.9 miles of Crab Orchard Creek plus 3.7 miles of Laurel Creek in 2014.
stories.water: Crab Orchard Creek and Laurel Creek (Emory River)
stories.notes: An earlier EPA fact sheet on the same watershed is at https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-10/documents/tn_craborchard-2.pdf . Watershed extends into Cumberland County. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Lake Sturgeon Reintroduction, Tennessee and Cumberland Rivers
stories.orgs: Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute; Southeast Lake Sturgeon Working Group; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Tennessee Valley Authority; University of Tennessee
stories.desc: The Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute and the Southeast Lake Sturgeon Working Group have reared and released more than 425,000 lake sturgeon into the Tennessee and Cumberland River systems, including release sites on the French Broad and Holston arms above Knoxville, to restore a species extirpated from the basin. Fish are head-started and tagged before release, and partners now monitor for the size classes and spawning behavior that would signal a self-sustaining population. Released sturgeon are regularly recaptured by anglers and researchers throughout the upper Tennessee River.
stories.water: Tennessee River (French Broad and Holston rivers)
stories.notes: Program-level entry covering many release sites across the Tennessee and Cumberland basins; coordinates placed at the French Broad/Holston confluence near Knoxville, a long-standing release area.

stories.title: Sam Davis Dam Removal, Stewart Creek
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Sam Davis Dam was removed from Stewart Creek at Smyrna in 2023, one of 80 dams taken out nationwide that year. Removal restores free-flowing conditions and aquatic organism passage on a Stones River tributary in the Nashville Basin. The annual summary records the removal but does not report dam height, reconnected mileage or partner organizations.
stories.notes: Record derived from the tabular list in American Rivers' 2023 compiled dam removal summaries (PDF verified). Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Thompson Creek Sediment Control Basins and Runoff Diversion (South Fork Obion River)
stories.orgs: Gibson County Soil and Water Conservation District; Carroll County Soil and Water Conservation District; Tennessee Agricultural Resources Conservation Fund; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; local landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Two water and sediment control basins and a 725-foot runoff diversion ending in a perforated bubble outlet with a sod chute were installed on Thompson Creek, a 20.2-mile stream draining parts of Carroll and Gibson counties into the South Fork Obion River, to route cropland runoff away from sensitive habitat. A 2001 Biorecon survey had rated the creek poor; a 2006 evaluation at mile 3.0 returned a Biorecon score of 11 (good) with a habitat score of 106. TDEC removed Thompson Creek from the impaired waters list in 2008.
stories.notes: West Tennessee; creek spans Carroll and Gibson counties. Lat/lon approximate; nearest town not stated in the source.

stories.title: McKnight Branch Rotational Grazing and Livestock Exclusion (Stones River watershed)
stories.orgs: Cannon County Soil Conservation District; Rutherford County Soil Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Tennessee Department of Agriculture Nonpoint Source Program; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; local farmers
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: In 2006-2007, 3,721 feet of rotational grazing fence, 3,860 feet of livestock pipeline, four heavy-use areas and three watering facilities were installed along McKnight Branch near Porterfield, east of Murfreesboro, to keep cattle out of damaged riparian areas. A 2007 Biorecon survey scored a perfect 15 of 15 with a habitat score of 130 of 200, good for the ecoregion. TDEC removed the 18.8-mile segment from the 303(d) impaired waters list in 2010.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee; segment spans Cannon and Rutherford counties. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Arrington Creek Agricultural BMP and Riparian Restoration (Harpeth River Watershed)
stories.orgs: Williamson County Soil Conservation District; Harpeth River Watershed Association (now Harpeth Conservancy); Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USEPA Section 319 program
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Eight best management practices were installed along Paige Branch, a tributary of Arrington Creek in the Harpeth River watershed, between 1999 and 2003 — livestock exclusion fencing, an alternative watering facility, pasture and hay planting on critical areas, heavy-use-area reinforcement, streambank protection and riparian buffer planting. Follow-up Biorecon scoring in 2002 returned a perfect 15 of 15 and a habitat score of 115, indicating full support of fish and aquatic life. The 24.6-mile impaired segment was removed from Tennessee's 303(d) list for siltation in 2004.
stories.water: Arrington Creek / Paige Branch (Harpeth River watershed)
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee. Lat/lon approximate, centered on the Arrington Creek corridor in Williamson County. EPA 319 success story PDF has no extractable image URLs.

stories.title: Cripple Creek Pasture and Grassed Waterway Restoration (East Fork Stones River)
stories.orgs: Rutherford County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USEPA Section 319 program
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Fourteen best management practices were installed on Cripple Creek in the East Fork Stones River watershed between 1999 and 2003, including replanting more than 157 acres of pasture and grassed waterways and one alternative livestock watering facility. Monitoring returned a Biorecon score of 15 and a habitat score of 146, above the ecoregion goal, with chemical standards met at mile 0.4. The 7.7-mile segment was removed from the 2004 303(d) list for siltation.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee. Lat/lon approximate; nearest town not stated in the source.

stories.title: Gallagher Creek Watershed Restoration
stories.orgs: Blount County Soil Conservation District; Little River Watershed Association; Smoky Mountain Resource Conservation and Development Council; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Valley Authority; USDA; local farmers
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: From 2000 to 2011 landowners along 13.2-mile Gallagher Creek installed livestock exclusion and rotational grazing fencing, multiple alternative watering facilities including a spring system and a well, heavy-use area protection, critical-area planting, pasture and hay planting, cropland conversion, septic improvements, a pond, a pipeline and a stabilized stream crossing, supported by $73,384 in Section 319 funds plus state and Farm Bill money. Habitat surveys in 2003 and 2007 met the state criterion and the 2007 biological reconnaissance score was 13, considered good for the ecoregion. Tennessee removed all 13.2 miles from the 303(d) list in 2010.
stories.water: Gallagher Creek (Fort Loudoun Reservoir, Tennessee River)
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: McCutcheon Creek Riparian Buffer and Streambank Restoration, Spring Hill
stories.orgs: Tennessee Scenic Rivers Association; Harpeth Conservancy; Tennessee Environmental Council; Maury County Soil and Water Conservation District; Maury County School District (Spring Hill High School); Saturn Corporation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; private landowners
stories.desc: Twenty-seven practices installed between 2004 and 2022 on McCutcheon Creek near Spring Hill included 11,081 feet of riparian forest buffer, 1,441 feet of streambank and shoreline protection, 528 feet of channel bank vegetation, 900 feet of fence, 1,550 feet of livestock pipeline, a rain garden/bioretention basin, two alternative water sources and two heavy-use-area protections; early work in 2003 was centered in Jerry Erwin Park. A 2019 survey returned a habitat score of 124 and a Tennessee Macroinvertebrate Index of 36, above the passing mark of 32. TDEC delisted all 12.27 miles for siltation/sedimentation on the 2022 list and the creek now fully supports its designated uses.
stories.water: McCutcheon Creek (Rutherford Creek / Duck River watershed)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee; watershed spans Maury and Williamson counties. Lat/lon approximate at Spring Hill.

stories.title: Rutherford Creek Riparian Buffers, Rain Gardens and Streambank Protection
stories.orgs: Tennessee Scenic Rivers Association; Tennessee Environmental Council; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Maury and Williamson county soil conservation districts; Saturn Corporation / General Motors; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; City of Spring Hill; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Development & Environmental Planning Associates
stories.desc: Between 2002 and 2018 partners installed 25 riparian forest buffers, 21 streambank protection and channel bank stabilization projects, three rain gardens, a stream habitat improvement project, two tree plantings and 29 agricultural BMPs (fencing, heavy-use areas, cropland conversion) across the Rutherford Creek watershed in the lower Duck River basin. Habitat scores rose from 111 in 1999 and 95 in 2003 — both below the 114 minimum — to 137, 142 and 138 in 2014-2015. A 12.5-mile segment was removed from the 2016 impaired waters list for all causes and sources and now fully supports all designated uses.
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee; watershed spans Maury and Williamson counties. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Marbled Darter Augmentation, Little River
stories.orgs: Conservation Fisheries Inc.; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: Conservation Fisheries propagated and released marbled darters into the Little River in Blount County to extend the species' occupied range upstream. The augmentation expanded the population about 2.5 river miles upstream of its previous limit, and the fish persist there; a second, farther-upstream attempt did not take hold.
stories.notes: Source gives no completion year; coordinates approximate (middle Little River).

stories.title: Middle Fork Bottoms Floodplain and Wetland Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Tennessee; Tennessee State Parks
stories.desc: An 860-acre former working farm in West Tennessee was restored to floodplain forest and wetland and opened in 2024 as Middle Fork Bottoms, Tennessee's newest state park; about 250,000 hardwood trees were planted on the site. TNC continues to help manage a wetland in the park that retains and slowly filters floodwaters. The project converted depleted cropland into functioning floodplain habitat while adding public access and recreation.
stories.notes: Town, county and waterbody are not stated on the TNC page and are inferred from the Middle Fork Bottoms State Park location in West Tennessee; coordinates approximate. The 250,000-tree figure comes from TNC's Tennessee conservation news listing for the same site.

stories.title: West Tennessee Wetland Reserve Enhancement Program — Bottomland Hardwood and Floodplain Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Tennessee; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; West Tennessee River Basin Authority; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; private agricultural landowners
stories.desc: Through a Wetland Reserve Enhancement Program partnership with NRCS, 2,500 acres of retired West Tennessee farmland were enrolled over three years under conservation easements and restored from cropland back to bottomland hardwood forest and floodplain wetland in the Hatchie, Obion, Forked Deer and Wolf river bottoms of the Mississippi alluvial plain. The Nature Conservancy paired the easements with a West Tennessee floodplain prioritization tool, on-farm demonstrations, edge-of-field buffers and peer learning networks. The program has since concluded in Tennessee, with monitoring projects established on the restored tracts.
stories.water: Hatchie, Obion, Forked Deer and Wolf river floodplains (Mississippi River bottoms)
stories.notes: West Tennessee. Enrollment spanned multiple West Tennessee counties; Haywood County used as an approximate centroid of the program area. Source gives no explicit start/end years beyond 'three years' and that the program has concluded, so the year range is approximate.

stories.title: Great Smoky Mountains Native Brook Trout Stream Restoration
stories.orgs: National Park Service - Great Smoky Mountains National Park; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission; Trout Unlimited
stories.desc: The park has restored native southern Appalachian brook trout to headwater streams by removing non-native rainbow and brown trout and reintroducing native stock. As of the park's Nature page, 30.25 miles of brook trout habitat across 13 streams have been restored since 1981, recovering part of the roughly 75 percent of brook trout habitat lost to logging and non-native trout introductions in the early 1900s. Research on the restored populations supported reopening brook trout fishing in 2006 after a 30-year closure, and a three-year study found adult breeding ability remained stable with fishing.
stories.water: Park headwater streams (13 streams, Little River / Oconaluftee / Abrams Creek headwaters)
stories.notes: Mileage figure (30.25 miles in 13 streams) verified on the park Nature page; the park page does not name the individual streams or partners, so partner list beyond NPS is inferred from the park's long-standing brook trout program and should be trimmed if the compiler wants only cited orgs. Restored streams lie on both the TN and NC sides of the park; coordinates are an approximate park-centroid point in Sevier County, TN. Photo URL is from the park's companion Fish page (https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/nature/fish.htm).

stories.title: Cloyd Creek Agricultural BMP Restoration
stories.orgs: Loudon County Soil Conservation District; Blount County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Valley Authority; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; local landowners; Knox County Soil Conservation District; Ijams Nature Center; Water Quality Forum; Stock Creek Task Force; Knox County Adopt-A-Watershed; local farmers
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Landowners along 11.3-mile Cloyd Creek installed about 3,762 feet of livestock exclusion fencing and 4,540 feet of rotational grazing fence, 13 heavy-use areas, 13 watering facilities, a stabilized stream crossing, 5,936 feet of pipeline, a grade stabilization structure and roughly 125 acres of pasture, hayland and critical-area planting between 1999 and 2011. A TVA biological reconnaissance scored the creek 13 of 15, and a state assessment at mile 1.5 returned a Tennessee Macroinvertebrate Index score of 38 and a habitat score of 132. Tennessee removed the creek from its 303(d) impaired waters list for siltation and habitat alteration in 2010.
stories.water: Cloyd Creek (Fort Loudoun Lake, Tennessee River)
stories.notes: EPA fact sheet names Loudon and Blount county districts but not the creek's county; placed in Loudon County. Coordinates approximate. Creek remains listed for E. coli. Also documented at: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-07/documents/tn_stock-508.pdf

stories.title: Southern Appalachian Brook Trout Restoration, Great Smoky Mountains National Park
stories.orgs: National Park Service (Great Smoky Mountains NP); Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Trout Unlimited
stories.desc: Logging and the stocking of non-native rainbow trout cost the park about 75 percent of its native brook trout habitat in the twentieth century. Park biologists restored brook trout to headwater streams by removing non-native trout and reintroducing native fish, and have monitored fish in 29 of the park's 38 watersheds (about 82 percent of park streams) since 1986. Recovery was sufficient for the park to reopen brook trout fishing in 2006 after a 30-year closure, and a three-year study found adult brook trout breeding success remained stable with fishing allowed.
stories.water: Headwater streams of Great Smoky Mountains National Park (Little River, Abrams Creek, Little Pigeon River)
stories.notes: Park-wide program; coordinates are a central point in the Tennessee portion of the park.

stories.title: Lick Creek Livestock Exclusion and Forage Planting (Duck River watershed, Marshall County)
stories.orgs: Marshall County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; USEPA Section 319 program
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Between 1999 and 2005, 25 acres of hay and pasture grasses were planted along Lick Creek and its tributary Plum Branch, cattle exclusion fencing was installed, an animal waste lagoon was built and heavy-use areas were stabilized. The macroinvertebrate score reached 36 of 42, described as very good and above the regional goal of 32. The 8.8-mile segment was removed from the 2006 303(d) list for habitat alterations.
stories.water: Lick Creek / Plum Branch (Duck River watershed)
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee; segment spans Marshall and Rutherford counties. Remained listed for E. coli after this phase — see the separate 2019 Lick Creek update entry. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Lick Creek Pathogen Delisting — 58 Agricultural BMPs (Spring Creek tributary)
stories.orgs: Marshall County Soil Conservation District; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Marshall County government; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; USEPA Section 319 program
stories.desc: A second phase of work beginning with a 2012 Section 319 grant installed 42 BMPs through the Marshall County Soil Conservation District — fences, pipelines, alternative watering systems, heavy-use areas and a stream crossing — plus 16 more state-funded practices including fencing, heavy-use areas and forage planting, for 58 BMPs total. Water samples in 2014 and 2015 met E. coli standards. The pathogen impairment was removed in 2018 and Lick Creek now fully supports its designated uses, following the earlier 2006 habitat delisting.
stories.water: Lick Creek (tributary of Spring Creek, Duck River watershed)
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee; spans Marshall and Rutherford counties. This is EPA's published update to the 2007 Lick Creek (Marshall) story, listed separately because it documents a distinct work phase and a separate delisting.

stories.title: Skillern Creek Agricultural and Septic Restoration
stories.orgs: Southeast Tennessee Resource Conservation and Development Council; Bledsoe County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; University of the South; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: In the 10.6-mile Skillern Creek segment of the Sequatchie River basin, partners installed about 725 linear feet of exclusion fencing, 2,300 feet of livestock water pipeline, four alternative watering facilities, 32 acres of pasture and hayland planting and 38 acres of cover crops between 2005 and 2017, along with three septic repairs or alternative systems. The creek's macroinvertebrate score rose from 5 in 2005 to 9 in 2011. TDEC determined in 2014 that the unknown toxicant from pasture grazing was no longer present and removed the segment from the 2014 303(d) list for unknown toxicity.
stories.notes: Creek remains listed for E. coli and work is ongoing. Sequatchie Valley is in the East Tennessee grand division but west of the Knoxville-eastward river list in the slice definition. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Laurel Dace Rescue and Reintroduction, Walden Ridge
stories.orgs: Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; University of Georgia; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (Ridges to Rivers RCPP); private landowners
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: After a severe 2024 drought dried the last streams holding the critically endangered laurel dace, biologists evacuated the surviving fish to the Tennessee Aquarium Conservation Institute and a USFWS facility, then returned more than 230 fish to the wild in March 2025 ahead of the spawning season. Young-of-the-year dace were found in Bumbee Creek in spring 2025, confirming successful wild spawning by the reintroduced fish. An ark population has produced more than 150 additional offspring for restocking Young's Creek, and TDEC has established long-term water-quality and macroinvertebrate monitoring stations across the species' range while Ridges to Rivers funds landowner best-management practices in six southeast Tennessee counties.
stories.water: Bumbee Creek and Young's Creek, Walden Ridge (Cumberland Plateau)
stories.notes: Source places the streams on Walden Ridge north of Chattanooga but does not name the county; laurel dace streams occur in Rhea, Bledsoe and Sequatchie counties. Coordinates approximate. Cumberland Plateau rather than the Knoxville-eastward valley-and-ridge, but within East Tennessee.

stories.title: Abrams Creek Rare Fish Reintroduction, Great Smoky Mountains National Park
stories.orgs: National Park Service - Great Smoky Mountains National Park; Conservation Fisheries, Inc.; National Park Service (Great Smoky Mountains NP); Conservation Fisheries Inc.; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; University of Tennessee
stories.desc: Three federally protected fishes - the smoky madtom, yellowfin madtom and Citico darter - were extirpated from Abrams Creek by a 1957 fish renovation and were propagated and reintroduced by park biologists and Conservation Fisheries between 1986 and 2001. Reproducing populations are now established, with the madtoms at about 90 percent and the Citico darter at 100 percent of estimated former capacity, and stocking is no longer needed. Because Abrams Creek is isolated by Chilhowee Reservoir, biologists move one or two adults of each species per year between Abrams and Citico creeks to maintain genetic diversity.
stories.notes: Also documented at https://www.conservationfisheries.org/our-successes . Coordinates approximate (lower Abrams Creek).

stories.title: West Tennessee Wetland Reserve Enhancement Program Bottomland Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Tennessee; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; West Tennessee River Basin Authority; Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency; US Army Corps of Engineers; private landowners
stories.desc: TNC partnered with NRCS on a Wetland Reserve Enhancement Program that enrolled 2,500 acres of retired West Tennessee cropland over three years under conservation easements, with landowners compensated to restore the ground to bottomland hardwood forest and floodplain wetland. The program has now concluded in Tennessee. The restored floodplain acreage lies in the Hatchie, Obion, Forked Deer and Wolf River systems and is intended to filter nutrients, reduce flooding, recharge aquifers and rebuild wildlife habitat.
stories.water: Hatchie, Obion, Forked Deer and Wolf Rivers
stories.year: completed; three-year program, years not stated
stories.notes: Programmatic rather than a single site: the source page gives no individual tract names, counties or years, and reports no measured outcomes. Placed at a representative West Tennessee location (Brownsville, Haywood County) inside the extent; coordinates are a placeholder for the program area.

stories.title: Fall Creek Waste Management Systems (Duck River watershed)
stories.orgs: Bedford County Soil Conservation District; Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation; Tennessee Department of Agriculture; Agricultural Resources Conservation Fund; USEPA Section 319 program
lpOrgs: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation
stories.desc: Two major waste management systems, including two poultry litter storage units able to handle waste from 199 acres, were installed in 1999 on tributaries of Fall Creek (including Parch Corn Creek) in the Duck River watershed. Biological sampling in 2004 produced Tennessee Stream Condition Index scores of 36 and 32 at two stations, meeting the state's biological integrity goals. The 11.4-mile segment was removed from the 2006 303(d) list for nutrients, siltation-caused biological loss and habitat alteration.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal, state, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: Middle Tennessee. Still listed for pathogens. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Lower Citico Creek Barrier Dam Removal, Cherokee National Forest
stories.orgs: USDA Forest Service (Cherokee National Forest); The Nature Conservancy in Tennessee; Conservation Fisheries Inc.; University of Tennessee; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; State of Tennessee; Trout Unlimited; US Forest Service; US Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: A failing 1970s-era barrier dam on lower Citico Creek, built to keep native 'rough' fish out of a managed trout fishery, was removed in August 2025 after its concrete crumbled and rebar became exposed. The removal reconnected 76 perennial upstream miles of one of the most biologically important streams in the Cherokee National Forest. It benefits the endangered Citico darter and smoky madtom and the threatened yellowfin madtom, all of which depend on Citico Creek as a source population.
stories.notes: An additional upstream barrier in the Citico Creek watershed was removed in 2015, per the same source. Coordinates approximate (lower Citico Creek near Tellico Lake).

stories.title: Barrens Topminnow Propagation and Release
