stories.title: Heron Bay oyster reef rebuilding (Mobile Baykeeper Holistic Oyster Restoration)
stories.orgs: Mobile Baykeeper; Alabama Commercial Fishermen Association; Salty Pirates Seafood; Isle Dauphine Oyster Company; Alabama Coastal Foundation; ADCNR; Alabama Dept. of Public Health; volunteers
stories.desc: In spring 2026 Mobile Baykeeper and commercial fishermen began laying burlap sacks of recycled shell on firm bottom and relic reefs in Heron Bay, west of the Dauphin Island causeway, to rebuild reef foundations for natural spat settlement; 13 of 28 planned reefs across several sites had been built by July 2026. Spat recruitment monitoring is the next step.
stories.notes: In progress; outcomes not yet reported.

stories.title: Bon Secour River Headwater Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of the headwaters of the Bon Secour River, treating erosion and altered hydrology in the upper watershed to reduce sediment delivery to Bon Secour Bay and improve stream and wetland habitat. Phase I was awarded in 2018 and phase II in 2020.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; location approximate.

stories.title: Coffee Island and Alabama Port living shorelines (ReefBLK breakwaters, 2010-2011) and 2023-2024 structure removal
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; Dauphin Island Sea Lab (Smee lab); ADCNR; volunteers
stories.desc: TNC installed 322 ReefBLK oyster-shell breakwater cages at Coffee Island in 2010 and 168 at Alabama Port in 2011 to protect eroding Mississippi Sound and Mobile Bay shorelines; too few oysters recruited to bind the structures and they deteriorated. TNC removed the Alabama Port units in 2023 and the Coffee Island units in July 2024, barging the debris to Bayou La Batre where volunteers recovered 495 live oysters that DISL relocated onto new reefs fronting the Lightning Point living shoreline; TNC is now building a two-mile rock breakwater at Coffee Island.
stories.water: Mississippi Sound (Coffee Island) / Mobile Bay (Alabama Port)
stories.notes: Mixed-outcome project; the Coffee Island rock breakwater replacement is in progress (TNC news Sept 2026).

stories.title: Dauphin Island Causeway Shoreline Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of the eroding shoreline along the Dauphin Island causeway in Mobile Bay, stabilizing the bank and rebuilding fringing marsh habitat. Phase I was awarded in 2018 and phase II in 2020.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Deepwater Horizon NRDA oyster cultch restoration, Mobile County reefs (524 acres)
stories.orgs: ADCNR Marine Resources Division; Alabama Deepwater Horizon NRDA Trustees (NOAA, USFWS, ADCNR, GSA, ADEM)
stories.desc: As a Phase III early-restoration project, the Marine Resources Division spread 65,540 cubic yards of limestone and shell cultch over 524 acres of public oyster reef in Mobile Bay and Mississippi Sound in 2015 to replace oyster production lost to the spill. Monitoring showed little productivity gain in the first three years but rising oyster density from 2019, and the reefs remain under a roughly 10-year monitoring program.
stories.water: Mobile Bay / Mississippi Sound public oyster reefs
stories.notes: Described in the Coastal Alabama Comprehensive Oyster Restoration Strategy (2021); NOAA project record https://www.gulfspillrestoration.noaa.gov/project?id=11 has no narrative.

stories.title: Restoration and enhancement of oyster reefs in Mobile Bay, Mississippi Sound and Bon Secour Bay (NFWF GEBF)
stories.orgs: ADCNR Marine Resources Division; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund; commercial oyster harvesters
stories.desc: With a $3.75M GEBF award (2013-2020) the Marine Resources Division placed about 50,000-60,500 cubic yards of cultch, planted roughly 41 million seed oysters and cultivated six 6-acre reef plots on public reefs in Mobile Bay, Mississippi Sound and Bon Secour Bay. The work restored roughly 600 acres of reef, increasing Alabama's 2,200 acres of viable reef by nearly 30 percent and testing advanced-stock planting to reduce oyster drill predation.
stories.water: Mobile Bay / Mississippi Sound / Bon Secour Bay
stories.town: Coden / Bayou La Batre (Cedar Point reefs)
stories.notes: Reef locations span both counties; coordinates placed on the Cedar Point reef complex.

stories.title: Lower Perdido Islands restoration (Walker and Robinson Islands, Orange Beach)
stories.orgs: Alabama Trustee Implementation Group (Deepwater Horizon NRDA); NOAA Transformational Habitat Restoration grant; City of Orange Beach; The Nature Conservancy; Moffatt & Nichol; Olsen Associates; Dauphin Island Sea Lab; CSA Ocean Sciences; MD Thomas Construction; US Army Corps of Engineers; Pensacola and Perdido Bays Estuary Program
lpOrgs: Pensacola and Perdido Bays Estuary Program
stories.desc: Crews pumped 170,000 cubic yards of sand to rebuild Walker Island (now Walker East and a new 26-acre Walker West) and Robinson Island near Perdido Pass, creating about 27 acres of dune, shrub, marsh and subtidal sand-flat habitat, adding riprap to Robinson Island and planting 200,000 native plants with volunteers; 4,000 shoal-grass sods were transplanted in 2024 to repair 1.5 acres of propeller-scarred seagrass. Completed September 2025, the islands now buffer seagrass beds from wakes and provide nesting and nursery habitat, and the project was named the Estuary Program's 2025 Project of the Year.
stories.notes: TNC page: https://www.nature.org/en-us/get-involved/how-to-help/places-we-protect/lower-perdido-islands/

stories.title: Restoration of the North Side of Dauphin Island
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources; Town of Dauphin Island
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of the north (bay) side of Dauphin Island, rebuilding marsh and stabilizing shoreline on the Mississippi Sound face of the island. Phase I was awarded in 2018 and a further phase in 2021.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Little Lagoon vegetated living shoreline (Bon Secour NWR)
stories.orgs: Alabama Trustee Implementation Group; US Fish and Wildlife Service (Bon Secour NWR); The Nature Conservancy; Mississippi State University; University of South Alabama
stories.desc: On a heavily eroded stretch of Little Lagoon's southwest shore inside Bon Secour National Wildlife Refuge, Deepwater Horizon trustees and partners planted an initial 500 black needlerush and smooth cordgrass plugs in November 2019, followed by 500 more and a planned 10,000-plant installation with a wave-reduction barrier in 2020. The pilot plantings were used to gauge wave energy and design the full vegetated shoreline to halt erosion of the refuge's lagoon edge.
stories.notes: NOAA lists the Little Lagoon Living Shoreline (project id=133) as In Progress; final planting totals not confirmed.

stories.title: Owl Creek-Little Hatchie River 319 Watershed Project
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Tippah County SWCD; USDA NRCS; Mississippi State University; private landowners
stories.desc: A Section 319 project in the Owl Creek-Little Hatchie River watershed installed 24,873 ft of livestock fencing, 54 streambank and shoreline protection practices, 144 grade stabilization structures, 35 tanks/troughs, 36 heavy-use area protections and 4 stream crossings on demonstration farms. MDEQ reports the project completed on schedule and within budget, with a public field day and outreach video documenting the practices.
stories.notes: Described in MDEQ FY2025 Section 319 annual report; field-day story at https://www.mswcc.ms.gov/news/commission-chronicals-may-june-2024. No delisting reported yet.

stories.title: North Tippah Creek NWQI Watershed Restoration (streambank protection, grade stabilization)
stories.orgs: USDA NRCS (National Water Quality Initiative); Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; U.S. EPA; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; USGS; Tippah County SWCD; local producers
stories.desc: More than $5 million in NWQI/EQIP practices, including grade stabilization structures, fencing, cover crops and stream and shoreline protection, were installed from 2012-2020 in the 35,521-acre North Tippah Creek-Tippah River watershed, saving an estimated 21,342 tons of soil per year. The M-BISQ score for the 3.99-mile impaired segment rose from 45.0 to 83.3 (threshold 71.6) and the creek was assessed as attaining aquatic life use for the 2022 cycle.
stories.water: North Tippah Creek (Tippah River / Hatchie basin)

stories.title: Caney Creek (Pickwick Reservoir Tributaries) Grade Stabilization and Planting
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; USDA NRCS; Tishomingo County SWCD; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Under the Pickwick Reservoir Tributaries Restoration and Protection Project, partners built 12 grade stabilization structures, a critical area planting, a pond, 55 acres of tree/shrub establishment, 128 acres of prescribed grazing and nutrient management on about 140 acres in the Coke Creek-Caney Creek watershed, with BMPs completed in 2009. The M-BISQ biological score rose from 48.1 (2001) to 87.9 (2011), and a 4.99-mile segment was assessed as attaining aquatic life use in 2014.
stories.notes: EPA NPS success story; location approximate.

stories.title: Yazoo Pass Grade Stabilization and Cover Crops
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Coahoma and Quitman County SWCDs; private landowners
stories.desc: A completed Section 319 project on Yazoo Pass in the Delta installed 39 grade stabilization structures, three check dams and 480 acres of cover crops to reduce gully and streambank erosion delivering sediment to the channel. MDEQ reports the project completed on schedule and within budget.
stories.notes: MDEQ FY2025 319 annual report; location approximate.

stories.title: Smith Creek Fish-Passage Culvert for the Yoknapatawpha Darter
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Lower Mississippi River FWCO and Mississippi ES Field Office); Calhoun County; Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks; Private John Allen National Fish Hatchery; University of Southern Mississippi
lpOrgs: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks
stories.desc: In 2017 the Service and Calhoun County replaced a failing, perched and undersized road culvert on Smith Creek with a bottomless arched culvert graded for fish passage, then began annual releases of hatchery-reared, tagged Yoknapatawpha darters, a Mississippi-endemic fish not seen in the creek since the 1980s. A February 2022 survey found 28 darters including 15 unmarked fish of multiple size classes, indicating natural reproduction in the reconnected stream.
stories.notes: FWS describes the site as 'near Oxford' in Calhoun County; coordinates approximate. Coordinate corrected to Calhoun County during QA (source says Calhoun Co.; earlier value fell in Lafayette Co.).

stories.title: Carmichael Creek-Town Creek Livestock and Streambank BMPs
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Lee County SWCD; private landowners
stories.desc: This completed Section 319 project in Lee County installed 950 ft of streambank and shoreline protection, 13,127 ft of livestock fencing, 26 grade stabilization structures, 17 heavy-use area protections, 13 watering facilities, a stream crossing, three sediment basins and 69 acres of vegetative cover and pasture planting. Estimated annual reductions exceed 2,851 tons of sediment, 13,058 lb nitrogen and 4,422 lb phosphorus.
stories.notes: MDEQ FY2023 319 annual report; location approximate.

stories.title: Sherman Creek-Panola Quitman Floodway Streambank and Grade Stabilization
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Tallahatchie County SWCD; private landowners
stories.desc: A two-phase Section 319 project on Sherman Creek in the Delta installed 15 grade stabilization structures, 231 ft of streambank and shoreline protection, 300 ft of diversion and three water and sediment control basins in Phase 2 (after a completed Phase 1). MDEQ estimates annual reductions of more than 1,323 tons of sediment, 2,562 lb nitrogen and 1,222 lb phosphorus toward the creek's sediment, nutrient and low-DO TMDLs.
stories.notes: MDEQ FY2025 319 annual report; location approximate.

stories.title: Buttahatchee River Livestock Exclusion and Pasture BMPs (Section 319 delisting)
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; USDA NRCS; Lowndes County SWCD; Monroe County SWCD; Mississippi Department of Health
stories.desc: Between 2005 and 2007, 59 agricultural BMPs were installed on about 4,702 acres along a 29-mile impaired segment of the Buttahatchee River, including 24,449 ft of livestock exclusion fencing, three watering troughs, 1,266 acres of pasture planting and 1,932 acres of nutrient management, plus mapping of failing septic systems. Post-BMP monitoring (2007-2010) showed fecal coliform meeting state standards and sediment loading cut by an estimated 19,462 tons; the segment was delisted in 2012.
stories.notes: Headwaters are in Alabama; the restored segment is in Mississippi.

stories.title: Broken Pumpkin Creek Agricultural BMPs
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Noxubee and Lowndes County SWCDs; private landowners
stories.desc: A completed Section 319 project installed 4,500 ft of fencing, 3,050 ft of terraces, two acres of grassed waterway, 89 acres of pasture and hayland planting, 278 acres of nutrient management, a pond, a heavy-use area and a grade stabilization structure in the Broken Pumpkin Creek watershed. MDEQ estimates annual reductions of about 964 tons of sediment, 6,565 lb nitrogen and 1,777 lb phosphorus.
stories.notes: MDEQ FY2023 319 annual report; location approximate.

stories.title: Fannegusha Creek Streambank and Livestock BMPs (EQIP; impaired-list removal)
stories.orgs: USDA NRCS; Holmes County SWCD; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; local producers
stories.desc: From 2008-2018 EQIP funded 82,439 ft of fencing, 24 grade stabilization structures, 21 ponds, 192 acres of critical area planting, 224 acres of prescribed grazing and other practices in the 29,084-acre Long Creek-Fannegusha Creek watershed to address eroding streambanks and cattle access. Estimated reductions of 1,627 tons of soil, 2,689 lb phosphorus and 12,425 lb nitrogen per year; the 2014 biological score was 30 points above the threshold and a 14.07-mile segment was removed from the impaired waters list.
stories.notes: EPA NPS success story; location approximate.

stories.title: Lake Washington Oxbow Sediment Reduction (dikes and grade stabilization)
stories.orgs: Washington County SWCD; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA; USGS
stories.desc: To restore the 2,965-acre Mississippi River oxbow listed for sedimentation, partners installed 139,712 ft of dikes, 153 grade stabilization structures, 13 water control structures and six rock outlet protections in the surrounding Delta cropland between 2008 and 2011. USGS edge-of-field monitoring found event concentrations down 35 percent or more for most constituents, and the lake was assessed as attaining aquatic life use in the 2018 and 2020 305(b) reports.

stories.title: Ellison Creek Grade Stabilization and Livestock Fencing
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Yazoo County SWCD; private landowners
stories.desc: A completed Section 319 project on Ellison Creek in the Loess Hills of Yazoo County installed eight grade stabilization structures, a stream crossing and 1,450 ft of livestock exclusion fencing to control headcutting and cattle access. MDEQ reports completion on schedule and within budget.
stories.notes: MDEQ FY2025 319 annual report; location approximate.

stories.title: Limekiln Creek (Bogue Chitto Creek Watershed Project) Delisting
stories.orgs: Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; USDA NRCS; Hinds County SWCD; Madison County SWCD; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Between 2005 and 2007, 77 practices covering about 2,024 acres were installed in the 28,880-acre Limekiln Creek watershed, including 25 water and sediment control basins, 13 grade stabilization structures, 14,642 ft of livestock fencing, a stream crossing and 16 acres of critical area and permanent vegetation plantings; NRCS added 12 more BMPs in 2009-2015. Estimated reductions of 9,525 tons of soil per year; the biological score rose from 30.9 to 45.5 and the creek was delisted in 2014.
stories.notes: Location approximate within watershed.

stories.title: Upper Little Bayou Pierre Watershed BMPs
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Claiborne and Copiah County SWCDs; private landowners
stories.desc: A Section 319 project that ended in fall 2022 installed a grade stabilization structure, six acres of critical area planting, 988 ft of fencing, a water and sediment control basin, 402 acres of nutrient management and 74 acres of pasture and hayland in the Upper Little Bayou Pierre watershed. Estimated reductions exceed 900 tons of sediment, 3,000 lb nitrogen and 1,300 lb phosphorus per year.
stories.water: Little Bayou Pierre (Bayou Pierre / Mississippi River)
stories.notes: MDEQ FY2023 319 annual report; location approximate.

stories.title: Bahala Creek Watershed Restoration (Section 319 delisting)
stories.orgs: USDA NRCS; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Copiah County SWCD; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; local producers
stories.desc: From 2005-2019 partners installed 18 grade stabilization structures, 38,777 ft of livestock exclusion fencing, 30 acres of critical area planting, heavy-use area protection and prescribed grazing in the Russell Creek-Bahala Creek watershed. Estimated annual reductions of 781 tons of soil, 6,709 lb phosphorus and 34,221 lb nitrogen; the 2020 M-BISQ biological score (44.7) exceeded the attainment threshold and Bahala Creek was removed from the 303(d) impaired list in 2022.
stories.notes: EPA NPS success story PDF; location approximate within watershed.

stories.title: Lake Hazle Sediment Control and Shoreline Revegetation
stories.orgs: Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Copiah County SWCD; City of Hazlehurst; Southwest Mississippi RC&D; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: The 22-acre city-owned Lake Hazle had nearly filled with silt; partners planted six heavily eroded sites, built a grade stabilization structure and two water/sediment control basins treating about 23 acres of the watershed. Soil savings were estimated at 2,240 tons per year, dissolved oxygen and nutrient criteria were met in 2001-2004 monitoring, and the lake was delisted in 2004 and fully supports aquatic life use.

stories.title: McCall Creek Sediment TMDL Success (EQIP fencing and heavy-use protection)
stories.orgs: USDA NRCS; Franklin County SWCD; Lincoln County SWCD; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; local producers
stories.desc: From 2007-2016 producers installed fencing, watering facilities, heavy-use area protection, tree/shrub establishment and pasture planting in the Beaver Creek-McCall Creek and Beaver Run Branch-McCall Creek watersheds to reduce sediment delivery under a 2009 TMDL. Both segments scored above the biological attainment threshold (2011 and 2016) and were listed as attaining aquatic life use / a TMDL success in the 2022 303(d) and 305(b) reports.

stories.title: Loch Leven Floodplain Reconnection (Lower Mississippi River)
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; USDA NRCS (Farm Bill); Nicholls State University; private landowner (Erik Piazza)
stories.desc: TNC and partners reconnected the roughly 6,000-acre Loch Leven island in Wilkinson County, long cut off by a 12-ft ring levee, to the Mississippi River's flood pulse by removing part of the levee and installing a box culvert, completed in 2019 as the largest floodplain reconnection on the Lower Mississippi. Monitoring has documented 28 species of young-of-year fish including alligator gar spawning on the floodplain, an estimated 40 percent nitrate removal, and the retention of sediment equal to about 1.2 million truckloads during the 2019 flood.
stories.notes: Completion year 2019 per TNC conservation news (https://www.nature.org/en-us/about-us/where-we-work/united-states/mississippi/stories-in-mississippi/conservation-news/); largely Farm Bill (WRE) funded.

stories.title: Magees Creek Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Tree Planting (delisting)
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; USDA NRCS; Walthall County SWCD
stories.desc: About 114 agricultural BMPs on more than 3,355 acres were implemented from 2005-2009 along two segments (12.2 miles) of Magees Creek, including roughly 52,000 ft of fencing to keep cattle out of the creek, 177 acres of tree planting, 350 acres of pasture planting, sediment basins, grade stabilization structures and animal waste facilities. Fecal coliform has met state standards since 2008, sediment loads fell by 7,841 tons per year, and MDEQ delisted both segments in 2012.
stories.water: Magees Creek (Bogue Chitto / Pearl River basin)
stories.notes: Watershed also touches Marion and Lawrence counties.

stories.title: Amazonian Apple Snail Removal, Lower Pascagoula River Marshes
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund)
stories.desc: Since 2014 (Phase I) and continuing under a $2.8 million Phase II award (2019, amended 2023), DMR crews and volunteers remove apple snail egg masses and live snails by hand and trapping throughout the Lower Pascagoula River's coastal swamps and marshes, where the snails strip submerged and emergent marsh vegetation. The program monitors infestation levels and conducts boater outreach to keep the invader out of brackish marsh in the Pascagoula system.
stories.notes: Ongoing control program; acres treated and quantitative outcomes not reported in source.

stories.title: Old Fort Bayou Urban BMPs and Marsh Restoration
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources (Gulf Coast National Heritage Area); Old Fort Bayou Watershed Implementation Team; St. Martin High School; Jackson County SWCD
stories.desc: A Section 319 project in the 32,079-acre Old Fort Bayou watershed combined an agricultural BMP component (cutting an estimated 150 tons of sediment per year) with an urban component that installed urban BMPs, restored marsh, built an outdoor classroom and trails at St. Martin High School, and extended the Old Fort Bayou Blueway to Bayou Talla with a boardwalk unveiled in July 2023. MDEQ selected Old Fort Bayou as its FY2024 NPS success story.
stories.notes: Marsh restoration acreage not quantified in the source.

stories.title: Orphan Creek Cattle Exclusion and Pasture Restoration (delisting)
stories.orgs: Mississippi Soil and Water Conservation Commission; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; U.S. EPA; USDA NRCS; Hancock County SWCD
stories.desc: From 2008-2011, 43 BMPs covering 533 acres were installed in the Dead Tiger/Orphan Creek watershed, including more than 2,800 ft of cattle fencing along Orphan Creek, 190 acres of nutrient management and 40 acres of pasture and hayland planting on erodible ground. Post-restoration M-BISQ scores rose from 51-53 to 76.5-82 (threshold 66), and the 6.2-mile segment was assessed as attaining aquatic life use and delisted in 2012.
stories.water: Orphan Creek (Jourdan River / Coastal Streams basin)
stories.notes: Location approximate within watershed.

stories.title: Woodland Cottage Pond and Longleaf Restoration / Dusky Gopher Frog Release
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partners for Fish and Wildlife; Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks; Memphis Zoo; Wildlife Mississippi; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service; private landowners Jim and Laura Currie
lpOrgs: Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries, and Parks
stories.desc: Over more than 20 years the landowners at Woodland Cottage replanted grazed and clear-cut land with longleaf pine, restored native groundcover and managed the stands with prescribed fire, restoring the ephemeral pond complex that breeding amphibians depend on. In June 2026 nearly 500 federally endangered dusky gopher frogs, reared by the Memphis Zoo, were released into the property's ponds. The restored habitat also benefits gopher tortoise, migratory birds and pollinators.
stories.water: ephemeral ponds, coastal Mississippi (Pearl/Jourdan River area)
stories.sector: Private landowner (with federal, state, NGO support)
stories.notes: Marginal fit: upland longleaf restoration that restored the hydrology/function of ephemeral breeding ponds; no named waterbody. Location approximate within Hancock County.

stories.title: Habitat Restoration and Conservation in Turkey Creek
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Land Trust for the Mississippi Coastal Plain
stories.desc: GEBF-funded habitat restoration and conservation in the Turkey Creek watershed at Gulfport, a historically African-American community's urban stream, combining floodplain and wetland restoration with land conservation to restore stream function and reduce flooding. Awarded in 2015.
stories.sector: Partnership (federal fund, state agency, land trust)
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Bayou Heron Boat Launch Living Shoreline (Grand Bay NERR)
stories.orgs: Grand Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve; Mississippi State University Coastal Extension; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources
stories.desc: In 2018 coir logs were installed along the eroding shoreline at the Bayou Heron boat launch and planted with smooth cordgrass and black needlerush to create a vegetated living shoreline. Photo monitoring shows the plantings have thrived through fall 2021.
stories.notes: Small demonstration-scale project; length not stated.

stories.title: Restoring Living Shorelines and Reefs in Mississippi Estuaries (Big Island and Deer Island components)
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Trustee Implementation Group; NOAA Restoration Center; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: This $30 million Phase IV early restoration project in the Back Bay of Biloxi, Grand Bay, Graveline Bay and St. Louis Bay comprises 1.8 miles of living shoreline and breakwaters, 137 acres of subtidal reef and 5 acres of intertidal reef. The Big Island component (5,200-ft outer riprap breakwater plus 2,800-ft inner breakwater of wave attenuation devices/OysterBreaks) and the Deer Island subtidal reef (expanded from 20 to 90 acres) were fully permitted in 2021 and moved to construction, while the St. Louis Bay living shoreline component is in permitting.
stories.water: Back Bay of Biloxi (Big Island, Deer Island)
stories.notes: Construction completion not confirmed on fetched pages; fact sheet https://www.mdeq.ms.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Mississippi-Project-Fact-sheet-Phase-IV-11_9_2020.pdf. Caller may wish to verify status before mapping.

stories.title: Mississippi Coastal Streams and Habitat Initiative
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality
stories.desc: An early GEBF award establishing a coastal streams and habitat restoration initiative in Mississippi, funding stream and wetland restoration work across the state's coastal watersheds. Awarded in 2013.
stories.notes: Programme-level award covering multiple coastal watersheds; pinned at a regional centre.

stories.title: Deer Island Oyster-Shell Breakwater and Reef (Mississippi GEMS)
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; Gulf of Mexico Community-based Restoration Partnership (NOAA, EPA Gulf of Mexico Program); Gulf of Mexico Foundation
stories.desc: On the northeast corner of Deer Island off Biloxi, DMR stacked and staked mesh bags of recycled oyster shell along about 800 linear ft of eroding shoreline to break wave energy, seeding live oysters at the base so a reef forms as the mesh rusts away. The $20,000 GCRP grant with DMR match was deployed beginning March 2010 as part of the larger effort to restore Deer Island to its pre-Katrina footprint.
stories.notes: Source is a DMR project summary written at deployment; outcomes not reported.

stories.title: Grand Bay NERR Intertidal and Subtidal Reefs (Bangs Bayou / Point aux Chenes Bay)
stories.orgs: Grand Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; U.S. Geological Survey; Mississippi State University
stories.desc: In 2021 the reserve built several artificial reefs of crushed limestone and oyster shell, intertidal reefs along Bangs Bayou and subtidal reefs in Point aux Chenes Bay, to reduce shoreline erosion and increase secondary productivity. USGS is tracking sediment accretion with shoreline transects and sedimentation tiles, MSU monitors vegetation and benthic invertebrates, and reserve staff sample the fish community using the reefs.
stories.water: Bangs Bayou / Point aux Chenes Bay (Grand Bay)
stories.notes: Effectiveness monitoring ongoing; no results yet reported.

stories.title: Grand Batture Habitat Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of the Grand Batture headland east of Pascagoula, rebuilding an eroding coastal landform and its associated marsh and nearshore habitat. Phase I was awarded in 2024.
stories.notes: Phase I award 2024; an earlier research pass found this at design stage, so treat as in progress.

stories.title: Tony Trapani Oyster Reef, Bay of St. Louis
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Mississippi Tidelands Fund; Mississippi Outdoor Stewardship Trust Fund
stories.desc: In summer 2024 TNC built a roughly 40-acre oyster reef in the Bay of St. Louis offshore of Pass Christian using 17,658 limestone pods stacked 1-2 ft high plus recycled oyster shell, expanding an existing 10-acre reef identified in MDEQ's oyster restoration program. The elevated reef in a harvest-closed area is designed to resist low oxygen and freshwater events and serve as brood stock for the Mississippi Sound while boosting recreational fish habitat.
stories.notes: Same project as NFWF 'Enhancement of St. Louis Bay Oyster Reef' (https://www.nfwf.org/sites/default/files/2020-04/ms-st-louis-bay-oysters-19.pdf). Monitoring results not yet published.

stories.title: Round Island Marsh Restoration with Dredged Material
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund)
stories.desc: Using more than $56 million in GEBF beneficial-use funding, MDEQ rebuilt Round Island off Pascagoula with dredged sediment, creating about 220 acres of island, marsh and beach habitat (constructed 2016). NFWF reports the restored island is already providing nesting habitat for shorebirds and seabirds, along with storm protection and recreation; a second GEBF phase is expanding beneficial-use sites at Greenwood Island, Wolf River and Beardslee Lake.
stories.notes: Supporting fact sheets: https://www.nfwf.org/sites/default/files/2020-04/ms-dredge-marsh-i-14.pdf and MDEQ Round Island page https://www.mdeq.ms.gov/marine-debris-removal-round-island-monitoring-services-form/ (island created 2016 from beneficial-use sediment).

stories.title: USM-ERDC Experimental Oyster Reef Restoration, Mississippi Sound
stories.orgs: University of Southern Mississippi Gulf Coast Research Laboratory; U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Ecosystem Management and Restoration Research Program
stories.desc: USM and ERDC built limestone base reefs on eight one-acre experimental plots within two 50-acre reef sites each near Bay St. Louis and Pascagoula, completing the base layer in 2024 with limestone gravel capping planned for 2025. The reefs test designs that maximize oyster recovery and will be monitored for use by tagged Gulf sturgeon.
stories.water: Mississippi Sound near Bay St. Louis and Pascagoula
stories.notes: Two project areas; coordinates given for the Bay St. Louis area. Monitoring results pending.

stories.title: Mississippi Oyster Cultch Early Restoration Phase I (western Mississippi Sound)
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; Deepwater Horizon NRDA Trustees
stories.desc: In fall 2012 and spring 2013, 141,321 cubic yards of limestone and 20,037 cubic yards of oyster shell were sprayed onto 1,430 acres of existing reef at Pass Christian (about 424 acres), Pass Marianne (809 acres), St. Joe's (100 acres) and Henderson Pass (about 100 acres) reefs in the western Mississippi Sound. Sampling 120 days after deployment found oysters growing on the new cultch; the $11 million project was monitored through 2020.
stories.water: Mississippi Sound (Pass Christian / Pass Marianne reefs)
stories.notes: Oyster reef enhancement for harvest-area reefs; coordinates are the Pass Christian reef area.

stories.title: Hancock County Marsh Living Shoreline (Deepwater Horizon early restoration)
stories.orgs: Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality; NOAA; Mississippi Trustee Implementation Group; Mississippi Department of Marine Resources; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
stories.desc: Along the Hancock County Coastal Preserve, Mississippi's largest contiguous salt marsh, MDEQ built about six miles of breakwaters (2017-2018), 46 acres of limestone oyster reef in Heron Bay and 46 acres of new marsh from dredged material (completed 2021), with Phase 6 adding 1.7 miles of breakwater in 2025 for 7.6 miles total. Shorelines that had eroded 6-10 ft per year have stabilized and in places gained 1.5-4 ft despite 13 tropical storms, bivalve density on the reefs exceeds project goals, and the $65.5 million project won second place worldwide in PIANC's Working with Nature awards.
stories.notes: Alternate links: https://www.gulfspillrestoration.noaa.gov/2021/07/living-shoreline-projects-move-forward-florida-wrap-mississippi (completion of marsh May 2021) and MS TIG 2025 annual update (Phase 6 completed Nov 2025).

stories.title: Pearl Creek Pond (Duke Field) Dam Removal
stories.orgs: U.S. Air Force (Duke Field, Eglin AFB range); listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory
stories.desc: A pond dam at Duke Field in Okaloosa County was removed from Pearl Creek in 2023, a military-lands aquatic connectivity project in the Yellow River basin of the Florida panhandle. Removal restores free flow and passage on a sandhill stream. The annual summary records the removal but does not report height, mileage or further partners.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2023 compiled summaries table (PDF verified), which gives the alternate name 'Duke Field Dam'. Air Force ownership inferred from that name. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Crooked Creek (Clearwater) Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Crooked Creek Dam, also recorded as the Clearwater Dam, was removed in Gadsden County in 2023, restoring free flow and aquatic organism passage on a tributary in the Apalachicola basin of the Florida panhandle. The annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2023 compiled summaries table (PDF verified). Exact site not given; lat/lon approximate within Gadsden County.

stories.title: Floridatown Park Shoreline Marsh Planting (Pace)
stories.orgs: Pensacola & Perdido Bays Estuary Program; EscaRosa Oyster Corps (AmeriCorps); Pace High School; Santa Rosa County
stories.desc: Oyster Corps members and Pace High School students planted more than 100 saltmeadow cordgrass plugs along the eroding Escambia Bay shoreline at Floridatown Park in May 2023, supplementing and monitoring a 2022 planting. In its first year the Corps recycled 57.75 tons of oyster shell and supplied 33,000 plants to regional restoration projects.
stories.notes: Small-scale volunteer planting.

stories.title: Crooked Creek Dam Removal, Apalachicola River Basin
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Panama City Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office; private landowner; Bipartisan Infrastructure Law
stories.desc: FWS biologists removed a longstanding dam on Crooked Creek, a tributary system of the Apalachicola River, on private land with the landowner's cooperation. The roughly $150,000 project reopened more than two miles of creek to endangered freshwater mussels, their host fish and Gulf sturgeon, covered about 10 acres including bank restoration with sod, plants and shrubs, and restored natural flow of roughly 1.5 million gallons of water annually.
stories.notes: Story confirms removal completed; exact completion date not stated. Location approximate within Gadsden County.

stories.title: Dam Removal and Stream Restoration in Florida (three barriers)
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program); Golden Triangle Resource Conservation & Development Council; private landowners
stories.desc: A $600,000 National Fish Passage Program package removing three barriers: an earthen dam on private land in Apalachicola River tributaries, a weir dam on the Myakka River, and a barrier on the Econlockhatchee River. The FWS project page lists 135 stream miles reopened. Expected beneficiaries include five federally listed freshwater mussels, Gulf sturgeon and Florida manatee.
stories.water: Apalachicola River tributaries; Myakka River; Econlockhatchee River
stories.notes: Three widely separated sites in one funded project; coordinates given for the Gadsden County (Apalachicola) component. Project status listed as Active with 135 stream miles reopened. The Gadsden component is likely the same work described at https://www.fws.gov/story/2024-05/fish-passage-and-bipartisan-infrastructure-law .

stories.title: Pensacola East Bay Oyster Habitat Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Santa Rosa County; Northwest Florida Water Management District; The Nature Conservancy in Florida; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund; Pensacola and Perdido Bays Estuary Program
lpOrgs: Pensacola and Perdido Bays Estuary Program
stories.desc: TNC constructed 33 oyster reefs along approximately 6.5 miles (about 34,300 linear feet) of shoreline in East Bay and Blackwater Bay within the Pensacola Bay System, the largest-scale estuarine habitat restoration TNC has undertaken in Florida. The project was funded by the NFWF Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund established after the 2010 Deepwater Horizon spill. Pre- and post-construction monitoring tracks oyster recruitment and the fish, crab and bird use the reefs attract, and the reefs are also intended to promote seagrass growth in their lee.
stories.water: East Bay and Blackwater Bay, Pensacola Bay System
stories.notes: Construction year not stated on the page (published 2018, updated 2022); year is approximate. Nearest town inferred; coordinates approximate within East Bay.

stories.title: Choctawhatchee Bay Smooth Cordgrass Shoreline Planting (Bluewater Bay)
stories.orgs: Coastal Conservation Association Florida; Okaloosa County Natural Resources; Choctawhatchee Basin Alliance; OysterCorps / Franklin's Promise Coalition; Duke Energy
stories.desc: In July 2025 partners planted about 4,000 smooth cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora) plugs along an eroding shoreline of Choctawhatchee Bay near Bluewater Bay Marina to stabilize sediment and build salt-marsh living-shoreline habitat.
stories.notes: Described in CCA Florida's 2025 habitat update; type could also be classed Living shoreline / coastal.

stories.title: Pensacola Bay Living Shoreline: White Island Habitat Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Florida Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: GEBF-funded living shoreline and habitat restoration at White Island in Pensacola Bay, protecting and rebuilding marsh and reef habitat on an eroding bay island. Awarded in 2021 with a 2025 amendment.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; amendment dated 2025 suggests work was still under way.

stories.title: Kelley Branch Dam and Stream-Crossing Removal (Apalachicola Bluffs and Ravines Preserve)
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy
stories.desc: In 2007 TNC removed a dam and a stream crossing from Kelley Branch, a steephead tributary of the Apalachicola River on its Apalachicola Bluffs and Ravines Preserve near Alum Bluff, structures that were degrading the channel and blocking fish passage. The preserve's work was an early Southeast example of small-dam removal for stream restoration; the restored reach is visible from the Kelley Branch spur trail.
stories.notes: Page gives no length or partner details; photo is of the Apalachicola River from Alum Bluff, not the project.

stories.title: Bayou Chico Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Escambia County; Florida Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of Bayou Chico in Pensacola, an industrialised urban bayou, combining sediment and habitat work to restore estuarine function and water quality. Awarded in 2014.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Pensacola Bay Living Shoreline – Project GreenShores Site II
stories.orgs: Florida DEP; NOAA; Florida Deepwater Horizon Trustee Implementation Group; City of Pensacola
stories.desc: A $10.8 million Deepwater Horizon early-restoration living shoreline along Pensacola's urban bayfront, building on the original Project GreenShores. Four acres of rock breakwaters were built to dampen wave energy and provide oyster reef habitat, with up to nine acres of salt marsh created behind them. Construction began in mid-2021 with completion scheduled for 2022; NOAA leads post-construction monitoring.
stories.notes: Completion not confirmed on the fetched page (construction scheduled to end March 2022). Alternate description at https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/feature-story/three-living-shorelines-creating-habitat-protecting-gulf-coast

stories.title: Panhandle Dune Ecosystem Restoration Project
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; University of Florida; Franklin's Promise Coalition; Eglin Air Force Base; National Park Service (Gulf Islands National Seashore); private landowners
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: A $6.4 million NFWF-funded effort (partly Deepwater Horizon settlement funds) stabilizing 21 linear miles of degraded Gulf-front dunes across six Panhandle counties by planting about 800,000 sea oats, bitter panicum, Gulf bluestem and beach elder and fencing off fragile sand. Plantings and fencing at Eglin Air Force Base are showing early success, and a second phase adds roughly 570,000 plants at Gulf Islands National Seashore. Companion work on Perdido Key is closing habitat gaps for the endangered Perdido Key beach mouse, whose population is now estimated at about 3,500 across a 17-mile stretch.
stories.town: Fort Walton Beach / Santa Rosa Beach area
stories.county: Escambia; Santa Rosa; Okaloosa; Walton; Bay; Gulf
stories.notes: Spans six counties; coordinates are a mid-point in Walton County. Coastal dune rather than in-water work, included as coastal habitat restoration with a described outcome.

stories.title: MK Ranch Hydrologic Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Florida Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: GEBF-funded hydrologic restoration at MK Ranch in the Florida Panhandle, restoring natural drainage patterns and wetland function on former ranch land to improve freshwater delivery and habitat downstream. Awarded in 2019.
stories.notes: Precise location not published in the GEBF list; coordinates are a Panhandle placeholder and should be refined before mapping at fine scale.

stories.title: Restoration of Florida's Coastal Dune Lakes
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Florida Department of Environmental Protection; Choctawhatchee Basin Alliance
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of Walton County's rare coastal dune lakes, a globally uncommon lake type found in only a handful of places worldwide, addressing shoreline erosion, stormwater inflows and habitat degradation around the lakes and their outfalls. Phase I was awarded in 2014 and phase II in 2018.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Suwannee Lake Fish Management Area Restoration
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida Legislature; Suwannee County
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Drained the 63-acre man-made Suwannee Lake, removed about 60,000 cubic yards of organic muck, added submerged log piles and varied bottom contours, planted native vegetation, improved angler access, then refilled and restocked with forage fish and Florida-strain largemouth bass (2013–2015, $600,000). Rebuilt the degraded sport fishery toward trophy bass production.

stories.title: Sweetwater Creek Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: A dam was removed from Sweetwater Creek in Liberty County in 2023, restoring free-flowing conditions on a steephead stream in the Apalachicola River corridor, a nationally significant hotspot for aquatic biodiversity. The annual summary records the removal but gives no height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.notes: Record derived from the 2023 compiled summaries table (PDF verified). Lat/lon approximate within Liberty County.

stories.title: M/V El Dorado Grounding Site Seagrass Restoration (North Bay)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; U.S. Coast Guard; NOAA; FEMA; St. Andrew and St. Joseph Bays Estuary Program; UF/IFAS Bay County Extension – Florida Sea Grant; Florida DEP
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
St. Andrew and St. Joseph Bays Estuary Program
stories.desc: After the 147-foot vessel El Dorado grounded on a seagrass bed in North Bay during Hurricane Michael (2018), the vessel was removed, the 1,000-foot extraction path and a 0.2-acre depression were filled to grade, and in May 2023 36 volunteers planted more than 1,400 bare-root Cuban shoal grass units harvested from nearby donor beds. Monitoring of regrowth continued through 2024.
stories.notes: Small footprint (0.2 acre); link is an FWC PDF fact sheet.

stories.title: West Bay Oyster Reef and Seagrass Restoration (St. Andrew Bay)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; St. Andrew Bay Watch; UF/IFAS Bay County Extension – Florida Sea Grant; Florida Dept. of Agriculture and Consumer Services; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Panama City Marine Institute; St. Andrew and St. Joseph Bays Estuary Program; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
St. Andrew and St. Joseph Bays Estuary Program
stories.desc: Along the western shoreline of West Bay, which had lost more than 200 acres of seagrass since the 1930s, FWC built more than five acres of low subtidal oyster reef from recycled and fossil shell, limestone and coir (2015-2019) and transplanted more than eight acres of bare-root Cuban shoal grass from donor beds (2019-2021). Volunteers contributed over 2,000 hours; the project pioneered coir-contained reefs and bare-root shoal grass transplanting in northwest Florida.
stories.notes: Link is an FWC PDF fact sheet.

stories.title: Oyster Reef Habitat Restoration in St. Andrew Bay
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: GEBF-funded construction of oyster reef habitat in St. Andrew Bay on the Florida Panhandle, placing cultch to re-establish reef on bay bottom that had lost its oyster habitat. Awarded in 2014.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list. Related to the FWC West Bay oyster and seagrass project already in this dataset.

stories.title: St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge Saltmarsh Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (St. Marks NWR)
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of salt marsh at St. Marks National Wildlife Refuge on Apalachee Bay, re-establishing tidal marsh habitat and natural hydrology within the refuge. Phase I was awarded in 2019.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Black Creek Tributary Stream-Crossing Stabilization for Black Creek Crayfish (Camp Blanding and Jennings State Forest)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida Department of Military Affairs (Camp Blanding Joint Training Center); Florida Forest Service; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: To cut erosion and turbidity from military, forestry and public vehicle crossings of blackwater tributaries of Black Creek, partners hardened about 55 stream crossings (3,800 tons of granite at 35 crossings on Camp Blanding; 160 tons of granite, 975 tons of topsoil, 282 tons of slag and new pipe at Jennings State Forest) and replaced culverts to restore flow. Protects habitat for the endemic Black Creek crayfish across ~1,750 acres; Camp Blanding received the USFWS Military Conservation Partner Award in 2018.
stories.notes: Completion year not stated; award received 2018.

stories.title: Tate's Hell State Forest Hydrologic Restoration
stories.orgs: Northwest Florida Water Management District; Florida Forest Service; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; State of Florida
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Across the ~205,000-acre Tate's Hell State Forest, acquired from timber companies beginning in 1994, the District and Florida Forest Service have been removing logging roads and roadside ditches (more than 800 miles were built), installing ditch plugs, flashboard risers, low-water crossings and new culverts, and revegetating with cypress, longleaf pine and wiregrass under a 2010–2020 Hydrologic Restoration Plan. Goal is to restore historic sheetflow and wetland hydrology and improve freshwater delivery to East Bay and Apalachicola Bay.
stories.water: Tate's Hell wetlands / East Bay tributaries
stories.notes: Page gives no quantities of roads removed or ditches plugged; described as a multi-decade effort.

stories.title: Apalachicola River Slough Restoration (East River, Douglas Slough, Spiders Cut)
stories.orgs: Apalachicola Riverkeeper; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (funder); First Line Coastal; Fishhunter Enterprise; Gulf Corps; Conservation Pathways; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; Franklin and Gulf counties
stories.desc: A $4.7 million NFWF-funded project removed dredge-spoil sand plugs from the mouth and channel of East River (about 14 river miles above Apalachicola) and cleared fallen trees and sand from Spiders Cut and Douglas Slough, which link the Apalachicola, Chipola and Brothers rivers. Begun in 2020 and now complete, the work restores freshwater and nutrient flow through the floodplain to East Bay, supporting oysters, blue crabs, tupelo swamp and the slough fishery; sand was reused for county roads and fish and vegetation surveys were conducted.
stories.water: Apalachicola River (East River, Douglas Slough, Spiders Cut)
stories.notes: Riverine floodplain hydrologic restoration feeding Apalachicola Bay; sites span Franklin and Gulf counties; completion year not stated on page.

stories.title: Santa Fe Spring Bank Restoration
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Alachua Conservation Trust
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: On a 254-acre Alachua Conservation Trust property acquired in 2020, FWC contractors removed a collapsing homestead from the eroding spring-run bank, regraded two bank sections along the Santa Fe River and the Santa Fe Spring run to natural slopes, stabilized them with riprap and natural-fiber matting, and planted native shrubs and grasses. Halted major erosion and sedimentation threatening habitat of freshwater mussels including the federally endangered oval pigtoe, and keeps the second-magnitude spring connected to the river.
stories.water: Santa Fe Spring / Santa Fe River
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (Santa Fe River, Columbia County side near High Springs).

stories.title: Franklin County Living Shoreline
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Florida Department of Environmental Protection; Franklin County
stories.desc: GEBF-funded living shoreline construction in Franklin County on Apalachicola Bay, using breakwaters and marsh planting to halt shoreline erosion and build oyster and marsh habitat. Awarded in 2020.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list. Related to the Cat Point living shoreline already in this dataset.

stories.title: Cat Point Living Shoreline (Apalachicola Bay)
stories.orgs: Florida DEP (Central Panhandle Aquatic Preserves / Apalachicola NERR); Florida Deepwater Horizon Trustee Implementation Group; UF/IFAS; Duke Energy; Conservation Corps of the Forgotten and Emerald Coasts
stories.desc: Deepwater Horizon early-restoration project that converted an eroding shoreline near Eastpoint into salt marsh: 16 breakwater structures forming a 1,300-foot backbone shield the shore, a protected zone behind them supports oyster restoration, and 20,634 native marsh grasses were planted. The site now provides nursery habitat for juvenile fish, crabs, shrimp and wading birds and received the 2023 ASBPA Best Restored Shores Award; monitoring continues through 2025.
stories.notes: Completion year not stated on page; construction and planting finished before the Oct 2023 award.

stories.title: Apalachicola Bay Oyster Restoration (Phases I and II)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida State University; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: A GEBF programme to rebuild oyster reef in Apalachicola Bay, which once held more than 10,000 acres of reef. Phase I was awarded in 2013 and Phase II in November 2019 at $20,057,000, targeting up to 1,000 acres of reef construction, with harvest management strategies for Apalachicola Bay and Suwannee Sound and FSU water-quality and hydrodynamic data used to select cultch deployment sites.
stories.notes: Phase II fact sheet lists status as active; treat as in progress rather than complete.

stories.title: Florida Panhandle Oyster Cultch Placement (Pensacola, St. Andrew, Apalachicola Bays)
stories.orgs: Florida Deepwater Horizon Trustees; Florida DEP; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Apalachicola National Estuarine Research Reserve
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: A $5 million Deepwater Horizon early-restoration project placed about 62,000 cubic yards of cultch (shell and limestone) over roughly 300 acres of existing oyster bars in Pensacola, St. Andrew and Apalachicola bays to provide settlement substrate for native oyster larvae. Placement was completed in April 2017; ANERR is monitoring oyster habitat enhancement in each bay for ten years.
stories.water: Apalachicola Bay (also Pensacola Bay and St. Andrew Bay)
stories.notes: Multi-bay project; coordinates placed on Apalachicola Bay, the largest component.

stories.title: Sweetwater Wetlands Park – Sweetwater Branch sheetflow restoration to Paynes Prairie
stories.orgs: City of Gainesville; St. Johns River Water Management District; Paynes Prairie Preserve State Park (Florida DEP)
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: Constructed a 125-acre treatment wetland and removed the 1930s drainage ditch that had carried Sweetwater Branch straight to Alachua Sink, restoring natural sheetflow across more than 1,300 acres of Paynes Prairie wetlands that had dried out. Completed in 2015, the project improves water quality entering the prairie, Alachua Sink and the Floridan aquifer, and created high-quality wetland habitat within the state preserve.
stories.water: Sweetwater Branch / Paynes Prairie / Alachua Sink
stories.notes: Described on SJRWMD Orange Creek Basin page; City of Gainesville park page would be an alternate link.

stories.title: Fanning Springs Spring-Run Restoration
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; The Nature Conservancy; Florida DEP (Fanning Springs State Park)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: A diver with a hand-held suction device removed and sifted more than 500 cubic yards of accumulated sediment from Fanning Springs and its run to the Suwannee River (November 2011–January 2012, $96,000), deepening parts of the spring by 2–3 feet. Restored the spring run and expanded winter warm-water refuge and access for manatees.

stories.title: Lake George / St. Johns River Eelgrass Restoration
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (Aquatic Habitat Conservation and Restoration)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: After Hurricane Irma (2017) eliminated eelgrass from Lake George and the middle St. Johns River, FWC began planting eelgrass inside fenced grazing exclosures in 2020; by 2025 more than 90 acres (about 1 million plants) were planted within 41 enclosures protecting over 155 acres, with another million plants planned for 2026 plus 350,000 bulrush across Lakes George, Dexter, Woodruff, Beresford, Monroe and Harney. Enclosures showed grazing was blocking natural recovery; eelgrass and other native SAV are re-establishing inside the protected plots.
stories.water: Lake George / St. Johns River / Silver Glen Spring
stories.notes: Project sheet: https://myfwc.com/media/ootfglzp/lake-george-eelgrass.pdf

stories.title: Recovery and Resilience of Oyster Reefs in Florida's Big Bend
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); The Nature Conservancy; University of Florida
stories.desc: GEBF-funded oyster reef restoration along Florida's Big Bend coast, rebuilding degraded nearshore reefs that support oystercatchers and nursery habitat for fish and crabs. Awarded in 2016.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; coordinates placed at Cedar Key as the centre of the Big Bend reef work.

stories.title: Ocklawaha Prairie Restoration Area – tussock removal and historic channel reopening
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (Aquatic Habitat Conservation and Restoration); St. Johns River Water Management District
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: On this 3,000-acre impounded former floodplain (purchased 1991; previous owner cleared the river channel and filled ditches), FWC used mechanical plant shredders to break up about 150 acres of floating tussocks created after Hurricane Irma, reconnected the north and south open-water pools, and cleared the southern 3.4 miles of the historic Ocklawaha River channel. Result: smaller tussock fields, return of native aquatic plants, improved water exchange and a travel corridor for fish and wildlife, and expanded deep-marsh refuge habitat.
stories.notes: FWC PDF gives no completion date; work followed 2017 Hurricane Irma. SJRWMD context page: https://www.sjrwmd.com/waterways/upper-ocklawaha-river/

stories.title: Sunnyhill Restoration Area – Ocklawaha River floodplain marsh restoration
stories.orgs: St. Johns River Water Management District; USDA
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: On about 2,800 acres of former floodplain farmland purchased in 1988, SJRWMD installed water control structures, built and enhanced levees and cleared vegetation to return flow to more than eight miles of the historic Ocklawaha River channel through a mosaic of wetland habitat adjoining Ocala National Forest. The restored channel and marsh now support wetland wildlife and miles of public trails.
stories.notes: Exact completion year not stated on the page.

stories.title: New Smyrna Beach Saltmarsh Restoration (Marine Discovery Center)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; NOAA Restoration Center; Marine Discovery Center; Costa del Mar; Wildlife Foundation of Florida; Volusia County
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: On the 22-acre former New Smyrna Beach High School site on Mosquito Lagoon, FWC removed more than 45,000 cubic yards of fill over five months in 2014 and graded a new marsh surface, restoring five acres of historic salt marsh; volunteers planted over 25,000 native plants. Shoreline terraces and seawall demonstrations, a kayak launch, trails and signage were added, and the marsh now serves as nursery habitat and a regional source of plants for other restoration projects. The living shoreline showed no visible damage during Hurricane Matthew (2016).
stories.notes: Link is an FWC PDF fact sheet; hurricane performance noted at https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/feature-story/three-living-shorelines-creating-habitat-protecting-gulf-coast

stories.title: Dragline-Ditched Coastal Salt Marsh Restoration (Volusia County)
stories.orgs: Volusia County Mosquito Control; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Coastal Wetlands Conservation Grant); Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; St. Johns River Water Management District
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: Mid-20th-century dragline mosquito ditching had removed up to 80% of vegetated marsh along Mosquito Lagoon. Using a county-owned amphibious excavator, spoil piles were cleared of vegetation and pushed back into the ditches and graded to marsh elevation, restoring 283 acres of coastal salt marsh (140 acres returned to proper elevation) for about $1.2 million between 2009 and 2012. Vegetated wetland area roughly doubled, black mangrove and glasswort colonized within months to years, fish and crustacean production increased (about 50 lb of resident fish per acre per year) and mosquito breeding did not rise.
stories.notes: Link is an FWC PDF fact sheet; coordinates approximate for the Volusia County marsh complex.

stories.title: Turtle Mound and Canaveral National Seashore Living Shorelines (UCF CEELAB)
stories.orgs: University of Central Florida CEELAB; National Park Service (Canaveral National Seashore); Florida State Parks; Marine Discovery Center; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Brevard County; Florida Sea Grant
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Since 2011 UCF has stabilized 7.3 km of eroding shoreline at culturally important shell-midden sites, beginning with Turtle Mound (2011) and Eldora House (2012) in Canaveral National Seashore using oyster-shell bags and planted mangroves and cordgrass. Sites completed by 2020 now have 90-100% vegetation cover with mangroves over 4 m tall; 2022 work used non-plastic materials with 88% mangrove survival, and 1,115 linear feet of highly eroded shoreline at Middle Island was stabilized in 2023. More than 10,600 volunteers have participated.
stories.notes: Program also includes sites at DeSoto National Memorial, Tomoka, Fort Mose, Washington Oaks and Gamble Rogers state parks; coordinates placed at Turtle Mound.

stories.title: Emeralda Marsh Conservation Area – levee breaching and reconnection to Lake Griffin
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; St. Johns River Water Management District; Lake County
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: On former muck farms diked in the 1950s on the northeast shore of Lake Griffin, FWC and SJRWMD excavated 2,270 feet of levee to create six internal and seven external breaches in Area 3, built four planted habitat islands from the spoil, and removed about 220 acres of floating tussock; across the conservation area roughly 2,000 acres of marsh have been reconnected to Lake Griffin. Filtered marsh water again reaches the lake, native plant diversity increased, and Area 3 now supports a bass fishery, waterfowl hunting and wildlife viewing.
stories.notes: Area 5 peat removal (3.4 million cu yd) is still in progress under a 2016–2031 lease: https://www.sjrwmd.com/projects/emeralda-marsh-project/

stories.title: Hunter Springs Park Living Shoreline
stories.orgs: Southwest Florida Water Management District; City of Crystal River
stories.desc: Replaced a degraded bulkhead at Hunter Springs Park on Kings Bay with a living shoreline of limestone rock, sand, gentler slopes and native plantings (sawgrass, needle rush) plus in-water eelgrass, completed October 2016 as the District's first living shoreline in a spring system. Restores shoreline habitat, reduces erosion and nutrient inputs to Kings Bay, and serves as a demonstration for waterfront homeowners.
stories.notes: Freshwater spring-fed bay (tidally influenced).

stories.title: Hunters Cove Eelgrass Revegetation (Kings Bay pilot)
stories.orgs: Southwest Florida Water Management District; Duke Energy Florida (Mariculture Center); FWC Fish and Wildlife Research Institute; UF/IFAS
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Pilot project that removed invasive Lyngbya algae from about 10 acres of Hunters Cove in Kings Bay, then laid eelgrass grown on coconut-coir mats onto the cleared bottom like sod, with exclosure fencing to keep manatees from grazing the plants before establishment (completed 2017). Provided manatee forage and habitat and generated planting lessons that informed the larger Kings Bay Restoration Project.

stories.title: Kings Bay Restoration Project (Save Crystal River Lyngbya removal and eelgrass planting)
stories.orgs: Save Crystal River (nonprofit, Rotary origin); Sea & Shoreline (contractor); Florida Legislature (state appropriations); City of Crystal River
stories.desc: Beginning with a 2015 state appropriation, contractors vacuum-removed Lyngbya algae and detrital muck (hundreds of thousands of pounds) from residential canals and open water of Kings Bay down to the natural sand bottom, then replanted native eelgrass in protective cages and maintained the plantings. The initial goal of 100 acres restored in Phases 1–5 was reached by July 2023; a further 85 acres (Phases 5–7) are underway, with restored canals showing clear water and dense eelgrass beds used by manatees.
stories.notes: Site figures (e.g., '890+ acres cleaned', '785,000+ lb removed') are ambiguously laid out; verify before citing. Homepage: https://savecrystalriver.com

stories.title: Pine Meadows Conservation Area Hydrologic and Habitat Restoration
stories.orgs: Lake County Division of Parks and Trails; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; St. Johns River Water Management District (former owner)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: On a wetland diked and drained for farming in the early 1970s, partners replaced failing water control structures, built a limestone access road, aerially treated exotic plants and used harvesters and shredders to remove floating tussocks (restoration began 2016; opened to the public May 2018). Water flow and retention were returned to near pre-farming conditions and native plants expanded as exotics were controlled.
stories.water: Pine Meadows (Trout Lake / Lake Eustis watershed)
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (north of Eustis).

stories.title: Three Sisters Springs Shoreline (Bank) Stabilization
stories.orgs: Southwest Florida Water Management District; City of Crystal River; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida DEP
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Restored about 1,100 feet of eroded, undercut shoreline around the Three Sisters Springs headsprings by hand-placing soil bags, setting limestone boulders with a barge-mounted excavator, and planting native wetland vegetation (April–November 2016, ~$777,000). Stabilized banks reduce sediment entering the spring vents, cut tree-fall hazards, add fish cover below the waterline and expand winter warm-water refuge for manatees.
stories.notes: FWC project sheet: https://myfwc.com/media/u0vl1tvv/three-sisters-springs-restoration.pdf Also documented at: https://www.swfwmd.state.fl.us/projects/springs/three-sisters-springs-canal-stabilization-project

stories.title: Three Sisters Springs Wetland Treatment Project
stories.orgs: Southwest Florida Water Management District; City of Crystal River; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: Converted about 6 acres of the 57-acre Three Sisters Springs property into a constructed wetland that intercepts runoff from more than 100 acres of commercial and residential land before it reaches Kings Bay, removed non-native and nuisance vegetation, planted bald cypress and sawgrass, and filled about 1 acre of a man-made lake to create forested swamp (built February 2015–2016). Re-creates wetland function lost to 1960s–70s dredge-and-fill and reduces nutrient loading to the springs.

stories.title: Lake Yale Tussock Removal and Habitat Restoration
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Lake County Water Authority; Lake County Parks and Trails
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Mechanical harvesters removed more than 10 acres of floating tussock mats that formed on the south end of Lake Yale (Harris Chain of Lakes) after a 2013 drought followed by Hurricane Irma's high water, hauling material to upland storage. Opened habitat for emergent and submersed native plants to recolonize and restored fishing, waterfowl hunting and boating access.

stories.title: Mosquito Lagoon Intertidal Oyster Reef Restoration (UCF CEELAB)
stories.orgs: University of Central Florida Coastal and Estuarine Ecology Lab (Dr. Linda Walters); Canaveral National Seashore / National Park Service; Indian River Lagoon NEP; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Marine Discovery Center; Coastal Conservation Association Florida; Brevard Zoo
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Since 2007 UCF and partners have restored 97 boat-wake-damaged intertidal oyster reefs (about 4 acres) in Mosquito Lagoon using oyster-shell mats and, since 2022, fully biodegradable materials, with help from more than 51,000 volunteers. Live oyster density on 2007 reefs remains about 896 per square meter, substrate for an estimated 14 million oysters has been supplied, and shoal grass has recruited naturally beside 26% of restored reefs.
stories.notes: Reefs span Volusia and Brevard portions of Canaveral National Seashore.

stories.title: Harris Bayou wetland restoration (Lake Harris–Lake Griffin reconnection)
stories.orgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: SJRWMD purchased the former S.N. Knight farm between Lake Harris and Lake Griffin in 1992 and restored its wetlands, creating the Harris Bayou flow-way that allows up to 1,000 cfs to move from Lake Harris to Lake Griffin and supplements Haynes Creek flow through the Harris Chain of Lakes. The restored bayou improves flood management and lake-level control while providing marsh habitat.
stories.water: Harris Bayou / Lake Harris / Lake Griffin
stories.notes: Acreage and completion year not stated on the page; photo is a .gif map.

stories.title: Chassahowitzka Springs Restoration (sediment removal)
stories.orgs: Southwest Florida Water Management District; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; Florida Division of Historical Resources
stories.desc: Vacuum-pumped accumulated sand and organic sediment that had washed in from residential canals and stormwater out of the Chassahowitzka headsprings into filter bags, deepening the spring area by 2–4 feet and removing an estimated 500 lb of phosphorus and 7,600 lb of nitrogen; work was timed outside manatee season. Restored bottom habitat and clarity for aquatic plants and animals; sediment was reused on nearby land and artifacts (including a ~2,000-year-old intact Native American bowl) were recovered.
stories.notes: Listed as completed on https://www.swfwmd.state.fl.us/projects/springs/chassahowitzka; photo is from the parent springs page.

stories.title: Lake Apopka Restoration – North Shore wetlands, Marsh Flow-Way and SAV replanting
stories.orgs: St. Johns River Water Management District; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida DEP; Florida Legislature; Orange Audubon; Friends of Lake Apopka
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Following the 1996 state-directed purchase of north-shore muck farms, SJRWMD converted thousands of acres of diked farmland back to wetlands, has operated a 760-acre Marsh Flow-Way since 2003 (filtering ~30% of lake volume per year and removing ~77,500 tons of solids and 38.9 tons of phosphorus), harvests ~750,000 lb of gizzard shad annually, and since 2021 has planted 174 acres (880,000 plants) of eelgrass and pondweed plus 28,000 floating-leaved lilies. Phosphorus is down 66% and clarity up 52% since the late 1980s; the 2024 survey found native SAV along 95% of the shoreline (none in 1994) and the North Shore now hosts 377 bird species.
stories.notes: Alternate article: https://www.sjrwmd.com/streamlines/progress-in-motion-the-continuing-restoration-of-lake-apopka/

stories.title: Moore Creek (C-20A) Mosquito Impoundment Restoration, Merritt Island
stories.orgs: Indian River Lagoon National Estuary Program; St. Johns River Water Management District; Florida DEP; NOAA; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Merritt Island NWR)
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: Mosquito-control dikes isolating salt marsh from the Indian River Lagoon were pushed into their borrow ditches and the surface graded with GPS-guided dozers to intertidal elevations. About 13.5 miles of dike were removed, returning roughly 83 acres to functioning tidal wetland, at about one-third of the budgeted cost; a further ~14 miles of dike removal has been permitted. Earlier SJRWMD impoundment restorations (43 miles of dike by 2011) reached ~50% vegetation cover in 2-3 years and became nearly indistinguishable from natural marsh within a decade.
stories.notes: Link is an IRLNEP podcast/transcript page; lagoon-wide, ~25,800 impoundment acres have been reconnected via culverts.

stories.title: Weeki Wachee Springs Restoration (headspring sediment and Lyngbya removal)
stories.orgs: Southwest Florida Water Management District; State of Florida; Hernando County; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida DEP; Weeki Wachee Springs State Park
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Contractors removed accumulated sand, silt, muck, debris and invasive Lyngbya algae and other exotic vegetation by hand and vacuum dredge from the spring vent to the park's boat dock, and replanted native vegetation (completed 2009, following a 2008 stormwater project treating runoff from US 19 and the park lot). Improved water quality and native habitat in the headspring and upper river.
stories.notes: No quantitative scale given on page. Also documented at: https://www.swfwmd.state.fl.us/projects/springs/weeki-wachee-channel-restoration-project

stories.title: Disney Wilderness Preserve Wetland Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; The Walt Disney Company; Greater Orlando Aviation Authority; State of Florida
stories.desc: On the former 8,500-acre Walker Ranch at the headwaters of the Everglades (Kissimmee basin), TNC restored drained pasture back to wetlands as mitigation for Disney and Orlando airport expansion, later adding 3,000 acres bought and restored by Disney in 2014; the 11,500-acre preserve now holds 3,500 acres of restored wetlands draining to Lake Russell and Reedy Creek. One of the earliest and largest wetland mitigation projects in the U.S., it served as a model for Florida's mitigation banking and the Everglades Headwaters NWR.
stories.notes: Page gives no ditch-fill quantities or hydrologic monitoring results.

stories.title: Bird Island Rookery Shoreline and Oyster Reef Restoration (Melbourne)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (Aquatic Habitat Conservation and Restoration); Marine Resources Council; Brevard Zoo
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: On an eroding mangrove rookery island in the Indian River Lagoon next to downtown Melbourne, FWC removed failed oyster-bag reefs and reused the shell to armor the island's shoreline, built new offshore breakwater reefs of limestone rock, dredged accumulated sand to raise elevation behind the breakwaters, and planted large red mangroves. The work improves nesting habitat for pelicans, herons, egrets and cormorants; Marine Resources Council and Brevard Zoo are monitoring.
stories.notes: Completion year not stated on the FWC PDF.
