stories.title: Crane Creek / M-1 Canal Flow Restoration (Melbourne)
stories.orgs: St. Johns River Water Management District; Brevard County; Florida DEP; City of Melbourne; City of West Melbourne
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
stories.desc: The M-1 Canal had rerouted roughly 5,300 acres of St. Johns River headwater drainage east into the Indian River Lagoon via Crane Creek. An operable weir, two pump stations, force mains and a stormwater treatment area west of I-95 were built (2023-2025, about $23 million) to return about 7 million gallons per day of freshwater and baseflow to the St. Johns River, cutting an estimated 24,000 lb/yr of nitrogen and 3,100 lb/yr of phosphorus from the lagoon. The system began operating in August 2025.
stories.water: Crane Creek / M-1 Canal (Indian River Lagoon and St. Johns River)
stories.notes: Hydrologic flow-restoration infrastructure benefiting the lagoon; borderline with water-quality projects.

stories.title: Ryckman Park Gabion-Corral Oyster Reef (Melbourne Beach)
stories.orgs: Restore Our Shores (East Coast Zoological Foundation / Brevard Zoo); volunteers
stories.desc: Starting in 2022 Restore Our Shores built a 900-square-foot plastic-free oyster reef at Ryckman Park in which shell-filled galvanized gabions corral loose recycled oyster shell, following earlier bagged-shell and gabion reefs in the Brevard County lagoon. After about a year of monitoring roughly 40,000 oysters had recruited and the reef supported more than 20 species; gabion reefs recruit about 40% more live oysters than the earlier mesh-bag method.
stories.notes: Program page rather than a single project page.

stories.title: Lake Conine Wetland Treatment and Shoreline Restoration (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: City of Winter Haven; Florida DEP Nonpoint Source Program; U.S. EPA (CWA 319); Florida Legislature
stories.desc: Built the Lake Hartridge stormwater treatment facility (sediment sump, 4-acre wetland detention area) and the South Lake Conine treatment project, which dredged organic soils, built berms, removed invasive plants and planted native aquatic vegetation in wetland marsh chambers treating a 328-acre drainage area. Lake Conine chlorophyll-a dropped from 46 µg/L (2007) to 16 µg/L (2020) and total phosphorus from 0.07 to 0.02 mg/L, now meeting state nutrient criteria.
stories.water: Lake Conine (Winter Haven Chain of Lakes)
stories.notes: Primarily stormwater-treatment wetlands; included because of constructed wetland, invasive removal and native planting components.

stories.title: Alligator Creek – Kapok Wetland and Floodplain Restoration (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: City of Clearwater; Southwest Florida Water Management District (SWIM); Pinellas-Anclote River Basin Board; Pinellas County; Florida DEP; U.S. EPA (CWA 319); UF/IFAS Extension
stories.desc: Removed a mobile home park from the 25-year floodplain of Alligator Creek and constructed 19.4 acres of herbaceous and forested wetlands on a 37-acre urban tract (Kapok Park) to restore floodplain function, stabilize the channel and treat runoff before it reaches Alligator Lake and Tampa Bay. Dissolved-oxygen exceedances fell from 48 of 90 samples (1999–2009) to 13 of 59 (2009–2013) and mean DO rose from 4.9 to 6.1 mg/L, above the state standard.
stories.notes: Listed on https://www.epa.gov/nps/nonpoint-source-success-stories-florida. Story does not explicitly state a 303(d) delisting.

stories.title: Kissimmee Chain of Lakes Revegetation and Tussock Management (Lake Kissimmee, Lake Hatchineha)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; University of Florida (Lake Rosalie research)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: From 2017–2024 FWC planted 686,635 native emergent plants (maidencane, Kissimmee grass, bulrush) in Lake Kissimmee, followed in 2025 by ~534,500 more grasses and bulrush plus 1,100 wetland trees and in 2026 by ~79,000 eelgrass and pondweed plants ($2.35 million, the agency's largest revegetation effort); on Lake Hatchineha 10 acres of dense tussock were shredded (2024–2025) and ~20 acres harvested (winter 2025–26). Everglade snail kites are already using the planted trees, and tussock removal improved fish habitat, wading-bird foraging and navigation.

stories.title: Alafia Banks Bird Sanctuary Living Shoreline Breakwater (Hillsborough Bay)
stories.orgs: Audubon Florida; The Mosaic Company; Port Tampa Bay; Living Shorelines Solutions; Cypress Gulf Development; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (Critical Wildlife Area)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: To stop erosion of Sunken Island and Bird Island, which host more than a dozen nesting waterbird species, Audubon installed breakwaters of concrete wave-attenuation devices along the islands' north shores in 500-foot sections with 12-foot gaps for marine life. The first 1,000 linear feet (2011-2014) were followed by about 5,000 feet completed in fall 2019, protecting over 6,000 feet of shoreline; calm water behind the structures provides foraging habitat and the concrete recruits oysters and barnacles. Invasive Brazilian pepper and lead trees were also removed.
stories.notes: Second article: https://www.audubon.org/florida/news/living-shorelines-protect-baby-birds

stories.title: Weedon Island Preserve Salt Marsh Restoration (St. Petersburg)
stories.orgs: Pinellas County Public Works and Parks & Conservation Resources; Southwest Florida Water Management District; U.S. Department of the Treasury (ARPA)
stories.desc: Across 41 acres of Weedon Island Preserve on Old Tampa Bay, Pinellas County removed man-made spoil mounds to expand black mangrove habitat and restored tidal flow by de-silting, dredging or filling historic mosquito ditches as a pilot for improved hydrology. Construction ran from spring 2024 to fall 2025 and is listed as complete, funded by ARPA, a SWFWMD grant and Penny for Pinellas.

stories.title: Saint Sebastian River Fish Habitat Restoration, Cypress Bend Community Preserve
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Peninsular Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office; Indian River County Conservation Lands Department; Friends of the Saint Sebastian River; local environmental NGOs
stories.desc: At the Cypress Bend Community Preserve, a former citrus grove bought by Indian River County, FWS led removal and treatment of invasive aquatic vegetation in priority areas identified by survey work, then replanted natives. About 1,500 emergent and submerged plants went in on the first trip, followed by 2,000 bare-root smartweed along the riverbank and more than 8,000 riparian and upland plants. The office continues monitoring native and invasive fish and plant species and is evaluating additional sites.
stories.notes: Combines invasive aquatic plant removal with riparian/in-stream native planting. Town not named in the story; Sebastian is the nearest named community.

stories.title: Fellsmere Water Management Area Wetland Restoration
stories.orgs: St. Johns River Water Management District; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Upper St. Johns River Basin Project)
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: About 10,000 acres of drained pasture and cropland in the St. Johns River headwaters west of Fellsmere were converted back to marsh and open water, including flooding Headwaters Lake after FWC sculpted lake and marsh bottoms for fish habitat. The floodplain restoration stores and treats stormwater, reduces freshwater discharges through the C-54 canal to the Indian River Lagoon, augments dry-season river flow, and supports snail kites, wood storks, wintering waterfowl and a popular bass fishery.
stories.water: Upper St. Johns River headwaters / Headwaters Lake
stories.notes: Freshwater floodplain project included because it reduces lagoon discharges; completion year not stated on page; may overlap with an inland slice.

stories.title: Upper St. Johns River Basin Project (Fellsmere, Six Mile Creek, Broadmoor marsh restoration)
stories.orgs: St. Johns River Water Management District; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Melbourne-Tillman Water Control District; Sun-Ag Inc.
lpOrgs: St. Johns River Water Management District
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Reconverted diked former pasture and cropland in the headwaters of the St. Johns River into a 166,500-acre system of marsh conservation areas and water management areas, including about 10,000 acres of restored wetland and open water at the Fellsmere Water Management Area and hydraulic reconnection of the Six Mile Creek and Broadmoor restoration areas to the river. Celebrated as complete in May 2016; stores up to 500,000 acre-feet of floodwater, reduces freshwater diversion to the Indian River Lagoon (Canal 1 rediversion cuts ~148,000 lb/yr nitrogen) and won the 2008 Thiess International Riverprize.
stories.water: Upper St. Johns River / Fellsmere WMA / Blue Cypress Marsh
stories.notes: Coordinates at Fellsmere Water Management Area; project spans ~2,000 sq mi.

stories.title: Clam Bayou Ecosystem Restoration (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: City of St. Petersburg; City of Gulfport; Southwest Florida Water Management District; Pinellas County; Florida DEP; U.S. EPA (CWA 319); UF/IFAS Extension
stories.desc: Restored or enhanced 24 acres of estuarine and coastal wetland habitat and built 20 acres of treatment ponds (including a 319-funded wet detention pond) treating runoff from about 2,560 urban acres draining to Clam Bayou and Boca Ciega Bay, plus boardwalks and a kayak launch. Estimated reductions of about 1,237 lb/yr nitrogen and 68,500 lb/yr suspended solids; chlorophyll-a fell below the impairment threshold from 2016–2019 and DEP scheduled the waterbody for 303(d) delisting in 2021.
stories.water: Clam Bayou Drain / Boca Ciega Bay
stories.notes: Tidal/estuarine site; may overlap with the coastal slice.

stories.title: Rock Ponds Ecosystem Restoration (Cockroach Bay, Tampa Bay)
stories.orgs: Southwest Florida Water Management District (SWIM Program); Hillsborough County Conservation and Environmental Lands Management; Tampa Bay Estuary Program; volunteers
stories.desc: The largest habitat restoration in Tampa Bay history converted 1,043 acres of former farmland and shell-mine pits adjacent to Cockroach Bay into 398 acres of estuarine and freshwater habitat (tidal channels, lagoons, marsh, islands, mudflats, limestone reefs, freshwater wetlands) and 645 acres of pine flatwoods and hammock, creating more than 16 miles of new shoreline. Work ran from 2009 to 2015 and moved 1.6 million cubic yards of earth and installed about 1.05 million plants (200,000 by 2,000 volunteers). Snook, tarpon, mullet, roseate spoonbills, manatees and widespread seagrass recruitment have been documented; the adjacent 500-acre Cockroach Bay restoration was completed in 2012.

stories.title: Robinson Preserve Coastal Habitat Restoration (Manatee County)
stories.orgs: Manatee County; NOAA Fisheries; RESTORE Council; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Mote Marine Laboratory; Tampa Bay Estuary Program; Southwest Florida Water Management District; Oyster River Ecology
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: A 482-acre former farm on lower Tampa Bay was restored in Phase 1 (completed 2008) by removing invasives, restoring wetlands and planting natives; a 150-acre donation and RESTORE-funded Phase 2 restored nearly 135 more acres of shellfish, seagrass, mangrove and salt/freshwater wetland habitat designed as snook and tarpon nursery with restricted-access water features. Monitoring found high numbers of juvenile snook, sheepshead and red drum, snook growth equal to or faster than other habitats, and tagged snook returning after spawning; the 700-acre preserve draws about 240,000 visitors a year and the $17 million effort supported 239 jobs. CCA Florida added 7.5 tons of recycled oyster shell in 2025.
stories.notes: Phase 2 completion year not stated on page.

stories.title: GT Bray Park Stream and Wetland Restoration (Bradenton)
stories.orgs: Sarasota Bay Estuary Program; Manatee County; City of Bradenton; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Two stormwater conveyance features draining to Sarasota Bay were retrofitted as habitat: a channelized stream on the park's west side was excavated (130,000 cubic yards) and invasive plants removed to create wetlands, and a stormwater pond was cleared of invasives and replanted. Over 10,000 native plants were installed by nearly 100 volunteers within a year of the September 2024 ribbon-cutting; created wetlands now stabilize banks and provide habitat for aquatic birds. Combined cost about $900,000.
stories.water: Stream/pond draining to Sarasota Bay (Palma Sola Bay watershed)
stories.notes: Urban stormwater-conveyance habitat retrofit; inland of the bay shoreline.

stories.title: FISH Preserve Coastal Wetland Restoration (Cortez)
stories.orgs: Florida Institute for Saltwater Heritage (FISH); Sarasota Bay Estuary Program; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Southwest Florida Water Management District; U.S. EPA; NOAA
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Multi-phase restoration of a 100-acre coastal preserve next to the historic Cortez fishing village on Sarasota Bay. Exotic vegetation was removed and new tidal waterways were excavated to reconnect flow to the bay and restore mangrove, marsh and aquatic habitat. The final phase was celebrated with a ribbon-cutting in November 2023; the site is now considered fully restored and supports osprey, mullet and wading birds.

stories.title: Kissimmee River Restoration Project
stories.orgs: South Florida Water Management District; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (Jacksonville District)
stories.desc: Backfilled 22 miles of the C-38 flood-control canal, removed two water control structures and reconnected remnant river channels, restoring continuous flow to 24 miles (44 miles of historic channel) of the meandering Kissimmee River and more than 40 square miles (about 20,000 acres) of floodplain wetlands between Lakes Kissimmee and Okeechobee. Construction completed with a July 2021 ribbon-cutting; wading birds, waterfowl (e.g., ring-necked duck, American avocet, black-necked stilt) and improved dissolved oxygen returned to restored reaches, with ecological response exceeding expectations per USACE.
stories.notes: Coordinates placed at the central restored reach (Phase I, near S-65B/C). Alternate link: https://www.saj.usace.army.mil/Missions/Environmental/Ecosystem-Restoration/Kissimmee-River-Restoration/

stories.title: Longboat Key Living Seawall (Bayfront Park)
stories.orgs: Sarasota Bay Estuary Program; Town of Longboat Key; Kind Designs; SBEP Citizen Advisory Committee volunteers
stories.desc: About 200 feet of vinyl seawall at Bayfront Park was retrofitted in 2025 with 3D-printed concrete panels textured like mangrove roots to add habitat relief and disperse wave energy, funded through the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. One year of citizen-science monitoring (Oct 2025 to Aug 2026) found barnacles larger and extending higher on the panels than on the control wall, with oysters, tunicates, sponges, gray snapper, baitfish, sea stars and crabs using the panels.
stories.notes: Demonstration-scale; monitoring ongoing.

stories.title: BayWalk Preserve Shoreline and Tidal Lagoon Restoration (Sarasota)
stories.orgs: Sarasota Bay Estuary Program; City of Sarasota; U.S. EPA; Florida DEP
stories.desc: SBEP's first shoreline restoration site, a 4.5-acre dredge-spoil-filled wetland on City Island, was restored beginning in 1990: volunteers removed trash and invasive plants, planted more than 20,000 natives, and crews regraded the shoreline to natural elevation and created tidal lagoons that serve as fish nurseries and wading-bird feeding grounds. After hurricane damage, a 2025 federally funded project removed collapsed boardwalks, replaced them with resilient structures, added interpretive signage and replanted salt-tolerant natives, reopening the site.

stories.title: Sarasota Bay Artificial Reef Module Deployments
stories.orgs: Sarasota Bay Estuary Program; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Reef Innovations; Aptim Environmental & Infrastructure; Sarasota and Manatee counties
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Roughly 1,350 concrete reef modules (reef balls, deep-cover, 3-tier cube, table-top and layer-cake designs) were added in 2013 and 2016 to six permitted estuarine reefs in Sarasota Bay (three each in Sarasota and Manatee counties). Diver and baited-video surveys in 2017-2018 recorded 13-15 fish species including juvenile gag grouper (up to 12 in one deep-cover module), gray snapper and sheepshead; 24 additional deep-cover modules were deployed in 2024.
stories.notes: Estuarine artificial reef habitat rather than shoreline work; sites span Sarasota and Manatee counties.

stories.title: FLOOR Oyster Reef Restoration, St. Lucie Estuary (Florida Oceanographic Society)
stories.orgs: Florida Oceanographic Society; 20 partner restaurants (shell recycling); volunteers
stories.desc: Through its Florida Oceanographic Oyster Restoration (FLOOR) program, the Society collected shell from local restaurants, cured and bagged it, and deployed it with more than 2,400 volunteers (over 6,000 hours) to build nearly 60,000 square feet of oyster reef in the St. Lucie Estuary and southern Indian River Lagoon, providing settlement substrate for new oyster larvae.
stories.water: St. Lucie Estuary / Indian River Lagoon
stories.notes: Program-level totals; individual reef dates not given on page.

stories.title: Lake Okeechobee Spoil Island Enhancement (northwest marsh)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (Aquatic Habitat Conservation and Restoration)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: In 2001 FWC removed a muck berm that was blocking flow into Lake Okeechobee's northwest marsh and used the material to build six in-lake islands (2.3–5.5 acres each), then planted them with more than 11,200 native trees, shrubs and ferns of 56 species (trials 2001–2011, large-scale planting 2012–2020) while controlling invasives. Plantings stopped erosion and created vertical structure now used by nesting and foraging birds (35 species banded, 34 more observed on one island), alligators, turtles and mammals.
stories.notes: County/coordinates approximate within the NW marsh.

stories.title: Blowing Rocks Preserve Lagoon Shoreline Restoration (Jupiter Island)
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; volunteers and community members
stories.desc: Beginning in 1985, TNC removed about 4,500 Australian pines and thousands of Brazilian peppers from this barrier-island preserve and replanted 14 acres on the ocean side plus 15,000 nursery-grown natives on the Indian River Lagoon side. More than 3,000 volunteers (78,000 hours) installed and repaired 12 tidal culverts, creating three-quarters of a mile of tidal creeks and four tidal ponds that reconnected spoil-altered shoreline to the lagoon. The preserve is now a model of large-scale native coastal habitat restoration.

stories.title: Lake Okeechobee Low-Water Muck Removal and Marsh Revegetation (1st Point, Fisheating Bay, Moore Haven Marsh)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (Aquatic Habitat Conservation and Restoration)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: During the 2026 low-water period FWC scraped 510 acres of muck from the 1st Point Connector area to expose sand bottom and reopen water movement into the interior marsh (building on a 2008 adjacent muck removal and 2011 Pearce Canal berm removal); in spring 2025 crews planted ~40,000 eelgrass, Kissimmee grass and bulrush plants over 8.25 acres in Fisheating Bay, 27,558 sawgrass plants across 6 acres of Moore Haven Marsh, and 380 trees on seven Fisheating Bay rookery islands. Native vegetation is regrowing from the seed bank on the scraped site and wading-bird rookery islands gained nesting structure.
stories.notes: Very recent; FWC page reports work complete but limited monitoring results.

stories.title: Don Pedro Island State Park Tidal Habitat and Hydrology Enhancement
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida DEP (Florida State Parks / Lemon Bay Aquatic Preserve); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Coastal Program; volunteers
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: A 12-foot dredge-spoil berm along a canal had blocked tidal exchange to salt marsh and mangroves beside Lemon Bay. From 2016 to September 2018, 8,477 cubic yards of spoil were removed along 994 feet of canal bank, reconnecting about 20 acres of wetland; the 2.79-acre excavation was replanted with 21,643 native marsh and mangrove plants and exotic plants were eradicated across about 70 acres, for $128,061. Restored tidal flow benefits juvenile fish, wading birds, manatees and the threatened golden leather fern.
stories.notes: Link is an FWC PDF fact sheet.

stories.title: Turtle Bay Recycled-Shell Oyster Reef Deployments (Charlotte Harbor)
stories.orgs: Coastal Conservation Association Florida; Ingman Marine; Clermont Oyster Bar; Abbotts Construction; Lee Reefs; Gasparilla Island Conservation and Improvement Association; Lake County
stories.desc: CCA Florida's fifth deployment at Turtle Bay in May 2025 placed 40 tons of recycled oyster shell, bringing the cumulative total to 130 tons of cultch on restored reef sites in the Charlotte Harbor system. A further 10 tons were placed at Cormorant Key in July 2025 with FDEP, SCCF and FWC. Statewide CCA Florida reported 205 habitat projects completed in 2025.
stories.notes: Annual update page covering many projects; Turtle Bay coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Benedict Key Mangrove and Oyster Restoration (Pine Island Sound)
stories.orgs: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation Marine Laboratory; SCCF Coastal Watch; Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (grant)
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: On Benedict Key, a bird-nesting island whose mangrove canopy was destroyed by Hurricane Charley in 2004, SCCF and more than 60 volunteers planted about 3,500 red mangrove propagules and placed about 27,960 pounds of fossil shell as wave-buffering oyster substrate across nine project areas in 2021. By early 2022 hundreds of propagules had leafed out, the first sign of successful re-establishment; Hemp Key received similar plantings.
stories.notes: Island coordinates approximate.

stories.title: SCCF Oyster Reef Restoration, Clam Bayou and San Carlos Bay (Sanibel)
stories.orgs: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation Marine Laboratory; SCCF Coastal Watch; University of Florida; Grow Oyster Reefs; On Island
stories.desc: Since 2009 SCCF's Marine Lab has restored about 4 acres of oyster reef beginning in Clam Bayou on Sanibel, with reefs built in 2016, 2018, 2023 (160 shell-cement tiles in San Carlos Bay) and 2025. Annual quadrat sampling shows restored reefs become statistically similar in oyster density and size to natural reference reefs within two years of construction.
stories.notes: Related page: https://sccf.org/2023/10/10/new-oyster-restoration-site-installed/

stories.title: Woodring Road Living Shoreline for Mangrove Restoration (Sanibel)
stories.orgs: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation; SCCF Coastal Watch; City of Sanibel; BESE Products; Government of the Netherlands; MANG
stories.desc: Along an eroding stretch of Woodring Road on Sanibel's bay side, volunteers installed biodegradable BESE habitat structures (made from potato-processing waste) with thousands of attached oyster shells and planted mangroves in December 2021 to trap sediment, shelter seedlings from wave action and seed oyster reef. Hundreds of mangroves have been planted at the site over several years and are monitored by SCCF as an alternative to riprap.
stories.water: Pine Island Sound / San Carlos Bay
stories.notes: Pilot scale; dimensions not given.

stories.title: Picayune Strand Restoration Project
stories.orgs: South Florida Water Management District; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; Florida Department of Environmental Protection
stories.desc: Removed roughly 260–285 miles of roads and tram roads, plugged 42–48 miles of drainage canals (Faka Union, Merritt, Miller) and built three large pump stations and a protection levee to re-establish sheetflow across 55,000 acres of a failed 1960s subdivision between Alligator Alley and Tamiami Trail. First CERP project to reach completion (ribbon-cutting January 2026); restored wetland hydrology benefits Florida panther habitat and improves freshwater delivery to Ten Thousand Islands NWR, Collier-Seminole State Park and Rookery Bay estuaries.
stories.water: Faka Union Canal / Picayune Strand wetlands
stories.notes: Completion news release: https://www.sfwmd.gov/news-events/news/sfwmd-and-usace-celebrate-completion-major-everglades-restoration-project

stories.title: Fruit Farm Creek Mangrove and Hydrologic Restoration (Marco Island)
stories.orgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission; Florida DEP (Rookery Bay NERR); City of Marco Island; NOAA
lpOrgs: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
stories.desc: Undersized 1930s culverts under San Marco Road had cut tidal flow to Fruit Farm Creek, a 2.5-mile tidal creek in Rookery Bay NERR, and sediment buildup worsened by Hurricane Irma killed more than 60 acres of mangroves. Two culvert sets were replaced, over half a mile of creek was dredged of excess sediment and utilities relocated (2021-Feb 2023, $2.74 million NOAA fishery-disaster funding), reconnecting about 209 acres of mangrove wetland to the Big Marco River; dead mangrove areas are recolonizing naturally and the creek again serves juvenile fish, shellfish and wading birds.
stories.water: Fruit Farm Creek / Big Marco River
stories.notes: Link is an FWC PDF fact sheet.

stories.title: Hole-in-the-Donut Wetland Restoration, Everglades National Park
stories.orgs: National Park Service - Everglades National Park; Miami-Dade County; National Park Foundation; Florida Department of Environmental Protection; Florida water management districts; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
stories.desc: About 6,300 acres of former rock-plowed farmland inside Everglades National Park are being restored to short- and medium-hydroperiod freshwater prairie wetland; 6,063 acres had been completed as of 2020, leaving roughly 237 acres. Crews remove invasive exotic vegetation (principally Brazilian pepper), mechanically clear woody growth and scrape the disturbed soil down to limestone bedrock, after which native wetland plants recolonize and typically form prairie within the first year. The site is an In-Lieu Fee mitigation project - the first of its kind in Florida and the only one in the National Park Service - funded by mitigation credits from permitted development in Miami-Dade and Broward counties.
stories.water: Taylor Slough / Everglades freshwater prairie wetlands
stories.year: 1989-2020 (6,063 of 6,300 acres complete; remainder in progress)
stories.notes: Substantially complete but not finished - 237 acres remained as of 2020 per the park page (page last updated 2022). Coordinates approximate the Hole-in-the-Donut area near the Research Road / Daniel Beard Center area east of Royal Palm, Miami-Dade County, FL.

stories.title: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park Seagrass Restoration (Key Largo)
stories.orgs: Coastal Conservation Association Florida; Sea and Shoreline; Florida State Parks
stories.desc: About 10,000 square feet of propeller-scarred seagrass bed in John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park was restored using sediment tubes and seagrass planting by Sea and Shoreline with CCA Florida support, completed by February 2025.
stories.water: Largo Sound / Florida Bay (John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park)
stories.notes: Described in CCA Florida's 2025 habitat update.

stories.title: Lake Providence Watershed Conservation (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana DEQ; USDA NRCS; East Carroll Parish SWCD; Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; Lake Providence Watershed Council; U.S. EPA; producers
stories.desc: To restore the 1,400-acre oxbow Lake Providence, 100% of producers whose cropland drains to the lake enrolled 12,393 acres in reduced fall tillage, cover crops/residue and nutrient management contracts (about $2.16 million NRCS, Oct 2016-2020). Total dissolved solids declined and LDEQ removed the impairment in its 2020 assessment, restoring the lake's fish and wildlife propagation use.
stories.notes: Agricultural BMP-driven lake delisting; no in-lake habitat work. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Tensas River NWR Bottomland Hardwood Reforestation
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Louisiana Dept. of Wildlife and Fisheries; Arbor Day Foundation; partners
stories.desc: On former cleared farmland within Tensas River National Wildlife Refuge in the Tensas River floodplain, the Service and partners are reforesting about 11,000 acres with native bottomland hardwoods (up to 20 species per site), with additional IRA-funded plantings (about 2,700 acres across Louisiana refuges) announced in 2024. The restored forest is projected to store 360 metric tons of carbon and rebuilds floodplain habitat for Louisiana black bear, waterfowl and other wildlife.
stories.notes: Floodplain reforestation rather than in-channel work; completion year not stated. Companion refuge page: https://www.fws.gov/refuge/tensas-river/what-we-do. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: 5L Land Development Wetland Reserve Easement – Boeuf River bottomland restoration
stories.orgs: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (ACEP-WRE); landowner Michael Liles / 5L Land Development; Northwestern State University ARGO lab
stories.desc: A more than 300-acre flood-prone pasture along the Boeuf River next to Boeuf WMA was enrolled in a permanent Wetland Reserve Easement (closed April 2025) and restored by the landowner under NRCS contract: 9.2 acres of hydrology restoration (shallow-water wetlands) in 2025 and 183 acres of bottomland hardwood established by February 2026. The easement reconnects wildlife corridors for Louisiana black bear and northern long-eared bat; drone imagery documents the before/after change.
stories.notes: Nearest town inferred from Boeuf WMA location; coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Turkey Creek Watershed Restoration (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana DEQ; Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; USDA NRCS; Northeast Soil and Water Conservation District; U.S. EPA; local producers
stories.desc: Beginning in 2003, producers in the 35,212-acre Turkey Creek subsegment (Ouachita River Basin) installed resource-management-system practices including 148,801 linear feet of fencing, 116 watering facilities, 27 grade-stabilization structures, conservation cover (752 ac) and prescribed grazing, while the Wetland Reserve Program restored 1,388 acres of wetlands in the watershed (about $4.6 million). Total dissolved solids exceedances fell from 65% of samples (1999) to 9% (2011-12) and LDEQ removed the TDS impairment.
stories.notes: Agricultural BMP / wetland-reserve story, not in-channel work. Parish not stated in the document; inferred from Turkey Creek Lake location. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Lake St. Joseph Watershed BMPs (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana DEQ; Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; USDA NRCS; LSU AgCenter; Tensas-Concordia SWCD; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Landowners implemented conservation cover, crop rotation, cover crops and irrigation water management on about 5,100 acres of the 14,000-acre Lake St. Joseph watershed ($467,141 in 319 funds plus $374,183 match and $691,444 Farm Bill funds, 2006-2014). Average turbidity in the oxbow lake fell from 68.9 NTU (1999) to 23.5 NTU (2013-14), meeting the 25 NTU standard, and LDEQ proposed removing the turbidity impairment in 2016.
stories.notes: Agricultural BMP-driven lake delisting; no in-lake habitat work. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Big Creek Watershed Livestock BMPs (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; Tangipahoa-St. Helena SWCD; Louisiana DEQ; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA National Water Quality Initiative; 27 cattle and dairy farmers
stories.desc: Twenty-seven cattle and dairy producers in the Big Creek / East Fork Big Creek watershed (a Tangipahoa River tributary) installed BMPs on 3,046 acres with $266,950 in 319 funds plus about $2 million from NRCS (2008-2015), including 463 acres of fencing, livestock water facilities, heavy-use area protection, shade structures, waste-facility closures, prescribed grazing (3,606 ac) and nutrient management. Fecal coliform met primary and secondary contact standards with no exceedances in 2014, and LDEQ delisted the creek in 2016.
stories.notes: Livestock exclusion/fencing on pasture; document does not confirm stream exclusion. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Bayou des Cannes Watershed BMPs (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; USDA NRCS; Louisiana DEQ; U.S. EPA; local landowners; Evangeline Parish SWCD
stories.desc: On the 68-mile Bayou des Cannes, NRCS (2009-2016) and LDAF (2015-2018) cost-share contracts installed about 9,100 acres of irrigation land leveling, 8,857 acres of nutrient management, 10,225 acres of crop rotation, plus grade-stabilization structures, fencing, prescribed grazing and shallow water for wildlife (about $3.9 million combined). TDS exceedances fell from 36% to 18% and LDEQ removed TDS as a cause of impairment in the 2018 Integrated Report.
stories.notes: Agricultural BMP-driven partial delisting (still listed for nutrients, turbidity, DO); no in-channel work. Coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-05/documents/la_mallet_508.pdf

stories.title: Bayou Nezpique Watershed BMPs and Riparian Buffers (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana DEQ; LDAF Office of Soil and Water Conservation; USDA NRCS; Evangeline SWCD and other SWCDs; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: From 2009-2013 about $1.06 million in Section 319 funds supported cost-share BMPs in nine of ten HUC-12s of the 611-square-mile Bayou Nezpique watershed, including 30 acres of riparian forest buffer, 5,240 acres of irrigation land leveling, 9,701 acres of nutrient management, 9,810 acres of crop rotation and 950 acres of prescribed grazing. TDS exceedances dropped from 25% (2003) to 8% (2011) and LDEQ delisted the bayou for TDS.
stories.notes: Mostly upland agricultural BMPs; riparian buffer component is small (30 ac). Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Henderson Lake Water Management Unit Spoil Bank Gapping
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA Atchafalaya Basin Program
stories.desc: Hydrologic restoration in the Atchafalaya Basin west of the Atchafalaya River: 25 indented gaps were cut through dredged-material spoil banks so river water can again flow into Henderson Lake and its cypress-tupelo swamp, improving circulation, dissolved oxygen and aquatic habitat. CPRA reported the project complete in its 2023 Year in Review.
stories.notes: Parish inferred from location (Henderson Lake is in St. Martin Parish). Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Maurepas Land Bridge Swamp Reforestation
stories.orgs: Pontchartrain Conservancy (formerly Lake Pontchartrain Basin Foundation); community volunteers
stories.desc: Since 2013 volunteers have planted thousands of bald cypress and other swamp trees on the clear-cut, salt-stressed land bridge between Lakes Pontchartrain and Maurepas to rebuild the swamp forest that buffers communities around Lake Maurepas and East Baton Rouge from storm surge. Most planted trees have survived, and a regeneration study begun in 2015 (600+ trees sampled) found natural recruitment of cypress, tupelo, red maple and green ash, strongest where soil salinity is lowest.
stories.water: Lake Maurepas / Lake Pontchartrain land bridge
stories.notes: Page gives no exact tree counts or acreage; parish and coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Bayou Bonfouca Marsh Creation (CWPPRA PO-104)
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (federal sponsor); CWPPRA
stories.desc: A $28 million marsh-creation project on the Lake Pontchartrain north shore near Slidell, using sediment dredged from the lake to rebuild several hundred acres of brackish marsh around Bayou Bonfouca. CPRA reported the project about 90% complete in November 2017, with completion following in 2018.
stories.notes: Linked CPRA page is a photo/video gallery (Nov 2017) with little text; the companion press release 'nears completion' is on the press-release index page 27. Final acreage and 2018 completion are from general knowledge and not verified on a fetched page. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Bayou Plaquemine Brule Watershed Restoration (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana DEQ; St. Landry and Acadia SWCDs; USDA NRCS (EQIP); Louisiana Dept. of Health and Hospitals; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: On the 55-mile Bayou Plaquemine Brule, 2004-2008 implementation covered about 70,656 acres of BMPs (rice irrigation water management, drill planting, rotational grazing and pasture fencing, grade-stabilization structures and pipelines in the Cole Gully sub-watershed) and replacement of more than 3,300 failing home sewage systems. Fecal coliform fell from as high as 37,000 to 164 cells/100 mL (2007) and LDEQ removed the entire 55-mile segment from the 303(d) list in 2008.
stories.notes: Agricultural/septic BMP-driven delisting; no in-channel work. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Bayou Queue de Tortue Watershed BMPs (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana DEQ; Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; USDA NRCS (EQIP, Gulf of Mexico Initiative, NWQI); Acadia and Vermilion SWCDs; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: On the 56-mile Bayou Queue de Tortue (Duson to the Mermentau River), 2004-2017 cost-share contracts installed 410 grade-stabilization structures, 4,639 acres of irrigation land leveling, 3,112 acres of shallow water for wildlife and thousands of acres of residue, nutrient and pest management (about $1.3 million match plus $108,350 in 319 funds). TDS was removed as an impairment in the 2014 Integrated Report and 2016 turbidity (84 NTU) was 44% better than predicted.
stories.notes: Agricultural BMP-driven partial delisting (turbidity still listed); no in-channel work. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Lake Arthur and Lower Mermentau River Watershed BMPs (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: USDA NRCS; Gulf Coast, Vermilion and Jefferson Davis SWCDs; Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; Louisiana DEQ; U.S. EPA; 23 landowners
stories.desc: From 2002-2011, 23 landowners implemented conservation practices on about 2,645 acres of rice, crawfish, soybean and pasture land in the 29,200-acre watershed, including 884 acres of wetland wildlife habitat, irrigation water management, residue management and prescribed grazing (about $264,000 Farm Bill and $85,800 Section 319 funds). Average dissolved oxygen rose from 4.7 to 7.8 mg/L, TSS fell from 27.5 to 12.3 mg/L, and the segment was delisted for sediment, turbidity and ammonia (2010) and for DO, nitrogen and phosphorus (2012).
stories.notes: Agricultural BMP-driven delisting with a wetland wildlife habitat component; no in-channel work. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: River Reintroduction into Maurepas Swamp
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (West Shore Lake Pontchartrain mitigation); RESTORE Council; Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group
stories.desc: A 5.5-mile controlled diversion channel from the Mississippi River at Garyville through Hope Canal is being built to deliver up to 2,000 cfs of fresh water, nutrients and sediment to roughly 45,000 acres of stressed cypress-tupelo swamp west of Lake Pontchartrain. Construction began at Hope Canal in 2024 (Reach 6 Phase 1 expected early 2026), with the river intake to begin in 2027 and completion estimated in 2030.
stories.water: Maurepas Swamp / Hope Canal / Mississippi River
stories.notes: In progress; included because the brief names it. Benefit acreage (~45,000 ac) from general knowledge; the page does not state it.

stories.title: Calcasieu Lake / West Cove Oyster Reef Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Louisiana; LSU AgCenter
stories.desc: TNC built artificial oyster reefs in Calcasieu Lake using metal gabion baskets filled with limestone and concrete plus rebar structures, part of a Louisiana coastal program that had created about nine miles of oyster reef habitat statewide as of 2024. LSU AgCenter monitoring documents consistent oyster recruitment, survival and growth on the reefs. At many reef sites shoreline erosion behind the reef is about 50% lower than at comparable sites without healthy reef habitat.
stories.notes: Per-site year and acreage are not broken out on the source page; the nine-mile figure is the statewide total as of 2024. Cameron Parish is not among the excluded parishes. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Cameron Creole Watershed Grand Bayou Marsh Creation (CWPPRA CS-54)
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (federal sponsor); CWPPRA
stories.desc: Dredged sediment was used to create and nourish more than 700 acres of marsh in the Cameron-Creole watershed east of Calcasieu Lake, Cameron Parish. CPRA celebrated completion in November 2019.
stories.notes: Only the CPRA press-release index page (listing 'CPRA Celebrates Completion of Cameron Creole Marsh Creation Project – More than 700 Acres of Marsh Created or Nourished in Cameron Parish', Nov 27 2019) could be fetched; the PDF was in a redirect loop. Coordinates approximate. Link is a paginated index that may shift over time; verify before citing.

stories.title: Cameron-Creole Freshwater Introduction (CWPPRA CS-49)
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (federal sponsor/engineering); CWPPRA; Tarpan Construction LLC
stories.desc: Hydrologic restoration that reconnected the Cameron-Creole Watershed on the east side of Calcasieu Lake to the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway so fresh water and sediment can again flow into 22,510 acres of marsh and open water that had suffered saltwater intrusion. The $9.4 million CWPPRA project (final debris-screen phase finished October 2021) was announced complete in January 2022.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (east side of Calcasieu Lake).

stories.title: Rabbit Island Restoration and Gabion Shoreline Protection (Calcasieu Lake)
stories.orgs: Louisiana Trustee Implementation Group (Deepwater Horizon NRDA); Louisiana CPRA; Louisiana Dept. of Wildlife and Fisheries; The Nature Conservancy; Cheniere Energy; Coastal Conservation Association
stories.desc: Rabbit Island, the only brown pelican colony in southwest Louisiana, had lost 89 acres (35%) to erosion. Dredged sediment from the Calcasieu Ship Channel raised the island and restored 102 acres of nesting habitat with more than 65,000 plantings; in December 2023, 810 limestone-filled gabion baskets were installed along the northeastern shore to limit erosion and seed a new oyster reef. In the first nesting season after restoration more than 11,600 colonial waterbird nests, including 561 brown pelican nests, were recorded versus about 370 expected.
stories.notes: Island restoration completed 2021 (CPRA press release Oct 2021); gabion breakwater completed Dec 2023. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: TNC Oyster Reef Restoration – Calcasieu Lake (West Cove) and Sabine NWR shoreline
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; LSU AgCenter (monitoring); Sabine National Wildlife Refuge / U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Louisiana CPRA
stories.desc: TNC and partners have built oyster-reef breakwaters along eroding marsh shorelines in southwest Louisiana, including Calcasieu Lake's West Cove and a project restoring oyster reef and salt marsh along Sabine National Wildlife Refuge and portions of Highway 27. Across TNC's roughly nine miles of Louisiana reefs, LSU AgCenter monitoring consistently finds strong oyster recruitment, survival and growth, and about 50% less shoreline erosion behind the reefs than at unprotected sites.
stories.notes: Program-level page; per-site length and build year are not stated. Coordinates approximate (West Cove, southwest Calcasieu Lake).

stories.title: Cameron Meadows Marsh Creation and Terracing (CWPPRA CS-66)
stories.orgs: Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority (CPRA); NOAA (federal sponsor); CWPPRA; Great Lakes Dredge and Dock; Lonnie G. Harper & Associates
stories.desc: Nearly 2 million cubic yards of sediment were dredged from the Gulf of Mexico and pumped 5 miles inland to build about 308 acres of marsh northwest of Holly Beach, plus 2.3 miles of earthen terraces (about 11 acres) to slow waves and trap sediment. Nearly 7,000 acres in the Cameron Meadows area had converted to open water; the $32 million CWPPRA project was announced complete in April 2022 and restores fish and wildlife habitat while buffering nearby communities from storms.
stories.water: Cameron Meadows marsh / Gulf of Mexico
stories.notes: Photo is from the companion NOAA Fisheries story (https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/feature-story/cameron-meadows-project-rebuild-hundreds-acres-marsh-louisiana). Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Boston Canal Watershed BMPs (EPA 319 success story)
stories.orgs: Louisiana DEQ; Louisiana Dept. of Agriculture and Forestry; USDA NRCS; Vermilion SWCD; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: In the 16,000-acre Boston Canal watershed (Vermilion-Teche Basin, half agriculture and half coastal marsh), producers installed more than 890,000 linear feet of field borders, 3,600+ acres of conservation crop rotation, 238 acres of cover crops and 1,800 acres of nutrient and pest management, plus 48 onsite wastewater pump-outs (2014-2018). Soil erosion fell by 3,049 tons, turbidity exceedances dropped from 52% to 8%, and LDEQ removed the turbidity impairment in 2020.
stories.notes: Agricultural BMP-driven delisting; no in-channel work. Parish inferred from Vermilion SWCD. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Oyster Bayou Marsh Creation and Terracing (CWPPRA CS-59)
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA; NOAA (federal sponsor); CWPPRA
stories.desc: Marsh creation and terracing project in the Oyster Bayou area southeast of Calcasieu Lake, Cameron Parish; CPRA announced in February 2019 that construction was complete and that about 1,200 acres of marsh had been created in Cameron Parish.
stories.notes: Only the CPRA press-release index page (listing 'CPRA creates 1200 acres of marsh in Cameron Parish', Feb 2019, which states construction is complete on Oyster Bayou Marsh Creation and Terracing) could be fetched; the PDF was in a redirect loop. Coordinates approximate. Link is a paginated index that may shift over time; verify before citing.

stories.title: Cameron Parish Shoreline Restoration (beach and dune east of Holly Beach)
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA (state-funded); Audubon Delta; Cameron Parish Sheriff's Office; volunteers
stories.desc: Offshore sediment was dredged and pumped onto 5 miles of eroded Gulf coastline east of Holly Beach (construction completed February 2014), followed by sand fencing in 2015 to rebuild dunes and keep drifting sand off the highway. In 2021 the restored beach hosted the first successful Black Skimmer nesting and fledging on the Louisiana mainland in a decade, with Least Terns, Wilson's Plovers and Common Nighthawks also nesting on the new dunes.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: TNC Oyster Reef Living Shoreline – Vermilion Bay
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; LSU AgCenter (monitoring); partners
stories.desc: One of TNC's first Louisiana oyster-reef living shorelines, built along eroding marsh edge in Vermilion Bay to buffer wave energy, stabilize the shoreline and create nursery habitat. TNC reports its Louisiana reefs (about nine miles total) show strong oyster recruitment and roughly 50% less shoreline erosion behind the reef than at unprotected control sites.
stories.notes: Program-level page; exact site, length and build year not stated on the page. Coordinates and parish approximate (could be Iberia side of the bay).

stories.title: Rockefeller Refuge Gulf Shoreline Stabilization (CWPPRA ME-18)
stories.orgs: NOAA Fisheries (federal sponsor); Louisiana CPRA; Louisiana Dept. of Wildlife and Fisheries; CWPPRA
stories.desc: About 3-4 miles of lightweight-aggregate breakwater with regularly spaced gaps for water and fish exchange were built along the Gulf shoreline of Rockefeller Wildlife Refuge, where erosion averaged more than 50 feet per year and the refuge had lost over 15,000 acres. Completed June 2020 at about $34-35 million, the structures protect more than 250 acres of coastal marsh, and oyster spat have settled and grown in the sheltered water behind the breakwater.
stories.water: Gulf of Mexico / Rockefeller Wildlife Refuge
stories.notes: Also listed as completed in CPRA's 2020 Year in Review (https://coastal.la.gov/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/In-Review.pdf). Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Cole's Bayou Marsh Restoration (CWPPRA TV-63)
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (federal sponsor); CWPPRA
stories.desc: Hydrologic restoration and marsh creation in the Cole's Bayou area of Vermilion Parish, using dredged sediment to rebuild marsh and water-control features to restore freshwater flow and reduce saltwater intrusion. CPRA announced completion in October 2019.
stories.notes: Only the CPRA press-release index (listing 'Louisiana CPRA Announces Completion of Cole's Bayou Marsh Restoration Project in Vermilion Parish', Oct 8 2019) could be fetched; the press-release PDF (http://coastal.la.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/2019.10.08-Coles-Bayou.pdf) was in a redirect loop. Acreage not verified; coordinates approximate. Link is a paginated index that may shift over time; verify before citing.

stories.title: Freshwater Bayou Shoreline Protection near Coles Bayou
stories.orgs: Louisiana CPRA
stories.desc: About 7,500 linear feet of foreshore rock dike was built along the eastern bank of Freshwater Bayou near Coles Bayou in Vermilion Parish to stop bank erosion from vessel wakes and protect the interior marshes behind it. CPRA listed the project among the eight projects completed in 2023.
stories.notes: Described in CPRA's 2023 Year in Review page; no dedicated project page found. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Vermilion Bay Oyster Reef Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Louisiana; LSU AgCenter
stories.desc: Vermilion Bay is one of four Louisiana sites where TNC has constructed artificial oyster reefs from limestone- and concrete-filled gabion baskets and rebar structures to rebuild reef habitat and buffer eroding marsh shoreline. Across the Louisiana program, about nine miles of oyster reef habitat had been created as of 2024. LSU AgCenter monitoring reports consistent oyster recruitment and growth and roughly 50% less shoreline erosion behind many of the reefs.
stories.notes: Parish, town, year and per-site scale are not stated on the source page and are inferred from the named waterbody; coordinates approximate. Vermilion Parish is not among the excluded parishes.

stories.title: Tanyard Creek Restoration, Bella Vista
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; Bella Vista Property Owners Association; Arkansas Game and Fish Commission
stories.desc: A 2,500-foot reach of Tanyard Creek and Avalon Branch (Little Sugar Creek / Elk River watershed) in Bella Vista was restored around 2013 with natural channel design, in-stream habitat and riparian restoration, and constructed wood benches. Post-restoration sampling documented the Neosho midget crayfish (multiple life stages, previously unrecorded in the creek), benefits to 13 Species of Greatest Conservation Need, and the restored channel held its riffles, pools and wood benches through the December 2016 flood.
stories.notes: Year from WCRC completed-projects list; partner list beyond WCRC inferred from page context (not explicit).

stories.title: Coler Creek Low-Water Crossing Removal and Channel Restoration
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; Peel Compton Foundation; Arkansas Game and Fish Commission Stream Habitat Program
stories.desc: At Coler Creek Preserve in Bentonville, a low-water crossing that blocked fish passage and endangered trail users was removed in 2023 and about 200 feet of channel and riparian area were restored with boulder grade-control structures and native plantings. Fish regained access to upper Coler Creek, in the McKisic Creek watershed that hosts 17 Species of Greatest Conservation Need.
stories.water: Coler Creek (McKisic Creek / Little Sugar Creek tributary)
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Little Sugar Creek Wetland and Stream Restoration at McKisic Creek
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; NWA Trailblazers; City of Bentonville
stories.desc: Along 1,500 linear feet of Little Sugar Creek at its McKisic Creek confluence in Bentonville, WCRC reduced bank erosion with natural channel design and toe-wood stabilization and converted about 2 acres of formerly mowed saturated floodplain into a herbaceous wetland by halting mowing, removing invasives and planting wetland and floodplain species. The wetland filters urban runoff and provides habitat alongside the stabilized channel.
stories.notes: Completion year from WCRC completed-projects list; coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.watershedconservation.org/projects/all-projects/little-sugar-creek-nwa-razorback-greenway-trail-bella-vista-arkansas/

stories.title: Town Branch Low-Water Crossing Removal, Bentonville
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Bentonville
stories.desc: A pre-1954 privately built low-water crossing on Town Branch in northern Bentonville near the Slaughter Pen trail area, which blocked fish migration and drove lateral channel migration and bank erosion threatening roads and utilities, was removed along with its access road in fall 2022 after storm damage. WCRC documented post-removal channel adjustment (a secondary channel and floodplain scour) and the need for follow-up stabilization.
stories.notes: Barrier (low-water crossing) removal rather than a true dam; listed as completed June 2024 by WCRC but page says site remains unstable without remediation.

stories.title: Town Branch Stream Restoration, Bentonville
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Bentonville; Walton Family Foundation
stories.desc: WCRC designed and oversaw construction of roughly 2,400 linear feet of restoration on Town Branch in Bentonville (completed January 2019), building riffles and pools fitted to the stream's morphology, rock vanes and toe-wood structures to stabilize banks and create aquatic habitat, and native riparian re-vegetation to protect park and trail infrastructure and improve water quality.
stories.notes: Walton Family Foundation funding noted in ANRD FY2019 annual report. Photo is pre-construction.

stories.title: Upper Osage Creek and Stoney Brook Restoration at Osage Park, Rogers
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Rogers
stories.desc: About 2,000 feet of Osage Creek and 800 feet of Stoney Brook in Rogers' Osage Park were restored (2020) with morphology-based riffles and pools, rock vanes and toe-wood structures, native riparian re-vegetation, invasive removal, and enhancement of several small floodplain wetlands to reduce phosphorus, nitrogen and sediment loading to the Illinois River.
stories.notes: Year from WCRC completed-projects list.

stories.title: Kings River Oxbow Streambank Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Arkansas; corporate volunteer partners (Walmart, FedEx, Cargill, Tyson Foods, Mahco); Walmart; FedEx; Pratt and Whitney; Cargill; Tyson Foods; Mahco (corporate volunteers)
stories.desc: TNC restored a three-quarter-mile eroding bank on the Kings River within its Kings River Preserve, roughly two miles downstream of Rockhouse Access, using natural channel design with a toe-wood structure and two in-channel rock structures. The bank had been retreating about 10 feet per year for nearly 70 years and shed 30,000 tons of sediment in 2016 alone; over 500 trees were planted along the riparian corridor. The work is estimated to keep 9,000 tons of sediment, 1,900 pounds of phosphorus and 4,100 pounds of nitrogen per year out of the river, which feeds Table Rock Lake.
stories.notes: Built fall 2016, damaged by spring 2017 floods and repaired summer 2017, with rock-structure modifications slated for 2018. County inferred from the Kings River Preserve location; coordinates approximate. Sediment/nutrient figures are estimates, not measured results.

stories.title: Dave Donaldson Black River WMA Hydrology and Greentree Reservoir Restoration
stories.orgs: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; Ducks Unlimited; contractors
stories.desc: Across the 36.7-square-mile Dave Donaldson Black River WMA, AGFC is restoring bottomland hardwood hydrology by improving or removing water-control structures and levees so the greentree reservoirs drain whenever the Black River allows, paired with silviculture (600 acres treated in 2025, 432-acre variable-retention harvest planned) to reverse red oak decline. Two years of survey and hydrologic modeling by Ducks Unlimited preceded design; construction is phased over about five years.
stories.notes: In progress; only forest treatments complete so far. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Illinois River Watershed Unpaved Roads BMP Demonstration (Haden and Lawson Roads)
stories.orgs: Illinois River Watershed Partnership; Benton County Road Department; Arkansas Natural Resources Division (Section 319 grant 19-800); Center for Training and Transportation Professionals
stories.desc: At two county-road stream crossings in Benton County, six demonstration BMPs were built in 2021-2022, including an open-bottomed box culvert with headwalls, a through-the-bank pipe, a high-water bypass of cabled precast concrete mats, a broad-based dip, berm removal and a raised road profile, to cut sediment delivery to Illinois River tributaries; 31 road personnel from 11 jurisdictions were trained on site.
stories.notes: Sediment-reduction road BMP project with an open-bottom culvert; coordinates approximate; link is the ANRD final report PDF.

stories.title: Osage Creek Stream Mitigation Bank
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; private donors; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (mitigation banking)
stories.desc: Over 6,000 feet of Osage Creek and tributaries near the creek's mouth on the Illinois River were restored (Oct-Dec 2015), with 5,000 feet of bank enhanced and preserved, using salvaged root-wad trees and rock diverted from Fayetteville construction sites and landfills. The restored reach showed no structural damage after the record April 2017 flood on the Illinois River and Osage Creek.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (near Osage Creek mouth on the Illinois River).

stories.title: War Eagle Creek Private Landowner Streambank Restoration
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; USDA NRCS Regional Conservation Partnership Program; Beaver Watershed Alliance; Beaver Water District; AR CommuniTree Project; NWA Karst Water Quality Improvement Program; private landowner
stories.desc: On a War Eagle Creek property that had lost about seven acres of land to bank erosion since 2001, WCRC built a toe-wood structure, brush mattresses and a rock vane, placed river-cane sod mats and salvaged willows, restored a tributary across the terrace, treated invasives and revegetated 6.1 acres with 2,255 potted native plants (completed spring 2026). The restoration is expected to keep roughly 4,700 tons of sediment per year out of War Eagle Creek and Beaver Lake.
stories.sector: Private landowner (NRCS RCPP) with NGO and utility
stories.notes: Exact site not disclosed; coordinates approximate on War Eagle Creek, county could be Madison or Benton.

stories.title: IRWP Riparian Restoration Program (Upper Illinois River Watershed)
stories.orgs: Illinois River Watershed Partnership; Walton Family Foundation; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division; USDA NRCS; municipalities; private landowners
stories.desc: From 2018 to 2024 this partner-driven, cost-share program enhanced 277 acres of riparian buffer, enhanced or protected 21.8 miles of stream, installed 90,701 linear feet of cattle-exclusion fencing and 94 BMPs in priority subwatersheds such as Osage Creek, including reforestation of Sager Creek in Siloam Springs and spring protection on participating farms.
stories.water: Illinois River tributaries (Osage Creek, Sager Creek)
stories.sector: Partnership (NGO, foundation, state, federal, private landowners)
stories.notes: Program-level entry aggregating many sites; coordinates placed at Sager Creek, Siloam Springs.

stories.title: Clear Creek E. coli Attainment through Riparian Buffers and Green Infrastructure
stories.orgs: Illinois River Watershed Partnership; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division; University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service and Arkansas Water Resources Center; Beaver Water District; Cities of Fayetteville and Springdale; Washington County Conservation District; U.S. EPA Section 319
stories.desc: Clear Creek (Illinois River watershed, listed for E. coli in 2006) was addressed with $2.3 million in 319 funds supporting 15 riparian-buffer demonstration sites and 4,892 acres of riparian buffer, 31+ rain gardens with 7,400 native plants, bioswales, porous pavement and 17 creek clean-ups removing about 3 tons of litter, engaging 4,000+ volunteers since 2008. E. coli exceedances dropped from 12.5 percent to 0 percent, and the 2018 303(d) list showed Clear Creek attaining the E. coli criterion for the first time since listing.
stories.notes: ANRD success story PDF (2025); formal delisting not explicitly stated.

stories.title: CommuniTree War Eagle Creek Riparian Planting
stories.orgs: Beaver Watershed Alliance; Beaver Water District; Arkansas Forests and Drinking Water Collaborative; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Forestry Division; Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership; Bass Pro Outdoor Fund; Har-Ber High School
stories.desc: Over 1,000 native tree and shrub seedlings were potted by volunteers at Beaver Water District in spring 2025, and more than 600 were planted along War Eagle Creek at the October 2025 landowner workshop to stabilize streambanks and restore riparian habitat in the Beaver Lake watershed, with the program continuing in 2026.
stories.notes: Planting site not precisely named; coordinates approximate on War Eagle Creek.

stories.title: Illinois River Turbidity Delisting (EPA 319 Success Story)
stories.orgs: Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; Arkansas Department of Environmental Quality; Benton and Washington County Conservation Districts; Illinois River Watershed Partnership; Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; University of Arkansas; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA; local landowners
stories.desc: Since 1998, roughly $9 million in Section 319 funds plus $7.5 million in partner match supported cost-shared agricultural BMPs, riparian plantings along the river, and urban rain gardens and low-impact-development projects across the upper Illinois River watershed in Benton and Washington counties. Turbidity exceedances on a 2.5-mile Ecologically Sensitive segment fell from 28 to 18 percent of samples, and ADEQ removed it from the 303(d) list in 2014.
stories.notes: Watershed-scale success story; coordinates approximate on the upper Illinois River.

stories.title: Re-Wilding Wildcat Creek: Riparian Restoration and Livestock Exclusion
stories.orgs: Illinois River Watershed Partnership; USDA Forest Service (Ozark-St. Francis NF, Wedington Unit); Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; Northwest Arkansas Master Naturalists; Siloam Springs High School; Burns & McDonnell; Rockline Industries; The Nature Conservancy
stories.desc: On an eroded reach of Wildcat Creek (Osage Creek tributary) in the Wedington Unit near Tontitown, partners built about 2.7 miles of fencing to exclude cattle from the creek, spring run, wet prairies and ponds, added two hardened-access ponds, planted 3,784 native trees, shrubs and grasses of 39+ species along 3,250 feet of creek, drove 300 live willow stakes on 300 feet of eroding bank and set 2,550 grass and sedge plugs along 500 feet of unstable bank (winter-spring 2026). The work is expected to stabilize banks and cut sediment, nutrient and bacteria loads to the Illinois River.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate within the Wedington Unit; outcomes are expected rather than measured.

stories.title: Buffalo River Watershed Livestock Exclusion and Streambank Protection (Crooked Creek CD, Project 20-400)
stories.orgs: Crooked Creek Conservation District; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division (Section 319); private landowners
stories.desc: In Marion and Baxter counties, the 319-funded Buffalo River Watershed Project wrote 200 conservation plans on 61,000 acres of pasture and installed 62,000+ feet of exclusion fencing and livestock water pipeline toward a goal of 7.25 miles of streambank protection, fencing cattle out of Buffalo River tributaries. The state estimates annual reductions of about 6,294 tons of sediment, 11,555 pounds of nitrogen and 6,196 pounds of phosphorus.
stories.notes: Program-level cost-share entry; coordinates approximate. Link is the ANRD 2023 NPS Annual Report PDF.

stories.title: Niokaska Creek Restoration at Sweetbriar Park
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Fayetteville; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; U.S. EPA Region 6 (Section 319); Elk River Construction
stories.desc: A 1,600-foot reach of Niokaska Creek in Fayetteville's Sweetbriar Park, where vertical cut-banks eroded up to 10 feet per year, was rebuilt with natural channel design including constructed floodplains, flow-deflecting rock structures, riffles and pools, adjacent wetlands, a grade structure at a water-line crossing and native revegetation (2009-2012). An April 2011 flood five times the design flow caused no tree loss and prevented an estimated 35-50 feet of bank erosion and loss of 5 percent of park land.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.watershedconservation.org/projects/gulley-park-restoration/

stories.title: Huntsville Dam Removal and War Eagle Creek Barrier Removals
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source; Beaver Watershed Alliance; Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Partners for Fish and Wildlife, National Fish Passage Program); USDA NRCS (RCPP); City of Huntsville; Madison and Washington Counties; The Nature Conservancy; University of Central Arkansas; Beaver Water District; Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership; landowners
stories.desc: A 12-foot-high by 160-foot-long dam on War Eagle Creek at Huntsville was removed in 2024 as the first of four barrier removals under a 2023-2027 RCPP, with more than 1,000 mussels of 12 species relocated beforehand; the program also restores about 7,200 feet of streambank, 4 acres of wetland and installs in-stream habitat structures. The dam removal reconnected 5.3 miles of stream, and the full set of removals aims to reconnect 434 miles of the Beaver Lake watershed's largest tributary.
stories.notes: Dam dimensions and mussel relocation figures come from the ANRD 2023 NPS Annual Report (https://media.ark.org/agri/2023-NPS-Annual-Report.pdf); the BWA page shows Huntsville Dam restoration nearing completion Dec 2024. Remaining barriers (e.g., Gar Hole, Washington Co. Rd 526) still in progress. Also documented at: https://www.americanrivers.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/DamRemovalCompiledSummaries_2024.pdf

stories.title: Scull Creek Streambank Restoration (Clear Creek watershed), Fayetteville
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Fayetteville
stories.desc: About 150 feet of eroding bank on Scull Creek, an urban stream draining 4.5 square miles through Fayetteville to Mud Creek and Clear Creek, were restored in winter 2025-26 with a stacked-rock toe revetment, a coir-mattress bankfull bench planted with native riparian species, and an upstream rock vane to keep storm flows off the restored bank. Post-restoration photos through May 2026 show the stabilized, vegetated bank.
stories.water: Scull Creek (Clear Creek / Illinois River watershed)
stories.notes: Construction dates inferred from dated photo filenames (Dec 2025-Jan 2026); coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Tanglewood Branch Restoration, Fayetteville
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Fayetteville
stories.desc: An urban reach of Tanglewood Branch in Fayetteville was reshaped with natural channel design (completed August 2022), forming bankfull benches and inner berms, boulder grade-control structures to hold bed elevation and pool depth, stacked rock walls on exposed banks, erosion-control fabric mattresses filled with topsoil, and graded floodplain terraces replanted with native trees, shrubs, grasses and wildflowers.
stories.notes: Completion date from WCRC completed-projects list; coordinates approximate; page images show the comparable Mullins Creek project.

stories.title: Bulldog Branch Restoration at Stadium Drive, University of Arkansas
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; University of Arkansas; City of Fayetteville; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; U.S. EPA Section 319(h); McClelland Consulting Engineers
stories.desc: About 550 linear feet of Bulldog Branch along Stadium Drive on the University of Arkansas campus were restored in 2021: the upstream section by hand with invasive removal and native riparian planting, and the downstream section (stormwater outfall to the Stadium Drive box culvert) with stacked rock toe protection, rock structures, floodplain features, coir soil-encapsulation blocks and native plantings on slopes and terraces.
stories.notes: Completion year from WCRC completed-projects list; page text gives limited detail. Also documented at: https://www.watershedconservation.org/projects/mullins-branch-stream-restoration/; https://www.watershedconservation.org/projects/all-projects/mullins-branch-at-uofa-phase-2/

stories.title: Strawberry River Livestock Exclusion Fencing (Projects 16-400 and 16-900)
stories.orgs: Izard County Conservation District; Sharp County Conservation District; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission (Section 319); private landowners
stories.desc: Two 319-funded pasture-improvement projects in the Strawberry River watershed (home to the endangered Arkansas fatmucket mussel) installed roughly 28,460 feet of fencing (11,420 ft in Izard County, 17,040 ft in Sharp County) with alternative water sources to exclude cattle from the river and tributaries, concluding in September 2019.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate; link is ANRD FY2019 annual report PDF.

stories.title: White River Streambank Restoration off Wyman Road
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Fayetteville; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; U.S. EPA Section 319(h); volunteers
stories.desc: An eroding bank of the White River a few miles above Beaver Lake, retreating about 14 feet per year and contributing an estimated 3,600 tons of sediment annually, was stabilized in February-April 2012 with a two-level boulder-and-wood toe bench built from donated highway-project trees, soil mattresses, and more than 700 potted native plants plus willow, sycamore and buttonbush cuttings. A flood one week after construction produced no measurable erosion on the formerly failing bank.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Brush Creek Streambank Restoration, Fayetteville
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; Beaver Water District; Beaver Watershed Alliance; USDA NRCS National Water Quality Initiative
stories.desc: A highly eroded streambank on Brush Creek near Fayetteville (Beaver Lake watershed) was restored in late 2023 with natural channel design: in-stream rock structures to correct flow, toe wood and erosion-control fabric on the reshaped banks, and constructed floodplains planted with sycamore and other hardwoods, silky dogwood, witch hazel, swamp milkweed and eastern gamagrass to build a vegetated riparian zone that slows floodwater.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (Brush Creek east of Fayetteville in the Beaver Lake watershed).

stories.title: White River Restoration at Noland Wastewater Treatment Plant
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Fayetteville; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; Arkansas Department of Environmental Quality; U.S. EPA Section 319(h); Beaver Water District; Beaver Watershed Alliance; Streamline Environmental LLC
stories.desc: An actively eroding White River bank near Fayetteville's Noland WWTP, retreating 8 feet per year and shedding over 4,800 tons of sediment, 11,000 pounds of nitrogen and 4,000 pounds of phosphorus annually, was rebuilt (Oct 2015-Dec 2016) with a toe-wood bench of salvaged trees, boulders and gravel, coir-wrapped topsoil lifts and about 500 trees, 4,000 shrubs and 1,000 grass plugs. Post-flood inspections found little to no measurable erosion along the formerly failing bank upstream of Beaver Lake.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Cato Springs Tributary Restoration at Mount Kessler Regional Park
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; City of Fayetteville; Beaver Water District; Beaver Watershed Alliance
stories.desc: More than 2,000 feet of an unnamed tributary to Cato Springs Creek (West Fork White River) in Fayetteville's Mount Kessler Regional Park, including nearly 1,000 feet of unstable bank, were restored using natural channel design, with invasive plant removal, native riparian planting, interpretive signage and removal and recycling of dumped tires, metal, vehicle parts and appliances from the eroding banks.
stories.notes: Completion year not stated on page (page last modified 2018). Photos only in site gallery.

stories.title: Cave Creek Low-Water Crossing Replacement, Buffalo River Watershed
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Arkansas; Newton County Road Department; Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; US EPA Section 319 Nonpoint Source Program
stories.desc: A 70-foot vented concrete slab crossing on Cave Creek, a Buffalo River tributary, was replaced in 2023 with a 100-foot span bridge. The county also abandoned 750 feet of creekside road and rebuilt it on the floodplain terrace away from the stream. The new structure reconnected six miles of stream to the Buffalo River and removed a chronic sediment source.
stories.notes: Nearest town inferred; coordinates approximate within the Cave Creek drainage of Newton County.

stories.title: West Fork White River Airport PL-566 Restoration
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; USDA NRCS (PL-566 / RCPP West Fork White River Watershed Initiative); Beaver Water District; Beaver Watershed Alliance
stories.desc: Approximately 1,600 feet of highly unstable channel and streambank on the West Fork White River east of the Fayetteville Executive Airport were surveyed, designed, permitted and restored between November 2020 and March 2021, extending a continuous restored footprint of nearly one mile with earlier adjacent work. Re-vegetation included invasive species removal and native plantings, improving habitat and water quality on a 303(d)-listed reach.

stories.title: West Fork White River Restoration at Drake Field (Fayetteville Airport)
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Fayetteville; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; U.S. EPA Section 319(h); Southern Excavating LLC; local landowners
stories.desc: WCRC restored 4,600 linear feet of the West Fork White River east of Drake Field, where bank erosion reached 26 feet per year and produced about 4,000 tons of sediment annually, using natural channel design, flow-deflection structures, a newly excavated channel and conversion of old channel to riverine wetlands. Revegetation used more than 15,000 bare-root seedlings, 5,000 live stakes and 4,000 pounds of seed over 10+ acres; the project (completed May 2014) eliminated accelerated erosion and cut sediment loading by over 98 percent.
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story credits the Airport site with keeping 15,000-20,000 tons of sediment out of the river over eight months.

stories.title: Prairie Grove Battlefield Riparian and Wetland Restoration
stories.orgs: Illinois River Watershed Partnership; Arkansas State Parks; United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians (River Cane Initiative); Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; Southeastern Grasslands Institute; Quail Forever; University of Arkansas; U.S. EPA Climate Pollution Reduction Grant
stories.desc: At Prairie Grove Battlefield State Park on the upper Illinois River, work that began in 2025 is restoring more than 800 acres, including 570 acres of prairie, wetland and wet prairie and 230 acres of floodplain woodland, through invasive control in riparian and woodland areas, hydrologic improvements for wetlands and springs, and reintroduction of river cane along streams for bank stabilization. Prairie planting and prescribed fire continue through 2029.
stories.notes: Early-stage; only site assessment and initial riparian invasive control reported complete.

stories.title: Rock Creek East Streambank and Habitat Restoration
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; USDA NRCS; private landowner family
stories.desc: Between September and November 2022, 250 feet of eroding streambank on Rock Creek between Greenland and West Fork (a Beaver Lake tributary via the West Fork White River) was restored for a private family with NRCS assistance. The page notes the West Fork White River was recently removed from Arkansas's 303(d) list for turbidity.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Rock Creek Streambank Restoration (Phase I and II) at West Fork
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; USDA NRCS (EQIP / RCPP West Fork White River Watershed Initiative); Beaver Watershed Alliance; Beaver Water District; Washington County Conservation District; private landowners
stories.desc: Eroding banks of Rock Creek just above its confluence with the West Fork White River (6-square-mile watershed) were rebuilt in two phases (2019 and June 2021) using toe-wood structures and native vegetation to create a stable bank profile with floodplain features. The work is part of the NRCS-funded effort that helped the upper West Fork come off Arkansas's impaired-waters list.
stories.water: Rock Creek (West Fork White River tributary)
stories.sector: Private landowner (NRCS EQIP) with NGO partners
