stories.notes: Phase I page: https://www.watershedconservation.org/projects/all-projects/rock-creek-streambank-restoration-west-fork-arkansas/

stories.title: West Fork White River Turbidity Delisting (EPA 319 Success Story)
stories.orgs: Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division; Watershed Conservation Resource Center; Beaver Watershed Alliance; City of Fayetteville; Ecological Conservation Organization; Audubon Arkansas; Beaver Water District; University of Arkansas; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Eighteen Section 319-funded projects since 1998 on the 27.2-mile West Fork White River (impaired for turbidity since 1998) included 800 feet of natural-channel-design relocation with six large rock/log structures and a 1-acre four-pond wetland (2007-2010), toe wood and soil-mattress bank stabilization and invasive removal at the Fayetteville Airport site (2007-2014), and conservation easements. The upper 16.5 miles met the state turbidity standard and were removed from the impaired list in 2018; a $4.3 million NRCS RCPP grant (2016) matched by $4.4 million continues the work.
stories.notes: Watershed-scale story overlapping individual WCRC sites listed separately.

stories.title: Cave Creek Crossing Replacement (Buffalo River tributary)
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Arkansas; Newton County Road Department; Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division; U.S. EPA Section 319 program
stories.desc: In 2023 a 70-foot vented concrete slab crossing on Cave Creek (County Road 4269/5070 at Gene Rush WMA) was replaced with a 100-foot single-pier bridge, and Newton County abandoned 750 feet of creek-side road and rebuilt it on the floodplain terrace. The project restored aquatic organism passage and reconnected about six miles of Cave Creek to the Buffalo National River while eliminating chronic erosion at the old slab.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (Cave Creek near Gene Rush WMA). Also documented in ANRD FY2022/FY2023 NPS annual reports ($140,346 319(h) + $176,847 county).

stories.title: West Fork White River Un-named Tributaries Restoration (EQIP)
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; USDA NRCS (EQIP practices 580 and 410); private landowner
stories.desc: Two unnamed pasture tributaries of the West Fork White River near West Fork that had incised and eroded laterally, delivering sediment and nutrients to the river and consuming pasture, were restored using stream-morphology-based channel dimensions, grade stabilization structures and native re-vegetation under EQIP streambank protection funding. Before-and-after photos document stabilized, vegetated channels.
stories.water: Unnamed tributaries, West Fork White River
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: West Fork White River at Dye Creek Road (PL-566)
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; USDA NRCS (RCPP / PL-566 West Fork White River Watershed Initiative); Beaver Water District; Beaver Watershed Alliance
stories.desc: Over a mile of the West Fork White River at Dye Creek Road near West Fork was restored during a 10-month construction season beginning January 2023, with the channel re-excavated to a stable self-sustaining form, rock structures to hold grade and deflect flood currents, toe-wood structures for bank protection and aquatic habitat, and riparian areas replanted to a native plant community. The project is part of the NRCS-funded initiative that helped the upper West Fork meet turbidity standards.

stories.title: Hazel Valley Low-Water Crossing Replacement, Middle Fork White River
stories.orgs: Beaver Watershed Alliance; USDA Forest Service (Joint Chiefs); Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Fish Passage Program; private landowners
stories.desc: A 90-foot low-water vented ford on the upper Middle Fork of the White River at Hazel Valley was replaced with a bridge built from repurposed rail-car decks (installed December 2024) to restore fish passage, reduce site erosion and restore natural stream dynamics. The project is expected to reconnect 507 miles of stream in the Beaver Lake watershed.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate; county (Washington vs. Madison) inferred from Hazel Valley location. Stream-miles figure is the stated expected outcome.

stories.title: West Fork White River Restoration at Brentwood
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; Arkansas Natural Resources Commission; U.S. EPA Section 319(h); local landowners; Beaver Watershed Alliance; Beaver Water District; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division; Flow State LLC
stories.desc: An 1,800-foot reach of the West Fork White River near Brentwood, where banks were retreating up to 13 feet per year and shedding about 1,960 tons of sediment annually, was rebuilt with natural channel design: the channel was relocated away from eroding banks, natural-material flow-deflection structures were installed, and the old channel was converted to four settling ponds that function as ephemeral wetlands. Completed September 2009, the project eliminated accelerated bank erosion, reduced sediment loading by over 96 percent and withstood an April 2011 flood.
stories.notes: Outcome is a projected reduction; coordinates approximate. Also documented at: https://www.watershedconservation.org/projects/all-projects/west-fork-white-river-brentwood-mountain-brentwood-arkansas/

stories.title: Squirrel Creek Streambank Stabilization at Peek's Park, Winslow
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; City of Winslow; Arkansas Highway and Transportation Department
stories.desc: About 260 feet of Squirrel Creek, a West Fork White River tributary running along Highway 74 in Winslow's Peek's Park, had toe erosion and invasive-dominated banks; the site was stabilized and revegetated (2018) within AHTD right-of-way, reducing sediment and nutrient inputs and improving aquatic and terrestrial habitat.

stories.title: Middle Fork Little Red River Low-Water Crossing Replacements at Arlberg
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Arkansas; Stone County Roads Department; Stone County Road Department
stories.desc: Two low-water crossings with undersized culverts on the Middle Fork of the Upper Little Red River near Arlberg were replaced with wider, higher crossings using large concrete box culverts; one new culvert alone passes more water than all the old pipes combined. The work reconnected 308 upstream stream-network miles, including 26 miles of the Middle Fork main stem, in a watershed that supports the endemic yellowcheek darter and rare mussels.
stories.notes: Completion year not stated on page; coordinates approximate near Arlberg.

stories.title: Jones Fork Creek (J. Pense) Streambank Stabilization above Lake Fort Smith
stories.orgs: City of Fort Smith Utilities Department (Watershed Management); Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division (Section 319 grant 20-600); U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; private landowner
stories.desc: About 1,220 feet of a 14-foot vertical eroding bank on Jones Fork Creek, 1.2 miles above Lake Fort Smith (Frog Bayou watershed), was re-sloped with a floodplain shelf, protected with bendway weirs, key-locks, 650 feet of longitudinal peaked stone toe and 12 locked-log structures, and planted with about 2,000 trees and willow/sycamore poles in a 30-foot riparian zone (Sept 2021; phase 2 repairs 2022). The project is projected to prevent roughly 21,000 cubic feet of bank loss per year to the drinking-water reservoir.
stories.sector: Public (municipal utility, state) with private landowner
stories.notes: Link is the ANRD final report PDF; coordinates approximate above Lake Fort Smith.

stories.title: Eagle's Nest Natural Channel Design Restoration, Upper Little Red River
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Arkansas; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division
stories.desc: TNC restored an eroding reach of the Upper Little Red River at the Eagle's Nest site using natural channel design and planted 1,200 trees on the rebuilt streambanks; the state's FY2019 nonpoint-source report credits the project with keeping about 1,240 tons of sediment per year out of the river, which supports the endemic yellowcheek darter and speckled pocketbook mussel.
stories.notes: Exact site and county not given in source; coordinates approximate on the Upper Little Red near Clinton. Link is the ANRD FY2019 annual report PDF.

stories.title: Speckled Pocketbook Mussel Reintroduction, Upper Little Red River
stories.orgs: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Arkansas Ecological Services, Greers Ferry National Fish Hatchery); Arkansas Game and Fish Commission
stories.desc: Since 2018 the endangered speckled pocketbook has been cage-cultured in Greers Ferry Lake and about 2,700 mussels have been released into native habitat in the upper Little Red River tributaries, including 288 stocked in the South Fork in May 2022, to stabilize the population of a species found nowhere else. Partners pair the releases with landowner sediment-reduction work in the watershed.
stories.water: South Fork and other forks, Little Red River
stories.notes: Population augmentation rather than physical habitat work; include at caller's discretion. 2022 stocking story: https://www.fws.gov/story/2022-05/mussels-stocked-south-fork-stabilize-little-red-river-population

stories.title: Johnson County Road 4220 Low-Water Crossing Replaced with Free Span
stories.orgs: Johnson County Road Department; Arkansas Department of Agriculture Natural Resources Division (Section 319(h) / Arkansas Unpaved Roads Program)
stories.desc: A routinely flooding low-water crossing on County Road 4220 in Johnson County was replaced with a free-span structure ($97,610 in 319(h) funds), ending overtopping and road-base erosion that delivered sediment to the stream; a similar free-span replacement on County Road 3271 was completed in FY2022.
stories.notes: Stream name not given; coordinates approximate at county seat. Link is ANRD 2023 NPS Annual Report PDF.

stories.title: Earl Buss Bayou DeView WMA (Oliver and Thompson Tracts) Greentree Reservoir Renovation
stories.orgs: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; Ducks Unlimited; North American Wetlands Conservation Act
stories.desc: Two outdated 4-foot water-control structures on the Thompson and South Oliver greentree reservoirs along Bayou DeView in Poinsett County were replaced with 15- and 18-foot remotely operated overshot gates (Phase 1 complete December 2023), with Phase 2 adding structures, rebuilt levees and spillways (2024) so spring floodwater moves through the bottomland hardwood forest more naturally and stressed red oaks can regenerate.
stories.sector: Public (state) with NGO and federal grant
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: Glaise Creek Water Control Structure and GTR Hydrology Restoration, Henry Gray Hurricane Lake WMA
stories.orgs: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission; Ducks Unlimited; North American Wetlands Conservation Act grant
stories.desc: A flow-restricting pinch point on Glaise Creek in Henry Gray Hurricane Lake WMA was replaced (2023-2025) with a 1,500-cubic-yard concrete structure with automated overshot gates spanning about 120 feet, allowing at least 10,000 cfs to pass so the bottomland hardwood greentree reservoirs can drain on a natural schedule; forest treatments and Nuttall oak reforestation accompany the work. Water-release footage in June 2025 confirmed the structure operating with debris passing over the gates.
stories.sector: Public (state) with NGO and federal grant
stories.notes: Coordinates from AGFC page.

stories.title: Maumelle River Bank Stabilization (Lake Maumelle)
stories.orgs: Watershed Conservation Resource Center; Central Arkansas Water
stories.desc: A 400-foot eroding bank of the Maumelle River above Lake Maumelle, the drinking-water supply for about 400,000 central Arkansans, was stabilized in 2011 with natural channel design including toe wood, a bankfull bench, flow-diverting structures and native riparian plantings. WCRC monitored and maintained the site for five years; the toe wood and structures also improved aquatic habitat.
stories.notes: Coordinates approximate (upper Lake Maumelle).

stories.title: Robinson Fork Fish Passage Improvement
stories.orgs: Arkansas Game and Fish Commission (project partner lead); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program)
stories.desc: A $2,000,000 National Fish Passage Program project removing five road-crossing barriers on the Robinson Fork of the Little River, stabilizing nearby stream reaches with natural channel design and providing safe public crossings. The work is expected to restore connectivity to over 150 miles of habitat, including for the federally threatened leopard darter.
stories.water: Robinson Fork of the Little River (Ouachita Mountains)
stories.notes: FY2024 National Fish Passage Program award; counties from the FY24 award listing. Coordinates approximate in the Polk/Sevier county area.

stories.title: Tuscumbia Access Riverbank Stabilization, Osage River
stories.orgs: Missouri Department of Conservation; Village of Tuscumbia
stories.desc: MDC closed the Tuscumbia Access on the Osage River in September 2026 to repair an eroding riverbank that threatened the boat ramp and river access. Construction finished ahead of schedule and the access reopened to the public in early October 2026; management of the site has since transferred from MDC to the Village of Tuscumbia.
stories.notes: MDC news release gives no length or cost. Miller County is inside the extent. The only images on the release are the MDC logo, so no project photo is available.

stories.title: Huzzah Creek Fish Passage Project
stories.orgs: Crawford County, Missouri (project partner lead); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program)
stories.desc: Two fish passage barriers on Huzzah Creek at John Coleman and Seller roads are being removed and replaced with climate-resilient bridges, building on a recent aquatic organism passage project on the same creek. The $1,459,850 project is expected to restore natural hydrology and open about 25 additional miles of stream habitat for the eastern hellbender and several endangered mussels, while reducing county maintenance costs and improving emergency access during high flows.
stories.notes: FY2024 National Fish Passage Program award; project page uses future tense. Boundary note: Ozark/Meramec basin in east-central Missouri; include only if that part of MO is inside the extent.

stories.title: Willhite Road Low-Water Crossing Replacement
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Missouri; Missouri Department of Conservation; Missouri Aquatic Connectivity Team; county road authority
stories.desc: A low-water crossing that blocked fish movement and flooded dangerously was removed and replaced with a free-span bridge, restoring aquatic organism passage along the stream and improving driver safety at high flows. The project is a demonstration site for the Missouri Aquatic Connectivity Team, co-led by TNC and MDC, which works to make barrier removal and bridge replacement standard practice statewide.
stories.water: Tributary in the Meramec/Huzzah Creek basin
stories.notes: TNC names the county (Crawford) but not the stream or exact year; lat/lon approximated to the Willhite Road area near Steelville.

stories.title: Huzzah Creek Bioengineered Streambank Stabilization
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Missouri; Missouri Department of Conservation; Ozark Land Trust; private landowner
stories.desc: Nearly 2,000 feet of eroding bank on Huzzah Creek was stabilized using bioengineering techniques - trees, root wads and live plantings rather than rock riprap - on private land in the Meramec basin. TNC continues to extend the approach with farmers elsewhere in the Huzzah watershed to reduce gravel and sediment loading to the Meramec River.
stories.notes: Year not stated on the source page; range inferred from TNC's Missouri stream restoration program. Approximate coordinates.

stories.title: Huzzah Creek Road Crossing Replacements for Fish Passage
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Missouri; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Missouri Department of Conservation; Missouri Aquatic Connectivity Team; Crawford County
stories.desc: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service awarded nearly $1.5 million to replace two barrier road crossings on Huzzah Creek, a high-quality Meramec River tributary. TNC describes it as the first fish passage project in Missouri funded by the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law; the replacements will reopen about 25 miles of river to fish and other aquatic organisms.
stories.notes: Funding awarded and project under way; TNC does not state a completion date. Approximate coordinates on Huzzah Creek in Crawford County.

stories.title: Drywood Creek and Second Nicolson Creek Abandoned Mine Land Reclamation
stories.orgs: Missouri DNR Land Reclamation Program; Missouri Geological Survey; Missouri State Parks; Missouri Department of Conservation; U.S. Office of Surface Mining; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Reclamation of 286 acres of abandoned coal mine land in the Drywood Creek headwaters removed highwalls and steep embankments, closed two collapsed mine shafts, neutralized acid impoundments and seeps, and regraded and revegetated spoil piles (Bison 160 acres, Prairie State Park 47 acres, Lester Davis 50 acres, Second Nicolson subwatershed 15 acres; over $2 million). Sulfate and chloride loads fell below the 970 mg/L TMDL target, macroinvertebrate communities now match a control stream, and 29.9 miles of Drywood Creek were delisted in 2016 with 3.0 miles of Second Nicolson Creek proposed in 2018.
stories.water: Drywood Creek and Second Nicolson Creek
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed/mine-land reclamation rather than in-channel work, but the documented outcome is restored aquatic life use in 33 stream miles. PDF link, no direct image URL.

stories.title: Upper Little Sac 319 Streambank Stabilization (642 linear feet)
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; U.S. EPA; City Utilities of Springfield; Greene County Soil and Water Conservation District
stories.desc: Under the $666,667 Upper Little Sac Section 319 grant, 642 linear feet of severely eroding streambank on the Upper Little Sac River was stabilized in August 2023. The project also included riparian corridor enhancement, bioretention, volunteer tree plantings and septic pump-out rebates aimed at reducing bacteria, sediment and nutrients in Springfield's drinking-water watershed.
stories.notes: Documented in the Watershed Committee of the Ozarks 2023 annual report (PDF). Project page: https://watershedcommittee.org/upper-little-sac-319/ . Exact site coordinates not published.

stories.title: Little Sac River Restoration and Improvement Project (LPSTP Streambank Stabilization)
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; City Utilities of Springfield; Greene County Soil and Water Conservation District; Missouri Department of Conservation; Greene County; Wildscape Environmental Services; River Research & Design; Missouri State University OEWRI
stories.desc: A $380,442 Section 319 project (with $225,222 local match) stabilized an eroding reach of the Upper Little Sac River using Longitudinal Peaked Stone Toe Protection, an engineered floodplain bench, bendway weirs, vegetated keys and live pole plantings, and installed prescribed grazing systems, vegetative bank buffers and alternative livestock watering on contributing farms. A November 2017 hands-on build and workshop trained 40 participants, and the project produced SWAT modeling and bacteria source-tracking reports for the Springfield/Greene County drinking water watershed.
stories.notes: Specific stabilization site coordinates are not published; lat/lon approximates the Upper Little Sac River north of Springfield.

stories.title: Fellows Lake Watershed Riparian Restoration and Livestock Exclusion
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; Missouri Department of Conservation; USDA NRCS; Greene and Polk County Soil and Water Conservation Districts; City Utilities of Springfield; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: A three-year Section 319 project (about $276,500) restored riparian corridors around Fellows Lake and the upper Little Sac River, restricted livestock access to the lake and streams, installed management-intensive grazing systems, and roofed livestock lots and improved manure storage. Missouri removed the 826-acre drinking-water reservoir from the Clean Water Act 303(d) impaired waters list in the 2004/2006 cycle for both mercury (fish tissue below 0.3 mg/kg) and nutrients, and taste-and-odor complaints at Springfield's utilities effectively ceased.
stories.water: Fellows Lake / upper Little Sac River
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed work extended into Polk County (both counties are inside the extent). PDF link, no direct image URL.

stories.title: Frisco Highline Trail Streambank Stabilization (Dear Future Challenge)
stories.orgs: Ozark Greenways; Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Wildscape Environmental Services; Ozarks Coca-Cola/Dr Pepper Bottling Co.
stories.desc: A $30,000 Dear Future Community Challenge award funded stabilization of an eroding stream bank along the Frisco Highline Trail inside Springfield's drinking-water supply area, using stone toe protection and native plantings. The work halted bank loss at the site and was paired with student engagement through the award to a local student whose idea shaped the project.
stories.water: Tributary of the Little Sac River along the Frisco Highline Trail
stories.notes: Stream name, exact year and project length are not stated on the source page; location approximated to the Frisco Highline Trail corridor between Springfield and Willard, inside the Little Sac water supply watershed.

stories.title: Little Sac Agricultural Demonstration Area Riparian Protection and Livestock Exclusion
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; City Utilities of Springfield; USDA NRCS; Greene County Soil and Water Conservation District; Missouri State University William H. Darr School of Agriculture
stories.desc: On City Utilities land between Fellows and McDaniel lakes, the Watershed Committee restored a demonstration farm with riparian protection, perimeter and interior fencing to exclude livestock from the Little Sac River, a hardened water crossing, a refurbished alternative watering system and rotational grazing paddocks. Completed in 2017-2018, the site now hosts landowner classes, tours and research on grazing practices that protect Springfield's drinking-water reservoirs.
stories.water: Little Sac River (between McDaniel and Fellows lakes)
stories.notes: Acreage not published. Funded by the Little Sac Restoration and Improvement Project, City Utilities and a Lucky's Market community grant.

stories.title: Springfield-Area Floating Wetland Installations (Valley Water Mill, Fellows and McDaniel Lakes)
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Missouri Department of Conservation; City Utilities of Springfield; City of Springfield; Ozarks Technical Community College; Watershed Natives; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; Missouri State University; James River Basin Partnership; Dickerson Park Zoo
stories.desc: Partners built, planted and maintained native-plant floating wetlands in Valley Water Mill Lake, Fellows Lake and McDaniel Lake - all Springfield water supply reservoirs - beginning in 2023 and expanding each year through 2026, with additional units at MDC's Bois D'Arc Conservation Area and Shepherd of the Hills Hatchery. The structures take up excess nutrients, shift the plant community away from algae, and add fish, pollinator and aquatic invertebrate habitat; protective cages were added to keep wildlife from grazing the roots.
stories.water: Valley Water Mill Lake, Fellows Lake, McDaniel Lake (Little Sac River basin)
stories.notes: Companion units at Shepherd of the Hills Hatchery (Taney County, also in extent). The photo URL is the only non-logo image on the source page and may not show the wetlands.

stories.title: Valley Water Mill Wetland Enhancement and Reservoir Sediment Removal (319)
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; Missouri State University (OEWRI); Intuition and Logic Engineers; Springfield-Greene County Park Board
stories.desc: A Section 319 project in the Valley Water Mill sub-watershed replaced reed canary grass with more than 30 native wetland species, excavated accumulated sediment from the Valley Water Mill reservoir, and completed a stream and reservoir assessment. The restored wetland now filters runoff reaching the lake, which is part of Springfield's water supply system.
stories.water: Valley Water Mill Lake and Sanders Branch
stories.notes: Year not stated on the source page; range inferred from related Watershed Committee grant history. No dedicated project page exists - details appear on the Completed Projects index.

stories.title: Jordan Creek Riparian Enhancement, Phase 1 (North Packer Road)
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Watershed Natives; Coca-Cola of the Ozarks
stories.desc: On the upper Jordan Creek corridor at the Coca-Cola of the Ozarks facility on North Packer Road in Springfield, crews controlled invasive vegetation and installed container-grown native trees, shrubs and herbaceous plants to rebuild the riparian buffer. Phase 1 was completed in 2023, with supplemental native seeding carried out in early 2024.
stories.notes: Documented in the Watershed Committee of the Ozarks 2023 annual report (PDF). Planted area not quantified; coordinates approximate the North Packer Road reach of Jordan Creek.

stories.title: Big Urbie Urban Watershed Stewardship Project (Jordan, Fassnight, South and Pea Ridge Creeks)
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; City of Springfield Storm Water Services; Greene County Resource Management; Missouri State University OEWRI; Missouri State Project WET; James River Basin Partnership; Ozark Greenways; Springfield Public Schools
stories.desc: A $1.1 million Section 319 project across the Jordan, Fassnight, South and Pea Ridge Creek watersheds in Springfield installed riparian corridor improvements and streamside tree plantings, rain gardens, tree box filters, bioswales, infiltration trenches, pervious pavement at two elementary schools, detention basin retrofits at Missouri State and Drury universities, and a 20,000-gallon rainwater harvesting system. Volunteer planting days and creek cleanups engaged 232 participants, and before-and-after water quality monitoring by OEWRI documented the results in three final reports.
stories.water: Jordan Creek, Fassnight Creek, South Creek, Pea Ridge Creek (James River basin)
stories.notes: Coordinates are a watershed centroid for urban Springfield; work was distributed across many sites.

stories.title: Upper James River and Little Sac River Riparian Plantings
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks; Missouri Department of Conservation; Watershed Natives; private landowners
stories.desc: Under cooperative agreements with MDC, the Watershed Committee installed and maintained more than 500 native woody shrubs and trees along streams in the Upper James River and Little Sac River watersheds in 2022, with further plantings at multiple sites in 2023. One documented planting site is on the James River in Webster County; the work rebuilds shade and bank-holding root mass on grazed headwater reaches.
stories.water: Upper James River and Little Sac River
stories.notes: Work spans Webster and Greene counties (both inside the extent). Exact planting sites are not published; coordinates approximate the James River in Webster County.

stories.title: South Creek Daylighting and Natural Channel Restoration (Sunset Street)
stories.orgs: City of Springfield; Olsson; James River Basin Partnership; Ozark Greenways; Missouri State University; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; Missouri Department of Conservation; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Crews removed 1.2 acres of concrete channel along a 1-mile reach of South Creek and rebuilt a meandering channel with pools and riffles, 14 hardwood log weirs, nine Newbury weirs, 115 tons of creek rock and 65 boulders. Eight acres were seeded with 30 native species, 103 native trees were planted in a 60-foot riparian corridor and 40 vegetated rain gardens were built. Post-project monitoring (2017-2020) showed aquatic macroinvertebrate health improve from poor-fair to good-excellent, with modeled reductions of 15% total nitrogen and phosphorus and 29% sediment.
stories.water: South Creek (tributary of Wilsons Creek, James River basin)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 nonpoint source success story (published Dec 2020). Wilsons Creek remains 303(d) listed for other parameters; story reports incremental improvement rather than a delisting. Link is a PDF, so no direct image URL.

stories.title: Wilsons Creek Section 319 Watershed Project
stories.orgs: James River Basin Partnership; Missouri Department of Natural Resources; U.S. EPA Region 7; City of Springfield
stories.desc: A multi-year Clean Water Act Section 319 grant completed in 2023 targeted the Wilsons Creek watershed in Springfield with riparian corridor protection work - tree planting, streambank stabilization and permanent corridor protection - alongside stormwater and septic best management practices. JRBP paired the on-the-ground work with macroinvertebrate sampling and basin-wide water quality snapshots to track recovery in this James River tributary.
stories.notes: The grants page confirms the project is complete (2017-2023) but gives no scale or quantified outcome; practice descriptions come from JRBP's Riparian Corridor Protection project page (https://www.jamesriverbasin.com/projects-1). JRBP also completed an earlier 'Riparian 319' grant (2010-2015) and a 'Stormwater 319' grant (2006-2010) in the same basin.

stories.title: Shoal Creek Restoration, Neosho
stories.orgs: Watershed Committee of the Ozarks / Watershed Natives; local partners
stories.desc: Proceeds from the Watershed Committee's Watershed Natives native plant sales were directed to a stream restoration project on Shoal Creek at Neosho in southwest Missouri, alongside the Garrison Springs community forest project. The newsletter reports the funding and the project but does not quantify the length restored or the techniques used.
stories.notes: Thinly documented - the Fall 2024 Watershed Committee newsletter names the project and its funding but gives no scale, methods or outcome. Included because the stream, town and county are unambiguous and inside the extent; verify before publishing.

stories.title: Ozark Hellbender Propagation and Reintroduction in Ozark Rivers
stories.orgs: Missouri Department of Conservation (Shepherd of the Hills Hatchery); Saint Louis Zoo Ron and Karen Goellner Center for Hellbender Conservation / WildCare Institute; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; U.S. Forest Service; National Park Service; Missouri State University; Missouri University of Science and Technology; University of Missouri
stories.desc: MDC's Shepherd of the Hills Hatchery at Branson and the Saint Louis Zoo rear federally endangered Ozark hellbenders and state-endangered eastern hellbenders from wild-collected eggs and captive breeding, using simulated gravel-bottom streams and artificial nest boxes, then release them into Ozark rivers. The Zoo achieved the world's first captive breeding of Ozark hellbenders in 2011, and by August 2022 the partnership had reintroduced 10,206 zoo-reared hellbenders (9,034 Ozark, 1,172 eastern) in Missouri - described by the agencies as the nation's most successful hellbender release program - against a modeled extinction risk above 96 percent without intervention.
stories.water: Ozark rivers (release rivers withheld for species protection); rearing at Shepherd of the Hills Hatchery, Lake Taneycomo
stories.notes: Release rivers (Current, Jacks Fork, Eleven Point and North Fork White basins) are deliberately unnamed by the agencies, so coordinates are given for the MDC rearing facility at Branson. Release-milestone detail is at https://stlzoo.org/news/10-000th-hellbender-released-to-the-wild .

stories.title: Elk River Streambank Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Missouri; Missouri Department of Conservation; private landowner
stories.desc: About 1,650 feet of severely eroding bank on the Elk River was restored with bioengineering - live plantings and woody material in place of riprap - on a reach that had been losing roughly 8,000 tons of soil per year. The work cut sediment and gravel delivery to one of southwest Missouri's clearest float streams and rebuilt riparian woody cover.
stories.notes: TNC gives restored length as both 1,600 and 1,650 feet; no completion year stated. Approximate coordinates on the Elk River in McDonald County.

stories.title: Pilot Grove Creek SCS Site 77 Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; original structure a Soil Conservation Service floodwater retarding dam
stories.desc: Soil Conservation Service Site 77, a floodwater-retarding dam on an unnamed tributary of Hickory Creek in Collin County, was removed in 2023. Removal of these aging NRCS-era structures restores free flow and aquatic organism passage on small prairie tributaries. The annual summary records the removal but does not report height, mileage or partners.
stories.water: Unnamed tributary to Hickory Creek (Pilot Grove Creek watershed)
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Collin County is in north-central Texas (Trinity/Sulphur divide) and may fall outside the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Giant Salvinia Containment and Control on East Texas Lakes
stories.orgs: Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; river authorities; local cities and lake controlling authorities
stories.desc: TPWD deploys floating containment booms combined with herbicide treatment and salvinia weevil releases to control giant and common salvinia on East Texas reservoirs, including Lake Fork, Lake Athens, Lake Naconiche, Houston County Lake, Lake Raven and portions of Caddo Lake. Statewide in FY2024-25 roughly 24,500 acres of giant salvinia and 21,250 acres of water hyacinth were treated across nearly 70 water bodies, with about 342,000 salvinia weevils released as biological control. Booms keep mats from spreading into open water and off boat ramps, protecting native aquatic vegetation and littoral fish habitat.
stories.water: Lake Fork, Lake Athens, Lake Naconiche, Houston County Lake, Lake Raven, Caddo Lake
stories.notes: Single entry covering several in-extent reservoirs named on one TPWD page (Wood/Rains, Henderson, Nacogdoches, Houston, Walker, and Marion/Harrison counties). Lat/lon is Lake Fork. Acreage totals are statewide and include out-of-extent waters.

stories.title: Vaquero Crossing Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Vaquero Crossing Dam on an unnamed tributary of Hart Branch in Parker County was removed in 2023, restoring free-flowing conditions and stream connectivity on a small Trinity/Brazos divide tributary. The annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Parker County is in north-central Texas and may fall outside the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Catfish Creek Watershed Restoration and Delisting
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension; Texas Water Resources Institute; Texas A&M Natural Resources Institute; Trinity Waters; Texas Wildlife Association; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Across the 165-square-mile Catfish Creek watershed draining to the Trinity River, private landowners adopted conservation plans on more than 26,000 acres, with prescribed grazing, upland wildlife management, forest stand improvement and nutrient management, supported by a landowner peer network and extensive outreach. Recent monitoring shows E. coli geometric means meeting the 126 cfu/100 mL contact recreation standard, and the 36-mile creek was removed from the Texas 303(d) impaired waters list in 2014.
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; headwaters are in Henderson County, also in extent. Watershed BMPs rather than in-channel work.

stories.title: Leon River and South Leon River Delisting
stories.orgs: TCEQ; Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Brazos River Authority; Upper Leon, Mills County and Hamilton-Coryell Soil and Water Conservation Districts; USDA NRCS; Texas A&M AgriLife; Hamilton County; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Water quality management plans on 4,058 acres added alternative water sources, prescribed grazing, cross-fencing, grassed waterways, grass planting and nutrient management across the Leon River watershed, with NRCS-assisted conservation practices reaching more than 388,600 acres in the Leon basin and 47,600 acres in the South Leon basin, plus repair or replacement of 10 failing on-site sewage facilities in Hamilton County in 2012. Monitoring from 2005-2012 showed E. coli geometric means of roughly 68-102 cfu/100 mL in three Leon River assessment units and about 117 cfu/100 mL in the South Leon River. All four assessment units, including the entire 17-mile South Leon River, were removed from the impaired waters list in 2014.
stories.water: Leon River (1221_01, 1221_04, 1221_05) and South Leon River (1221B_01)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local districts, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; watershed spans Comanche, Erath, Hamilton, Coryell and Mills counties. Mills County is NOT on the in-extent list but the named reaches below Proctor Lake are in Comanche/Hamilton/Coryell.

stories.title: Toledo Bend Reservoir Tenaha Creek Arm Aquatic Life Use Restoration
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Shelby County Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Texas A&M Forest Service; TCEQ; local landowners
stories.desc: The Tenaha Creek Arm of Toledo Bend Reservoir was listed in 2000 for low dissolved oxygen that failed its aquatic life use, driven by nutrient runoff from poultry, grazing and forestry operations. Landowners implemented 26 water quality management plans on 4,155 acres plus NRCS conservation plans on 31,142 acres, covering waste utilization, nutrient management, grazing management, poultry mortality management and forestry best management practices, backed by forestry BMP education and effectiveness monitoring from 2002 to 2009. Monitoring in 2007-2009 met state dissolved oxygen standards and the arm was removed from the impaired waters list in 2010.
stories.water: Toledo Bend Reservoir, Tenaha Creek Arm (segment 0504_06)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; delisting restored the aquatic life use (dissolved oxygen), making this an aquatic-habitat outcome. Watershed BMPs rather than in-channel work.

stories.title: Leon River and Pecan Creek Grazing Land Restoration
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; TCEQ; Brazos River Authority; Upper Leon and Hamilton-Coryell Soil and Water Conservation Districts; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: In the 1,375-square-mile Leon River watershed, 13 certified water quality management plans on about 2,950 acres and NRCS practices on more than 4,600 acres installed alternative livestock water sources, prescribed grazing, cross-fencing, grassed waterways, grass planting and nutrient management, keeping cattle off stream banks and reducing runoff. Post-restoration E. coli geometric means fell to 123.81 cfu/100 mL on Pecan Creek and 121.83 cfu/100 mL on the upper Leon River, both below the standard. Pecan Creek's entire 11.9-mile segment was delisted in 2010 and the 3.9-mile upper Leon River segment in 2012.
stories.water: Pecan Creek (1221C_01) and upper Leon River (1221_07)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local districts, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; watershed spans Comanche, Erath, Hamilton and Coryell counties, all in extent.

stories.title: Attoyac Bayou Riparian and Grazing Land Restoration, Neches Basin
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Texas Water Resources Institute; TCEQ; USDA NRCS; Nacogdoches, Piney Woods, Rusk and Shelby Soil and Water Conservation Districts; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Along 82 miles of Attoyac Bayou in East Texas, 20 certified water quality management plans covering more than 2,000 acres added alternative livestock water, prescribed grazing, cross-fencing, animal mortality and composting facilities and nutrient management, while NRCS EQIP practices reached more than 13,700 additional acres with prescribed grazing, range planting, forestry practices, livestock pipelines and conservation cover. Total investment exceeded $2 million including about $617,800 in CWA section 319(h) funds. Long-term E. coli geometric means dropped below the 126 cfu/100 mL standard and TCEQ delisted a portion of the bayou in the 2016 Integrated Report.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local districts, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; also spans Rusk, San Augustine and Shelby counties, all in extent. Work is watershed BMPs (grazing/riparian management) rather than in-channel construction.

stories.title: Sulphur Creek Grazing Land Restoration and Delisting
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Texas A&M AgriLife Research; Hill Country Soil and Water Conservation District; USDA NRCS; TCEQ; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: On Sulphur Creek, a tributary of the Lampasas River in the eastern Hill Country, eight water quality management plans covering about 1,929 acres of mostly grazing operations and NRCS-assisted practices on more than 3,000 additional acres installed alternative livestock water, prescribed grazing, pasture and range planting, cross-fencing, nutrient management, brush management, prescribed burning and cover crops between 2013 and 2018. E. coli geometric means from 2011-2018 data fell to 45.51 cfu/100 mL, well below the 126 cfu/100 mL contact recreation standard, and TCEQ removed the upper creek from the 303(d) list in the 2020 Texas Integrated Report.
stories.water: Sulphur Creek (AU 1217B_02), Lampasas River / Brazos basin
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local district, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story. The PDF does not name the county; Sulphur Creek runs through Lampasas, Lampasas County, which is in extent. Link is a PDF.

stories.title: Navasota River and Cedar Creek Watershed Restoration
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Texas Water Resources Institute; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Research; Brazos County, Bedias Creek, Navasota and Robertson County Soil and Water Conservation Districts; USDA NRCS; TCEQ; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Six water quality management plans covering about 3,666 acres, mostly poultry and grazing operations, added alternative water sources, prescribed grazing, cross-fencing, mortality and composting facilities and nutrient management, while NRCS EQIP practices reached more than 4,200 additional acres with prescribed grazing, cover crops, livestock pipelines, troughs and ponds. Education covered riparian protection, feral hogs, livestock and septic systems. Three assessment units were delisted in sequence: Navasota River AU 1209_02 in 2012 (101.51 cfu/100 mL), Cedar Creek AU 1209G in 2014 (117.05), and Navasota River AU 1209_03 in 2018 (54.48).
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local districts, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; spans Brazos, Robertson, Grimes and Leon counties, all in extent.

stories.title: Neusch Dam Removal, James River
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Neusch Dam was removed from the James River in Mason County in 2024, restoring free-flowing conditions on a Llano River tributary that is a stronghold for Texas Hill Country spring-fed stream fauna. The 2024 annual summary records the removal but does not report height, reconnected mileage or partner organizations.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Mason County is in the central Texas Hill Country and may fall outside the project extent; included per the brief's instruction to flag rather than drop. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: San Gabriel River Ranch Lake Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: A ranch lake dam on Lackey Creek in Williamson County was removed in 2021, draining the impoundment and restoring free-flowing stream conditions in the San Gabriel River system. American Rivers' 2021 report records the removal but gives no height, reconnected mileage or partners.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Williamson County is in central Texas and may fall outside the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Wolf Pen Creek Grow Zone Stream Restoration, College Station
stories.orgs: City of College Station Parks and Recreation; Texas Water Resources Institute; Texas Commission on Environmental Quality; Texas Riparian Association
stories.desc: An 850-foot reach of Wolf Pen Creek in Wolf Pen Creek Park was converted from mown turfgrass to a native-plant Grow Zone in December 2024, with native seeding and the end of routine mowing so deep-rooted vegetation could stabilize the banks. The site survived two intense flood events in its first six months with most plantings intact, and project staff report visibly more stable banks, abundant pollinator use and native fish using the vegetated margin for cover during floods. Erosion monitoring compares the Grow Zone to an upstream mown control using erosion pins, cross-section surveys, the Bank Erosion Hazard Index and Wolman pebble counts.
stories.notes: Installation complete; quantitative erosion monitoring results not yet published. Demonstration site for TWRI's Urban Riparian and Stream Restoration Program.

stories.title: Upper Brushy Creek WS Site 10B Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Upper Brushy Creek Water Control and Improvement District; listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory
stories.desc: Watershed Site 10B, a floodwater-retarding structure on a tributary of Chandler Branch in the Upper Brushy Creek watershed, was removed in Williamson County in 2021. Removal restores free flow on a small Brazos-basin tributary. The 2021 report records the removal without height, mileage or further partner detail.
stories.water: Tributary of Chandler Branch (Upper Brushy Creek)
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - Williamson County, central Texas, may fall outside the extent. District ownership inferred from the structure name. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Jamestown Tributary Stream Rehabilitation, Little Walnut Creek
stories.orgs: City of Austin Watershed Protection Department; Austin Water
stories.desc: About 2,500 feet of eroding streambank on the Jamestown Tributary of Little Walnut Creek in north Austin is being stabilized using natural limestone boulders, mechanically stabilized earth walls and graded slopes, with native vegetation planted along the restored banks and large concrete debris removed from the channel. The $8.2 million project also upsizes storm drain and wastewater lines and replaces the Fairfield Drive crossing with a pedestrian-friendly bridge. Construction began May 2026 with completion estimated winter 2027.
stories.notes: In progress. Funded by Austin drainage utility fees and 2018 bonds.

stories.title: Austin Grow Zones Riparian Reforestation Program
stories.orgs: City of Austin Watershed Protection Department; TreeFolks; Austin Civilian Conservation Corps; Keep Austin Beautiful; The Other Ones Foundation
stories.desc: Austin's Watershed Protection Department manages creekside Grow Zones along 45 creeks and tributaries totaling more than 90 miles, where mowing is halted so riparian forest can re-establish and, where tree diversity is limited, seedlings are planted at roughly one tree every three feet. Ready! Set! Plant! volunteer events run with TreeFolks each fall and winter install 25-30 native tree and shrub species. The program also includes the Onion Creek floodplain, where 815 flood-prone properties bought between 1999 and 2021 were converted to public open space and restored riparian land.
stories.water: Austin-area creeks including Onion Creek, Walnut Creek, Williamson Creek
stories.notes: Program-level entry; the page does not give per-site acreage or dates. Lat/lon is the Onion Creek / Yarrabee Bend floodplain restoration area.

stories.title: Healthy Creeks Initiative Arundo Removal, Texas Hill Country
stories.orgs: Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; private landowners; local river authorities; nonprofit partners
stories.desc: TPWD's Healthy Creeks Initiative treats Arundo donax (giant reed/carrizo cane) along Hill Country rivers using targeted aquatic-approved herbicide applied at no cost to landowners, to restore stream function, reduce erosion and improve habitat for Guadalupe bass. Begun as a 2015 pilot, by the end of 2024 the program had enrolled more than 380 landowners across five watersheds (Blanco, Guadalupe, Llano, Medina and Pedernales), eight counties and about 300 river miles, with roughly 52 additional miles added in FY2025. Native riparian vegetation has re-established on treated reaches, and two elephant ear species were added to the target list in 2025.
stories.water: Blanco, Guadalupe, Llano, Medina and Pedernales rivers
stories.notes: Covers Bandera, Blanco, Comal, Gillespie, Hays, Kerr, Kimble and Kendall counties, all inside the extent. Lat/lon is a representative point (Kerrville, Guadalupe River). Mileage figures from TPWD's FY24-25 statewide AIS management summary, https://tpwd.texas.gov/landwater/water/aquatic-invasives/media/Statewide_AIS_Management_FY24-25.pdf, which was also verified.

stories.title: Buescher State Park Aquatic Vegetation Control
stories.orgs: Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: Targeted invasive and nuisance aquatic plant control at the lake in Buescher State Park cleared dense surface vegetation that had closed off the shoreline. TPWD's FY2024-25 statewide aquatic invasive species report documents the work with before-and-after photographs and reports that treatment restored access for bank angling and reopened littoral habitat.
stories.notes: Described in a statewide report rather than a dedicated project page; no acreage given. Link is a PDF.

stories.title: Guadalupe River Above Canyon Lake Restoration, Kerrville
stories.orgs: TCEQ; Upper Guadalupe River Authority; City of Kerrville; Kerr County; Texas Department of Transportation
stories.desc: A 3.5-mile reach of the Guadalupe River through Kerrville was restored to contact recreation use through 23 pet waste stations in riverside parks, bird deterrent structures on three sections of the SH16 bridge, waterfowl-feeding signage and limited removals, annual river and low-water-crossing cleanups that removed thousands of pounds of litter, and major wastewater collection repairs (about 42,675 feet of line replaced, 16 lift stations, 100 manholes) from 2011 to 2015. More than $548,851 was spent including over $329,000 in CWA 319(h) funds. Assessment unit 1806_04 was delisted in 2012 (geomean 87.25 cfu/100 mL) and 1806_06 in 2014 (97.3 cfu/100 mL).
stories.water: Guadalupe River above Canyon Lake (segment 1806, AUs 1806_04 and 1806_06)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story. CAVEAT: the work is largely wastewater infrastructure, pet/bird waste management and in-stream litter cleanups rather than physical habitat restoration; included because it is a documented river-reach delisting with on-the-ground in-channel cleanup work. Lower confidence than the other entries.

stories.title: Bessie Heights Wetland Restoration, Neches River Marsh
stories.orgs: Deepwater Horizon Texas Trustee Implementation Group; Texas General Land Office; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; NOAA; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: Selected in the Texas Trustee Implementation Group's first restoration plan (2017), the Bessie Heights project restores subsided brackish marsh in the Bessie Heights complex along the lower Neches River in Orange County, an area converted to open water by subsidence and erosion. Dredged and borrow sediment is used to rebuild marsh elevations and re-establish emergent vegetation. The project was still listed as In Progress in the Texas TIG project tracker.
stories.water: Bessie Heights marsh / lower Neches River, Sabine Lake system
stories.notes: The NOAA project page (https://www.gulfspillrestoration.noaa.gov/project?id=100) is JavaScript-driven and returned only a title; the TX TIG Restoration Plan 1 PDF linked here describes the project and its Orange County location. Status is also shown on https://www.gulfspillrestoration.noaa.gov/restoration-areas/texas . Approximate coordinates.

stories.title: Restoration of JD Murphree WMA Water Management Infrastructure
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: GEBF-funded restoration of the water management infrastructure at the J.D. Murphree Wildlife Management Area near Port Arthur, rebuilding the levees, water control structures and pumps that maintain marsh hydrology across the area's coastal wetlands. Awarded in 2017.
stories.water: J.D. Murphree WMA marshes / Salt Bayou
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Upper Cibolo Creek Riparian Restoration and Delisting, Boerne
stories.orgs: City of Boerne; Upper Cibolo Creek Watershed Partnership; Cibolo Nature Center; Cow Creek Groundwater Conservation District; Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Texas Water Resources Institute; Texas A&M AgriLife; TCEQ; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Partners planted bald cypress in the riparian zone along Upper Cibolo Creek through Boerne to filter runoff, buffer and stabilize the banks, and added pet-waste stations, waterfowl-feeding signage, low-impact development standards and new city master plan requirements for riparian buffers and protected riparian corridors. About $758,842 was spent through 2020, including $455,305 in Clean Water Act section 319(h) funds. The E. coli geometric mean dropped from 476 cfu/100 mL at listing to below the 126 cfu/100 mL standard, and TCEQ removed the segment from the 303(d) impaired waters list in the 2018 Integrated Report.
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story. Link is a PDF.

stories.title: Memorial Park Land Bridge and Prairie Restoration, Houston
stories.orgs: Memorial Park Conservancy; The Nature Conservancy; City of Houston
stories.desc: Gulf Coast prairie and wetlands were restored on both sides of Memorial Drive in Houston's Memorial Park, with The Nature Conservancy supplying thousands of pounds of native seed harvested from its coastal preserves including Mad Island Marsh and Nash Prairie. The land bridge opened in 2023. Reported outcomes include restored pollinator and wildlife habitat, improved stormwater management in the Buffalo Bayou watershed and greater storm resilience.
stories.water: Buffalo Bayou watershed / Galveston Bay drainage
stories.notes: Coastal prairie wetland restoration in the upper Galveston Bay watershed rather than on the bay shoreline.

stories.title: Salt Bayou Watershed Restoration Program (Keith Lake Fish Pass and GIWW crossing)
stories.orgs: Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Texas General Land Office; Jefferson County; Deepwater Horizon Texas Trustee Implementation Group; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
stories.desc: Guided by the 2013 Salt Bayou Watershed Restoration Plan, partners restored the mouth of the Keith Lake Fish Pass to re-balance tidal exchange, restored the watershed crossing at the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway, and restored marsh inside the conservation lands of McFaddin NWR and the J.D. Murphree WMA. These hydrologic fixes reduced saltwater intrusion into roughly 100,000 acres of the largest remaining coastal marsh complex on the upper Texas coast. The beach-ridge rebuild at McFaddin was the final phase.
stories.water: Salt Bayou / Keith Lake / Sabine Lake drainage
stories.notes: Linked page describes the Keith Lake Fish Pass, GIWW crossing and marsh phases as already restored. Lat/lon at the Keith Lake Fish Pass.

stories.title: Enhancement of Buffalo Lake Marsh Complex
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: GEBF-funded enhancement of the Buffalo Lake marsh complex on the upper Texas coast, restoring marsh hydrology and habitat within the coastal wetland system. Awarded in 2019.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; county inferred from the upper-coast marsh complex, verify before fine-scale mapping.

stories.title: Galveston Bay Sustainable Oyster Reef Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Texas; Galveston Bay Foundation; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund)
stories.desc: A $2.5 million GEBF project restoring 40 acres of degraded oyster reef in upper Galveston Bay using high-relief structures and segmented reef complexes. Fifteen acres are a harvest-restricted sanctuary supplying larvae to 25 acres of commercial reef, which was to stay closed to harvest for its first two years. Awarded November 2015.
stories.notes: Fact sheet lists status as active with the construction bid package complete; completion not confirmed on the sheet.

stories.title: Rich Sanctuary Freshwater Wetland and Coastal Prairie Restoration
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (Wetland Reserve Program)
stories.desc: The 192-acre Rich Sanctuary in Chambers County, adjacent to Trinity Bay, was converted from abandoned farmland back to a functioning wetland and coastal prairie system under the NRCS Wetland Reserve Program. Work included excavating shallow wetland depressions and planting native coastal prairie grasses. The restored complex contributes to the more than 780 acres of wetland Galveston Bay Foundation reports restoring to date.
stories.notes: Completion year not stated on the source page. Approximate coordinates in Chambers County adjacent to Trinity Bay.

stories.title: Sea Rim State Park Coastal Dune Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: GEBF-funded coastal dune restoration at Sea Rim State Park on the upper Texas coast, rebuilding the dune ridge that protects the marshes behind it from saltwater intrusion and storm overwash. Awarded in 2013.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; dune restoration protecting marsh hydrology behind the ridge.

stories.title: Marsh Mania 2022 Smooth Cordgrass Plantings (Trinity Bay, Kemah, Sweetwater Preserve)
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; Trinity Bay Discovery Center; ExxonMobil; CITGO; Coca-Cola Southwest Beverages; Reliant/NRG; Transocean; United Airlines
stories.desc: 120 volunteers planted 15,400 smooth cordgrass stems in a single day, restoring about 7 acres of wetland at three Galveston Bay sites: 1.5 acres at the Trinity Bay Discovery Center in Beach City (3,500 stems), 3 acres at GBF headquarters in Kemah (5,000+ stems) and 2.5 acres at Sweetwater Preserve on Galveston Island (7,000+ stems). The event is part of a program that by 2022 had restored over 220 acres at 99 sites around the bay with more than 8,000 volunteers since 1999.
stories.water: Trinity Bay / Galveston Bay / West Bay
stories.notes: Three sites across Chambers and Galveston counties; coordinates at the Trinity Bay Discovery Center, Beach City. No non-logo article image was available.

stories.title: McFaddin Beach and Dune Restoration (Salt Bayou Watershed)
stories.orgs: Deepwater Horizon Texas Trustee Implementation Group; Texas General Land Office (CEPRA and Surface Damage funds); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Jefferson County; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund; Gulf Coast Ecosystem Restoration Council (RESTORE); GOMESA
stories.desc: More than 14 miles of eroded Gulf beach and dune ridge fronting McFaddin National Wildlife Refuge were rebuilt with offshore and upland sediment, and more than 150,000 native dune plants were installed to stabilize the new dunes. The restored ridge closes breaches that were letting Gulf saltwater pour into the Salt Bayou estuarine marsh complex behind it. Construction finished at the end of 2024; the Texas Trustees contributed $18 million and will monitor plant survival and sand movement for five years.
stories.water: Gulf shoreline fronting Salt Bayou marsh / McFaddin NWR
stories.notes: A 2017 pilot restored 2.9 miles of the same shoreline. Total project cost estimated at $87 million across funding sources.

stories.title: Panther Springs Creek Restoration
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority; City of San Antonio
stories.desc: Under the City of San Antonio 2017-2022 bond program, SARA designed and built a channel restoration on Panther Springs Creek in north San Antonio to improve conveyance in the existing natural channel and eliminate excessive ponding. Work included survey, environmental investigations and permitting, property acquisition and construction, at an adopted budget of $1.1 million. Completed in December 2023.
stories.notes: Project page does not detail restoration techniques or outcomes. Approximate lat/lon (Stone Oak area, Salado Creek watershed). A second, still-active phase is listed separately.

stories.title: Shipe Woods Breakwater and Marsh Restoration, Trinity Bay
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation
stories.desc: Galveston Bay Foundation's 14.26-acre Shipe Woods property on the eastern shoreline of Trinity Bay had lost more than 100 feet of shoreline in ten years. In 2013 a 725-foot rock breakwater was constructed offshore, and volunteers planted smooth cordgrass in the protected water behind it. The planted marsh has since spread behind the breakwater, halting the shoreline retreat.
stories.notes: Described in the Living Shorelines section of the GBF habitat page; approximate coordinates on the eastern Trinity Bay shoreline.

stories.title: Geronimo Creek Riparian Restoration Demonstration Site
stories.orgs: Texas Water Resources Institute; Irma Lewis Seguin Outdoor Learning Center; Guadalupe-Blanco River Authority; Geronimo and Alligator Creeks Watershed Partnership
stories.desc: A riparian buffer was installed on Geronimo Creek at the Irma Lewis Seguin Outdoor Learning Center using natural bank stabilization techniques and native vegetation, with planting on an approximately 100-foot reach. The buffer holds soil, stabilizes the bank and filters runoff, especially during flood flows. The restored site was monitored against an unrestored upstream reference reach for bank erosion and total suspended solids, and results showed measurable benefits from the increased bank vegetation.
stories.notes: Page gives no explicit project dates (last modified Aug. 2022). Photo is the site header image, not a project photo.

stories.title: Marsh Mania 2024 Marsh Planting at Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Anahuac NWR); Exploration Green Conservancy; Aramco; CITGO; United Airlines; Port Houston; Transocean
stories.desc: At the 25th annual Marsh Mania, volunteers planted 11,000 smooth cordgrass stems at Anahuac National Wildlife Refuge on East Galveston Bay, plus 600 coastal prairie plants at GBF headquarters and 1,700 freshwater wetland stems at Exploration Green. 105 volunteers contributed 436 hours across the planting events. The event series has restored more than 221 acres of coastal habitat around Galveston Bay with over 8,500 volunteers since 1999.
stories.notes: Primary planting site was Anahuac NWR; coordinates given for the refuge.

stories.title: Trinity Bay Dual Sanctuary and Commercial Harvest Oyster Reef
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; The Nature Conservancy; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Texas Water Development Board; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund
stories.desc: More than 20,000 tons of limestone cultch were placed in southwestern Trinity Bay to create 40 acres of new oyster habitat: 25 acres opened to commercial harvest and 15 acres built with dredge-resistant larger material as a permanent broodstock sanctuary. Tidal current measurement and modelling by the Texas Water Development Board sited the sanctuary so its larvae would seed the harvestable reefs. Announced January 2021, the reef was closed for two years to allow oysters to populate it; it is described as the first project of its kind in Galveston Bay.
stories.notes: Approximate coordinates in southwestern Trinity Bay; the reef straddles the Chambers/Galveston county water boundary.

stories.title: Candy Abshier WMA Shoreline Protection and Marsh Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: GEBF-funded shoreline protection and marsh restoration at the Candy Abshier Wildlife Management Area on Galveston Bay at Smith Point, armouring an eroding bay shoreline and rebuilding the marsh behind it. Awarded in 2015.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Galveston Bay Foundation Kemah Headquarters Living Shoreline
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation
stories.desc: A 905-linear-foot living shoreline was built in summer 2021 at the Galveston Bay Foundation headquarters on Galveston Bay in Kemah, combining an offshore rock breakwater, planted native marsh grass and a secondary bulkhead at the land-water edge. The restored intertidal marsh behind the breakwater covers about three acres. During Hurricane Beryl's landfall the breakwater measurably reduced wave energy and surge while the marsh held soil in place and the shoreline did not erode.
stories.notes: Storm performance reported after Hurricane Beryl (2024).

stories.title: Marsh Mania 2023 Salt Marsh Planting at Candy Abshier WMA
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (Candy Abshier WMA); Aramco; Marathon Petroleum Foundation; CITGO; United Airlines; Transocean; Ports America
stories.desc: More than 90 volunteers planted 14,200 marsh grass stems at the Candy Abshier Wildlife Management Area at Smith Point on Galveston Bay during the 24th annual Marsh Mania. The planting rebuilt salt marsh fringe at a site best known as a hawk-watch and migratory bird stopover. Cumulatively the program had restored more than 213 acres of salt marsh around Galveston Bay by 2023.

stories.title: East Salitrillo Creek Natural Channel Design Pilot
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority; City of Converse; Judson Independent School District
stories.desc: About a quarter-mile of East Salitrillo Creek through the Judson High School campus in Converse was rebuilt using natural channel design after urban runoff destabilized the channel and lateral migration threatened utilities, roads and athletic fields. Work included partial stream realignment, root wads and log/boulder vanes on outside bends, boulder and log grade-control structures, and rock-lined plunge pools at two tributary junctions. Two bioswales with littoral shelves and a boulder cascade were added on the west side to treat school-campus stormwater before it reaches the creek, reducing erosion and downstream sediment delivery.
stories.notes: Construction began Jan. 10, 2011. The two photos cited are the page's before/after stream restoration images and are not explicitly captioned as East Salitrillo Creek.

stories.title: Oyster Reef Restoration in East Bay, Galveston Bay
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: GEBF-funded oyster reef restoration in East Bay, part of the Galveston Bay system, placing cultch to rebuild reef lost to storms and sedimentation. Awarded in 2013.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Galveston Bay Foundation Oyster Shell Recycling and Volunteer Reef Restoration
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; participating Houston, Clear Lake and Galveston restaurants; bayfront property owners; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: Galveston Bay Foundation collects shucked oyster shell from nearly 40 restaurants between Houston and Galveston, cures it for at least six months, and returns thousands of pounds a year to Galveston Bay as reef substrate. Volunteers build shell-bag breakwaters parallel to eroding shorelines, while bayfront property owners grow spat-on-shell in dock-hung oyster gardens each May-June and transplant inch-long oysters to restoration reefs in the fall. Larger reefs are built by contractors using river rock, limestone or concrete rip-rap topped with recycled shell, and reef health and growth are monitored to refine the technique.
stories.notes: Ongoing program rather than a single site; program description also at https://www.galvbay.org/habitat . Start year not stated on the source pages.

stories.title: Marsh Mania 2026 Volunteer Coastal Habitat Restoration
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; Port Houston; CITGO; Aramco; Del Papa Distributing; Bass Pro Shops and Cabela's Outdoor Fund; John P. McGovern Foundation; Odfjell; Houston Pilots; Exploration Green Conservancy
stories.desc: 136 volunteers and 21 team captains logged 421 hours restoring 1.37 acres of coastal habitat with about 7,100 native plants across four sites: 0.37 acres of freshwater habitat at Paul Hopkins Park on Dickinson Bayou (2,200 smooth cordgrass), 0.25 acres of coastal tallgrass prairie plus 0.25 acres of freshwater habitat at the Gessner Center in Kemah, and 0.5 acres of freshwater wetland at Exploration Green (3,000 plants). More than 95 volunteers propagated the plants over 250 hours from May to August beforehand.
stories.water: Dickinson Bayou / Clear Lake / Galveston Bay tributaries
stories.notes: Multi-site event; coordinates at Paul Hopkins Park on Dickinson Bayou. Exploration Green is in Harris County (Clear Lake City).

stories.title: Dickinson Bay Oyster Reef Restoration
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; Restore America's Estuaries; NOAA; Freese and Nichols; Deepwater Horizon Texas Trustee Implementation Group; Texas General Land Office; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: Galveston Bay Foundation built four recycled-shell reef mounds in 2018 and 2022 (about 0.4 acres from 750 cubic yards of recycled shell), then in summer 2026 added ten large mounds of rip-rap capped with 4-6 inches of recycled oyster shell, creating roughly 2 more acres of reef where Dickinson Bayou meets Galveston Bay. The mixed-material design was adopted after monitoring showed the shell-only mounds went anoxic below 8-10 inches. Monitoring has documented oysters up to 6.5 inches plus crabs, shrimp, fish and mussels, and about 1,610 spat-on-shell from the volunteer oyster gardening program had been transplanted onto the reefs by December 2025.
stories.water: Dickinson Bay / Dickinson Bayou, Galveston Bay
stories.notes: Approximately 2.4 acres of reef in total across phases. Merged during QA with a duplicate record describing the same project (https://www.gulfspillrestoration.noaa.gov/2022/05/major-milestone-completed-new-bird-rookery-island).

stories.title: Dollar Bay / Moses Lake Marsh Terrace and Breakwater Restoration
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; CCA Texas (Habitat Today for Fish Tomorrow); Building Conservation Trust; Ducks Unlimited; Shell; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Coastal Program; NOAA; Texas General Land Office; City of Texas City
stories.desc: The final phase of a two-decade effort restored 73 acres of intertidal marsh in the Dollar Bay-Moses Lake complex, where subsidence and erosion had converted historic marsh to open water. Work built wave-attenuating breakwaters along about 1,500 feet of shoreline and constructed 47 marsh terraces raised to elevations that support estuarine emergent vegetation, followed by volunteer smooth cordgrass planting. It completed earlier breakwater phases of 1,600 feet (2002), 2,400 feet (2012) and 1.3 miles (2018), and adjoins a 106-acre coastal prairie tract GBF acquired as an upland buffer.
stories.water: Dollar Bay / Moses Lake, Galveston Bay
stories.notes: Funding announcement with additional detail at https://www.galvbay.org/post/galveston-bay-foundation-receives-2-3-million-grant-to-restore-marsh-along-galveston-bay ($2.3M NFWF GEBF plus $1M National Coastal Resilience Fund; >$5.7M total).

stories.title: San Pedro Creek Culture Park Urban Stream Restoration
stories.orgs: Bexar County; San Antonio River Authority; City of San Antonio
stories.desc: A concrete flood-control ditch running through downtown San Antonio from the tunnel inlet near Fox Tech High School to the confluence with Apache Creek was reconstructed as a naturalized linear park and creek corridor. The project restores natural habitat and water quality along more than 2 miles of creek while removing roughly 30 acres and 38 structures from the 100-year floodplain. Completed in phases between 2012 and 2025 at a cost of about $303 million.
stories.notes: Project page states habitat and water-quality restoration goals but gives no habitat metrics; the quantified figures are floodplain and length. Primarily an urban stream/culture park project.

stories.title: Upper San Antonio River Green Infrastructure Restoration (AU 1911_07)
stories.orgs: City of San Antonio; San Antonio River Authority; San Antonio Water System; Texas Water Resources Institute; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Research; TCEQ; Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: In the Salado Creek-San Antonio River watershed, partners built low impact development and green stormwater infrastructure including permeable pavement, a bioswale, bioretention areas, a rain garden and rainwater harvesting at the Mission Library, plus a permeable parking lot, nine bioretention cells and seven rainwater cisterns at two SARA campuses, alongside River Walk sidewalk washing capture, grackle reduction, 173 pet waste dispensers in 75 parks and feral hog management. Monitoring estimated the SARA sites alone remove 46 percent of the annual bacterial load from stormwater runoff. Samples from 2011-2018 gave a geometric mean of 118.56 cfu/100 mL and the 2020 Integrated Report found the unit fully supporting recreational use. Total cost about $2.08 million.
stories.water: Upper San Antonio River (AU 1911_07), Salado Creek watershed
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story. Classified here as Wetland/floodplain because the work is distributed green stormwater infrastructure (bioretention, bioswales, rain gardens) rather than in-channel restoration.

stories.title: First Freshwater Mussel Reintroduction in Texas, Mission Reach of the San Antonio River
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Inks Dam National Fish Hatchery); Utah State University; The Meadows Center for Water and the Environment; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
stories.desc: Hatchery-propagated yellow sandshell mussels raised at Inks Dam National Fish Hatchery were released in May 2024 into the restored Mission Reach of the San Antonio River just south of downtown San Antonio, the first freshwater mussel reintroduction in Texas. About 5,000 more mussels were scheduled for release beginning that July, with juveniles of pistolgrip, pimpleback and threeridge to follow. Some mussels are PIT-tagged and are being tracked with visual surveys to measure survival and reproduction.
stories.notes: Same boundary uncertainty as the Otilla Dam entry. Species restoration into an engineered river-restoration reach rather than habitat construction itself.

stories.title: Guadalupe Bass Reintroduction, Upper San Antonio River
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Texas State University; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation
stories.desc: After in-channel habitat was rebuilt in the Mission Reach, partners collected, tagged and stocked Guadalupe bass (Micropterus treculi) into reaches of the upper San Antonio River where the Texas state fish had been extirpated. More than 60,000 fish were released into the Mission Reach and roughly 84,000 more at four additional upper-basin sites from 2015 onward. A 2017 genetic study confirmed the stocked fish were genetically pure and were spawning, documenting a re-established, reproducing population.
stories.notes: Project page is marked Completed but gives no fish counts; the numbers (60,000 and 84,000) and the 2017 genetics result come from the SARA ecosystems page, https://www.sariverauthority.org/services/river-health/ecosystems/, which was also verified.

stories.title: Mission Reach Streambank Erosion Repairs
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority; Bexar County
stories.desc: A rolling program of bank repairs along the restored Mission Reach of the San Antonio River, funded at about $5.1 million under an interlocal agreement with Bexar County. Completed repairs are located downstream of Mitchell Street, at the confluence with San Pedro Creek, downstream of Espada Dam, and near the Lone Star Brewery. The repairs protect the hike-and-bike trail system and reduce sediment loading to the restored river channel.
stories.notes: Page lists the project as Active although the stated end date (June 30, 2023) has passed; several individual repair sites are described as completed.

stories.title: Otilla Dam Removal, San Antonio River
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority (project partner lead); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program)
stories.desc: Removal of the Otilla Dam, a deteriorating 1920s irrigation dam on the San Antonio River that is a public safety hazard and a full barrier to aquatic species including American eel, burrhead chub and Guadalupe bass. The $1,000,000 National Fish Passage Program project is expected to reconnect about 30 miles of upstream river habitat and reduce flood risk.
stories.notes: Boundary uncertainty: south-central Texas, San Antonio River basin draining to San Antonio Bay. Include only if the Texas portion of the extent reaches Bexar County. FY2024 National Fish Passage Program award; no completion status given.

stories.title: Mission Reach Ecosystem Restoration Project, San Antonio River
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; Bexar County; City of San Antonio; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Texas State University; National Fish and Wildlife Foundation
