stories.desc: An 8-mile straightened flood-control channel of the San Antonio River south of downtown was reconfigured into a functioning river ecosystem, with more than 100 acres of constructed aquatic features (riffles, pools, embayments) and over 350 acres of native riparian and grassland plantings, including more than 20,000 native trees and shrubs. Follow-up work includes prescribed burning, invasive plant control and periodic stem-density management to keep the restored floodplain within its design capacity. Monitoring since 2015 has documented returning bird communities (Interior Least Tern, Black-capped Vireo) and successful Guadalupe bass reproduction in the restored reach.
stories.notes: Construction of the USACE/SARA ecosystem restoration project was substantially completed in 2013; adaptive management (stem density, prescribed fire, erosion repair) continues. Lat/lon is mid-reach near Mission Concepcion.

stories.title: Freshwater Mussel Reintroduction, Mission Reach
stories.orgs: San Antonio River Authority; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
stories.desc: Building on a 2017 Mission Reach Mussel Survivability Study and a propagation feasibility project, SARA and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service are propagating four native freshwater mussel species and placing them into the restored Mission Reach, where mussel beds had been nearly eliminated but survive in remnant channels. Species recovered during relocation events include yellow sandshell, pistolgrip, pimpleback, threeridge and washboard. The five-year release schedule is timed to the maturation period of the slowest-developing species.
stories.notes: In progress; propagation feasibility confirmed but no completed release counts published. Budget $484,052.

stories.title: Pierce Marsh Wetland Restoration (Beneficial Use of Dredged Material)
stories.orgs: NOAA; Deepwater Horizon Texas Trustee Implementation Group; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers; Texas General Land Office; Ducks Unlimited; Galveston Bay Foundation; The Nature Conservancy
stories.desc: More than 280,000 cubic yards of sediment dredged from federally maintained navigation channels were pumped up to seven miles to rebuild 115 acres of intertidal marsh within the 800-acre Pierce Marsh complex on West Galveston Bay. Dredging phase one finished in January 2022 and phase two in early 2024, after which Galveston Bay Foundation led vegetative planting and Ducks Unlimited monitored sediment settlement. The work converted subsided open water back to vegetated wetland habitat for fish, shellfish and birds.
stories.notes: Dredged-material placement complete 2024; marsh planting and monitoring continuing. Lat/lon approximate for the Pierce Marsh complex south of Hitchcock.

stories.title: Lower Colorado River Grazing and Cropland Restoration
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; Texas Water Resources Institute; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Research; Lower Colorado River Authority; Colorado, Wharton and Matagorda County Soil and Water Conservation Districts; USDA NRCS; TCEQ; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: On the lower Colorado River above Matagorda Bay, 33 site-specific water quality management plans covering more than 14,700 acres of grazing, rice and row-crop land added alternative water sources, prescribed grazing, cross-fencing, nutrient management and grade stabilization structures, with NRCS EQIP practices on more than 10,000 additional acres and LCRA Creekside Conservation plans for three landowners. Outreach covered feral hogs, riparian areas, septic systems and livestock. The tidal reach's Enterococcus geomean fell from 152 to 31 cfu/100 mL and was delisted in 2014; the reach below La Grange fell from 140 to 114 cfu/100 mL E. coli and was delisted in 2018.
stories.water: Colorado River (AUs 1401_01 tidal and 1402_02 below La Grange)
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, river authority, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; spans Colorado, Wharton and Matagorda counties, all in extent.

stories.title: Upper San Antonio River Urban and Rangeland Restoration (AU 1911_02)
stories.orgs: TCEQ; Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA; San Antonio River Authority; City of San Antonio; Karnes and Wilson County Soil and Water Conservation Districts; Texas A&M AgriLife Research
stories.desc: Low impact development at the San Antonio Mission Public Library (infiltration structures, bioswales, roof rainwater collection and rain gardens) and runoff-diverting power washers on the River Walk were combined with rural grazing practices, including prescribed grazing, range planting and alternative watering facilities, under 12 water quality management plans covering 1,706 acres. About $1.85 million was invested from 2007, including $1.11 million in CWA section 319(h) funds. The E. coli geometric mean dropped from 184 to 106 cfu/100 mL between the 2006 and 2016 Integrated Reports, and the assessment unit was delisted in 2016.
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; AU lies southeast of San Antonio in Wilson County, with Karnes County rangeland work. Both in extent.

stories.title: Bird Island Cove Habitat Restoration, West Galveston Bay
stories.orgs: Deepwater Horizon Texas Trustee Implementation Group; Texas General Land Office; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; NOAA
stories.desc: Bird Island Cove, on the bayside of Galveston Island adjacent to Galveston Island State Park, was engineered under the Texas TIG's first restoration plan and funded for $5 million construction in the second plan. The work restores intertidal marsh behind an existing breakwater, building on earlier marsh restoration in the cove, and includes replanting marsh grass. The project is now listed in Monitoring/Operations and Maintenance status, indicating construction is complete.
stories.water: Bird Island Cove / West Galveston Bay
stories.notes: The NOAA project page (https://www.gulfspillrestoration.noaa.gov/project?id=325) renders only a title; details come from the TX TIG Restoration Plan 2 PDF linked here, and status from https://www.gulfspillrestoration.noaa.gov/restoration-areas/texas . Approximate coordinates.

stories.title: Sweetwater Lake Living Shoreline, Sweetwater Nature Preserve
stories.orgs: Galveston Bay Foundation; Aramco Americas; volunteers
stories.desc: On the eroding western shoreline of Sweetwater Lake within the 449-acre Sweetwater Nature Preserve on Galveston Island, volunteers have hand-built up to 1,900 linear feet of offshore breakwater from mesh bags of recycled oyster shell and planted smooth cordgrass marsh behind it. The shoreline had been retreating one to two feet per year. Volunteer work has run since 2014; one 2022 event alone put about 3,000 Spartina alterniflora stems in the ground in two hours, and the reef now also provides oyster and nursery habitat for fish, shrimp and crabs.
stories.notes: Project description and 1,900-foot target also documented at https://www.galvbay.org/habitat

stories.title: Hydrological Restoration of Brazoria National Wildlife Refuge Wetlands
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Brazoria NWR)
stories.desc: GEBF-funded hydrologic restoration of wetlands at Brazoria National Wildlife Refuge on the upper Texas coast, repairing water control infrastructure and restoring marsh hydrology across refuge wetland units. Phase I was awarded in 2017 and phase II in 2020.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list.

stories.title: Freeport Nearshore Artificial Reef (George-Vancouver Site)
stories.orgs: Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Deepwater Horizon Trustees (Phase III Early Restoration); Callan Marine LTD
stories.desc: Beginning in December 2016, 800 concrete pyramids were deployed at the George-Vancouver nearshore artificial reef site about six miles off Freeport to create hard-bottom habitat in an otherwise featureless mud bottom. The reef was one of three Texas artificial reef projects funded as compensation for recreational use lost to the Deepwater Horizon spill. The structures are expected to support reef fish, corals and other invertebrates and provide accessible fishing and diving.
stories.water: Gulf of Mexico nearshore off Freeport
stories.notes: Nearshore marine reef rather than estuarine habitat; included because it is within state nearshore waters off an in-extent county. Site photo on the page shows the related Kraken ship-to-reef sinking.

stories.title: Dressing Point Island Rookery Island Restoration, East Matagorda Bay
stories.orgs: Deepwater Horizon Texas Trustee Implementation Group; Texas General Land Office; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Galveston Bay Foundation
stories.desc: Dressing Point Island in East Matagorda Bay is being rebuilt and armored as part of the Phase IV Early Restoration Texas Rookery Islands project, which restores four eroding colonial waterbird nesting islands. The island design was revised in 2023 to address continuing erosion and construction cost inflation, with implementation expected from 2024. Funds freed by dropping the Smith Point island were redirected to Dressing Point and Rollover Bay.
stories.notes: In progress as of the linked 2023 update; included because it is a funded, designed construction project within the Texas Rookery Islands program. Approximate coordinates for Dressing Point Island.

stories.title: Clive Runnells Family Mad Island Marsh Preserve Wetland Restoration
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy; Ducks Unlimited; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center
stories.desc: On the 7,063-acre Mad Island Marsh Preserve on the mid-Texas coast, The Nature Conservancy worked with Ducks Unlimited and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to create more than 500 acres of seasonally flooded wetlands and to enhance freshwater wetlands and coastal marshes for wintering waterfowl, alongside 3,500 acres of managed native coastal prairie. Management continues with prescribed fire, invasive species control and native seed harvest. The preserve supports more than 250 bird species including whooping crane, and the adjacent Matagorda County-Mad Island Marsh Christmas Bird Count has ranked first in the nation for species tallied for more than a decade.
stories.notes: Wetland creation dates to the 1980s-1990s; management and restoration ongoing.

stories.title: Mad Island Marsh Shoreline Protection and Coastal Ecosystem Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); The Nature Conservancy in Texas
stories.desc: GEBF-funded shoreline protection and coastal ecosystem restoration at TNC's Clive Runnells Family Mad Island Marsh Preserve on Matagorda Bay, protecting eroding marsh edge and restoring coastal wetland habitat. Awarded in 2016 with a further shoreline protection award in 2019.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; fills part of the Texas mid-coast gap.

stories.title: Lower San Antonio River Ranchland Restoration and Delisting
stories.orgs: Texas State Soil and Water Conservation Board; U.S. EPA; TCEQ; USDA NRCS; Karnes, Wilson and Victoria County Soil and Water Conservation Districts; San Antonio River Authority; City of San Antonio; local landowners
stories.desc: Across the 1,210-square-mile lower San Antonio River watershed, ranchers voluntarily installed alternative livestock water sources, prescribed grazing, cross-fencing, nutrient management and grass planting under 25 certified water quality management plans covering 15,961 acres, plus NRCS EQIP practices on 40,291 acres. Long-term E. coli geometric means dropped to 109.53 and 110.64 cfu/100 mL in the two impaired assessment units, below the 126 cfu/100 mL standard. Both units of the 153-mile river reach were removed from the impaired waters list in 2014 and now support all designated uses.
stories.sector: Partnership (state, federal, local districts, private landowners)
stories.notes: EPA 319 success story; spans DeWitt, Goliad, Karnes, Refugio, Victoria and Wilson counties, all in extent.

stories.title: Oyster Lake Shoreline Protection and Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Texas Parks and Wildlife Department
stories.desc: GEBF-funded shoreline protection and habitat restoration at Oyster Lake on the Matagorda Bay system, stabilising an eroding shoreline and restoring the marsh and oyster habitat behind it. Awarded in 2014.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; fills part of the Texas mid-coast gap.

stories.title: Matagorda Nearshore Artificial Reef
stories.orgs: Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Deepwater Horizon Trustees (Phase III Early Restoration); Callan Marine LTD
stories.desc: About 1,600 concrete pyramids were placed roughly 60 feet deep at the Matagorda nearshore artificial reef site, approximately ten miles offshore of Matagorda County, following completion of the Freeport deployment in winter 2016-17. The reef creates hard structure in open sand and mud bottom to support reef fish and invertebrates and to restore lost recreational fishing and diving opportunity.
stories.water: Gulf of Mexico nearshore off Matagorda
stories.notes: Nearshore marine reef off an in-extent county. Approximate coordinates; photo is the shared article image.

stories.title: Egery Flats Marsh Restoration
stories.orgs: National Fish and Wildlife Foundation (Gulf Environmental Benefit Fund); Texas Parks and Wildlife Department; Coastal Bend Bays & Estuaries Program
stories.desc: GEBF-funded marsh restoration at Egery Flats on the Aransas River delta at the head of Copano Bay, restoring tidal marsh and the hydrology connecting the river to the bay. Awarded in 2014.
stories.notes: Award year from the GEBF project list; the delta straddles the Refugio/San Patricio line, both inside the extent.

stories.title: Little Cabin Creek Grazing Land Restoration
stories.orgs: Craig County Conservation District; Delaware County Conservation District; Ottawa County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA; participating landowners
stories.desc: Across the 102,000-acre Little Cabin Creek watershed, landowners implemented prescribed grazing on about 15,400 acres, integrated pest management on 5,800 acres, brush management on 1,900 acres, forage and biomass planting on 2,400 acres, about 15,300 feet of fencing, 13,700 feet of livestock pipeline and 46 ponds between 2002 and 2015. The E. coli geometric mean in the 32.3-mile stream fell from 237 CFU/100 mL in 2004 to 101 CFU/100 mL by 2014, and the creek was removed from Oklahoma's 303(d) list for E. coli in 2014.
stories.water: Little Cabin Creek (Big Cabin Creek / Neosho River)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans Craig, Ottawa and Delaware counties, all inside the extent.

stories.title: Upper Honey Creek Riparian Exclusion and Stream Channel Restoration
stories.orgs: Delaware County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA Region 6; Oklahoma Office of the Secretary of Energy and Environment; Oklahoma Blue Thumb; participating landowners
stories.desc: From 2006 to 2014, work in the 79,000-acre Honey Creek watershed included riparian livestock exclusion on 384 acres, about 350,000 linear feet of cross-fencing, 48 ponds and 222 water tanks as alternative water, prescribed grazing on 2,820 acres, 238 heavy-use area protections, alum treatment and off-site transport of poultry litter, and replacement of 16 failing septic systems. About 3,600 feet of stream channel and riparian wetland were restored directly. The upper segment's E. coli geometric mean fell to 63 CFU/100 mL and it was removed from the 2012 303(d) list for E. coli.
stories.water: Honey Creek, upper segment (Grand Lake O' the Cherokees)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Distinct from the lower Honey Creek story; includes roughly 3,600 ft of in-channel and riparian wetland restoration.

stories.title: Lower Honey Creek Conservation Systems (Grand Lake)
stories.orgs: Delaware County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA Region 6; Oklahoma Office of the Secretary of Energy and Environment; Oklahoma Blue Thumb; participating landowners
stories.desc: Between 2006 and 2017 landowners in the 79,000-acre Honey Creek watershed installed prescribed grazing on 6,728 acres, riparian protection on 2,734 acres, about 491,762 feet of fence, 50,012 feet of livestock pipeline, nutrient management on 4,179 acres, 37 waste storage facilities and 48 ponds, at a cost of more than $3.29 million. The recreation-season E. coli geometric mean fell from 134 CFU/100 mL to 14 CFU/100 mL. Oklahoma proposed removing lower Honey Creek, which enters Grand Lake O' the Cherokees, from its 2018 303(d) list for E. coli.
stories.water: Lower Honey Creek (Grand Lake O' the Cherokees)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Headwaters reach into Benton County AR and McDonald County MO; the restored/delisted segment is in Delaware County, OK.

stories.title: Beaty Creek Watershed Restoration (Lake Eucha)
stories.orgs: Oklahoma Conservation Commission; Delaware County Conservation District; Benton County (AR) Conservation District; Oklahoma Department of Agriculture; Oklahoma State University Cooperative Extension; USDA NRCS; USDA Farm Service Agency; Arkansas Soil and Water Conservation Commission; local producers and poultry integrators
stories.desc: About 100 cost-share contracts across the 13-mile Beaty Creek watershed established 335 acres of riparian buffer, 31 miles of cross fencing, more than 150 alternative livestock water sources, 56 heavy-use area protections, 16 feeding/waste storage facilities and 27 septic replacements over 2000-2004. Mean E. coli and Enterococcus fell significantly and an OSU paired-watershed analysis estimated a 31 percent drop in phosphorus loading to Lake Eucha (flow-weighted phosphorus fell from 0.220 to 0.191 mg/L). Beaty Creek was nominated for removal from Oklahoma's 2006 303(d) list for E. coli.
stories.water: Beaty Creek (Lake Eucha / Spavinaw Creek basin)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed extends into Benton County, Arkansas; the Oklahoma portion is in Delaware County, inside the extent.

stories.title: Pryor Creek Riparian Buffer and Wetland Restoration
stories.orgs: Oklahoma Conservation Commission; Craig County Conservation District; Mayes County Conservation District; Rogers County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; participating landowners
stories.desc: In the 146,775-acre Pryor Creek watershed, landowners installed prescribed grazing on 37,178 acres, 191 acres of riparian forest buffer, 62 acres of wetland restoration, 55,615 feet of fencing, 14,021 feet of livestock pipeline, 35 ponds, two composting facilities and two waste storage facilities between 2002 and 2015. The E. coli geometric mean on the lower 4.97-mile segment fell from 135 CFU/100 mL to 25 CFU/100 mL, and Oklahoma removed the stream from its 2014 303(d) list for E. coli.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans Craig, Mayes and Rogers counties; Craig and Mayes are inside the extent, Rogers is not. The delisted lower segment is in Mayes County.

stories.title: Bull Creek Turbidity and Bacteria Reduction
stories.orgs: Oklahoma Conservation Commission; Mayes County Conservation District; Rogers County Conservation District; Wagoner County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: Landowners along the 17-mile Bull Creek installed prescribed grazing on 3,860 acres, brush management on 908 acres, 4,171 linear feet of fencing, 12,550 feet of terraces, conservation crop rotations on 732 acres and 10 ponds between 2004 and 2010. Turbidity exceedances of the 50 NTU standard fell from 25-35 percent of samples to 6 percent, and the E. coli geometric mean fell from 317 to 123 colonies/100 mL. Bull Creek was nominated for removal from the 2010 303(d) list for both turbidity and E. coli.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. BOUNDARY CAVEAT: watershed spans Mayes, Rogers and Wagoner counties; only Mayes is inside the listed extent, so part of this project lies outside.

stories.title: Ranger Creek Grazing Land Restoration (Fort Gibson Lake)
stories.orgs: Cherokee County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA; Oklahoma Locally Led Cost Share Program
stories.desc: Landowners in the 23,324-acre Ranger Creek watershed, about 60 percent grazing land, installed prescribed grazing on 2,179 acres, pest management on 2,430 acres, brush management on 447 acres, nutrient management on 473 acres, nine ponds and 408 feet of livestock pipeline from 2002 to 2017. E. coli violations fell from 50 percent of samples in 2002 to a geometric mean of 30 CFU/100 mL by 2014 and low dissolved oxygen violations fell from 25 percent to 9 percent. Oklahoma delisted the 7.94-mile creek for both E. coli and DO in 2014, and it now fully supports its fish and wildlife propagation use.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Also documented at: https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2018-09/documents/ok_fourteenmile_1745_508.pdf

stories.title: Illinois River Watershed Riparian Protection Program (Oklahoma)
stories.orgs: Oklahoma Conservation Commission; Grand River Dam Authority; Oklahoma Scenic Rivers Commission; USDA NRCS; Cherokee County Conservation District; Land Legacy; Cherokee Nation; poultry industry; participating landowners
stories.desc: Over roughly 25 years across the 577,550-acre Oklahoma portion of the Illinois River basin, hundreds of landowners signed 30-year riparian easements ($2,250/acre) that funded livestock exclusion fencing, buffer strips and streambank stabilization, alongside poultry litter export and storage, septic replacement, cedar removal and no-till conversion; a 2010 NRCS EQIP special initiative added more than $21 million in practices. Five Oklahoma river segments were removed from the bacteria impaired-waters list by 2016 and phosphorus loads declined basin-wide. The Illinois River, Barren Fork and Flint Creek are state scenic rivers.
stories.water: Illinois River, Barren Fork and Flint Creek
stories.notes: EPA in-depth Section 319 success story. Projects spanned Adair, Cherokee and Delaware counties, all inside the extent; point coordinates are for Tahlequah.

stories.title: Peacheater Creek Paired-Watershed Riparian and Grazing Restoration
stories.orgs: Oklahoma Conservation Commission; Adair County Conservation District; Cherokee County Conservation District; Oklahoma Department of Agriculture; Oklahoma State University Cooperative Extension; USDA NRCS; USDA Farm Service Agency; U.S. EPA National Nonpoint Source Monitoring Program; local producers
stories.desc: Eleven landowners in the 16,209-acre Peacheater Creek watershed (a Baron Fork / Illinois River tributary above Lake Tenkiller) installed riparian buffers, alternative livestock water, heavy-use feeding and waste storage areas, improved pasture management and septic repairs, and exported poultry litter, at a cost of about $800,000 between 1998 and 2002. Compared with the untreated Tyner Creek control, phosphorus loading dropped about 71 percent and total nitrogen loading about 58 percent. Median streambank erosional area fell from 4.1 to 1.7 square feet, the macroinvertebrate IBI rose from 29 to 34, and median fish counts rose from 89 to 275.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 / National NPS Monitoring Program. Adair and Cherokee county conservation districts were partners; both counties are inside the extent.

stories.title: Brazil Creek Riparian Forest Buffers and Grazing Management
stories.orgs: Haskell County Conservation District; Latimer County Conservation District; Le Flore County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: More than 110 landowners in the 156,448-acre Brazil Creek watershed, on the edge of the Ouachita National Forest, installed 143 acres of riparian forest buffer, prescribed grazing on 3,091 acres, nutrient management on 1,328 acres, brush management on 1,053 acres, about 90,887 feet of fencing, 13 waste facilities and 33 ponds from 2002 to 2020. By 2008 fewer than 10 percent of dissolved oxygen samples in the 17.83-mile creek fell below criteria, and the DO impairment was removed from the 303(d) list that year. The creek fully supports all other assessed warm water aquatic community parameters.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans Haskell, Latimer and Le Flore counties, all inside the extent.

stories.title: Peaceable Creek Grazing Land Restoration
stories.orgs: Pittsburg County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA; participating landowners
stories.desc: Landowners in the 93,000-acre Peaceable Creek watershed near McAlester installed prescribed grazing on about 6,947 acres, nutrient management on 3,240 acres, forage and biomass planting on 1,019 acres, about 30,552 feet of fence, 108 ponds, plus brush management, prescribed burning and pest management between 2000 and 2018. Turbidity was removed from the impaired list in 2006 and sulfate and E. coli in 2016, with sulfate exceedances falling from 11 percent of samples to zero and the E. coli geometric mean dropping from 149 to 58 CFU/100 mL on the 17.14-mile segment.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story.

stories.title: Caney Boggy Creek Sediment and Turbidity Reduction
stories.orgs: Oklahoma Conservation Commission; Coal County Conservation District; Pittsburg County Conservation District; Hughes County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA (Blue Thumb); participating landowners
stories.desc: In the 65,000-acre Caney Boggy Creek watershed, landowners installed prescribed grazing on roughly 4,800 acres, integrated pest management on 2,522 acres, nutrient management on 607 acres, cross-fencing, ponds, wildlife habitat management, prescribed burning and about 12,385 acres of firebreaks beginning in 2007. Base-flow samples exceeding the 50 NTU turbidity criterion fell from 20 percent in 2008 to 7 percent in 2010 and 0 percent by 2014. The 26.5-mile creek was removed from the 2010 turbidity impairment list and partially attains its fish and wildlife propagation use.
stories.water: Caney Boggy Creek (Clear Boggy / Red River basin)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. BOUNDARY CAVEAT: watershed spans Hughes, Coal and Pittsburg counties; Coal and Pittsburg are inside the listed extent, Hughes is not.

stories.title: Big Eagle Creek Forest and Riparian Restoration (Mountain Fork)
stories.orgs: Talihina Conservation District; Little River Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA
stories.desc: About 20 landowners in the 218,754-acre Big Eagle Creek watershed planted 740 acres of trees and shrubs, prepared 639 acres for planting, carried out forest stand improvement on 130 acres, prescribed burning on 698 acres, brush management and prescribed grazing on 145 acres each, 72,037 feet of firebreaks, 5,381 feet of fencing, 8 ponds and animal waste facilities between 2002 and 2020. Samples below the dissolved oxygen criterion dropped from 19 percent in 2008 to under 5 percent in 2018, and the 20.5-mile creek, a Mountain Fork tributary, was removed from the 2018 303(d) list, now partially supporting its Cold Water Aquatic Community use.
stories.water: Big Eagle Creek (Mountain Fork, Little River)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans Le Flore and McCurtain counties, both inside the extent.

stories.title: Ouachita National Forest Low-Water Ford Replacements
stories.orgs: Ouachita National Forest / USDA Forest Service (project partner lead); U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Fish Passage Program)
stories.desc: Four concrete low-water fords on tributaries of the Glover and Mountain Fork rivers are being removed and replaced with passable structures. The $1,000,000 project is a high priority because this is the only watershed where the threatened leopard darter occurs; it also benefits the Ouachita shiner and improves safe vehicle access to camping and fishing in the national forest. FWS lists 14 stream miles reopened.
stories.water: Glover River and Mountain Fork River tributaries (Little River basin)
stories.notes: FY2023 National Fish Passage Program award; status listed as In Development. Coordinates approximate within the Ouachita National Forest portion of McCurtain County.

stories.title: Glover River Forest and Grazing Land Restoration
stories.orgs: Little River Conservation District; Pushmataha County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry (Forestry Services); Oklahoma Conservation Commission; Oklahoma Water Resources Board; participating landowners
stories.desc: Across the 220,000-acre Glover River watershed, landowners installed tree and shrub establishment on 518 acres, forest stand improvement on 280 acres, prescribed grazing on 3,070 acres, brush management on 226 acres, 12,633 feet of fencing, 11,900 feet of firebreaks, 11 ponds and 5 waste storage facilities between 2004 and 2017, with ODAFF forestry BMPs guiding harvest operations. Turbidity criterion violations in the 33.95-mile river fell from 20 percent of samples to 9 percent, and the Glover was removed from the turbidity 303(d) list in 2014. It is one of Oklahoma's few remaining free-flowing rivers, draining to the Little River.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Watershed spans McCurtain and Pushmataha counties, both inside the extent.

stories.title: Pennington Creek Livestock Exclusion and Riparian Protection
stories.orgs: Oklahoma Conservation Commission (Blue Thumb); Johnston County Conservation District; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA; Tishomingo National Wildlife Refuge; Chickasaw Nation; City of Tishomingo; local landowners
stories.desc: Landowners along Pennington Creek, the sole drinking-water source for Tishomingo, installed 15,948 feet of fencing and 500 feet of pipeline to keep livestock out of the creek, plus four ponds, two watering facilities, a heavy-use area protection, a grade stabilization structure, prescribed grazing on 1,018 acres and nutrient management on 1,773 acres. Enterococcus fell from a geometric mean of 104 CFU/100 mL in 2006 to 26 CFU/100 mL in 2012, well below the 33 CFU threshold. Oklahoma recommended delisting the creek in 2012 and it now fully attains its designated uses.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Chickasaw Nation and Tishomingo NWR participated in Blue Thumb volunteer training in the watershed.

stories.title: Rock Creek Forest, Riparian and Feral Swine Restoration
stories.orgs: Little River Conservation District; USDA NRCS; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; U.S. EPA; Oklahoma Blue Thumb; participating landowners
stories.desc: Across the 28,587-acre Rock Creek watershed, landowners carried out forest stand improvement on 1,356 acres, brush management on 1,334 acres, prescribed grazing on 3,465 acres, feral swine eradication across 450 acres, filter strips, 13 comprehensive nutrient management plans and about 43,671 feet of fencing between 2002 and 2017. Turbidity violations in the 12.35-mile creek fell from 18 percent of samples in 2008 to 8 percent by 2014. Rock Creek was removed from Oklahoma's 2014 303(d) list for turbidity and now partially supports its fish and wildlife propagation use.
stories.water: Rock Creek (Little River basin, flows into Arkansas)
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story. Includes 450 acres of feral swine (invasive animal) management affecting the stream.

stories.title: Mineral Bayou Grazing and Sediment Reduction
stories.orgs: Bryan County Conservation District; Oklahoma Conservation Commission; USDA NRCS; U.S. EPA; Oklahoma Blue Thumb; participating landowners
stories.desc: At least 20 landowners in the 25,120-acre Mineral Bayou watershed, mostly managed pasture, installed 575 acres of prescribed grazing, about 7,500 feet of fence, 11 ponds, nutrient management, pasture planting and brush management between 2005 and 2018 to increase plant cover and reduce bare soil and sediment delivery. Turbidity exceedances on the 15.53-mile segment fell to 6 percent by 2014 and stayed low through 2020. Mineral Bayou was removed from the 303(d) impaired list in 2014 and now fully supports its warm water aquatic community use.
stories.notes: EPA Section 319 success story.

stories.title: Big Creek Agricultural and Wetland Restoration (Big Oaks NWR)
stories.orgs: Indiana Department of Environmental Management; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Big Oaks National Wildlife Refuge); Central Muscatatuck watershed partners; participating landowners
stories.desc: Guided by the Central Muscatatuck watershed plan, partners addressed nutrients from fertilizer, livestock and failing septic systems in the Big Creek watershed with cover crops, livestock exclusion fencing, a watering facility on a heavy-use protection pad, and pasture and hayland planting, plus wetland construction and vegetative planting at the adjacent Big Oaks National Wildlife Refuge. A 2019 fish survey showed higher index of biological integrity scores than the 2006 baseline. Three Big Creek segments and one unnamed tributary were removed from Indiana's 303(d) impaired waters list in 2022.
stories.notes: EPA FY2022 Section 319 Success Story Recap (the linked PDF is the only verifiable page reachable for this story; the Indiana state success-story page was blocked). BOUNDARY CAVEAT: Big Oaks NWR and the Big Creek watershed span Jefferson, Ripley and Jennings counties; Jefferson and Ripley are inside the listed extent, Jennings is not. Coordinates approximate, at Big Oaks NWR.

stories.title: Hickey Martin Dam Removal, Henderson Creek
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Hickey Martin Dam was removed from Henderson Creek in Lawrence County in 2023, restoring free flow on a tributary in the East Fork White River system of south-central Indiana. The annual summary records the removal without height, reconnected mileage or partner detail.
stories.water: Henderson Creek (East Fork White River basin)
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - south-central Indiana; confirm against the Indiana county list for the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Corydon North Bridge (Gupta) Dam Removal, Big Indian Creek
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Corydon North Bridge Dam, also recorded as the Gupta Dam, was removed from Big Indian Creek at Corydon in Harrison County in 2024. Removal restores free-flowing conditions and aquatic organism passage on a southern Indiana karst stream draining directly to the Ohio River. The annual summary records the removal but does not report height, mileage or partners.
stories.notes: Southern Indiana, directly on the Ohio River drainage - likely inside the extent, but confirm against the Indiana county list. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Stewart Lake Dam Removal, Stony Creek tributary
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Stewart Lake Dam on a tributary of Stony Creek in Ross County was removed in 2021, restoring free-flowing stream conditions in the Scioto River basin of south-central Ohio. American Rivers' 2021 report records the removal but gives no height, reconnected mileage or partners.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - south-central Ohio, Scioto basin; confirm against the Ohio county list for the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Dieckbrader Lake Dam Removal, Salt Lick Creek tributary
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; removing parties not named in the source
stories.desc: The Dieckbrader Lake Dam on a tributary of Salt Lick Creek in Brown County was removed in 2023, draining the impoundment and restoring free-flowing stream conditions in a direct Ohio River tributary watershed. The annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.water: Tributary to Salt Lick Creek (Ohio River basin)
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - far southern Ohio on the Ohio River; confirm against the Ohio county list for the extent. Lat/lon approximate.

stories.title: Strait Creek Stream Restoration (Ohio Mitigation Program)
stories.orgs: The Nature Conservancy in Ohio (Ohio Stream and Wetland In-Lieu Fee Mitigation Program)
stories.desc: TNC's Ohio Mitigation Program restored Strait Creek by re-meandering a straightened stream bed back toward its natural planform and rebuilding the riparian corridor. Paired 2019 and 2022 aerial photos on the project page show the before and after condition of the restored channel. The site is one of the program's flagship stream restorations in its first decade of work.
stories.notes: BOUNDARY CAUTION: the source page does not state the location. Strait Creek is a known Ohio Brush Creek tributary in Adams/Highland counties, southern Ohio, draining to the Ohio River; assumed inside the extent but unconfirmed. Linear feet, partners and completion date are not given on the page. Coordinates approximate.

stories.title: JM Stuart Station Ash Pond No. 10 Dam Removal
stories.orgs: Listed in American Rivers' national dam removal inventory; structure associated with the retired J.M. Stuart generating station
stories.desc: An ash pond dam on an unnamed tributary of Three Mile Creek at Manchester in Adams County was removed in 2022 as part of decommissioning work at the retired J.M. Stuart power station on the Ohio River. Removal restores free-flowing conditions on the tributary and eliminates an impoundment associated with coal-combustion residuals. The annual summary records the removal without height, mileage or partner detail.
stories.water: Unnamed tributary to Three Mile Creek (Ohio River)
stories.notes: BOUNDARY UNCERTAIN - far southern Ohio on the Ohio River. Utility association inferred from the structure's name. Lat/lon approximate.
